**Sūrat al-Nisā'** (The Women)

Al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Sūrat al-Nisā' was revealed at Medina."

Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Zayd ibn Thabit.

Al-Nahhas claimed that it is Meccan, relying on the fact that the verse ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾ [al-Nisā': 58] and the verses following it were, by consensus, revealed at Mecca concerning the matter of the key of the Ka'bah. But this reliance is weak. The revelation of one verse or several verses of long sūrahs, most of which were revealed at Medina, does not necessarily make the whole sūrah Meccan, especially since the more probable view is that whatever was revealed after the Hijrah is Medinan.

Whoever examines the occasions of revelation of its verses will recognise the refutation of his claim. Among what also refutes it is the report of al-Bukhari from 'Ā'ishah, who said: "Sūrat al-Baqarah and Sūrat al-Nisā' were not revealed except while I was with him." Her entry into his household took place after the Hijrah, by consensus.

It has also been said that it was revealed at the time of the Hijrah.

Its verses number one hundred and seventy-five, though it has been said six, and it has been said seven. So stated al-Suyuti in *al-Itqān* (*al-Itqān fī 'Ulūm al-Qur'ān*, a work of Qur'anic sciences).

Al-Hakim narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Indeed, in Sūrat al-Nisā' there are five verses that would not please me to have in exchange for them the world and all that is in it: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisā': 40], and ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisā': 31], and ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisā': 48], and ﴿And if they, when they wronged themselves, had come to you﴾ [al-Nisā': 64]."

'Abd al-Razzaq also narrated from him: "Five verses of al-Nisā' are dearer to me than the whole world: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisā': 31]; and His saying: ﴿And if there is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾ [al-Nisā': 40]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisā': 48]; and His saying: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness of Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisā': 110]."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Eight verses were revealed in Sūrat al-Nisā' which are better for this Ummah than all that the sun rises upon and sets upon. The first of them is: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you and to accept your repentance, and Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisā': 26]. The second: ﴿And Allah intends to accept your repentance, but those who follow desires intend that you deviate into great deviation﴾ [al-Nisā': 27]. The third: ﴿Allah intends to lighten for you, and mankind was created weak﴾ [al-Nisā': 28]." Then he mentioned the saying of Ibn Mas'ud in the same way, meaning regarding the remaining five.

**A subtle point:** This sūrah was named *al-Nisā'* because what was revealed in it concerning women's rulings is more than what was revealed in other sūrahs.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

**Concerning the interpretation (ta'wīl) of His saying, the Exalted:**

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and [be mindful of] the wombs. Indeed Allah is ever, over you, an Watcher﴾ [1].

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾: that is, fear Him lest you oppose Him in what He has commanded you or forbidden you.

Then He drew their attention to His being characterised by complete and overwhelming power, to reinforce the command to piety and to emphasise the obligation to comply with it, by way of encouragement and warning, through His saying: ﴿who created you from one soul﴾, that is, He originated you from a single origin, namely the soul of your father Adam. His creating them in this wondrous manner indicates great power, and whoever is able to do the like is able to do everything, including punishing them for their disobedience.

Therefore, reflection upon this leads to guarding oneself against the causes of His wrath. Likewise, His making them as offshoots (*ṣinwān*) branching from a single root is among the reasons for avoiding neglect of the rights of brotherhood among them, as is indicated by what follows of guidance concerning maintaining kinship ties, caring for orphans, justice in marriage, and other matters.

It is established in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* from the narration of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali that: "When that group from Mudar came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they were wearing rough garments (meaning, due to their nakedness and poverty), he stood and addressed the people after the noon prayer, and in his sermon he said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul﴾ [al-Nisā': 1] until he finished the verse. Then he said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 18]. Then he urged them to give charity, saying: 'A man gives from his dinar, from his dirham, from his measure of wheat, from his measure of dates...'" and he mentioned the rest of the hadith.

Likewise it was narrated by Aḥmad and the authors of the Sunan, from Ibn Mas'ud, in the *khuṭbat al-ḥājah* (the sermon of need).

In it: "Then he recites three verses, of which this is one: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾" and the verse, and ﴿and created from it its mate﴾, that is, from its own self, meaning from its own kind, so that there may be between them what necessitates affection and mutual support, for kinship of nature is the cause of attachment. He clarified this with His saying: ﴿And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves spouses that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [al-Rūm: 21].

﴿And dispersed from both of them﴾: that is, He spread forth from that soul and its mate who was created from it, by way of procreation and propagation, ﴿many men and women﴾, that is, many, and He omitted to state their number explicitly, being content with the attribute mentioned.

﴿And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another﴾: this is a repetition of the command and a reminder of another of the reasons for complying with it, for one person's asking another by Allah, the Exalted, by saying: "I ask you by Allah and I adjure you by Allah," seeking compassion, requires guarding oneself against opposing His commands and prohibitions.

The linking of piety to the Glorious Name is for added emphasis and for greater intensity in urging compliance, by instilling awe and inspiring reverence, and because the mutual asking is conducted by Him and not by any of His other names or attributes.

**Note on the grammar of** ﴿*tasā'alūna*﴾: its original form is *tatasā'alūna*, and one of the two *tā'*s was dropped for lightness. It was also read with the *tā'* of the reflexive form (*tafā'ul*) assimilated into the *sīn*, because they are close in articulation (both being voiceless). It was also read as *tas'alūna* from the triliteral root, meaning "you ask others by Him." The first and second readings have been explained as one another. The reflexive form may be understood as reflecting plurality of agents, as in your saying: "We saw the crescent and we saw it together (*tarāyaynāhu*)." So stated Abu al-Su'ud.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿*wa-l-arḥām*﴾ (and the wombs): Ḥamzah read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with the pronominal suffix in the genitive (*bihi*), while the rest read it in the accusative, as a conjunction with the Glorious Name. The meaning is: "Fear Allah, and [fear] the wombs, lest you sever them, for severing them is something which must be guarded against." Or it is a conjunction with the place (*maḥall*) of the preposition-and-genitive phrase, as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd and 'Amr." The reading "*tasā'alūna bihi wa-bi-l-arḥām*" supports this, for they used to couple them in asking and in appealing to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: "I ask you by Allah and by the womb." By coupling them with His Glorious Name, He, glory be to Him and exalted, has indicated that the maintaining of their ties holds a lofty station with Him, as in His saying: ﴿And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents﴾ [al-Nisā': 36]; and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not worship except Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isrā': 23].

It is related by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The womb is suspended from the Throne, saying: 'Whoever joins me, Allah joins him, and whoever severs me, Allah severs him.'"

They also both narrated from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The one who severs ties will not enter Paradise." Sufyān said in his narration: "That is, one who severs the ties of kinship."

Al-Bukhari narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'Āṣ, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The one who maintains ties is not the one who merely reciprocates, but the one who maintains ties when they are severed from him."

They both also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him maintain his ties of kinship." The hadiths encouraging the maintenance of kinship ties and warning against severing them are numerous.

* *

**A caution:**

The verse indicates the permissibility of asking by Allah, the Exalted, so said al-Razi. The reasoning is that He, the Exalted, affirmed them in this asking, since they believed in His greatness, and He did not disapprove of it from them. Yes, whoever is led by asking by His name, the Exalted, to laxity regarding His dignity, and to making Him an object of disregard for not revering Him, and a means to the *sāsāniyyah* gates (a term for ulterior or base ends), this is absolutely forbidden.

On this basis is to be understood what has been reported of the curse upon one who asks by the Face of Allah, as we shall mention. Numerous hadiths have come in this regard.

Among them, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever seeks refuge in Allah, grant him refuge; whoever asks you by Allah, give to him; whoever invites you, respond to him; whoever does you a kindness, reciprocate it. If you do not find anything to reciprocate with, then pray for him until you know that you have reciprocated." Narrated by Imam Aḥmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim.

Imam Aḥmad and Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever seeks refuge in Allah, grant him refuge; whoever asks you by the Face of Allah, give to him."

From Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever is asked by Allah and gives, seventy good deeds are recorded for him." Narrated by al-Bayhaqi with a weak chain.

In al-Bukhari, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us with seven things," and he mentioned among them: "fulfilling the oath" (*ibrār al-qasam*).

Abu Dawud and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtārah* narrated with a sound chain, from Jabir, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Nothing is asked by the Face of Allah, the Exalted, except Paradise."

Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Cursed is the one who asks by the Face of Allah, and cursed is the one who is asked by the Face of Allah and then refuses his petitioner, so long as he does not ask for something evil." Al-Suyuti said: "Its chain is good." (*ḥasan*)

The ḥāfiẓ al-Mundhiri said: "Its narrators are the narrators of the Ṣaḥīḥ except his teacher (that is, al-Tabarani), Yahya ibn 'Uthman ibn Salih, who is trustworthy (*thiqah*), though there is discussion about him."

*Hujran* (with a *ḍammah* on the *hā'* and a *sukūn* on the *jīm*): that is, so long as he does not ask for a base matter that is not fitting. It is possible that he meant: so long as he does not ask with a base request, expressed in base speech. End.

From Abu 'Ubaydah, client of Rifa'ah, from Rafi', that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Cursed is the one who asks by the Face of Allah, and cursed is the one who is asked by the Face of Allah and then refuses his petitioner." Narrated by al-Tabarani.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not inform you of the worst of people? A man who is asked by the Face of Allah and does not give." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "Ḥasan gharīb", and by al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Hibban in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not inform you of the worst of creatures?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "The one who is asked by Allah and does not give."

﴿Indeed Allah is ever over you a Watcher﴾: that is, observing all your conditions and deeds, seeing them and knowing them, so that not even an atom's weight in the earth or in the heavens escapes Him, as He said: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness﴾ [al-Burūj: 9]. And in the hadith: "Worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."

This is guidance and a command to observe Allah's watchfulness. The person must watch over the state of his own soul and take care lest Satan seize an opportunity against him so that he perishes in heedlessness.

(p-١١٠٠)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad [of yours] for the good [of theirs], and do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is ever a great sin.﴾ [2]

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ begins an explanation of the sources and occasions of taqwa (piety, guarding oneself against wrongdoing), by imposing what corresponds to them as commands and prohibitions.

The mention of matters concerning orphans first serves to show the complete care for their affairs, and because they are linked to the kinship ties (al-arham), since the address is to the guardians (awliya’) and executors (awsiya’), and guardianship is rarely entrusted to outsiders.

The yatim (orphan) is one whose father has died, from yutm, meaning isolation (infirad), and from it comes "the unique pearl" (al-durra al-yatima). Morphological analysis requires that the term apply to both the young and the old, but the Law (al-shar‘) has restricted it to one who has not reached puberty (al-hulum), as Abu Dawud related with a sound chain (isnad hasan) from ‘Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "There is no orphanhood after reaching puberty (ihtilam)."

There are several interpretations of the verse:

The first: that by orphans is meant adults in whom right judgment has been observed, used metaphorically with regard to what they were, because of the recent passing of their childhood, and as an indication of the obligation to hasten in handing over their property to them at that time, as though the name "orphan" still remained and had not yet disappeared.

The second: that by them is meant adults in the literal sense, in accordance with the original usage of the language.

The third: that by them is meant children, and by "giving" (al-ita’) is meant what the guardians and executors provide to them of maintenance and clothing, not handing over the property itself. This is far-fetched.

The fourth: that by them is meant what has been mentioned, and by "giving them" (ita’ihim) the property is meant that the guardians and executors, the wicked rulers and their judges, should not covet it, and should withhold their snatching hands from it, until the orphans, when they reach maturity, are given it intact and not diminished. Thus the figurative use of "giving" here is by employing it for its necessary meaning, which is leaving the property intact, since it is only given when it is in that state.

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: This interpretation is strong because of His saying after some verses: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property﴾ [al-Nisa’ 4:6]. This shows that the first verse is an exhortation to preserve it for them so that it may be given to them when they reach maturity and sound judgment, and the second is an exhortation to actual handing over when maturity and sound judgment are attained.

It is also strengthened by His saying after the first verse: ﴿and do not substitute﴾ etc., for all of this is a discipline for the executor as long as the property is in his hand and the orphan is in his care.

As for the first interpretation, the import of the two verses is one, namely the command to give in the literal sense. It is freed from repetition by saying that the first is like a general statement (mujmala) and the second is like a clarifying statement (mubayyina) of the condition of giving: maturity and perceived sound judgment. And Allah knows best.

﴿and do not substitute the bad for the good﴾, that is: do not exchange the forbidden, which is the property of orphans, for the lawful, which is your own property and what is permitted to you of gains and the provision of Allah spread across the earth, so that you consume that in its place.

﴿and do not consume their property along with your own property﴾ is a prohibition of another wrong that they used to practise, that is: do not consume it while joined to your own property and mixed with it for the sake of expanding your wealth. ﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is the consuming, ﴿is ever a sin﴾, that is, a great wrong (ḥūb) (p-١١٠٢) — it was also read with a fatha on the ḥa’ — and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿great﴾ is an intensification in clarifying the greatness of the sin of the consuming mentioned, as though it were said: it is among the great sins.

* *

Note:

An exception to this is the amount of the customary wage (ajr al-mithl) when the guardian is poor, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him consume in accordance with what is reasonable﴾ [al-Nisa’ 4:6]. So said al-Baydawi, and Abu al-Su‘ud followed him.

In my view, there is no need to restrict this prohibition to the poor in this verse, because it concerns the wealthy, as shown by His saying: ﴿to your own property﴾. Therefore its context does not include the poor, and we will clarify that.

A subtle point:

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: He has already forbidden them to consume the property of orphans alone and together with their own property, so why is the prohibition on consuming it together with theirs mentioned? I answer: Because when they are wealthy without needing the property of orphans, through the lawful wealth Allah has provided them, and yet they still covet it, the ugliness is greater and the blame more fitting. Also, they used to do so, so He censured their action and reproached them for it, so that it would be a stronger deterrent for them. End.

Al-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: The people of rhetoric (ahl al-bayan) say: when the prohibited matter has degrees, the way of eloquence is to prohibit the lowest of them as a means of alerting to the highest, as in His saying: ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾ [al-Isra’ 17:23]. When you consider this principle in relation to this verse, you find at first glance that it contradicts it, since the highest degree of consuming the property of an orphan in the prohibition is that he consumes it while being wealthy and free of need for it, and the lowest is that he consumes it while being poor and in need of it. So the principle mentioned would require that the prohibition of consuming the property of an orphan be directed at one who is poor and in need of it, so that the prohibition on the wealthy would follow by way of greater priority (al-awla). In that case, it is necessary to establish a point that clarifies the benefit of specifying the highest form for the prohibition in this verse.

We say: The most eloquent speech (p-١١٠٣) is that whose modes of benefit are multiple. There is no doubt that the prohibition of the lesser, although it conveys the prohibition of the higher, also has another noble benefit that is not derived from the prohibition of the lesser. That is because the more ugly the forbidden matter is, the more the soul recoils from it and the less inclined it is toward it.

There is no doubt that what is firmly established in souls is that consuming the property of an orphan while being wealthy is the most ugly form of consuming. So it was singled out for prohibition, as a means of condemning those who fall into it, so that when their aversion to consuming his property in this shameful form becomes firmly established, that brings them to abstain from consuming his property altogether.

In this there is training of the addressee in turning away from what is forbidden, and this benefit would hardly be attained if the prohibition were restricted to consuming it in poverty, since natures in that case do not help one to refrain, as they help in the first case. What confirms the attention to this meaning is that He specified consumption, although taking the orphan's property in any manner is forbidden, whether by hoarding, by mixing, by spending it on the pleasures of marriage for instance, or otherwise. However, the wisdom of restricting the prohibition to consumption is that the Arabs used to regard excess in eating as shameful, considered gluttony (al-bitna) to be bestial, and blamed whoever made it his habit. This is not so with other pleasures, for they often boast of excess in marriage and regard it as one of the adornments of this world. Since consumption was for them the ugliest of pleasures, the prohibition was specified for it, so that once the soul recoils from it by its accustomed nature, that leads it to recoil from diverting the property of an orphan to all other pleasures or other uses, whether eating or otherwise.

A similar example of restricting the prohibition to the higher case is His saying: ﴿Do not consume usury, multiplied manifold﴾ [Al ‘Imran 3:130]. He specified this form, because the soul is more aided in desisting from it.

Opposite to this consideration regarding prohibition is another consideration regarding command. Sometimes it singles out the lower form of command as a way of alerting to the higher, and sometimes it singles out the higher form for the same benefit of training mentioned. Do you not see His saying, after some verses of this surah: ﴿And when relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, provide for them﴾ [al-Nisa’ 4:8] — the verse goes on. How He specified the case of their presence, even though it is the higher in comparison with their absence? This is because Allah, exalted is He, knew the stinginess of souls regarding property. If He had commanded the support of relatives and orphans from the inherited property without mentioning the situation of their being present at the division, souls would not have been moved toward this kindness as they are when they are present. In contrast, when they are present, the soul's nature softens and recoils from taking abundant wealth while a kinsman is present and deprived, not helped or assisted. So when it is commanded in this situation to give support, complying with the command becomes easy for it and it becomes accustomed to obeying the command against the nature, and then it is trained by that to support a kinsman in all cases, whether present or absent.

Therefore, observing this and similar benefits is hardly to be found except in the Mighty Book, and only the skilled and discerning, aided by success, will attain it. We ask Allah to guide us along this path. So take this principle as your foundation: if the prohibition singles out the lower, it is for the benefit of alerting to the higher; if it singles out the higher, it is for the benefit of training in restraint from ugliness in general, from restraint from the uglier. A similar consideration applies to the command. And Allah is the Granter of success. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 1 of 4):

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:
﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you may not incline toward injustice.﴾ [3]
﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾, i.e., that you will not be equitable, ﴿with the orphans﴾, i.e., the orphan girls.
Al-Zamakhshari said: The female orphans are called "yatama" just as the males are, and it is the plural of "yatima" by metathesis (al-qalb), as it is said "ayama" (widows), whereas the original is "aya'im" and "yata'im."
﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾, i.e., those whom your souls find agreeable in respect of beauty and loveliness, or intellect, or righteousness among them.
﴿Two, three, or four﴾. The meaning of the verse: If you, O guardians of orphans, fear that you will not be equitable toward them when you marry them, by mistreating them in companionship or by diminishing their dowry, then marry others besides them, from among the strangers, for they are many, and Allah has not constricted you.
So the verse is a warning against entanglement in injustice and a command to take precaution, and that in other than them there is ample room up to four.
Al-Bukhari narrated from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that a man had an orphan girl in his guardianship, and he married her, and she had a palm tree (ʿadhq, i.e., a date palm), and he would keep her under his control and she had no share of his own self. So this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾. He said: I think she was his partner in that palm tree and in his property. Also narrated by Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i.
In another narration from them on the authority of ʿA'isha: She is the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, sharing with him in his property, and her guardian is attracted to her wealth and beauty, so the guardian wants to marry her without being equitable concerning her dowry, giving her the like of what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and give them the highest custom of their dowry. Then they were commanded to marry what seems good to them of women other than them.
ʿUrwah said: ʿA'isha said: Indeed the people asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a ruling after this verse, and Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127].
ʿA'isha said: And the saying of Allah in another verse: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] refers to one of you being averse to his orphan when she is little in wealth and beauty.
She said: So they were forbidden to marry, out of desire for wealth and beauty, the orphan women whom they were averse to, except with justice, because of their aversion to them when they are lacking in wealth and beauty.
In another narration concerning His saying: ﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127] to the end of the verse, ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: She is the orphan girl who is in the charge of a man, who has shared with him in his property, so he is averse to marrying her, and he dislikes that she be married to another, for then he would enter into his property, so he withholds her; so Allah forbade them from that.
Abu Dawud, may Allah have mercy on him, added: Rabi'ah said concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans﴾ he said: He says: Leave them, if you fear, for I have made lawful to you four.
Subtleties:
The first: "ma" in His saying "what seems good to you" (ma tāba lakum) is a relative pronoun, and "ma" was used in place of "min" because the two may replace each other, so each one occurs in place of the other, as in His saying: ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5], and His saying: ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 5], and ﴿of them is one that walks on its belly, and of them is one that walks on two legs, and of them is one that walks on four﴾ [al-Nur: 45]. Some said: its use here is good because it refers to women, who are deficient in intellect.
The second: In preferring the command to marry them over the prohibition of marrying orphans, although the latter is the primary intent, there is additional gentleness in drawing them away from that, for the soul is naturally inclined to covet what it is forbidden. Likewise, describing women as "good" (ṭayyib), in the manner indicated, contains emphasis in attracting and encouraging inclination toward them, and all of this is for the sake of turning them away from marrying orphans. Abu al-Su'ud conveyed this.
The third: The scholars agreed that this stipulation mentioned in the verse has no implication (mafhum) in the sense that it is permissible for one who does not fear being unjust toward orphans to marry more than one.
The fourth: "Mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿa" are numbers formed by a distributive pattern (ʿudila ʿan aʿdad mukarraraa), and their position is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the subject of "ṭāba," emphasizing what the description of goodness conveyed concerning encouragement toward them and attraction to them, by widening the scope of permission. That is: marry the good ones for yourselves, numbering this count, two by two, three by three, and four by four, as you wish.
If you say: what is permitted to the marrying man in gathering is that he may combine two or three or four; so what is the meaning of the repetition in "mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿa"? I say: the address is to all, so repetition was necessary so that every man who wishes to gather may attain what number he wishes from the count that was permitted to him, just as you say to a group: divide this wealth, which is a thousand dirhams, two dirhams each, three each, and four each; and if you had used the singular it would have had no meaning.
If you say: why did the conjunction come with "wa" (and) rather than "aw" (or)? I say: as it came with "wa" in the example I have set for you. Had you said: divide this wealth two dirhams each or three each or four each, you would have informed that it is not permissible for them to divide it except in one of the types of this division, and it is not permissible for them to combine them, making part of the division in pairs, part in threes, and part in fours. The meaning of permitting the combining of types of division, which "wa" indicates, is lost.
Its clarification: "wa" indicates the general permission that the marrying men may take from the women whom they wish to marry by way of gathering, whether they wish to differ in those numbers or to agree in them, with what lies beyond that forbidden to them. Conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.
A Weighty Inquiry:
Al-Razi said: A people (Sada, like Hata, a place near Zabid in Yemen, per al-Qamus) went to the view that it is permissible to marry any number one wishes, and they argued from the Qur'an and the report:
As for the Qur'an: they held to this verse from three aspects:
The first: that His saying "so marry what seems good to you of women" is a general statement covering all numbers, since there is no number but that its exception from it is valid, and the rule of exception is to remove what would otherwise have been included.
The second: that His saying "two, three, or four" is not suitable as a specification of that generality, because specifying some numbers by mention does not negate the establishment of the ruling for the rest. Rather we say: mentioning these numbers indicates the lifting of hardship and restriction absolutely, for when a man says to his son, "do whatever you wish, go to the market, to the city, to the orchard," it is an explicit delegation to him of the reins of choice absolutely and the lifting of restriction and hardship from him absolutely, and it is not a specification of permission to those mentioned things but a permission for what is mentioned and what is other than it. So likewise here. Also, mentioning all numbers is impossible, so when some numbers are mentioned after "so marry what seems good to you of women," that is an indication of the availability of permission for all numbers.
The third: that the "wa" is for absolute gathering, so His saying "two, three, or four" conveys the permissibility of this collection, which amounts to nine; indeed the truth is that it conveys eighteen, because "mathna" is not an expression for two only but for two and two, and likewise the rest.
As for the report, it is from two aspects:
The first: that it is established by tawatur that "he ﷺ died leaving nine (wives)," and then Allah commanded us to follow him, saying "follow him," and the least level of a command is permissibility.
The second: that the sunnah of a man is his way, and marrying more than four was the way of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, so that was a sunnah for him. Then he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me." The apparent meaning of this hadith requires blame to fall upon one who abandons marrying more than four, so at least it establishes the basic permissibility.
Know that the basis of the jurists for establishing the limit rests on two matters:
The first: the report, which is what was narrated: that Ghaylan embraced Islam while under him were ten wives, and the Messenger ﷺ said: "Keep four and separate from the rest."
And it was narrated that Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah embraced Islam while under him were five wives, and he, peace be upon him, said: "Keep four and separate from one."
Know that this path is weak for two reasons:
The first: that since the Qur'an indicates the absence of a limit, to restrict it by this report would be abrogating the Qur'an with a solitary report, which is impermissible.
The second: that the report is a particular event, so perhaps he, peace be upon him, only ordered him to keep four and separate from the rest, because combining more than four with the rest is impermissible, either due to kinship or due to nursing.
In sum, this possibility stands in this report, so the Qur'an cannot be abrogated by its like.
The second path: the consensus of the jurists of the major cities that it is impermissible to exceed four, and this is the reliable basis, and against it there are two questions:
The first: that consensus neither abrogates nor is abrogated, so how can it be said that consensus abrogated this verse?
The second: that in the community there are some eccentric groups who do not hold the prohibition of exceeding four, and consensus is not established in the face of the dissent of one or two.
As for the answer to the first: consensus reveals the occurrence of an abrogating text in the time of the Messenger ﷺ.
As for the answer to the second: the dissenter from this consensus is among the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah), so his dissent is not regarded. End of al-Razi's words. His saying "from the people of innovation" may not be taken in its generality, as you will see.
Imam al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in "Wabl al-Ghamam": What the imams of language and grammar have transmitted to us, and which has become as though agreed upon among them, is that the distributive form in numbers indicates that the counted thing, when it is multiplied, requires numerous numbers for its completion, so the form of the singular distributive carries the force of those numbers. If the coming of a people, for example, was two by two, or three by three, or four by four, and they were thousands gathered together, and you said "the people came to me mathna," this form conveys that they came two by two, until they were complete.
If you said: "mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿa," this conveys that the people came to you at times two by two, and at times three by three, and at times four by four. These forms indicate the quantity of the number of occasions of coming, not the quantity of the total number of the people, for nothing of that is derived from them at all; rather the most that is derived from them is that their number is great, a multiplicity such that encompassing it is difficult.
Similarly, if you say: "I married women mathna," its meaning is that I married them two by two, and there is no evidence in it that each occasion of these occasions did not enter into his marriage except after the first had left; just as there is no evidence in your saying "the people came to me mathna" that the two others did not reach you except after the first two had departed from you. Having established this, His saying, exalted is He, "mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿa" conveys the permissibility of marrying women two by two, three by three, and four by four.
What is meant is the permissibility of marrying each occasion of these occasions at some time, and there is in this no reference to the quantity of their number; rather from the forms is derived the multiplicity without specification, just as we have set forth regarding the coming of the people.

Nor is there in it any proof that the second group was after separation from the first group. As for the one who claims that the imams of language and grammar have transmitted to us something that contradicts this, this is the place to benefit from it, so let him graciously share it with us. As for Ibn 'Abbas, even if it is authentically reported from him regarding the verse that he limited men to four, he is one individual among the individuals of the Ummah.

As for the clamor of claiming consensus, how trivial it is and how easy its matter is for one whom this uproar does not alarm. How can a consensus be valid when the Zahiriyyah, Ibn al-Sabbagh, al-'Imrani, al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim (the star of the Family of the Messenger), a group of the Shi'ah, and a host of the verifying later scholars have opposed it? The Noble Qur'an also contradicts it, as we have explained.

It is also contradicted by the practice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is established by mass transmission (tawatur), from his gathering between nine or more at some times. ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7] ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21] ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 31]. The claim of exclusivity requires evidence, and the original presumption of innocence (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah) remains in force; only a sound transmitter whose excuses are cut off can transmit away from it.

As for the hadith of his (ﷺ) command to Ghaylan, when he embraced Islam while having ten wives, to choose four of them and separate from the rest, as narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban, although it has several chains, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "All of them are defective (ma'lulah)," and others among the hadith scholars have criticized it for other defects. Such a matter cannot stand as a transfer away from the Qur'anic evidence, the prophetic practice upon which he (ﷺ) died, and the original presumption of innocence.

Whoever authenticates this hadith for us in a manner that establishes proof, or brings us evidence in its meaning, may Allah reward him with good. There is no enmity between anyone and the truth. The scholar must give ijtihad its due, especially in matters of editing and affirmation (maqamat al-tahrir wa al-taqrir), as we do in many researches. If something troubles his chest, let his caution be in practice, not in establishing what is correct. Beware of shying away from clearly stating the truth that your faculty reaches, out of deference to gossip, especially in situations where many men shrink back. For you will not be asked on the Day of Resurrection about what the servants approve of from you, but about what the Worshipped One approves of. When the river of Allah comes, the stream of Ma'qal is nullified, and whoever reaches the sea considers the streams insignificant. End of quote.

Al-Shawkani, may his secret be sanctified, said in Nayl al-Awtar: The hadith of Qays ibn al-Harith (and in another narration, al-Harith ibn Qays) has in its chain Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, whom more than one of the imams have declared weak.

Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi said: "I know of no hadith from al-Harith ibn Qays other than this one."

Abu 'Umar al-Namari said: "He has only one hadith, and it has not come through a sound route."

In the same sense is the hadith of Ghaylan al-Thaqafi, from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "Ghaylan al-Thaqafi embraced Islam while having ten wives in the pre-Islamic period, and they embraced Islam with him, so the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him to choose four of them." Narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi. Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'ah ruled that the mursal version is more authentic.

al-Hakim related from Muslim that this hadith is among those in which Ma'mar erred in Basra. He said: "If a trustworthy narrator relates it from him outside Basra, we will rule for its authenticity." Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi took the outward judgment and narrated it through several routes from Ma'mar, from the people of Kufa, the people of Khurasan and the people of Yamamah, from him.

The Hafiz said: "This does not benefit anything, for all of these only heard from him in Basra. Even if they heard from him elsewhere, his narration that he related outside his own town is confused (mudtarib), for he used to narrate from his books in his town accurately, but when he traveled and narrated from memory, he erred in things, as the people of knowledge agreed, such as Ibn al-Madini, al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ya'qub ibn Shaybah and others."

al-Athram related from Ahmad that this hadith is not authentic, and that practice is not based on it, and he gave as its defect Ma'mar's singular transmission of it in its connected form and his narrating it outside his town.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "All its routes are defective."

al-Daraqutni extensively traced its routes in al-'Ilal.

Ibn 'Uyaynah and Malik related it from al-Zuhri as a mursal report.

'Abd al-Razzaq related it from Ma'mar in the same way.

Bahr ibn Kunayz al-Saqqa' agreed with Ma'mar in connecting it from al-Zuhri, but he is weak. Likewise Yahya ibn Sallam connected it from Malik, but Yahya is weak.

On this topic there is a report from Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah, in al-Shafi'i, that he embraced Islam while having five wives, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Keep four and separate from the other." In its chain is an unknown man, for al-Shafi'i said: "Some of our companions related to us from Abu al-Zinad, from 'Abd al-Majid ibn Sahl, from 'Awf ibn al-Harith, from Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah, who said: I embraced Islam, and he mentioned it." Also on this topic are reports from 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud and Safwan ibn Umayyah in al-Bayhaqi.

His saying: "Choose four of them" has been used by the majority as evidence for the prohibition of exceeding four. The Zahiriyyah held that a man may marry nine, perhaps their basis being the Almighty's saying: ﴿two, three, or four﴾, and the sum of these, not considering the justice involved, is nine.

This was attributed to Ibn al-Sabbagh, al-'Imrani and some of the Shi'ah.

It was also attributed to al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim, but Imam Yahya denied this attribution, and the author of al-Bahr reported it from the Zahiriyyah and some unknown people.

They answered the hadith of Qays ibn al-Harith mentioned above with what was previously said regarding it, and answered the hadith of Ghaylan al-Thaqafi with what was previously said about it, and likewise answered the hadith of Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah with what we previously mentioned, that its chain contains an unknown man. They said: A matter as great as this is not to be satisfied with such things, especially since it is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered between nine or eleven, and the Almighty has said: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21].

As for the claim that he was specifically exempted from the limit of four, that is the point of dispute, and no proof has been established for it.

As for the Almighty's saying: ﴿two, three, or four﴾, the waw in it is for conjunction, not for choice. Moreover, the word mathna is used to denote "two by two," and it indicates the inclusion of whatever numbers possess the attribute of being in pairs, even if they reach the greatest multitude, beyond thousands. For you say: "The people came to me mathna," i.e., two by two, and likewise "thulath and rubaʿ" (three by three, four by four). This is known in the language of the Arabs and no one doubts it.

Thus the aforementioned verse indicates by its basic wording that a person may marry two women two-by-two, three three, and four four. It is not a condition of this that the second group arrives in the number only after he has separated from the first group. For there is no doubt that it is correct, linguistically and customarily, for a man to say to a thousand men with him: "These came to me two by two, or three by three, or four by four." Then the verse indicates permission to marry a large number of women, whether the waw is for conjunction or for choice, because addressing a group with a ruling is equivalent to addressing each one of them. It is as if Allah, glorified and exalted, said to every individual among people: "Marry what is good for you of women, two, three, or four." Moreover, the original presumption of innocence remains, and by itself it suffices for permissibility until a sound transmitter is found who transmits away from it.

It may be answered that the totality of the hadiths mentioned in this chapter are not below the rank of hasan li-ghayrihi, so together they stand as proof, even though each one of them is not free from criticism. This is supported by the fact that the original status of private parts is prohibition, as al-Khattabi explicitly stated, so one may not proceed with any of them except with evidence. Also, this disagreement is preceded by consensus on the impermissibility of exceeding four, as stated in al-Bahr.

In al-Fath it says: The scholars agreed that among his special privileges (ﷺ) was exceeding four wives whom he gathered together. The Hafiz mentioned in al-Fath and al-Talkhis the wisdom in the multiplicity of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), so refer to that. End of quote.

He, may his secret be sanctified, said in his tafsir Fath al-Qadir, and he (the author) had used the verse as evidence for the prohibition of exceeding four: They explained this by saying that it is an address to the whole Ummah, and that every man who marries has the right to choose whatever number of this he wishes, just as it is said to a group: "Divide this money," which is a thousand dirhams (or this money which is in the bag), "two by two, three by three, and four by four."

This is accepted when the amount being divided has been stated in total or its place has been specified. But if it is absolute, as when one says: "Divide the dirhams," meaning what they earned, the meaning is not like this, and the verse belongs to the latter category, not the former. Moreover, whoever says to a group dividing a large specific sum of money: "Divide it mathna and thulath and rubaʿ," and they divide part of it among themselves two by two, part three by three, and part four by four, this would be the Arabic meaning.

It is known that when someone says: "The people came to me mathna," and they are a hundred thousand, the meaning is that they came to him two by two, just as: "The people came to me thulath and rubaʿ."

The address to the whole is equivalent to the address to each individual, as in His saying: "Kill the polytheists," and "Establish the prayer and give the zakat," and similar. The meaning of His saying: ﴿So marry of women what is good for you, two, three, or four﴾ is that each one of you should marry of women what is good for him, two and two, three and three, four and four. This is what the Arabic language requires. Thus the verse indicates the opposite of what they used it to prove. This is supported by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one﴾, for it, although an address to all, is equivalent to an address to each individual.

It is therefore better to derive the prohibition of exceeding four from the Sunnah rather than from the Qur'an. As for the reasoning of those who used the verse to permit marrying nine, by considering the conjunctive waw, as if he said: "Marry the total of this stated number," this is ignorance of the Arabic meaning. Had he said: "Marry two, three and four," that statement would have had some basis, but with the use of the expression of distribution, no. Allah, glorified be He, used the conjunctive waw rather than "aw" (or) because choice would imply that only one of the stated numbers is permissible and not others, and that is not the intent of the Qur'anic wording.

Al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Umar that Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi embraced Islam while having ten wives, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Choose from among them" (and in one wording, "Keep from among them") "four, and separate from the rest." This hadith was narrated in various wordings through several routes.

And from Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Dili, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had five wives, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Keep four and separate from the other.'" Al-Shafi'i related it in his Musnad.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 3 of 4):

Ibn Majah and al-Nahhas narrated in his *Tarikh*, "From Qays ibn al-Harith al-Asadi, who said: I embraced Islam and I had eight wives. I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Choose four of them and divorce the rest.' So I did." These are corroborating reports for the first hadith, as al-Bayhaqi said.

He (may Allah sanctify his secret) also said in his book *al-Sayl al-Jarrar al-Mutadaffiq 'ala Hada'iq al-Azhar*: As for the argument for the prohibition of a fifth wife, and the impermissibility of exceeding four, based on the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿two, three, or four﴾, it is not sound, as I have clarified in my commentary on *al-Muntaqa*, which we have already mentioned.

However, the argument for this based on the hadith of Qays ibn al-Harith, the hadith of Ghaylan al-Thaqafi, and the hadith of Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah is what should be relied upon, even though each of them has some criticism. Yet the consensus on what they indicate has made it among the matters agreed upon for acting by.

The consensus has been reported by the author of *Fath al-Bari* and by al-Mahdi in *al-Bahr*. The attribution of a contrary view to the Zahiriyyah (the literalist school) is not established, for some of their own scholars who knew their school best have denied it. End of quote.

**Appendix:**

Al-Darqutni narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "A slave may marry two women, divorce twice, and a slave-woman observes a waiting period of two menstrual cycles."

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: Those who hold that a slave may not marry more than two women have adhered to this. It is narrated from 'Ali, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Nasir, the Hanafis, and the Shafi'is. It is not hidden that the statement of a Companion is not a proof for one who does not hold it to be a proof. Yes, if the consensus of the Companions on this were established, it would be evidence for those who hold consensus to be a proof. However, it has been narrated from Abu al-Darda', Mujahid, Rabi'ah, Abu Thawr, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Salim that it is permissible for him to marry four, like a free man. The author of *al-Bahr* reported this from them. End of quote.

So the better course is to affirm firmly that he falls under the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women﴾, and that the ruling for him applies to him and against him as it does to free men, unless there is a proof that requires opposition, as in the well-known cases where the rulings of the two differ.

﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾, i.e., among these numbers, ﴿then [marry only] one﴾, i.e., choose that one. It is also read in the nominative case, meaning: then one is sufficient for you. ﴿Or those your right hands possess﴾, i.e., of slave-women, whatever their number. This is because they do not bear the same rights as free women, and they have no fixed turn in the division.

The "or" (*aw*) is for equivalence, i.e., for choice. The number is taken from the context and from the contrast with "one."

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made equal in ease and facility between one free woman and slave-women, without any restriction or fixing of a number. By my life, they are less burdensome, less troublesome, and lighter in expense than free wives (*mahair*). It does not matter whether you take many of them or few, whether you divide equally among them or not, whether you withdraw from them or not. End of quote.

﴿That﴾, i.e., limiting oneself to one or to concubinage, ﴿is more suitable﴾, i.e., closer, ﴿that you not incline [to injustice]﴾, i.e., that you not deviate or oppress. This is because the matter is eliminated entirely in the first case by the absence of its locus, and in the second case by the absence of its danger. This contrasts with choosing a number among free wives, where the forbidden inclination is expected, because the locus and the danger are both present. This is if "ta'ulu" is taken as the imperfect of *'ala*, meaning "to act unjustly and to deviate from the truth," which is the view chosen by most exegetes.

Among the possible readings is that it is the imperfect of *'ala* meaning "his dependents became many." Al-Qamus says: "'Ala fulan 'awlan and 'iyalah: his dependents increased, like a'wala and a'yala."

On this interpretation, Imam al-Mahayimi (may Allah sanctify his secret) limited himself in his tafsir, saying: "That is, closer to not having many dependents, so that contentment is possible with it, to the extent that one is not compelled to wrong the property of orphans." End of quote.

This interpretation was also narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, and al-Shafi'i.

As for the statement of Ibn Kathir on this tafsir: "Here there is an issue, for just as the multiplication of free wives may cause a large household, so too the multiplication of concubines may be feared" — its answer, as al-Razi said, is in two ways:

First: what al-Qaffal (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned, namely that when concubines increase, he may require them to earn, and when they earn they spend on themselves and also on their master, and then the dependents decrease. But when the woman is free, the matter is not the same, so the difference is clear.

Second: that when a woman is a slave, if the master is unable to support her he sells her and rids himself of her. But if she is free, he must support her, and custom shows that as long as the husband keeps his wife she does not demand her dower from him. When he tries to divorce her, she demands her dower, and so the husband falls into distress. End of quote.

**Two points of caution:**

**The first:** Some exegetes said: The verse indicates that rights become obligatory through marriage. It also indicates that whoever fears falling into what is impermissible, the act that calls to that wrong becomes ugly for him. So it is not permissible for one who knows that he consumes the property of an orphan to marry more than one wife. Likewise, whoever knows that he will betray a deposit and not guard it may not accept it. The verse also indicates that justice is obligatory among wives, and that whoever knows he will not be just is not allowed more than one. It indicates that marrying a minor girl without her father or her grandfather is permissible, and the jurists have well-known positions on this.

**The second:** Concerning the secret of what the verse points to regarding the improvement of offspring, one of the scholars of sociology among the Muslim philosophers said in an article titled "Islam and the Improvement of Offspring," something to this effect: For thousands of years mankind has continually sought to improve the livestock it owns, such as horses, cattle, and sheep, so that its benefit from them would increase. So he chooses noble males for the females of these animals, having the qualities he desires, in order to obtain from them offspring more beneficial to him than their mothers.

The desire of people in this age to improve beneficial kinds of animals has increased. They have bred and refined them by choosing suitable males, until they obtained a breed of fine horses that outrun the wind, covering 16 meters in a second. They obtained a breed of cattle that yields fifty *uqqa* in one day, and a breed of goats and sheep whose hair or wool is as soft as silk. Their improvement did not stop at animals but extended to plants. Through this they obtained trees with abundant and delicious fruit, and they benefited greatly, in a way that their forebears could not achieve.

Indeed, mankind has thought about improving the dumb animals and plants, and has known the benefits in them, so it has striven toward them in the way that knowledge approves, and has reaped the fruits of that effort. But they did not think about improving what is more important than all of that: improving the intelligent animal. The wicked are more numerous than the righteous, the cowardly more than the brave, the liar more than the truthful, and the lazy more than the energetic. Had they improved their offspring, there would not be found among people one who is born sick and lives sick, so that society does not benefit from his existence, and such people are many.

Among this generation there arose two philosophers, one German and one English. They began teaching, through their writings based on proofs, the obligation of improving human offspring by humans, enumerating the benefits of improvement for the species, and explaining to the public that the advancement sought cannot be achieved without it. They began to blame people for their care in improving livestock and their neglect of improving themselves, which is far more important. They mentioned ways for this:

(Among them) preventing those with chronic defects and diseases, and those guilty of great crimes, from marriage, so that their line may end, since it generally comes out in their likeness.

(Among them) permitting multiple wives for the outstanding men, so that their offspring multiply. They said: If society follows this artificial selection for many generations, the final human offspring, by the law of heredity, will be free from disease, good in disposition, not inclined to evil, strong, sharp of heart, and outstanding in the sciences they learn. It will be like a higher species than present humanity. The most important method they proposed for the advancement awaited by mankind in the future is the method of multiple wives in the present for outstanding people. For preventing those with chronic diseases and criminals from marriage only serves to strengthen the offspring and make it naturally inclined to good, and nothing more; it does not make it more intelligent than its parents or of loftier perceptions.

The multiplicity of wives for outstanding Muslim men was brought by Islam more than thirteen hundred years before these two philosophers. It permitted them to have up to four, so that their offspring would increase, and so the number of outstanding people would increase, through whom alone great works in this world are accomplished. So this is one of the social discoveries of this religion.

Their consent to this was made a condition for it, so that there would be no injustice to their rights. A wise woman prefers to be the wife of an outstanding man, even if he has other wives, rather than to be the wife of a foolish man, even if he has her alone. This is because she knows that her children from the first will produce more outstanding offspring than those from the second.

As for the non-outstanding among them, religion prevents them from marrying more than one wife, so that their offspring does not multiply. Allah, the Exalted, said in His Clear Book, addressing the believers: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one﴾. The address in this verse is to the whole community. It permits every Muslim to marry more than one woman, up to four, if he perceives in himself the ability to be just among them. Otherwise it becomes obligatory for him to limit himself to one, lest he wrong them.

The ability to be just among four women depends on great intellect, skill in management, and profound wisdom in dealing, which are only attainable by one who is outstanding among men, possessing a level of intellect that raises him above his peers. When such an outstanding man marries more than one wife, his offspring multiply, and thus outstanding people multiply.

A people whose outstanding members are numerous is more capable of prevailing in the struggle for survival than other peoples, as history shows us.

Then Allah, in another place, addressed those who fear they will not be just among women, who are the non-outstanding among Muslims, saying: ﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives, even if you should strive to do so﴾ [al-Nisa: 129]. In this verse, which in meaning complements the first, He commanded them not to take more than one wife, because they are at a level of intellect below that of the outstanding. With them they will not be able to achieve justice among wives, which depends on great intellect that makes it easy for its possessor to satisfy them all, as the outstanding and the shrewd among people manage to do. He prohibited those who have not attained the capacity for justice from marrying more than one, lest injustice by men toward women occur, which is frequent among the middling, and among those lower than them on the ladder of advancement. And lest the offspring of the non-outstanding multiply, which is the more important matter, so that the community remains in its place of decline.

Earlier it was explained that the address in His words, ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾, in the first verse is to the whole community, but the condition of justice restricts it to those among them who are just, namely the outstanding (al-nabigun) who are capable of achieving justice among wives because of the fullness of their intellect.

The purpose of this category of Muslims being commanded to marry more than one wife, up to four, is to increase their offspring, so that society benefits from the abundance of their likes, as we have previously stated. But the outstanding man's offspring generally do not become outstanding merely by the multiplicity of wives, for the average or inferior wife generally produces children who are average or inferior, even if their father is elevated. Thus the desired benefit of plurality of wives, which is the improvement of offspring, is not achieved.

Rather, to attain this lofty goal it is necessary that outstanding men marry outstanding women, so that their children may be like them in distinction or more distinguished than them, by the law of the sequence of heredity. This is only accomplished if outstanding men choose their spouses well, so that they "marry what seems good to them." The outstanding man does not find it good to be joined except with one who combines distinction like his own with fine beauty, for keeping company with a foolish woman is not something that is good for the elevated intellectual. Good is sought among beautiful faces. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾, and He did not say "and marry of women." In His words, ﴿two, three, or four﴾, there is an indication of the three levels of the man's distinction. It is as if He intended that the one whose distinction is small should not exceed being joined to two; that the one whose distinction is average should not exceed being joined to three; and that the one whose distinction is higher than the first two may be permitted to be joined to four.

As for those who fear that they will not be just, they must not exceed being joined to one wife, because they are people who, despite all their eagerness, will not be able to act justly among women, due to the deficiency of their intellect in managing the household and their lack of distinction. There is a human being whose distinction is greater than every distinction, namely Muhammad (ﷺ), whom God chose, for the fullness of His wisdom, as a messenger from Him to mankind. God permitted him to be joined to more than four, because of his capacity to be just among them.

I think that, after reading what I have set forth, you will acknowledge, if you are among the fair-minded, that Islam came more than thirteen hundred years ago with a law of marriage, upon which alone the improvement of the offspring of mankind depends, which some of the philosophers of the West have begun in this century to urge. That law is plurality of wives, after the general opinion in the West had been censuring it. Here is Islam establishing the greatest principle for progress, which is the permission of plurality of wives, who become lawful to outstanding Muslim men, by reason of the fullness of their beauty and intellect, men who, because of the fullness of their intellect, do not fear that they will fail to be just among them. But the Muslims did not comply with God's command. They permitted this plurality to every Muslim, both to those who fear they will not be just and to those who do not fear. So the offspring were corrupted. What helped bring about this corruption is that the capacity for it came to be restricted, by the decree of ignorance, to wealth that is gathered by the usurper, the thief, and the earner, so the offspring of the wrongdoers multiplied and the offspring of the just, people of sound intellect, diminished. His discourse ends, and it is a wonderful deduction.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

{And give the women their dowries graciously; but if they willingly give you something of it, then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure} [4]

{And give} means: bestow upon. {the women} means: those whom you have been commanded to marry. {their dowries} means: their mahr (bridal gifts), the plural of ṣadaqah on the pattern of samurah, which is the mahr. {graciously} means: a gift not to be reclaimed by stratagem that compels them to return it. The word niḥlah (with the vowel of the nūn either kasra or ḍamma, as transmitted by Ibn Durayd) is a verbal noun from naḥala, whose verbal noun is nuḥl (with ḍamma), meaning a gift without return. The expression of giving the mahr as niḥlah, although it is obligatory upon husbands, serves to convey the sense of giving out of complete contentment and goodwill.

Two benefits:

First: this address is either to the husbands, as reported from ʿAlqamah, al-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah, and preferred by al-Zajjaj, since what precedes it is addressed to those who marry, namely the husbands; or it is to the guardians of the women, because the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah would not give the women any part of their mahr.

Therefore they would say to the one to whom a daughter was born: "May the nāfijah be pleasant for you," meaning that you will take her mahr in camels and add them to your camels, so that your wealth swells, i.e., you magnify it.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: the nāfijah is what a man takes as a gift when he marries off his daughter. God Most High forbade this and commanded that the right be given to its people. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Abu Salih, and the preference of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

Second: al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: It may be that the intended meaning of giving (ītāʾ) is handing over, and it may be that the intended meaning is undertaking an obligation. God Most High said: {until they give the jizyah willingly} [al-Tawbah: 29], meaning until they guarantee it and commit to it. According to the first sense, the meaning is that they were commanded to pay the mahrs they had named for them; according to the second, the meaning is that intimacy is not made lawful except in exchange for an obligatory consideration, whether it was named or not, except what was specially granted to the Messenger ﷺ regarding the woman who gave herself in marriage (al-mawhūbah).

Then he said, may God have mercy on him: It is possible that the statement comprises both meanings together. And God knows best.

{But if they willingly give you something of it} The pronoun refers to the ṣadaqāt, and its masculine form is because it is treated as the equivalent of that (i.e., the gift). That is: if they release to you some of the mahr with willing hearts, seeking to win your affection, not out of shyness that befalls them from you or from others, nor from being compelled to give up of it due to the harshness of your characters and the badness of your dealings.

{then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure} means: take it and dispose of it as owners. The mention of eating is specific because it is the greatest of the forms of financial disposal.

Hanīʾan marīʾan are two adjectives derived from (hanuʾa al-ṭaʿām wa-marua) when food is smooth and free of any disturbance. It has been said: the hanīʾ is what comes to you without hardship or consequence, and the marīʾ is that whose outcome is praiseworthy. Both are an expression of permissibility and emphasis on allowance, and the removal of any consequence, since women are like men in their dispositions and gifts.

* *

Note:

Some exegetes said: the verse has several fruits:

Among them: that marriage necessarily requires a bridal gift.

Among them: that it is a right obligatory for the woman like other debts.

Among them: that she may dispose of it as she wishes, and the verse does not distinguish between whether she has taken possession of it or not. For this reason some jurists said: she may sell her mahr before taking possession of it; and others said: she may not sell it until she takes possession, like ownership by purchase.

Among them: that it is removed from the husband by her release of it with her goodwill. Shurayh held that she may rescind it if she retracts, and argued from the verse.

al-Shaʿbi reported that a woman came with her husband to Shurayh over a gift she had given him, and she sought to take it back. Shurayh said: Return it to her. The man said: Did not God say: {if they willingly give you something}? He said: If her soul had been content with it, she would not have taken it back.

It is also reported from him: I will have her rescind what she gave, and I will not accept it, because women are deceived.

It is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he wrote to his judges: women give out of desire or fear; whichever woman gave something and then wished to take it back, that is hers. Transmitted by al-Razi.

I say: What Shurayh held and what was reported from ʿUmar is sound jurisprudence and a masterful deduction, for the verse indicates the narrowness of the path in this matter and the necessity of caution, in that the condition is built upon willing contentment of the soul. It did not say "if they give you as a gift," to inform that what is considered is the soul's being genuinely content with what is given; and her retraction shows that her soul was not content, and this is clear.

(p-1125) The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them words of kindness.﴾ [5]

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them, and speak to them words of kindness.﴾ Know that the verse admits several interpretations that the noble wording allows:

(p-1125) The first: that by *al-sufaha'* (the foolish, those of weak judgment) is meant orphans, as was related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The address is then to the guardians, who were forbidden to give the orphans their property for fear that they would waste it, because of the weakness of their intellect, since the *safih* is one who is light in forbearance. The property is attributed to the guardians, though it belongs to the orphans, by treating its being specific to its owners as though it were specific to the guardians. Thus their property is as if it were the guardians' own property, because of the kinship and common kind that binds them together, as a form of emphasis in urging them to preserve it. This is like His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [An-Nisa: 29] [An-Nisa: from verse 29], meaning that some of you should not kill others, where the people of their kind are referred to as themselves, as an emphasis in deterring them from killing. So their killing is as if it were the killing of themselves. This is confirmed by the fact that He describes the property as the means of livelihood of its owners by describing it as the means of livelihood of the guardians, in His saying: ﴿which Allah has made a means of support for you﴾, meaning: Allah has made it something by which you stand and are sustained. So if you waste it, you will be ruined.

As for His saying: ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾, it means: make it the source of their provision and clothing, by trading and seeking profit, so that their expenses come from the profits and not from the principal of the wealth.

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and speak to them words of kindness﴾, it means: gentle speech by which their hearts are made content. Among this is that the guardian promise them a fine promise, by saying: "When you become righteous and mature, we will hand over your property to you."

The second: that by *al-sufaha'* is meant people in general and children. This was related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others. The address is then general, and the prohibition applies to everyone who would single out the property that Allah has entrusted to him and give it to his wife and children, and then look at what is in their hands. He called them *sufaha'* only to belittle their intellect and to censure the making of them custodians over themselves.

Ali ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Do not single out your property, which Allah has entrusted to you and made your livelihood, and give it to your wife or your daughter, and then look at what is in their hands. Rather, keep your property and manage it, and you yourself should be the one who spends on them from its clothing, support and provision.

The third: that by *al-sufaha'* is meant everyone who does not have the intellect adequate to preserve property. This includes women, children, orphans, and everyone described by this attribute.

Al-Razi said: This view is preferable, because specification without evidence is not permissible.

Al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: In this verse is the restriction (*hajr*) upon the *safih* (the one who squanders property, a spendthrift), that he is not to be permitted to dispose of his property, that he is to be provided for from it and clothed, and that it is not to be spent on charitable gifts. It is also said to him in kind words: "If you become mature, we will hand over your property to you; we are only being cautious for your benefit."

Those who hold that a *safih* who has reached maturity is to be restricted use the generality of the verse as evidence, whether this condition arose after maturity or was present from the time of maturity. So do those who hold that a person who is deceived in sales is to be restricted, and those who hold that one who gives charity to a restricted person, on the condition that it remains in his hand, is not to be heard in that matter.

A subtle point:

In His saying: ﴿which Allah has made a means of support for you﴾ there is an exhortation to guard property and not to waste it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The early generation used to say: "Wealth is the weapon of the believer. Leaving wealth about which Allah will hold me to account is better for me than being in need of people."

It is related from Sufyan, who had merchandise that he turned over: "Were it not for it, the Banu al-Abbas would have trampled me."

And from another, when it was said to him: "It brings you close to the world," he said: "If it has brought me close to the world, it has certainly kept me away from it."

They used to say: "Trade and earn, for you live in a time when, if one of you is in need, the first thing he consumes is his religion." And sometimes they would see a man at a funeral, and they would say to him: "Go to your shop." End of quotation.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Test the orphans until, when they reach marriageable age, if you perceive in them sound judgment, then release to them their property. Do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up. Whoever is wealthy should abstain, and whoever is poor may eat in a reasonable manner. When you release their property to them, then have witnesses against them. And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.﴾ [6]

(p. 1127) ﴿Test the orphans﴾ meaning: examine their intellects and their knowledge of managing affairs. ﴿Until, when they reach marriageable age﴾ meaning: by their having a wet dream (ihtilam) or by their reaching fifteen years, because of what is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ presented me on the day of Uhud when I was fourteen years old, and he did not permit me. Then he presented me on the day of the Trench when I was fifteen, and he permitted me."

Nafi' said: "I came to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who was then caliph, and related this hadith to him. He said, 'This is indeed the dividing line between the minor and the adult,' and he wrote to his governors that they should assign stipends to those who had reached fifteen."

Similarly, [the sign is] the growth of coarse hair around the private parts, because of what Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan narrated from Atiyyah al-Qurazi, who said: "We were presented to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Qurayzah. Whoever had grown [hair] was killed, and whoever had not grown it was released. I was among those who had not grown it, so he released me." At-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih."

﴿If you perceive﴾ meaning: you witness and ascertain ﴿in them sound judgment﴾ meaning: uprightness in their religion and preservation of their property. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is related from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and many other imams. ﴿Then release to them their property﴾ meaning: without delay.
