The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that whoever reaches maturity without being of sound judgment, whether through squandering, incapacity, or immorality, his property is not handed over to him, because that would be a corruption of the property.

﴿And do not consume it﴾ O guardians ﴿extravagantly and hastily, [fearing] that they will grow up﴾ meaning: wastefully and hurrying to consume it before they grow up, or [it means] because of your extravagance and haste regarding their growing up. You squander its expenditure, saying, "We will spend as we wish before the orphans grow up, and then they will snatch it from our hands."

﴿Whoever is wealthy﴾ among the guardians ﴿should abstain﴾ meaning: he should keep himself far from consuming the orphan's property, for it is for him like carrion and blood. Let him be content with what Allah Most High has given him of provision. ﴿And whoever is poor﴾ whose preoccupation with the orphan's property prevents him from earning, and whose neglect of it leads to its loss, ﴿may eat in a reasonable manner﴾ meaning: in proportion to his essential need and the wage of his effort and service.

This is as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Aisha (p. 1128), who said: "[He may eat] in a reasonable manner, in proportion to his care for it." Al-Bukhari also narrated it.

Ibn Kathir said: The jurists said: He may take the lesser of two things: the customary wage for his like, or the amount of his need. As for whether he must repay it when he becomes well-off, there are two opinions:

The first: he does not repay, because he consumed it in return for the wage of his work and he was poor. This is the sound view among the followers of al-Shafi'i, because the verse permitted eating without a substitute.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that "a man asked the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I have no property, and I have an orphan.' He said: 'Eat from your orphan's property, without extravagance, without squandering, and without accumulating property for yourself, and without protecting your property with his property,' or he said, 'ransoming your property with his property.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it with the wording: "Eat in a reasonable manner, without extravagance." Abu Dawud, an-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah also narrated it.

Ibn Hibban in his Sahih and Ibn Mardawayh in his Tafsir narrated from Jabir that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah! With what may I discipline my orphan?' He said: 'With what you would discipline your own child, without protecting your property with his property, and without accumulating property from him.'"

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from ath-Thawri, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, who said: "A Bedouin came to Ibn Abbas and said: 'I have orphans in my custody, and they have camels, and I have camels, and I give milk from my camels to the poor. What is lawful for me from their milk?' He said: 'If you are seeking their stray animals, and treating their mange, and repairing their watering trough, and tending to them, then drink without harming the offspring and without excessive milking.'" Malik narrated it in his Muwatta'. It is with this view, that there is no repayment, that 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Ikrimah, Ibrahim an-Nakha'i, Atiyyah al-Awfi, and al-Hasan al-Basri (p. 1129) say.

The second opinion: he must repay, because the property of the orphan is forbidden, and it is only permitted out of necessity, so he repays its equivalent, like consuming another's property by the one in dire need.

Ibn Abi ad-Dunya narrated from Harithah ibn Mudarrib, who said: "Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'I have placed myself with regard to this property in the position of the guardian of an orphan. If I am well-off, I abstain; if I am in need, I borrow; and when I become well-off, I repay.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated in his Sunan: "Abu al-Ahwas related to us from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to me: 'I have only placed myself with regard to Allah's property in the position of the guardian of an orphan. If I am in need, I take from it; when I become well-off, I return it. And if I am well-off, I abstain.'" Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is sahih."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim likewise narrated it through Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿then let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾, that it means "by way of a loan." He said: It is also related from Ubaydah, Abu al-Aliyah, Abu Wa'il, Sa'id ibn Jubayr (in one of the narrations), Mujahid, ad-Dahhak, ash-Sha'bi, and as-Suddi something similar.

Fakhr ad-Din ar-Razi said: Some scholars restricted this lending to the principal of property, such as gold, silver, and other things.

As for taking from the milk of livestock, using slaves, and riding animals, it is permitted for him if it does not harm the property. This is the view of Abu al-Aliyah and others, and they argued that Allah Most High said: ﴿When you release their property to them﴾, so He made the decision regarding property to be its release to them. The quotation ends.

I say: All of these are possible, since there is no explicit text from either of the two foundational sources (the Qur'an and Sunnah) regarding any one of them. The scrupulousness (wara') is not hidden.

﴿When you release their property to them﴾ meaning: after maturity and sound judgment, ﴿then have witnesses against them﴾ meaning: at (p. 1130) the time of release, [confirming] that they have received it, for that is more effective in averting suspicion and further from dispute.

As-Suyuti said: In it is the command to call witnesses, recommended by some and obligatory according to others. It is also derived from it that the statement regarding the release is the statement of the minor, not the guardian, so his claim is not accepted without evidence.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ meaning: sufficient as a witness against you regarding the release and receipt, or as the one who calls you to account. So do not oppose what He has commanded you. The placement of this concluding phrase here is not hidden, for the guardian of an orphan will be held accountable for what is in his hand.

In it is a warning to the guardian of the orphan, and an informing of him that Allah Most High knows his inner state just as He knows his outer state, so that he does not intend or do with his property anything that is not lawful, and that he upholds complete trustworthiness in that until his property reaches him.

It is established in the Sahih of Muslim that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'O Abu Dharr, I see you are weak, and I love for you what I love for myself. Do not take charge over two people, and do not be in charge of an orphan's property.'"

Then Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the rulings on inheritance with His saying:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, whether it is little or much, a share ordained.﴾ [7]

﴿For men﴾ means: the sons and the relatives. ﴿a share﴾ means: a portion. ﴿of what the parents and the close relatives leave﴾ means: those who have died. ﴿And for women there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, whether it is little or much﴾ means: of the property. ﴿a share ordained﴾ means: a specified, obligatory portion due to them.

The mention of the ruling concerning women independently, rather than inserting it within the rulings concerning men by saying "for men and women, etc.", is for the sake of giving attention to their matter, and to indicate from the outset the disparity between the two groups' shares, and to emphasize the nullification of the ruling of the Jahiliyyah (Pre-Islamic Ignorance). For they used not to give inheritance to women and children, and they would say: "None inherits except one who thrusts with spears, defends the enclosure, and seizes the spoils." The verse has been cited as evidence for the inheritance of *dhawu al-arham* (distant kin not counted among the sharers or agnatic heirs), since they are among the close relatives. This is a sound inference, and there is no proof for anyone who has attempted to repel it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 8:

(p-1131) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And when the division [of the estate] is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them kind words.﴾ [8]

﴿And when the division [of the estate] is attended﴾, i.e., the division of the inheritance, ﴿by relatives﴾ (dhawu al-qaraba), those who are kin but do not inherit, ﴿[He] mentioned them first because giving to them is charity and maintaining ties of kinship﴾, ﴿and orphans﴾, the weak through the loss of their fathers, ﴿and the needy﴾, the weak through lacking what suffices them of wealth. ﴿Provide for them from it﴾, i.e., give them something from the inheritance, ﴿and speak to them kind words﴾ by speaking gently to them and invoking blessings upon them, such as: "May Allah bless you."

Ibn Kathir said regarding this verse: The meaning is that when these poor people, from among the relatives who do not inherit, and the orphans and the needy, attend the division of abundant wealth, their souls long for some of it when they see this one taking and that one taking, while they are in despair and are given nothing. So Allah, exalted is He, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful, commanded that something be set aside for them from the estate, as an act of kindness toward them, charity to them, benevolence to them, and a consolation for their brokenness, just as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-An'am: 141] [al-An'am: part of verse 141]. He also censured those who carry off wealth secretly for fear that the needy and those in want would notice them, as He reported about the companions of the garden: ﴿When they swore that they would surely harvest it in the morning﴾ [al-Qalam: 17] [al-Qalam: part of verse 17] ﴿So they set off while whispering to one another﴾ [al-Qalam: 23] ﴿that no needy person shall enter it today against you﴾ [al-Qalam: 24] [al-Qalam: 23-24] (p-1132) ﴿Allah destroyed them, and there are similar [fates] for the disbelievers﴾ [Muhammad: 10] [Muhammad: 10]. Whoever denies the right of Allah over him, He punishes him in the most precious of what he possesses. For this reason it came in the hadith: "Charity has never mixed with wealth without ruining it," meaning that withholding it is the cause of the complete loss of that wealth. End of quotation.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: It is muhkam (definitive) and not mansukh (abrogated); and in another wording from him: it remains in force and is acted upon.

It has been reported from a group of the Companions and the Successors regarding this verse that it is obligatory upon the heirs, to the extent that their souls are content with it.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated in his "Musannaf" that Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr divided the inheritance of his father Abd al-Rahman, while Aisha was alive, and he did not leave in the house any needy person or any relative except that he gave them from his father's inheritance, and he recited: ﴿And when the division [of the estate] is attended by relatives﴾, the verse.

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, who said: There are three Madinan, definitive verses which many people have neglected: ﴿And when the division [of the estate] is attended﴾; the verse of seeking permission: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty﴾ [al-Nur: 58]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created you from male and female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], the verse.

Here many exegetes have mentioned reports from some of the earlier scholars that this verse is abrogated by the verse of inheritance; but this is very weak. Indeed, the one who holds the view of abrogation has strayed far from grasping the secret of the verse regarding this noble virtue it urges, namely aiding those mentioned from the inherited wealth. A noble soul recoils from taking abundant wealth while a relative stands present, deprived, neither helped nor assisted. The verse is clear in itself, plain in its meaning, as plain as the sun at midday; it is not abrogated, nor will the Hour come [before it is upheld].

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ [9]

﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ There are several interpretations of the verse:

The first: It is a command to guardians (awsiya') that they should fear Allah, exalted is He, and be mindful of Him regarding the affairs of orphans, treating them as they would wish their own weak offspring to be treated after their death.

The second: It is a command to those who attend the sick person (al-'uwwad) at the time of making a bequest, that they should fear their Lord, or fear the sick person's children and feel for them the compassion they feel for their own children, so that they do not allow him to harm them by diverting the wealth away from them.

The third: It is a command to the heirs to show compassion toward the weak relatives, orphans and needy who are present at the division [of the estate], imagining that if they were their own children and were left behind them weak like them, would they permit their deprivation?!

The fourth: It is a command to those making bequests that they should consider the heirs and not be extravagant in the bequest, as is established in the two Sahihs, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he entered upon Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas to visit him, [Sa'd] said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have wealth, and none inherits from me except one daughter. Shall I give two-thirds of my wealth in charity?" He said: "No." He said: "Then half?" (p-1134) He said: "No." He said: "Then a third." He said: "A third, and a third is much. Indeed, that you leave your heirs wealthy is better than that you leave them dependent, begging from people."

And in the Sahih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "If the people reduced it to a quarter? For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The third, and the third is much (or great).'"

The first interpretation was related by Ibn Jarir through al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Kathir said: "It is a good opinion, reinforced by what follows of the threat regarding consuming the wealth of orphans unjustly."

Al-Razi transmitted from al-Qadi: this interpretation is more fitting with what precedes and follows of the verses concerning orphans, for Allah, exalted is He, made the last of what urged them to preserve the orphan's wealth to be that He alerts them to the state of their own selves and their offspring if they imagine it; and there is no doubt that this is among the strongest motivations and incentives toward this aim.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The appropriate speech from guardians is that they should not harm orphans, and should address them as they address their own children, with good manners and warmth, calling them "my son" (ya bunayya) and "my child" (ya walidi). And from those sitting with the sick person is that they should say to him, when he wishes to make a bequest: "Do not be extravagant in your bequest, lest you harm your children," like the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Sa'd: "That you leave your child wealthy is better than that you leave them dependent, begging from people." And from those dividing the inheritance is that they should soften their speech and make it gracious to those present.

A subtle point:

It is necessary to understand His saying, exalted is He, "taraku" (they leave) as meaning "approaching," so that "khafu" (they would be anxious) can validly be its predicate, since there is no fear after the actual occurrence of death and the leaving of heirs. A parallel is His saying: (p-1135) ﴿Then when they have reached their term, retain them in good manner or release them in good manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231], meaning: they have approached the end of their term. And in this metaphorical use of expressing the approach to leaving by the leaving there is a wondrous secret: it is the instilling of fear through a state in which no hope of life remains, nor any hope of protecting weak offspring. This state, although it belongs to this world, is, because of its nearness to the Hereafter and its adherence to departure, counted within its domain, and is expressed by what is used to express the state following departure, namely "leaving." Thus in al-Intisaf.

* *

A note:

Some exegetes said: it is obligatory for a person to love for his brother what he loves for himself, and to love for the offspring of other believers what he loves for his own offspring; and that the guardian of an orphan must not harm the orphan, but must speak to him as he speaks to his own children, with good manners and warmth, and should address the orphan as "my son" (ya bunayya) and "my child" (ya walidi). Many reports concerning tenderness toward orphans have come down. End of quote.

In the verse there is also an indication of guiding fathers who fear leaving behind weak offspring to piety in all their affairs, so that their children may be preserved and aided by special care from Him, exalted is He. Its implication also contains a warning that their children will be lost if they lack the fear of Allah, exalted is He; and an indication that the piety of forebears preserves their descendants. Righteous men preserve their weak offspring, as in the verse: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father was righteous﴾ [al-Kahf: 82], to its end, for the two boys were preserved, by the blessing of their father's righteousness, in their persons and their wealth.

(p-1136) The Discussion of the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly - they are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blaze.﴾ [10]

﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly﴾ meaning: in the manner of injustice, [committed] by the heirs, or by the wicked guardians and their judges, unlike the consumption of the poor one who oversees their property in proportion to his wage, as has passed.

﴿They are only consuming fire into their bellies﴾ meaning: that which draws them to the Fire and leads them to it. ﴿And they will burn﴾ meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿in a blaze﴾ meaning: a fire that is kindled.

Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Barzah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There will be raised on the Day of Resurrection a people from their graves, their mouths blazing with fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! Who are they?" He said: "Have you not seen that Allah said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly⦆ - the verse."

A subtle point:

Al-Zamakhshari said: "In their bellies" means: filling their bellies. It is said: "So-and-so ate in his belly and in part of his belly." The poet said:

"Eat in part of your bellies, that you may abstain, for your time is a lean time."

Al-Nasir said: Similar to it is: "Hatred has already appeared from their mouths" - meaning they choked on it and said it with the full of their mouths. The mention of the bellies is intended to depict the eating for the listener, so that the heinousness of this crime becomes firmly established in his mind through greater depiction. And for the sake of emphasizing the censure of the wrongdoer who devours the orphan's property, the eating was singled out, because it is the most hideous of the states in which the orphan's property is consumed. And Allah knows best.

* *

(p-1137) A Note:

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim and others narrated that when this verse was revealed, whoever had an orphan in his custody went and separated the orphan's food from his own food, and his drink from his drink, and he would set aside for him some of his food and keep it for him until he ate it or it spoiled. This became hard on them, so they mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿They ask you concerning orphans. Say: Reforming them is best﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220] - the verse. So they mixed their food with his food and their drink with his drink. This has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Some of the ignorant have said that this verse was abrogated by that one. This is far-fetched, because this verse concerns the prohibition of injustice, and this does not become abrogated by that. Rather, the intent is that mixing with orphans' property - if it is in the way of injustice - is among the greatest gates of sin, as in this verse; and if it is in the way of nurturing and kindness, it is among the greatest gates of righteousness, as in His words: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220].

And he, may Allah have mercy on him, said before that: How strongly this threat indicates the vastness of His mercy, the abundance of His pardon and His bounty; for when the orphans reach the utmost extreme of weakness, Allah's care for them reaches the utmost extreme.

[p-1138] The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the portion of two females. And if they are [only] daughters, more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he leaves; and if there is only one, for her is half. And for his parents, to each one of them is a sixth of what he leaves, if he has a child. But if he has no child and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third. And if he has brothers, for his mother is a sixth, after any bequest he [i.e., the deceased] makes or debt. Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit. [This is] an obligation from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [11]

﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾: This begins the detailed explanation of the rulings on inheritance that were stated in summary in His words, exalted is He: ﴿For men is a share﴾ [an-Nisa: 7], and so on.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This noble verse, the one after it, and the verse that concludes this surah are the verses of the science of inheritance (ʿilm al-fara'id), which is derived from these three verses and from the hadiths related on this subject, which serve as an explanation of them. End of quote.

The meaning: Allah commands you and enjoins upon you, concerning the inheritance of your children after your death, ﴿for the male﴾, i.e., among them, ﴿the like of the portion of two females﴾, i.e., their share, whether combined or separate.

As for the first: each male is counted as equal to two females, as in the case of a son with two daughters, or a son's son with two daughters of a son, and so on for the lower generations. Thus his share is diminished, and he takes two shares, just as they together have two shares.

As for the second: he [the male] has the whole, which is double the share of a single daughter, because she is assigned half when she is alone. This necessarily implies that the male, when alone, has double her share when she is alone, and that is the full amount. So what is mentioned here is the inheritance of the male in general, whether together with females or alone, as the author of al-Intisaf (al-Zamakhshari) has verified.

* *

A note: al-Suyuti said: Those who hold that the children of a son are included in the word "children" (awlad) have cited this verse, since there is consensus on their inheriting, but not the children of a daughter.

[p-1139] Subtleties:

The first: The wisdom behind doubling the male's share is that he needs to bear the burden of maintenance, endure the hardship of trade and earning a living, and bear difficulties. He is more in need of wealth. Also, if the female's share were complete, despite her being of lesser intellect and greater desire, she would squander it on desires in extravagance. And because she may spend only on herself, whereas he spends on himself and his wife.

The second: He did not say, "For the male is double the share of the female," because "double" applies to two times and more, so it would not be an explicit text. Nor did he say, "For the two females is the like of the share of the male," nor "For the female is half the share of the male," giving precedence to the male by showing his superiority over the female. Nor did he say, "For the male is two times the share of the female," because the "like" in quantity is not multiplied except by a multiplicity of persons, and that was not considered here.

The third: The choice of the terms "male" and "female" over what was mentioned first, "men" and "women," is to make explicit the equality of the adults and children of both groups in entitlement, without any consideration of puberty or adulthood at all, as is the claim of the people of the Jahiliyyah, who did not give inheritance to children, nor to women.

The fourth: Some scholars inferred from this verse that He, exalted is He, is more merciful to His creation than a mother is to her child, since He enjoined parents concerning their children, so it is known that He is more merciful to them than they are.

As occurs in the authentic hadith, when [the Prophet] (ﷺ) "saw a woman among the captives whose child had been separated from her, and she began to search for her child. When she found him among the captives, she took him, pressed him to her chest and nursed him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: Do you think this woman would throw her child into the fire while she is able not to do so? They said: No, O Messenger of Allah. He said: By Allah! Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman to her child."

[p-1140] ﴿And if they are [only] daughters﴾: i.e., the children, and the feminine form is according to the predicate, which is His words, ﴿daughters﴾, meaning pure daughters with no male among them. ﴿More than two﴾ is a second predicate or an adjective of "daughters," i.e., daughters exceeding two. ﴿For them is two-thirds of what he leaves﴾: i.e., of the deceased, which is indicated by the context.

* *

A note: The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that two-thirds is the prescribed share for three or more daughters when there is no male with them. No prescribed share is named for two daughters.

The scholars differed regarding their prescribed share. The majority held that, if they are alone without sons, they are entitled to two-thirds.

Ibn 'Abbas held that their prescribed share is one-half. The majority argued by analogy with two sisters, for Allah, glorified is He, said concerning them: ﴿If there are two, they have two-thirds﴾ [an-Nisa: 176]. So they equated two daughters with two sisters in their entitlement to two-thirds, just as they equated sisters, when more than two, with daughters in sharing the two-thirds.

It was also said that the verse contains an indication that two daughters have two-thirds, because when a single female with her brother has one-third, two daughters alone have two-thirds. This argument was used by Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash and al-Mubarrid.

Al-Nahhas said: This argument, according to those versed in reasoning, is flawed, because the disagreement concerns two daughters when they are alone without sons. Also, the opponent may say: If he leaves two daughters and a son, then the two daughters have one-half. This is evidence that this is their prescribed share.

The argument of the majority may be reinforced by the fact that when Allah, exalted is He, prescribed for a single daughter one-half when she is alone, by His words, ﴿And if there is only one, for her is half﴾, the prescribed share of two daughters when alone is above the prescribed share of one, and analogy with the two sisters [who get two-thirds] requires that two daughters be limited to two-thirds.

It was also said that "above" (fawqa) is superfluous, and the meaning is: if they are two females, as in His words, ﴿so strike above the necks﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], i.e., the necks.

Al-Nahhas and Ibn 'Atiyya rejected this, saying: This is an error, because adverbs and all nouns may not be added in the speech of the Arabs without meaning.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Also, the expression "above the necks" is the eloquent one, and "above" is not superfluous, but has a definite meaning, because striking the neck must be above the bones at the joint, not at the brain, as Durayd ibn al-Simma said: "Lower it from the brain and raise it from the bone; thus I used to strike the necks of heroes." End of quote.

Also, if the word "above" were superfluous as they claim, He would have said, "for the two of them is two-thirds of what he leaves," and not "for them [feminine dual/plural] is two-thirds of what he leaves."

The clearest argument for the majority is what Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, [p-1141] al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Jabir, who said: "The wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' came with her two daughters by Sa'd to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, these are the two daughters of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'. Their father was killed with you at the battle of Uhud as a martyr. Their uncle took their wealth and left them with no property, and they cannot be married unless they have property. He said: Allah will decide concerning that. Then the verse of inheritance was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to their uncle and said: Give the two daughters of Sa'd two-thirds, their mother one-eighth, and what remains is for you." They related it through several chains, from 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil, from Jabir.

Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound hadith which we know only through the narration of 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil. Sharik also related it from 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil in his narration. Thus [it is cited] in Fath al-Bayan.

﴿And if she is only one﴾: i.e., the newborn female, ﴿one﴾: i.e., a single woman with no brother or sister with her, ﴿then for her is half﴾: i.e., half of what he leaves. She is not given the full amount because she is deficient. For this reason she was not assigned the two-thirds which is the share of a son with her. Then, after the inheritance of the children, He mentioned the inheritance of the parents, saying: ﴿And for his parents﴾: i.e., the deceased. This is a pronoun referring to what is not explicitly mentioned, which is permissible because the context indicates it. By "the two parents" is meant the father and the mother, and the dual is used according to the form of "father" by way of prevalence (taghlib). ﴿To each one of them is a sixth of what he leaves﴾ of the wealth ﴿if he has a child﴾, male or female. ﴿But if he has no child﴾, male or female, ﴿and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third﴾: i.e., a third of the wealth of what he leaves, and the remainder is for the father. The male receives the like of the portion of two females. But the mother was assigned a third, by placing her in the position of a daughter together with a son, not alone; this is a lowering of her rank, because the daughter stands in place of the deceased in general, as stated by al-Mahayimi.

﴿And if he has brothers﴾: i.e., for the deceased, whether full brothers, or brothers from the father or from the mother, male or female, ﴿then for his mother is a sixth﴾, meaning the mother of the deceased receives a sixth of the estate, ﴿after any bequest he makes or debt﴾. Here the phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: these stated shares are distributed among the heirs only after carrying out a bequest the deceased makes, up to one-third, and after paying off a debt owed by the deceased.

It is read in the seven canonical readings: "yuwsi" (he makes a bequest) with both the passive and the active voice.

[p-1143] Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: The scholars of the early and later generations agreed that debt takes precedence over bequest.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and the authors of the exegeses related, through the chain of Ibn Ishaq, from al-Harith ibn 'Abdullah al-A'war, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "You recite this verse: ﴿after a bequest he makes or debt﴾, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided on debt before bequest. And the full-blooded relatives of the mother inherit from each other, to the exclusion of the half-blood relatives [from the father]. A man inherits from his full brother [from both parents] to the exclusion of his half-brother [from the father]."

Al-Tirmidhi then said: We know it only through the narration of al-Harith, and some scholars have spoken about him. But he was a memorizer of the rules of inheritance, careful with them and with calculation. Allah knows best.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: The verse indicates that inheritance is divided only after the payment of debt and the execution of bequests. It also indicates the legitimacy of bequest. Those who hold that bequest takes precedence over debt in the estate have used the mention of bequest first as evidence. Those who held that bequest is delayed answered that it was mentioned first so that it would not be neglected. Those who permitted bequest of any amount, whether little or much, even if it exhausts the wealth, and those who permitted bequest to an heir or to a disbeliever, whether a combatant or a protected non-Muslim, used its generality as evidence. Those who said that debt prevents the transfer of the estate into the ownership of the heir used it as evidence, and those who said that debt for Hajj and zakat takes precedence over inheritance used the generality of His words, ﴿or debt﴾. End of quote.

Imam Ahmad and Ibn Majah related with a sound chain from Sa'd ibn al-A'wal that "his brother died and left three hundred dirhams and a family, so I wanted to spend them on his family. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: Your brother is held back by his debt, so pay it off on his behalf. He said: O Messenger of Allah, I have paid it off on his behalf, except for two dinars which a woman claims, and she has no proof. He said: Give it to her, for she is right."

[p-1144] A subtlety:

Fa'idah: Describing the bequest with His words, ﴿he makes﴾, is an encouragement toward bequest and a recommendation of it.

The choice of "or" (aw), which conveys permissibility, in His words "or debt," over "and" (waw), is to indicate that both are equal in being obligatory, and that both precede the division, whether together or separately. The mention of bequest before debt, although it is later in ruling, is, as we have mentioned, to display full concern for its execution, since it is the object of likely neglect in carrying it out, and for its regular occurrence. This is unlike debt. This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit.﴾ That is: you do not know which of those who inherit from you, from your ascendants and your descendants, is more beneficial to you in this world and in the next. The meaning is: Allah prescribed the obligatory shares (al-fara'id) as they are, in wisdom. Had He left that to you, you would not have known which of them is more beneficial to you, and you would have distributed the wealth without wisdom. The difference in the shares follows the difference in benefit, and you do not know its degrees. So Allah undertook that Himself as a favour from Him, and did not leave it to your effort, because of your inability to know the proper measures. This clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) that reinforces the matter of the division, and a refutation of what was practised in the Jahiliyyah.

Al-Samarqandi said: It is also said that the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, taught you the division of inheritances, and that you do not know which of you is nearer in death, so that the other would inherit from him. End of quotation.

﴿An obligation from Allah.﴾ It is in the accusative as an absolute infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for an omitted verb, meaning: Allah prescribed that as a prescription. Or it is in the accusative in relation to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah enjoins you﴾, since it carries the sense of: He commands you and imposes upon you.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing﴾, that is, of the interests and the ranks, ﴿Wise﴾, that is, in everything He decrees and ordains. Thus within this is included the explanation of the shares of the male and the female, by way of primary inclusion.

[p. 1145]

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is a quarter of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for them is a quarter of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt. And if a man or a woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants (kalalah), and he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they share in a third, after any bequest that is made or debt, without harm. An ordinance from God; and God is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.﴾ [12]

﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ of the property, ﴿if they have no child﴾, male or female, from you or from others, ﴿but if they have a child﴾ in the manner that has been detailed, ﴿then for you is a quarter of what they leave﴾ of the property, and the remainder goes to the rest of the heirs, ﴿after any bequest they make or debt﴾, meaning: after their bequest has been carried out and their debt has been settled. ﴿And for them is a quarter of what you leave﴾ of the property, ﴿if you have no child﴾, male or female, from them or from others, ﴿but if you have a child﴾ in the manner that has been detailed, ﴿then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt﴾. The discussion of this is as has already preceded, and in the repetition of the mention of bequest and debt there is an evident concern for their importance.

*A subtle point:*

The verse contains an indication of the superiority of men over women. When He mentions the men in this verse, He addresses them directly, and when He mentions the women, He refers to them in the third person. Moreover, God addresses men seven times in this verse, and mentions women in the third person fewer times than that. This indicates the preference of men over women, just as they are preferred over them in the share. Thus it is derived from al-Razi.[p. 1146]

﴿And if a man leaves neither ascendants nor descendants (yurathu kalalah), or a woman﴾, meaning: a woman who is inherited in the same way, ﴿and he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that﴾, meaning: the brothers and sisters from the mother's side, ﴿more than one﴾, ﴿they share in a third﴾, in which males and females are equal.

Al-Majd said in *al-Qamus*: *al-Kalalah* is: one who has neither child nor parent; or what is not of lineage by direct descent; or one whose lineage is linked to yours, such as a paternal cousin and the like; or it is brothers from the mother's side; or distant paternal cousins; or everything other than parent and child; or it is from the 'asabah, the one from whom brothers from the mother's side inherit. These are seven sayings reported from the imams of the language.

Ibn Barri said: Know that *al-kalalah* in origin is the verbal noun of (*kalla al-mayyit yakillu kallan wa kalalatan*): he is *kall* when he leaves no child nor parent who inherit from him. This is its original meaning.

He said: Then *al-kalalah* may be used of the person, not of the event, so that it becomes a name for the deceased heir, even though originally it was a name for the event, in the sense of their saying: *hadha khalq Allah*, meaning: the creature of God.

He said: It is also permissible that it be a name for the heir, in the sense of their saying: *rajul 'adl*, meaning: just (*'adil*), and *ma' ghawr*, meaning: sunken (*ghair*).

He said: The first is the choice of the Basrans, that *al-kalalah* is a name for the deceased, and the tafsir of the verse came in accordance with it: that *al-kalalah* is one who leaves neither child nor parent. When you take it to mean the deceased, its grammatical position in the verse can be in two ways:

One of them: it is the predicate of *kana* (was), its estimated sense being: "if the deceased was *kalalah*," that is, *kall*, having neither child nor parent.

The second way: its accusative is as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the pronoun in *yurathu* (is inherited), that is, "is inherited while being *kalalah*," and *kana* is then the complete verb which does not require a predicate.

He said: It is not correct that it be the incomplete *kana*, as al-Hawfi stated, because its predicate can only be *al-kalalah*, and there is no benefit in His saying *yurathu*. The sense would be: "if there occurs or is present a man who dies *kalalah*," that is, is inherited while being *kalalah*, meaning *kall*.

If you take it to mean the event and not the person, its accusative may take three forms:

One: its accusative is as a verbal noun, by omitting a modifier, the estimated sense being: "is inherited with a *kalalah* inheritance," as al-Farazdaq said:

> *You inherited the spear-shaft of kingship, not by kalalah*

meaning: you inherited it through inheritance of nearness, not inheritance of distance.

And 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl said:

> *'Amir did not make me a chief through kalalah* ∗∗∗ *God refused that I should be exalted through a mother or a father*

And from this is their saying: "He is a paternal cousin *kalalah*," meaning: distant in lineage; and when they want nearness they say: "He is a paternal cousin *dinyah*."

The second way: *al-kalalah* is a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial state, in the sense of their saying: "Zayd came running" (*rakdan*), meaning: running. "He is my paternal cousin *dinyah*," meaning: near; and "my paternal cousin *kalalah*," meaning: distant in lineage.

The third way: it is the predicate of *kana*, by omitting a modifier, its estimated sense being: "if the deceased was one possessing *kalalah*."

He said: These are five aspects of the accusative of *al-kalalah*:

The first: that it is the predicate of *kana*.

The second: that it is a circumstantial state.

The third: that it is a verbal noun by omitting a modifier.

The fourth: that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state.

The fifth: that it is the predicate of *kana* by omitting a modifier. This is the way followed by the people of Basra and the scholars of the language, namely that *al-kalalah* is a name for the deceased and not for the heir.

He said: Some of the people of the language, namely the people of Kufa, have permitted that *al-kalalah* be a name for the heir, and they argued for this with several things, among them:

The recitation of al-Hasan (*wa in kana rajulun yurithu kalalatan*) with a *kasra* on the *ra'*, so that *al-kalalah* on the apparent reading of this recitation is the heirs of the deceased, namely the brothers from the mother's side.

They also argued by the statement of Jabir, that he said: "O Messenger of God, only *kalalah* inherit from me."

If the proof of this view is established, the accusative of *kalalah* is then also in the same way as it stands in the fifth aspect of the first view, namely that it is the predicate of *kana* with an omitted modifier, so that the second is the first; its estimated sense being: "if a man who is inherited from possesses *kalalah* (heirs who are kalalah)," as you say: "one with kinship among whom there is no child nor parent." He said: Likewise, if you make it a circumstantial state of the pronoun in *yuwrithu*, its estimated sense being: "one possessing *kalalah*."

He said: Ibn Jinni, regarding the recitation of the one who read (*yurathu kalalatan*) and (*yuwarrithu kalalatan*), held that the two objects of *yurithu* and *yuwarrithu* are omitted, meaning: his heir bequeaths his property. He said: On this view, *kalalatan* remains in its first state which I mentioned, so its accusative is as the predicate of *kana* or as a verbal noun, and *al-kalalah* is for the deceased and not for the heir.

He said: The apparent meaning is that *al-kalalah* is a verbal noun which applies both to the heir and to the deceased, and a verbal noun may sometimes refer to the agent and at other times to the object. And God knows best.

Ibn al-Athir said: The father and the son are the two extremities of a man. If he dies and leaves neither of them, he has died having lost his two extremities, so the loss of the two extremities is called *kalalah*.

In *al-Asas*: Among the figurative usages is: "So-and-so was *kalla kalalah*," when he had neither child nor parent, meaning: he failed to reach the close kinship that touches him.

Al-Azhari said: God mentioned *al-kalalah* in Surat al-Nisa' in two places:

One of them is His saying: ﴿And if a man leaves neither ascendants nor descendants (yurathu kalalah), or a woman, and he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth﴾.

The second place is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning *al-kalalah*: if a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, then for her is half of what he leaves﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], the verse.

So here He made *al-kalalah* refer to the full sister and the full brother, and He gave the single sister half of what the deceased left, and to two sisters two-thirds, and to the brothers and sisters together all the property between them, the male receiving the equivalent of the share of two females.

And in the first verse He made the brother and sister from the mother's side a third, each one a sixth. Thus the context of the two verses makes clear that *al-kalalah* sometimes includes brothers from the mother's side, and at other times brothers and sisters from the father and mother.

The verse of the poet shows that the father is not *kalalah*, and that all the other guardians among the 'asabah after the child are *kalalah*. It is his saying:

> *For the father of a man is more protective of him* ∗∗∗ *and the guardian of the kalalah does not become angry*

He meant: the father becomes angrier for him when he is wronged, and the guardians of the *kalalah*, who are the brothers, paternal uncles, paternal cousins and all other relatives, do not become angry for a man with the anger of a father. End of quotation.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said: "I have formed an opinion concerning *al-kalalah*. If it is correct, it is from God alone, without partner; and if it is in error, it is from me and from Satan, and God is free of it": that *al-kalalah* is everything other than child and parent.

* *

*A note:*

The scholars agreed on what is meant by His saying: ﴿and he has a brother or a sister﴾: it is the brother and sister from the mother's side.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and others among the early generation recited: "and he has a brother or a sister from a mother" (*min umm*), and likewise Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, explained it in what Qatadah narrated from him.

Al-Karkhi said: An irregular recitation (*qira'ah shadhdhah*) is like a solitary report (*khabar al-ahad*), because it does not come from opinion.

Al-Shafi'i permitted absolute argument by it, as al-Buwayti related from him, in the chapter on suckling and in the chapter on the prohibition of combining (two sisters in marriage). This is the view of the majority of his companions, because it is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), and the absence of the specific Qur'anic status of a reading does not entail the absence of the specific status of its being a report.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that the brothers here are the brothers from the mother's side.

He said: There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that the inheritance of the brothers of the full or the paternal side is not like this. Their consensus therefore indicates that the brothers mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if they are brothers and sisters, men and women, then the male receives the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa': 176] are the brothers of both parents, or of the father.

*A subtle point:*

The singular pronoun in His saying ﴿and he has a brother﴾ either refers back to the deceased, which is understood from the context, or to one of them (the man or woman), and the masculine form is for the sake of prevalence. Or it refers to the man, and his ruling is sufficient without the ruling for the woman, because the conjunction indicates that they share in it.

﴿after any bequest that is made or debt, without harm﴾: a circumstantial state of the pronoun in ﴿yuusi﴾ [al-Nisa': 11] (according to the reading in which it is active), meaning: not bringing harm upon the heirs, such as bequeathing more than a third. Or it is from the agent of a hidden verb indicated by what is mentioned (according to the reading in which it is passive). The restriction of this condition to this context is because heirs are the likely object of a deceased person's neglect toward them.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Harm in bequest is among the major sins." al-Nasa'i narrated it in his *Sunan* from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (*mawquf*), and this is the sound version, as Ibn Jarir said.

﴿An ordinance from God﴾: a verbal noun emphasizing an omitted verb, its tanwin for the sake of magnification, like His saying: ﴿an obligation from God﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. Or it is in the accusative governed by *ghayra mudarr* (without harm), as an object, since it is an active participle relying on the one it qualifies, or it is negated in meaning, so it governs the explicit object. The reading with the genitive (idafah) supports this, meaning: not causing harm to the ordinance of God and His covenant regarding the heirs.

﴿And God is All-Knowing﴾ of the one who causes harm and others, ﴿Most Forbearing﴾, who does not hasten punishment, so let no one be deceived by the delay.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿These are the limits of Allah. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger – He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. And that is the great achievement.﴾ [13]

﴿These﴾ – the rulings – ﴿are the limits of Allah﴾: His rulings and His obligations, the bounded limits which may not be transgressed. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ – in the division of inheritances and other matters – ﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., beneath their trees and dwellings. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ – they will not die nor be removed. ﴿And that is the great achievement﴾ – the abundant salvation through Paradise.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits – He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment﴾ [14]

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ in the division of inheritances and other matters, ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ by overstepping His rulings and obligations through deviation and injustice, ﴿He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein eternally, and for him is a humiliating punishment﴾. That is: because he changed what Allah has decreed and opposed Allah in His ruling. This arises only from not being content with what Allah has apportioned and decreed, and for this He recompenses him with humiliation in a painful, lasting punishment.

Abu Dawud narrated in the chapter "Harm in the Bequest" (al-Idrar fi al-Wasiyyah) of his Sunan, from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a man or a woman may work by obedience to Allah for sixty years, then death attends them, and they cause harm in the bequest, so the Fire becomes obligatory for them."

Abu Hurayrah recited: ﴿after any bequest﴾ [an-Nisa': 12] up to: ﴿That is the great achievement﴾ [an-Nisa': 13]. It was also narrated by at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.

Imam Ahmad narrated it with a fuller version, and its wording is: "Indeed, a man may work with the deeds of the people of good for seventy years, then when he makes a bequest he deviates in his bequest, so he is sealed for him with the worst of his deeds, and he enters the Fire. And indeed, a man may work with the deeds of the people of evil for seventy years, then he is just in his bequest, so he is sealed for him with the best of his deeds, and he enters Paradise." He said: Then Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 13] up to His words: ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾."

Then, after explaining the rulings on inheritances, Exalted is He clarified some of the rulings relating to women with His words:

(p-1152) The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And those of your women who commit obscenity, bring against them four witnesses from among you. And if they testify, then confine them to their houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way.﴾ [15]

﴿And those of your women who commit obscenity﴾, that is, the grave indecency, which is adultery, ﴿of your women﴾, ﴿bring against them﴾, that is, demand from those who accuse them, ﴿four witnesses from among you﴾, that is, from among the Muslims. ﴿And if they testify﴾ against them with it, ﴿then confine them to their houses﴾, that is, keep them locked in them and do not allow them to go out, to protect them from exposing themselves through it to indecency. ﴿Until death takes them﴾, that is, until it completes taking their souls. In this there is a magnification of death and a presentation of it in the form of one who undertakes seizing and taking souls. Or, ﴿until the angels of death take them﴾. ﴿Or Allah ordains for them a way﴾, that is, He prescribes for them a specific ruling. The expression of it as "the way" (al-sabil) may be to indicate that it is an uncertain path. This is what Abu al-Su'ud said.

The Sunnah (the prophetic practice, as a second source of law after the Qur'an) has clarified that Allah, exalted is He, fulfilled His promise and made a way for them. This is what Imam Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan collections related from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "When revelation came down upon the Prophet ﷺ, he would be distressed by it and his face would darken. When it was lifted from him, he said: 'Take from me, take from me, [three times]. Allah has made a way for them: the previously married (thayyib) for the previously married, and the virgin for the virgin. The previously married receives one hundred lashes and stoning, and the virgin receives one hundred lashes and a year of exile.'" This is the wording of Imam Ahmad.

Likewise, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related it, and his wording from Ubadah is: "When revelation came down upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it was recognized in him. When the verse ﴿or Allah ordains for them a way﴾ [al-Nisa': 15] was revealed and the revelation was lifted, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Take your precaution. Allah has made a way for them: the virgin for the virgin, one hundred lashes and a year of exile; and the previously married for the previously married, one hundred lashes and stoning with stones.'"

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

﴿And the two of you who commit it among you, harm them. But if they repent and amend, then leave them alone. Indeed, Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful.﴾ [16]

﴿Wallatani﴾ is read with the nun lightly stressed or heavily stressed. ﴿Ya'tiyanaha﴾ means "the immorality." ﴿Minkum﴾ means "from among the men." ﴿Fa-adhuhuma﴾ means "harm them by reviling and reproaching them, so that they will feel remorse for what they did." ﴿Fa-in taba wa-aslaha﴾ means "if they repent and set right their deeds." ﴿Fa-a'ridu 'anhuma﴾ means "cease the harm and reproach, and overlook and conceal [their fault]," for repentance and reform prevent them from deserving blame and punishment. ﴿Inna Allaha kana tawwaban﴾ means "toward whoever repents." ﴿Rahiman﴾ means "of vast mercy." This clause is the reason given for the command to turn away.

* *

**Note:**

The ruling stated in these two verses has been abrogated (*mansukh*), partly by the Book and partly by the Sunnah.

Imam al-Shafi'i said in *al-Risalah* (in the chapters on the abrogating and the abrogated (*al-nasikh wa'l-mansukh*)), after mentioning these two verses [376]: "Then Allah abrogated the confinement and harm in His Book, saying: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterous man, flog each of them one hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2]."

[377] The Sunnah indicates that the hundred lashes apply to unmarried adulterers (*al-bikrayn*), according to the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit mentioned earlier.

He then said: [380] "The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ indicates that the hundred lashes apply to free unmarried persons, and are abrogated for married persons (*al-thayyibayn*), and that stoning applies to free married persons." He then said: [381] "Because the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'Take from me; Allah has indeed made a way for them: the virgin with the virgin, a hundred lashes and exile for a year; the married with the married, a hundred lashes and stoning' was the first revelation, and by it the confinement and harm of the two adulterers were abrogated."

[382] "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stoned Ma'iz and did not flog him, and commanded Unays to go to the wife of the man of Aslam, and if she confessed, to stone her, this indicated the abrogation of flogging for the two free married adulterers, and the stoning was established against them. For everything that comes after a first is, always, the last." End of quotation.

* *

His words ﴿fa-adhuhuma﴾ are a command to harm in an unrestricted way; He did not specify its form or its measure. The word *adha* (harm) is used frequently for speech, as in His words: ﴿They will not harm you except with some harm﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111]. Turning away (*i'rad*) means refraining from harming. The wrongdoer continues to be harmed, forbidden, and reproached until he repents. The least of this is to shun him, so he is not addressed with pleasant speech. This is a muhkam (clear, definitive) ruling: whoever commits immorality must be harmed by rebuke that deters him until he repents. This is not limited to a specific measure or form, except what is deterrent to him and calls toward the desired outcome, which is his repentance and reform. Allah linked it to repentance and reform. So when these are absent, the command to turn away cannot apply.

As for one who repents by abandoning the immorality but does not reform, the scholars disagreed: is the reform of deeds a condition of repentance? There are two opinions. This resembles His words: ﴿But if they repent and establish prayer and give zakat, then let them go on their way﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. He made releasing them conditional upon repentance and righteous action, even though once they utter the two testimonies of faith (*al-shahadatayn*), it becomes obligatory to refrain from them. Then, if they pray and pay zakat, well and good; otherwise they are punished for abandoning the act. This is because the Lawgiver, in the case of repentance, prescribed restraint from harming him, and the matter remains suspended until completion. Likewise, the one who repents from immorality.

This verse is among those used as evidence for discretionary punishment (*ta'zir*) by harm. And harm, though commonly used for speech, is not restricted to it. Compare His saying to one who spat toward the qiblah: "You have indeed harmed Allah and His Messenger." Likewise His saying concerning Fatimah: "What harms her harms me." And His saying to one who ate onions: "The angels are harmed by what harms the children of Adam."

Does confession of the sin count as part of repentance? If the sin is established by his own confession, and then he denies it and denies the witnesses, or if it is established by the testimony of witnesses, there is dispute. Ahmad stated that there is no repentance for one who denies. He cited the story of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: a group was brought to him who had been witnessed against for heresy (*zandaqah*); some of them confessed and repented, and he accepted their repentance, while a group denied and he killed them. The Prophet ﷺ also said to 'A'ishah: "When the servant confesses and then repents, Allah repents toward him." So whoever sinned secretly should repent secretly, as in the hadith: "Whoever has been afflicted with any of these filthy things should conceal himself." And in the Sahih: "All of my community will be forgiven except those who openly display [their sins]." Thus, when sin appears from a servant, repentance must also appear. With denial, repentance does not show, for the denier claims he did not sin. This is why the early generation (*al-salaf*) applied this ruling to one who openly displayed innovation or wickedness, for this is the most evident state of the misguided and this is the most evident state of those who earned wrath.

Among the harm is preventing him, when able, from leading prayer, from judgeship, from issuing religious rulings, from transmitting hadith, and from giving testimony. When unable, one does what he can.

He did not tie the harm to the testimony of four witnesses, and this is not a case of applying the unrestricted to the restricted (*haml al-mutlaq 'ala'l-muqayyad*). That would require the ruling to be identical, as in manumission (*al-i'tq*). When two things agree in genus but not species, such as the unrestricted hands in tayammum and their restriction to the elbows in wudu', they are not equated.

The Companions and the Successors did not apply the unrestricted to the restricted in His words: ﴿And your mothers-in-law, and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], and His words: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]. They said: the condition (consummation) applies only to stepdaughters. They said: leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified. The unspecified is the unrestricted, and that for which a condition is stated is the restricted. But they disagreed whether death is equivalent to consummation, in two opinions. This is because the ruling differs, and the restriction is not equivalent across the individual cases. The prohibition of one genus is not like the prohibition of another genus. Just as the prohibition of blood, carrion, and pork, being distinct genera, does not make restricting blood to "poured forth" (*masfuh*) require carrion and pork to be poured forth. Here the restriction is the stepdaughter's condition of her mother's consummation. Consummation with the mother cannot be replicated in the case of the wife of a father or the mother of a wife: for by consummating the wife, one consummates her herself; and in the case of the mother, by her daughter.

Likewise, the Muslims did not apply the unrestricted to the restricted in the requirement of testimony. Rather, when Allah mentioned in the verse on debts: ﴿Then a man and two women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in the matter of revocation: ﴿two men﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], they left each in its own situation. This is because the cause of the ruling differs: it is property in one case and sexual relations in the other.

Just as the establishment of the hadd (prescribed punishment) for immorality and for slander concerning it required four witnesses, the contracts of exchange and of marriage are not analogized to that. In the hadd for slander, three rulings are mentioned: eighty lashes, and the rejection of their testimony forever, ﴿And they are the wicked ones﴾ [al-Nur: 4]; ﴿except those who repent after that and reform, for Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nur: 5]. Repentance does not lift the flogging if the one slandered demands it, but it lifts the wickedness (*fisq*) without hesitation. Most scholars said it lifts the prohibition on accepting testimony.

If a person is widely known for immorality, he is not stoned, as in the Sahih: "If she bears a child resembling the husband, then he has lied about her; and if she bears one resembling the man who accused her, then he has spoken truly about her." She bore a child with the disliked attribute. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Were it not for the oaths, there would have been a matter between me and her." It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "This is the woman about whom he said: 'If I were to stone anyone without evidence, I would stone her.'" He said: "No. That is a woman who used to openly display evil in Islam." This shows that he does not stone anyone except with evidence, even if evil is manifest about the person. The hadith indicates that resemblance has an effect in that matter, but it was not evidence (*bayyinah*).

Likewise, it was established from him regarding a funeral, when they praised one of the dead with evil and the other with good, that he said: "You are the witnesses of Allah on earth." And in the Musnad from him that he said: "Soon you will know the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire." They said: "O Messenger of Allah! How is that?" He said: "By good praise and by bad praise." So he made general reputation (*al-istifadah*) a proof and evidence in these rulings, but did not make it a proof for stoning.

Likewise, the testimony of People of the Book against Muslims is accepted regarding a bequest during travel. And the testimony of children regarding wounds is accepted if they give it before separating, according to one of the two reports.

If a witness testifies that he saw a man and a woman, or a boy, under a blanket, or in a privy, or with their trousers undone, and in addition there is something that indicates this, such as the blanket being in a place outside its usual place, or one of them having a lamp he had lit, which he saw and extinguished, the extinguishing is evidence of their concealment of what they were doing. If what they were concealing was nothing but what the witness testified to, that is among the greatest clarity regarding what he testified to. This is a door of great benefit in religion.

It is among what the Law came with, which many judges and jurists have neglected, claiming that no one is punished except by witnesses who saw directly or by heard confession. This contradicts what the Sunnah has been transmitted with continuous attestation (*tawatur*), and the Sunnah of the rightly guided Caliphs, and what hearts created upon knowing good and rejecting evil affirm.

His words, exalted is He, also indicate this: ﴿O you who believe, if a wicked person brings you news, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6], and so on.

In it there are several indications:

First, He did not command verification upon the arrival of every wicked person with every news, for among news there is what is forbidden to verify, and among it there is what is permitted to leave unverified, and among news there is what includes punishment for some people, because He gave as reason the fear of striking people in ignorance (*jahalah*).

If every people struck by news were in this condition, the distinction between the just and the wicked would not occur. Rather, this is one indication that striking people by news of this kind did not produce distinction between the just and the wicked. Rather, this is one indication that striking people by the news of a single just person is not forbidden absolutely.

This indicates the acceptance of the testimony of a single just person in the category of punishments, for the occasion of the revelation of the verse indicates this. It was revealed upon a single report that a people had waged war through apostasy or breach of covenant.

It also indicates that whenever the report of a wicked person is accompanied by another indication that confirms its truth, the matter becomes clear, and the command to verify no longer applies. So striking that people becomes permissible. How, then, is the report of a just person, with another indication?

For this reason, the more correct of the two opinions is that such a thing constitutes a *lawth* (a presumptive indication) in the *qasamah* (oath procedure for homicide). When the oaths of the swearers are added, that becomes clear evidence (*bayyinah*) that makes the blood of the person sworn against permissible.

His words ﴿in ignorance﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6] make the feared outcome striking a people without knowledge. So when they are struck with knowledge, the fear is removed. This is the criterion that the Qur'an indicates, as He said: ﴿except one who testifies to the truth and they know﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 86], and He said: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra': 36].

Also, it was given as the reason the fear of regret, and that arises only from punishing one innocent of the sin, as in the Sunan: "Avert the hudud by doubts, for the Imam's error in pardoning is better than his error in punishing." When he has knowledge that he punished only a guilty person, he will not regret, and there is no error in it.

Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad mentioned that exile (*taghrib*) came in the Sunnah in two places: one is adultery, and the second is the effeminate man (*al-mukhannath*), as Umm Salamah narrated: "The Prophet ﷺ entered upon her while with her was an effeminate man, who was saying to 'Abd Allah, her brother: 'If Allah opens Ta'if to you tomorrow, I will guide you to the daughter of Ghaylan, for she advances with four and retreats with eight.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Expel them from your houses.'" It was narrated by both (al-Bukhari and Muslim). In another wording: "These should not enter upon you." In another narration: "I think this one knows such things. Let him not enter upon you after today." Ibn Jurayj said: "He is Hit."

[p. 4439] Another said: Hinb.
It was also said: Mati'.
Some have mentioned that they were three: Nahim, Hayt, and Mati'.
They were not accused of the great immorality (zina). Their effeminacy was only soft speech, dyeing of the hands and feet, and play like the play of women.

In the Sunan it is related that he ordered an effeminate man (mukhannath, a man who imitates women) to be exiled, and he was sent to al-Naqi'.

Since Allah commanded that these people be removed from the houses, it is known that the one who gives himself to men is worse than these, and he is more deserving of exile. The mukhannath brings corruption to both men and women, because when he imitates women, they may keep his company while he is a man, and so he corrupts them. And when a woman sees a man behaving effeminately, she may become masculine and keep company with both kinds. She may choose intercourse with women, just as he chooses intercourse with men.

As for his corrupting men, it is that he enables them to do the act with him, through their seeing him and their desire for him. When he goes out to a land and finds there someone who does the act with him, then his exile is according to its measure, in a place where no one else is with him. If his going out is feared, he is to be restricted, since this is the meaning of his exile.

For this reason the scholars disagreed about the exile of the muharib (one who wages war on society and spreads terror):
Is it to expel him such that he cannot take refuge in any land, or to imprison him, or is it according to what the ruler (imam) sees of this and that?
There are three narrations from Ahmad. The third is the most just and the best.
For his exile such that he cannot take refuge in any land is not possible, because the subjects are dispersed, differ, and differ in their aspirations. And his subsistence may not be provided, because he needs maintenance.

It is narrated that when Hinb complained of hunger, the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to enter Madinah from one Friday to the next, asking for what would sustain him. What the Shari'ah has brought of exile is a kind of hijrah (withdrawal), and it is not like the exile of the three who were left behind (in the Tabuk account), nor their boycott. For he (the Prophet) did not prevent them from the gatherings of people and from attending their assemblies for prayer and other things. That is because Allah created the children of Adam needing one another's help. Whoever's company is harmful deserves removal from among them, because it is harm without benefit. For when a child sees another child doing something, he imitates him.

Gathering with fornicators and sodomites contains the greatest corruption and harm to men, women, and children. Therefore the sodomite and the fornicator must be punished in a way that includes their reproach and distancing.

The essence of hijrah is abandoning evil deeds and their people. Likewise is the abandonment of those who call to innovations (bid'ah), the abandonment of the immoral (fussaq), and the abandonment of whoever [p. 4440] mixes with and helps all of these. Likewise, whoever abandons jihad, which is not beneficial for them without it, is punished by their abandoning him, because he did not address them in righteousness. Whoever does not abandon these people is one who has left what is commanded and committed what is forbidden.

This is abandoning what is commanded of association, and this is committing what is forbidden of it. Each of them is punished by what suits its offense.

What the Shari'ah has brought of commands, punishments, expiations, and other things, is done according to capacity. If the Muslim cannot fight all the polytheists, he fights those he is able to fight. If he cannot punish all the transgressors, he punishes those he is able to punish. If exile and imprisonment cannot be applied to all people, then exile and imprisonment are according to capacity. This is what is commanded, for a little good is better than leaving it altogether, and repelling part of the evil is better than leaving all of it.

Likewise the mutashabbihah (woman who imitates men) is imprisoned, as is her case when she commits fornication, for the kind of imprisonment is among what was prescribed for the kind of immorality.

Among what enters into this: 'Umar exiled Nasr ibn Hajjaj from Madinah to Basra when women were infatuated with him. He had first ordered that his hair be cut, to remove his captivating beauty, but when he saw that he was among the most beautiful of people in face, it grieved him, and he exiled him to Basra. This man did not commit a sin for which he was punished, but there were women who were tempted by him, so he ordered the removal of his captivating beauty. For his moving from his homeland is something that weakens his resolve and body, and he knows that he is being punished.

This is from the category of separating those who are feared to fall into immorality and infatuation before it occurs, and it is not from the category of punishment.

'Umar used to exile for wine-drinking to Khaybar, as an increase in the punishment of its drinker.

Among the strongest things that stir up immorality is the recitation of poetry by those in whose hearts is a disease of passionate love and love of immoralities. And if the heart is in a state (of corruption), it causes disease in it, as some of the salaf said:
Singing is the incantation (ruqyah) of fornication.
The ruqyah of the snake is that by which the snake is drawn out of its hole. The ruqyah of the eye and of the fever, and the ruqyah of fornication, meaning that it calls to it and draws out of a man the evil matter, just as wine is the mother of evil things.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Singing produces hypocrisy in the heart, as water produces herbs.

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And incite whoever you can among them with your voice, and urge against them your horsemen and your footmen﴾ [al-Isra: 64]. Inciting them with his voice occurs through singing, as whoever among the salaf said, and through other sounds like wailing and the like. These sounds necessitate the agitation of corrupt hearts and souls toward that, and cause their swift movement and turbulence, until Satan continues to play with these people more than children play with a ball. The soul is in constant motion. If it becomes still, it is by the permission of Allah; otherwise it is always moving. Some have likened it to a ball on a smooth surface, which never stops rolling on it.

In a hadith traced to the Prophet: "The heart is more changeable than a cooking pot when it boils vigorously." And in another hadith: "The likeness of the heart is the likeness of a feather in a desert, which the wind turns over."

In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar: "The oath of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was: 'No, by the Turner of hearts.'" In Muslim, from him, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "O Turner of hearts, turn our hearts to Your obedience." In al-Tirmidhi: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say often: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." It was said: O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you and in what you have brought; do you fear for us? He said: "Yes. The hearts are between two of the fingers of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He turns them however He wills."

End of the words of Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him.

Note: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: Regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each of them﴾ [al-Nur: 2], it is obligatory to apply the hadd (prescribed punishment) to the fornicator and the fornicatress, and that it is one hundred lashes, that is, for the unmarried, as the Sunnah has clarified. Those who made the hundred lashes obligatory on the slave, the dhimmi, and the muhsan (married person), and then stoning, used its generality as evidence. Ahmad related from Ali that a muhsanah (married woman) was brought to him, and he flogged her on Thursday and stoned her on Friday, then said: "I flogged her by the Book of Allah and stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The Kharijites used the verse as evidence that the hadd for the muhsan is flogging without stoning, saying: "Because it is not in the Book of Allah." Abu Hanifa used it as evidence that there is no exile (taghrib), since it does not mention it. In the verse there is a refutation of whoever says that if a slave commits fornication with a free woman he is stoned, and with a slave woman he is flogged. And of whoever says that a sane woman is not subject to hadd if a insane man fornicates with her, or an adult woman if a boy fornicates with her, or the reverse.
