And of whoever says there is no hadd on one who fornicates with a woman of the enemy or a Muslim woman in the lands of war, or in the army of the rebels (ahl al-baghy), or with a Christian woman absolutely, or with the slave woman of his wife, or with a mahram, or with one who takes into herself the penis of a sleeper. Whoever made it obligatory on the coerced, on one who fornicates with the slave woman of his son, and on one who has intercourse with a dead woman, used its generality as evidence.

Ibn al-Faras said: From His words ﴿flog﴾ it is deduced that he is stripped of his clothing, because flogging requires direct contact with the body. From His words ﴿one hundred lashes﴾ it is deduced that it is not sufficient to strike with them all together in one blow, whether the person is healthy or sick. In His words, the Exalted: ﴿And let not compassion for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 2] is an exhortation to establishing the hudud and a prohibition against suspending them. It is not permissible for the imam or anyone else to pardon them, and in this there is a refutation of whoever permitted the master to pardon. Whoever said that the flogging for fornication is more severe than the flogging for slander and drinking used it as evidence. In His words, the Exalted: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2] etc., there is a recommendation that a gathering be present when she is flogged. The minimum is four, the number of witnesses to fornication. It was said ten, and it was said three, and it was said two.

End.

It was previously mentioned from Ibn Jarir that the particle "aw" (or) linguistically may apply to one, so it is to be noted. And His words, the Exalted:

[p. 1154]

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

﴿Repentance is only accepted by Allah from those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [17]

﴿Repentance is only accepted by Allah﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh point), brought to explain that Allah's acceptance of repentance is not absolute. This is indicated by His description of Himself as *Tawwab* (Ever-Relenting) and *Rahim* (Most Merciful). Rather, it is restricted by what the noble text itself will state.

The phrase ﴿al-tawba﴾ (repentance) is the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence), and ﴿for those who do evil﴾ is its *khabar* (predicate).

The phrase ﴿'ala Allah﴾ (from Allah) is connected to what the predicate is connected to, namely the sense of being established (*istiqrar*). The meaning of repentance being "upon Him" (*'alayhi*, i.e., His obligation) is that acceptance proceeds from Him, may He be exalted. The word ﴿'ala﴾ (upon) indicates certainty of realization, because of the prior promise, so that it is as though it were one of the things obligatory upon Him, glorified is He. By ﴿evil﴾ (*su'*) is meant disobedience, whether minor or major. So says Abu al-Su'ud.

The phrase ﴿bi-jahala﴾ (in ignorance) is connected to an omitted element that falls as a *hal* (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of ﴿ya'malun﴾ (they do). That is, they are engaged in it while being ignorant and foolish. Alternatively, it is connected to ﴿ya'malun﴾, with the *ba'* being causal, meaning that they do it because of ignorance. By *jahl* (ignorance) is meant foolishness, in committing what is not befitting for a rational person, not the lack of knowledge. For whoever does not know does not need to repent. Ignorance in this sense is a real usage found in the language of the Arabs, as in the verse:

*So we act in ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant.*

﴿then repent soon after﴾ means: from a near time. The apparent meaning of the verse is the condition that repentance occur immediately after the disobedience, without delay. By doing so, one attains the degree of its certain acceptance as a favour. For by postponing it and procrastinating, one enters the company of the persistent [p. 1155]. Thus the verse contains guidance to hasten to repentance after the sin, and to turn back to the Master immediately after it. The obligation of repentance being immediate is beyond doubt, for knowing that sins are destructive comes from faith itself, and faith is obligatory immediately. Its full treatment is in *al-Ihya'* (*Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din*, The Revival of the Religious Sciences, by al-Ghazali).

Having understood this, what many exegetes have mentioned, that the meaning of His words ﴿soon after﴾ is the time before the arrival of death, is far from the wording of the verse and its secret, which guides to it. I mean the urgency to repentance before the poisons of sins work upon the spirit of faith, seeking refuge in Allah, may He be exalted.

(If it is asked): From where is the acceptance of repentance before the arrival of death derived?

(We say): It is derived from the verse that follows it, and from the abundant hadiths on this, not from His words ﴿soon after﴾ in the way they interpreted it. This is because the second verse, His words ﴿Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says: "Indeed, I have repented now"﴾ [an-Nisa: 18], is explicit that the time of the death throes is the time when repentance is not accepted. Thus what lies beyond it remains within the scope of acceptance.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of a servant as long as he has not begun the death rattle (*gharghara*)."

Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi also narrated it, and al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib" (a good hadith, rare in its chain).

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: "Whoever repents a year before his death, it is accepted from him; whoever repents a day before his death, it is accepted from him; whoever repents an hour before his death, it is accepted from him."

(Ayyub said): So I said to him: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only said: ﴿Repentance is only accepted by Allah from those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after﴾." He said: "I am only relating to you what I heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Imam Ahmad, Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh narrated similarly.

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever repents before the sun rises from its west, Allah will accept his repentance."

al-Hakim narrated it as a raised (*marfu'*) report: "Whoever repents to Allah before he begins the death rattle, Allah accepts it from him."

Ibn Majah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud with a good chain: "The one who repents from a sin is like one who has no sin."

His words ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness﴾ mean: He accepts their repentance. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾.

**The interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:**

﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾ [18]

﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them﴾ at the moment of the death throes (*al-nizaʿ*), ﴿he says﴾ at the moment of witnessing what he is facing, ﴿"Indeed, I have repented now"﴾, so that does not benefit him, and it is not accepted from him. ﴿Nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾, so their regret and their repentance do not benefit them, because at the very moment of death they see the punishment.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Dharr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah accepts the repentance of His servant and forgives His servant as long as the *ḥijāb* has not descended." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! What is the *ḥijāb*?" He said: "That the soul dies while it is associating partners with Allah."

For this reason, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We have prepared (*aʿtadnā*)﴾, meaning: We have readied (*aʿdadnā*), ﴿for them a painful punishment.﴾

(p-١١٥٧) Allah's words: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ are a prohibition of what the people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic era) used to do to women by way of harm and oppression.

Al-Bukhari narrated, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "When a man died, his guardians had more right to his wife. If some of them wished, one of them would marry her; if they wished, they would give her in marriage; and if they wished, they would not give her in marriage. They had more right to her than her own family. So this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you﴾ to the end of the verse."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others also narrated it. The wording of Abu Dawud, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, is: "A man would inherit the wife of his relative and then restrain her until she died, or until she returned to him her dowry. So Allah prohibited that," i.e., He forbade it.

Al-Suyuti said: "In this there is evidence that a free person cannot be conceived as being owned, nor as falling under possession, and that in no way does a free person come under the category of property."

The reading of ﴿kurhan﴾ with a fatha and with a damma on the kaf are two readings, meaning either: while they are unwilling to that, or: compelled to it. The restriction by "unwillingness" does not indicate permissibility when it is absent, because singling out a thing by mention does not indicate the negation of what is other than it, as in His words: ﴿and do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31] [al-Isra': part of verse 31].

﴿And do not restrain them in order to take back part of what you have given them﴾ The address is to the husbands, as most exegetes hold.

Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, that the verse concerns a man who has a wife whom he dislikes keeping as a companion, and she has a dowry from him, so he harms her so that she will ransom herself with it.

Al-'adl (restraining) means confinement and constriction.

(p-١١٥٨) That is: it is not lawful for you to constrict them in order to take back part of what you have given them, i.e., of the dowry, by making them give you part of it under compulsion, so that you take it from them.

﴿unless they commit a clear immorality﴾ i.e., fornication (zina), as a group of the Companions and the Successors said. That is, if she commits zina, then you have the right to reclaim from her the dowry you gave her, and to press her until she relinquishes it to you, and to seek khul' (divorce by compensation) from her, as the Exalted said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 229], to the end of the verse.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others that the clear immorality is ill-conduct (nushuz) and disobedience. Ibn Jarir chose that it encompasses all of that: fornication, disobedience, ill-conduct, foul speech and other things. That is, all of this permits pressing her until she releases him from her right or part of it, and he separates from her.

Ibn Kathir said: "This is good, and Allah knows best."

Abu al-Su'ud said: "(mubayyinah) is in the form of the active participle from (bayyana), meaning 'making clear'. It has also been read in the passive form, and in the active form from (abana), meaning 'becoming clear', i.e., clearly ugly through ill-conduct, bad character, harming the husband and his family with foul and abusive speech. And this is supported by the reading of Ubayy: ﴿unless they commit indecency against you﴾." End of quotation.

In al-Iklil (al-Suyuti's work), it is said: "A group used the words ﴿some of what you have given them﴾ as evidence for prohibiting khul' in exchange for more than what he gave her." End of quotation.

Then the Exalted explained the right of companionship with wives in His words: ﴿And live with them﴾ i.e., keep company with them ﴿in kindness﴾ i.e., with fairness in action and graciousness in speech, so that you do not become the cause of their fornication by abandoning them, or the cause of their ill-conduct or bad character. In that case it is not lawful for you (to take back anything).

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: In the verse is the obligation of kindness, including fulfilling the dowry, maintenance, equitable distribution, gentleness in speech, and refraining from beating and harshness without wrongdoing.

Whoever holds that she is owed service when she is of those who do not serve themselves has used its generality as evidence.

﴿But if you dislike them﴾ i.e., you dislike the companionship with them, ﴿then perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah places in it much good﴾ i.e., perhaps He will place that good in them, by granting you from them a righteous child in which there is much good, and by granting you abundant reward in the Hereafter for spending on them and being good to them, contrary to natural inclination.

In al-Iklil, al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: "In this verse is the recommendation of keeping (a wife) in kindness even if it is against the desire of the soul, and in it is evidence that divorce is disliked."

Muslim narrated in his Sahih, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let not a believing man hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one trait in her, he will be pleased with another."

(Yafrak), with a fatha on the ya' and the ra', means: he hates.

A subtle point:

Abu al-Su'ud said: The mention of the first verb, despite its being dispensable, and the restriction of causation to the second, serve to extend its object (generalize), to convey that the ordering of abundant good from Allah, the Exalted, is not restricted to a disliked thing over another disliked thing, but is a divine custom operating universally, according to what wisdom requires; and that what we are discussing is one of its instances. And in it is an emphasis on urging non-separation and generalizing the guidance, which is not hidden.

A noble note on the recommendation regarding women and kindness to them:

This noble and comprehensive verse suffices in this matter, which is His words: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾

Ibn Kathir said: That is, make your words to them good, and beautify your actions and your appearance according to your ability, just as you like that from them, so do likewise with them, as the Exalted said: (p-١١٦٠) ﴿And they have rights similar to those of men over them, according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 228].

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of you is the best of you to his family, and I am the best of you to my family." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi from 'A'ishah, Ibn Majah from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Tabarani from Mu'awiyah.

He (ﷺ) said: "The best of you is the best of you to women." Narrated by al-Hakim from Ibn 'Abbas.

He (ﷺ) said: "The best of you is the best of you to his family, and I am the best of you to my family. Only a noble man honours women, and only a base man humiliates them." Narrated by Ibn 'Asakir, from Ali (peace be upon him).

On the authority of 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas (may Allah be pleased with him): that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) during the Farewell Pilgrimage say, after praising Allah, extolling Him, and admonishing and exhorting, then saying: "Beware! Treat women well, for they are prisoners with you; you possess nothing from them other than that, except that they commit a clear immorality. If they do so, then forsake them in their beds and strike them with a non-severe striking. If they obey you, then seek no way against them. Beware! You have a right over your wives, and your wives have a right over you. Your right over them is that they not let anyone you dislike tread upon your bedding, nor let anyone you dislike enter your houses. Beware! Their right over you is that you be good to them in their clothing and their food." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

His words (awan) mean: prisoners, plural of 'aniyah.

On the authority of Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the right of one's wife over him? (p-١١٦١) He said: 'That you feed her when you eat, clothe her when you are clothed, do not strike the face, do not revile her, and do not forsake her except within the house.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud.

On the authority of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no amusement except three: a man training his horse, his shooting with his bow and arrows, and his playing with his family.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud.

In another narration by him: "Everything a man amuses himself with is vain, except his training of his horse, his shooting from his bow, and his playing with his family."

Ibn Kathir said: It was among the character of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was pleasant in companionship, constantly cheerful, playful with his family, gentle with them, generous in spending on them, and would laugh with his wives. To the extent that he would race 'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with her), seeking to win her affection by that. She said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raced me and I outran him, and that was before I had become heavy with flesh. Then I raced him after I had become heavy with flesh, and he outran me, and he said: 'This is for that.'"

He (ﷺ) used to gather his wives every night in the house of the one with whom he was spending the night. Sometimes he would eat dinner with them, then each one would depart to her own dwelling. He would sleep with one of his wives under one covering, removing his upper garment from his shoulders and sleeping in his waist-wrap.

When he had prayed the 'Isha' prayer, he would enter his house and converse with his family briefly before sleeping, thereby being companionable with them (ﷺ). Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Certainly you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]. End of quotation.

(p-١١٦٢) Al-Ghazali said in al-Ihya', in (The Etiquettes of Companionship and What Occurs During the Continuance of Marriage): The second etiquette: good character with them and bearing harm from them, out of compassion for them due to the deficiency of their intellect. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And live with them in kindness﴾ and He said, in magnifying their right: ﴿And they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 21] [al-Nisa': part of verse 21]. And the Exalted said: ﴿and the companion by your side﴾ [al-Nisa': 36] [al-Nisa': part of verse 36]; it was said: this is the wife.

Then he said: Know that good character with her is not merely withholding harm from her, but bearing harm from her and forbearance at her recklessness and anger, following the example of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His wives used to answer him back in speech, and one of them would forsake him for a day until night. "The wife of 'Umar argued with 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he said: 'Do you argue with me?' She said: 'The wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) argue with him, and he is better than you.'"

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say to 'A'ishah: 'I know when you are pleased with me and when you are angry with me.' She said: I said: 'How do you know that?' He said: 'When you are pleased with me, you say: No, by the Lord of Muhammad! And when you are angry, you say: No, by the Lord of Abraham!' She said: I said: 'True, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah! I only forsake your name.'"

(p-١١٦٣) Then al-Ghazali said:

The third: to go beyond bearing harm to playfulness, jesting and sportiveness, for that is what comforts the hearts of women. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to joke with them and descend to the level of their intellects in their actions, to the extent that it is narrated "that he (ﷺ) raced 'A'ishah on foot; she outran him one day and he outran her on some other day, and he (ﷺ) said: 'This is for that.'"

Al-'Iraqi said: Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra, and Ibn Majah narrated it in the hadith of 'A'ishah with a sahih chain.

'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "I heard the voices of some people from Abyssinia and others, and they were playing on a day of festival. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Would you like to see their play?' I said: 'Yes.' So he sent for them and they came, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood between the two doors, placing his palm on the door, and I placed my head on his shoulder. They began playing and I was looking on, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept saying: 'Enough for you!' And I would say: 'Do not hurry' (twice or thrice). Then he said: 'O 'A'ishah! Enough for you!' I said: 'Yes.'"

In a narration of al-Bukhari she said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) shielding me with his cloak while I looked at the Abyssinians playing in the mosque, until I was the one who grew weary. So estimate the measure of a young girl, eager for amusement."

'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It is fitting for a man to be among his family like a child; when they seek what he has, he is found to be a man."

Luqman (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "It is fitting for the intelligent man to be among his family like a child, and when he is among the people he is found to be a man."

(p-١١٦٤) The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jabir: "Why not a virgin, you playing with her and she with you?" Narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

A Bedouin woman described her husband after he had died, saying: "By Allah! He was smiling when he entered, silent when he left, eating what he found, and not asking about what was missing." End of quotation, with adaptation.

Then the Exalted forbade taking anything of the dowry of women from one who wishes to separate from them, in His words: [the passage ends here]

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And if you desire to replace one spouse with another, and you have given one of them a great amount of wealth, do not take back anything from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾ [20]

﴿And if you desire to replace one spouse﴾, meaning: to marry a woman you desire, ﴿in place of a spouse﴾ you are averse to, by divorcing her. ﴿And you have given one of them﴾, meaning: one of the wives—the word "spouse" here is generic. ﴿A great amount of wealth﴾, meaning: much money as dower. ﴿Do not take back anything from it﴾, meaning: not even a little, let alone a lot. ﴿Would you take it by slander﴾, meaning: falsely. ﴿And manifest sin﴾, meaning: clear. The interrogative is for denunciation and reproach, meaning: would you take it while being slanderers and sinners?

(p-1165) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ [21]

﴿And how could you take it?﴾ This is a denunciation of taking it following a prior denunciation, and a repulsion from it after a repulsion, in the manner of wonder; that is, "By what means would you deem the dower lawful?"

﴿When you have gone in unto one another﴾, that is, have reached one another, ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾, that is, a firm and emphatically confirmed pledge, with extra emphasis, whereby its breaking becomes difficult, as a thick garment is difficult to tear.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The solemn covenant is the right of companionship and intimacy. Its description as "solemn" is for its strength and greatness. For they have said: "Companionship of twenty days is kinship; so what of that which has passed between the spouses of union and mingling?" End of quotation.

Al-Shihab al-Khafaji said: I say rather, they have said:

*"The companionship of a single day is a near kinship, and a bond that the discerning one recognizes."*

Or the solemn covenant is what Allah the Exalted has bound upon them concerning their affairs by His saying: ﴿Then retain them in kindness or release them with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], or the words of the guardian at the contract: "I have married you under what is in the Book of Allah: retaining with kindness or releasing with good treatment."

Note on several points:

The First: His saying: ﴿And you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ [al-Nisa': 20] is evidence for the permissibility of giving a large amount of wealth as dower.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, had forbidden its excess and then retracted that.

As Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu al-'Ajfa' al-Sulami who said: "I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say: Beware, do not exaggerate (p-1166) the dowers of women. Beware, do not exaggerate the dowers of women. For if it were a nobility in this world or piety before Allah, the most deserving of it would be the Prophet (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not give any of his wives a dower, nor was any of his daughters given a dower, more than twelve ounces. And a man is tried by the dower of his wife."

And he said once: "And a man may become heated over his wife's dower until it becomes enmity in his soul, and until he says: 'I have toiled for you the sweat of a waterskin.'" It was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, and al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sound hadith.

Abu Ya'la narrated from Masruq who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab mounted the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and then said: O people! What is this excess in the dowers of women? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions' dowers among themselves were four hundred dirhams or less than that. If excess in this were piety before Allah or nobility, you would not have preceded them in it. So I will certainly know that no man has increased a woman's dower beyond four hundred dirhams."

He said: Then he descended, and a woman of Quraysh confronted him and said: "O Commander of the Believers! You forbade the people to increase women's dowers beyond four hundred dirhams?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Have you not heard what Allah revealed in the Qur'an?" He said: "And which of that?" She said: "Have you not heard Allah say: ﴿And you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ [al-Nisa': 20], to the end of the verse?" He said: Then he said: "O Allah, forgive! Every person knows better than 'Umar." Then he returned and mounted the pulpit and said: "O people! I had forbidden you to increase women's dowers beyond four hundred dirhams; so whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes, let him do so."

Abu Ya'la said: And I think he said: "Whoever is content in his soul, let him do so." Its chain is good and strong, as Ibn Kathir said.

In *al-Hujjat al-Balighah* there is the following text: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not fix the dower at a limit that neither exceeds nor falls short, since customs in displaying concern differ, and desires have various degrees, and they have classes in haggling; so it is not possible to fix it upon them, just as the price of desirable things cannot be fixed at a specific limit. For this reason he said: "Seek even an iron ring." However, he prescribed for the dowers of his wives twelve ounces and a nash, that is, half. End of quotation.

(p-1167) Something has also been reported indicating recommendation to lighten it and disliking exaggeration in it.

Abu Dawud and al-Hakim narrated, and al-Hakim graded it sound, from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best dower is the easiest of it."

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: I have married a woman from the Ansar. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: Have you looked at her? For there is something in the eyes of the Ansar. He said: I have looked at her. He said: For how much did you marry her? He said: For four ounces. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: For four ounces? It is as if you are hewing silver from the side of this mountain; we do not have what we can give you, but perhaps we will send you on an expedition from which you may obtain something. So he sent a detachment to the Banu 'Abs, and sent that man among them."

The Second: Almighty Allah specifically mentioned the one who gave a heap of gold in the prohibition, as an alert from the higher to the lower; for if this, despite the great amount of wealth he expended on his wife, is forbidden from reclaiming a small, trifling thing (p-1168) from it in this manner, then one who gave only a trifle is forbidden from reclaiming it all the more.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿And you have given﴾ [al-Nisa': 20], and Allah knows best, is: "And you had given," since the intention of exchange, outwardly, occurs after the giving of the wealth and the settling of the marriage. Thus is it in al-Intisaf.

The Third: They agreed that the dower becomes firmly due by consummation, and differed regarding its becoming firmly due by mere seclusion (khalwa). The root of this is that "afda" (gone in) in His saying: ﴿when you have gone in unto one another﴾ may be taken as a metaphor for intercourse, following the Qur'anic manner of using metaphor for what is shameful to mention; and seclusion is not shameful to mention, so it does not need a metaphor, and it may be kept on its apparent meaning.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: Ifda' in reality means reaching the end, and from it: ﴿and they have gone in unto one another﴾, that is, reached and retired. This is so; and the metaphor is more eloquent and closer in this context. What favours it is that He, exalted is He, mentioned this in the context of wonder, saying: "And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another?" Wonder is only complete if this going-in was a strong cause of affection and love, and that is intercourse, not mere seclusion. So it is obligatory to take "ifda'" as referring to it. Al-Razi mentioned this from several aspects.

Then he said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how could you take it?﴾ is a word of wonder, that is: "For what reason and for what purpose would you do this? For she has given herself to you, made her very self your pleasure and enjoyment, and complete intimacy and perfect affection have arisen between you both. How, then, is it fitting for a sensible person to reclaim from her something he gave her by his own goodwill? This is not fitting for one who has sound nature and upright taste."

The Fourth: In *al-Iklil*: whoever prohibited khul' absolutely cited this verse, and said it abrogates the verse of al-Baqarah.

Others said: this verse is abrogated by that one.

Others said: there is neither abrogation nor abrogated, but rather it concerns taking without her good pleasure. End of quotation.

(p-1169) I say: The third view is the one to be preferred, because each of the two verses, that of al-Baqarah and this one, concerns a specific case known from the context of the noble arrangement. For His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿And if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon them for what she gives up for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] is explicit that if the wife dislikes her husband's form, or his character, or the deficiency of his religion, or fears sin by abandoning his right, she is permitted to ransom herself from him, and it becomes lawful for him to take the ransom from what he gave her, by His saying there: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take from what you have given them anything, except that both fear they will not keep within the limits of Allah. And if you fear...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], and so on.

The wisdom in the permissibility of taking is clear: it is to compensate the husband for what afflicts him of lowliness from her seeking khul' from him and her dominance over him then, and to recover what, if taken from him, would be in the form of the wronged, since he did not incline to separation nor desire it. So it is of Divine justice that he not be made to suffer both the loss of enjoyment and the loss of wealth.

As for this verse, it concerns another ruling, which is when he wishes to exchange his wife because his gaze has aspired to another, without her ransoming herself from him, or wanting to free herself from him. Then he begrudges what he gave her and regrets that she should keep it, while he does not desire her and she has no weight in his soul. So it is resolved that he should take nothing of what he gave her at all after consummation; for if taking were permitted to him then, it would be clear injustice, since it is taking without any fault on her part. Thus, leaving in her hand what he gave her is a compensation for the pain of his turning away from her and casting her off, out of mercy from Him, exalted is He, and justice in both matters.

So the one who holds abrogation has missed the secret of both rulings. Would that I knew what he says concerning the hadith narrated in al-Bukhari and others, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the wife of Thabit: "Will you return to him his garden?" She said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said to her husband: "Accept the garden and divorce her." (p-1170)

It cannot be said: perhaps the one who holds abrogation of khul' relied on His saying: ﴿And how could you take it?﴾, with what it contains of terrifying the taking and repelling from it, as we have mentioned. For we say: the indicators of abrogating or abrogated rulings are taken only from complete sentences in both sources; so they are not taken from a condition without its consequent, for example, or the reverse; nor from a subject without its predicate, or the reverse; nor from an emphasizing particle without what it emphasizes; and so on.

In our case, if the general prohibition of taking were taken from His saying: ﴿And how could you take it?﴾, the inference would be from the emphatic without considering what it emphasizes, and this is invalid; for His saying: ﴿And how?﴾ is a denunciation of what preceded, connected to it, and what comes before it is specific. And even if the one who holds abrogation claims that His saying: ﴿And if you desire to exchange one spouse for another﴾ [al-Nisa': 20] is general, covering the one who is divorced by khul' and the one whom divorce is intended for, we say: this is false and corrupt; for the case the verse addresses is his desire to separate from her from the outset, so it does not apply to the one who seeks khul', since exchange is not intended with another initiated by the husband. In sum, whoever reads the opening of the two verses as each being a ruling on its own, with no connection between them, has no basis for abrogation in them; and abrogation is not to be resorted to by personal opinion. Claims of abrogation in verses have multiplied among later scholars in this way without strong basis, rather based on what appears outwardly without careful reflection. So reflect on this.

In the Two Sahihs: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the pair who performed mutual curse, after they had finished cursing one another: "Allah knows that one of you is a liar; will any of you repent?" He said it three times. The man said: "O Messenger of Allah, what of my wealth?" (p-1171) meaning what he gave as dower. He said: "You have no wealth. If you were truthful, then it is for what you made lawful of her private part; and if you lied about her, then it is further from you than she is."

In the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others, from Busrah ibn Akthам: that he married a virgin secluded in her chamber, and then she was found pregnant from fornication. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him; so he decided for her the dower, separated them, ordered her to be lashed, and said: "The child is a slave for you, and the dower is in exchange for the private part."

Then Almighty Allah explained which women are forbidden to marry and which are not, and He, glorified is He, said:

(p-1172) The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an abomination and hatred and an evil way.﴾ [22]

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married﴾ through marriage (*nikah*, the contract of marriage) or ownership of the right hand (*milk al-yamin*, ownership of a slave-woman), even if they were not your mothers. ﴿Except what has already passed﴾, that is, other than what happened in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period), for it is pardoned for you, and you will not be held accountable for it. ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination﴾, that is, a very ugly deed, because it resembles marrying one's mothers. ﴿And hatred﴾, that is, detestation with Allah and with people of noble character. For this reason, the Arabs used to call this marriage "the marriage of hatred" (*nikah al-maqt*), and they called the man who married in this way "maqit" (a detested one). This was said by Ibn Sidah.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-maqt* is the most intense hatred. When they knew that this was called *al-maqt* in the Jahiliyyah, they were informed that it had always been reprehensible and detested. ﴿And an evil way﴾, that is, an evil path, since it involves violating the sanctity of the father.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated: "When Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, and he was among the righteous Ansar, his son Qays proposed to his wife. She said: 'I only consider you a son, and you are among the righteous of your people. But I will go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' So she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Indeed, Abu Qays has died.' He said: 'Good.' Then she said: 'Indeed, his son Qays has proposed to me, and he is among the righteous of his people, and I used to consider him a son. So what do you think?' He said to her: 'Return to your house.' Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married﴾ up to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid everything that is forbidden except the wife of the father and the combining of two sisters. So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed﴾ and ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ [An-Nisa': 23] [An-Nisa': part of verse 23]."

A subtle point:

Al-Razi said: The degrees of ugliness are three: ugliness in intellects, ugliness in revealed law, and ugliness in customs. So His saying, ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination﴾, indicates rational ugliness; His saying ﴿and hatred﴾ indicates legal ugliness; and His saying ﴿and an evil way﴾ indicates ugliness in convention and custom. When these aspects are all combined in something, it has reached the extreme of ugliness. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir said: Whoever engages in this after this has apostatized from his religion, so he is to be killed, and his property becomes spoils for the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*).

This is as narrated by Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan, through several chains, from al-Bara' ibn Azib, and in one narration from his paternal uncle, that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to a man who had married his father's wife after him, to kill him and take his property."

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers, and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage; but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame on you. And the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [23]

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ by lineage, that you marry them. This includes the grandmothers, from the father's or the mother's side. ﴿And your daughters﴾ by lineage. This includes the daughters of descendants, however far down. ﴿And your sisters﴾ from the mother, or from the father, or from both. ﴿And your paternal aunts﴾, that is, the sisters of your fathers and your grandfathers. ﴿And your maternal aunts﴾, that is, the sisters of your mothers and your grandmothers. ﴿And your brothers' daughters﴾ by lineage, in whatever manner they are related. ﴿And your sisters' daughters﴾ by lineage, in whatever manner they are related, and their children are included among the daughters. ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾. Al-Mahayimi said: "Because the milk is a part of her, and it has become a part of the nursling, so it is as if it were a part of her, and she resembles his origin (asl)," end of quote.

Two matters are considered regarding nursing:

The first: the amount by which this meaning is realized. The unrestricted ruling has been specified and its general statement explained in the Sunnah as five sucklings, based on the hadith of ʿĀ'isha in Muslim and others: "There was revealed in the Qur'an that ten known sucklings establish prohibition. Then they were abrogated (naskh) by five known sucklings. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died while they were still among what is recited of the Qur'an."

The second: that the nursing should occur at the beginning of the formation of the body and the shaping of the infant's form, and that is before weaning. Otherwise it is nourishment, in the same position as all other foods that occur after the shaping and the formation of the body, like a youth who eats bread.

From Umm Salama, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Nothing is prohibited by nursing except what ruptures the intestines and occurs before weaning." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, and also by al-Hakim.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no nursing except that which occurs within the two years." Al-Bayhaqi authenticated its being a statement of Ibn ʿAbbas (mawquf).

Al-Suyuti said in "al-Iklil": "Whoever prohibits by the general application of the verse has used it as evidence for the nursing of an adult," end of quote.

Permission for it has been transmitted for a need that arises. Muslim and others narrated from Zaynab bint Umm Salama, she said: "Umm Salama said to ʿĀ'isha: 'The youth who has reached maturity (al-ghulam al-ayfa') enters upon you, and I do not like him to enter upon me.' ʿĀ'isha said: 'Do you not have in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) an example?' And she said: 'The wife of Abu Hudhayfa said: "O Messenger of Allah! Salim enters upon me and he is a man, and Abu Hudhayfa has some feeling about him." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Suckle him until he may enter upon you."'" Al-Bukhari narrated something similar from the hadith of ʿĀ'isha too.

This hadith was narrated from the Companions by: the Mothers of the Believers, Sahla bint Suhayl, and Zaynab bint Umm Salama. A large group of the Followers (tabiʿun) narrated it, and then a great multitude narrated from them.

ʿAli, ʿĀ'isha, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, Ibn ʿUlayya, Dawud al-Zahiri, and Ibn Hazm went to this view, while the majority (al-jumhur) went to the opposite.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: "A group of the early generations (al-salaf) adopted this opinion, among them ʿĀ'isha, but most of the people of knowledge did not adopt it. They preferred over it the hadiths that set a time limit for nursing that establishes prohibition, namely before weaning, or in infancy, or within the two years, for several reasons:

The first: their number, and the singularity of the hadith of Salim.

The second: that all the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) other than ʿĀ'isha - may God be pleased with them - were on the side of prohibition.

The third: that it is more cautious.

The fourth: that the nursing of an adult does not produce flesh nor spread bone, so there is not realized through it the partial unity (al-ba'diyya) which is the cause of prohibition.

The fifth: that it is possible this was specific to Salim alone, and for this reason nothing of that came except in his story.

The sixth: 'That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon ʿĀ'isha and there was a man sitting with her, and that was difficult for him and he became angry. She said: "He is my milk-brother." He said: "Look to your milk-brothers, for the nursing is only from hunger (al-majāʿa)."' Agreed upon, and the wording is Muslim's."

As for the story of Salim, there is a way of understanding it: that this was a case of necessity, for Salim had been adopted by Abu Hudhayfa and raised by him, and there was no way for him to avoid entering upon his household. So when the need calls for something like this, the view upon it is among the matters in which ijtihad (independent reasoning) is permissible. Perhaps this way is the strongest of the ways, and our shaykh used to incline toward it," end of quote.

He means Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya, may God be pleased with them both.

﴿And your milk-sisters﴾. Al-Razi said: "He, exalted is He, specified in this verse the prohibition of mothers and sisters by way of nursing. However, the prohibition is not restricted to them, because He (ﷺ) said: 'What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by nursing.'

We knew that the matter is so by the indication of these verses. That is because when He, exalted is He, called the nursing woman a mother, and the nursing woman a sister, He drew attention to the fact that He placed nursing in the position of lineage. He, exalted is He, prohibited by means of lineage seven categories. Two of them are those connected by way of birth, namely mothers and daughters. Five of them are by way of brotherhood, namely sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brothers' daughters, and sisters' daughters. Then when He, exalted is He, after that began to address the situations of nursing, He mentioned from these two categories one example, as an indication for the rest. He mentioned from the category of birth-relation the mothers, and from the category of brotherhood-relation the sisters, and by mentioning these two examples from these two categories He drew attention to the fact that the situation in the matter of nursing is like that in lineage. Then He (ﷺ) confirmed this explanation by his clear statement: 'What is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by nursing.' So the clear hadith became in agreement with the implication of the verse, and this is a subtle explanation," end of quote.

A subtle point:

Some exegetes, at this point, dealt with jurisprudential branches whose only basis is analogies (aqyisa).

Al-Razi said: "Whoever speaks on the rulings of the Qur'an must mention only what he derives from the verse, and as for anything beyond that, it belongs only in books of jurisprudence (fiqh)."

﴿And your wives' mothers﴾, that is, the roots (usul) of your spouses. ﴿And your stepdaughters﴾ is the plural of rabiba, in the sense of marbuba (one who is raised). Al-Azhari said: "The rabiba of a man is the daughter of his wife from another (husband)," end of quote.

She was named that because he raises her generally, as he raises his own child.

﴿Under your guardianship﴾ is the plural of hajr (with the first letter either fathah or kasrah), that is, in your upbringing. It is said: "So-and-so is in the hajr of so-and-so" if he is in his upbringing. The reason for this metaphor is that everyone who raises a child seats him in his lap (hajr), so hajr became an expression for upbringing. The secret of their prohibition is that they then resemble daughters, though the resemblance is only realized if they are ﴿from your wives with whom you have consummated marriage﴾, because then they are the daughters of your spouses, like the daughters of one's own loins. Consummation (al-dukhul) with them is a metaphor for intercourse, as in their saying: "He built upon her" (bana ʿalayha), and "He drew the veil upon her" (darab ʿalayha al-hijab), that is, you made them enter the screen. The ba' (with) is for transitivity. ﴿But if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, there is no sin upon you in marrying their daughters if you have separated from them or they have died.

* *

Notes:

The first: Some of the early generations held that the condition of consummation in His words, exalted is He, ﴿with whom you have consummated marriage﴾ refers to both the mothers and the stepdaughters. So they said: neither the mother nor the daughter is prohibited merely by the contract with the other, until one consummates with her, based on His words: ﴿But if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿAli - may God be pleased with him - concerning a man who married a woman and divorced her before he had consummated with her: "May he marry her mother?" He said: "She is in the position of the stepdaughter."

It is also narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbas. Among the Shafiʿis, Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabuni adopted this view, as transmitted by al-Rafiʿi from al-ʿAbbadi. It is also narrated from Ibn Masʿud the like of it, then he retracted it. Muʿawiya hesitated on it, as narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from Bakr ibn Kinana, that his father married him to a woman in al-Ta'if. He said: "I did not have intercourse with her until my paternal uncle died leaving her mother, and her mother had much wealth. My father said: 'Do you want her mother?'" [He said:] "I asked Ibn ʿAbbas and informed him, and he said: 'Marry her mother.'" He said: "I asked Ibn ʿUmar and he said: 'Do not marry her.' I informed my father of what the two of them said, so he wrote to Muʿawiya, and he informed him of what they had said. Muʿawiya wrote: 'I do not make lawful what Allah has prohibited, nor prohibit what Allah has made lawful, and you and that matter; there are many women other than her.'" He did not forbid, nor did he permit me, so my father turned away from her mother and did not marry me to her.

The majority held that the mother is prohibited by the contract with the daughter, and the daughter is not prohibited except by consummation with the mother. They said: the condition applies only to the mothers of the stepdaughters.

It is narrated on this from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whatever man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her daughter; and if he has not consummated with her, then let him marry her daughter. And whatever man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her mother, whether he has consummated with her or not." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi.

The hadith scholar Ibn Kathir said: "This report is gharib (singular in its chain), and there is scrutiny in its isnad."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Some scholars made His words, ﴿with whom you have consummated marriage﴾, a qualifier of both the preceding and the following women, and this is not so, because a single qualifier does not apply to two qualified nouns with different governing particles. This is because the first women are in the genitive by the construction (idafa), and the second by 'from' (min). It is not permissible to say: 'I passed by your women and I fled from the beautiful women of Zayd,' with 'the beautiful ones' being an adjective for both these women and those women."

Al-Nasir said in "al-Insaf": "The well-known view of the majority is the generality of the prohibition of the mother of the wife, and the restriction of the prohibition of the stepdaughter to consummation with the mother, as is the apparent meaning of the verse. This distinction has a secret and a wisdom: the one who marries the daughter of a woman does not, after the contract and before consummation, avoid conversation between himself and her mother, and speech and intimate talk, so the need calls for immediately establishing the prohibition, to cut off his desire for the mother so that he treats her as one of the unmarriageable kin. This is not so for the one who contracts with the mother, for he is far from addressing her daughter before consummation with the mother; so the need does not call for hastening the spread of the prohibition. But if consummation with the mother occurs, the cause of frequent mixing with the stepdaughter has been established, and then the need calls for spreading the prohibition between them. And God knows best."

The second: Whoever did not prohibit marriage to an adult stepdaughter, one whom he did not raise, has used as evidence His words, ﴿under your guardianship﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, who said: "I had a wife who died, and she had borne me children, and I was grieved over her. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib - may God be pleased with him - met me and said: 'What is wrong with you?' I said: 'The woman has died.' He said: 'Does she have a daughter?' I said: 'Yes, and she is in al-Ta'if.' He said: 'Was she under your guardianship?' I said: 'No, she is in al-Ta'if.' He said: 'Then marry her.' I said: 'Then where is the word of God: ﴿and your stepdaughters under your guardianship﴾?' He said: 'She was not under your guardianship; that applies only when she is under your guardianship.'"

Ibn Kathir said: "Its isnad is strong and established to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, on the condition of Muslim." To this view went the Imam Dawud ibn ʿAli al-Zahiri and his companions, and Abu al-Qasim al-Rafiʿi related it from Malik, may God have mercy on him, and Ibn Hazm adopted it.

The majority of scholars hold that the prohibition on stepdaughters (rabā'ib) applies absolutely, whether or not they are in the man's guardianship (hijr). They said: the address in His words ﴿those who are in your guardianship﴾ comes in the form of what is usual and typical, since the normal situation of such girls is to be in the custody of their mothers under the protection of their husbands. It does not intend that they are in fact in this state.

The benefit of describing them thus is to strengthen and complete the reason for the prohibition. It is also the point behind naming them "stepdaughters" (rabā'ib) rather than "daughters of the women." Their being close to being raised by these men, and the honour of being moved about in their laps and under their protection and upbringing, strengthens the closeness and resemblance between them and the men's own children. This calls for treating them as their daughters, rather than restricting the prohibition to their actually being in their laps. So Abu al-Su'ud established this.

In al-Intisaf: the benefit of describing them thus is to single out the most extreme form of what is forbidden for the prohibition. The prohibition on marrying a stepdaughter whose mother he has consummated marriage with is general, covering all cases, whether she is in the husband's guardianship or living far away in distant lands. But his marrying her while she is in his guardianship is the most abhorrent form, and the natural disposition recoils from it most. So she was singled out for the prohibition, to help the natural disposition submit to the rulings of the religion. Then this becomes a training and a gradual step toward regarding everything forbidden in all its forms as abhorrent. And God knows best.

In the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim): "Umm Habibah, may God be pleased with her, said: O Messenger of God, marry my sister, the daughter of Abu Sufyan." (In a wording of Muslim: "Izzah, daughter of Abu Sufyan.") He said: "Would you like that?" She said: "Yes. I am not going to be exclusive to you, and I love that my sister should share in the good with me." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That is not lawful for me." I said: "We have heard that you intend to marry the daughter of Abu Salamah." He said: "The daughter of Umm Salamah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Even if she were not my stepdaughter in my guardianship, she would still not be lawful for me. She is the daughter of my brother through nursing. Thuwaybah nursed me and Abu Salamah. So do not offer me your daughters or your sisters." (In a narration of al-Bukhari: "Even if I had not married Umm Salamah, she would not be lawful for me.")

Ibn Kathir said: He made the basis for the prohibition the mere fact of his marrying Umm Salamah, and ruled the prohibition on that basis alone.

Third: It is well known that the meaning of "consummated" (dakhaltum) in His words ﴿you have consummated with them﴾ is the euphemistic sense, which is intercourse, because this is the style of the Mighty Book in its parallels, in eloquence and courtesy. Accordingly Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it so. The indication of the verse is then explicit that the prohibition is conditional upon intercourse, and it does not cover anything else, such as touching, kissing, or looking at her private parts. Whoever established the prohibition of stepdaughters by this consideration noted that the meaning of "entering" (dukhul) is broader than intercourse, since it is said: "He entered with her" when he kept her and brought her into the house.

In Fath al-Bayan: What should be relied upon in such a disagreement is to examine the meaning of "entering" either in the Shariah or in the language. If it is specific to intercourse, there is no basis for attaching anything else to it, such as touching, looking, or other things. If its meaning is broader than intercourse, such that it applies to what involves some kind of enjoyment, then that is the basis of the prohibition. End of quote.

In Sharh al-Qamus by al-Zabidi: "He entered with his wife" is a euphemism for intercourse, and its use has become predominant for lawful sexual relations. A woman who has been entered with is "consummated." I say: from this comes "al-dukhlah," for the night of the wedding procession. End of quote.

﴿And the wives of your sons﴾, that is, the women with whom your descendants have had intercourse by marriage or by right of possession (ownership of a slave-woman). It is the plural of "halilah" (a wife), so called because she is lawful to her husband.

His words ﴿who are from your loins﴾ exclude adopted sons (al-ad'iya') whom they used to adopt in the Jahiliyyah, as He said: ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need of her, We married her to you, so that there would be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37], and He said: ﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4].

So the purpose of the restriction is to make lawful the wife of an adopted son, refuting the claims of the Jahiliyyah. It is not to make lawful the wife of a son through nursing or the wives of grandsons. It is as if it were said: unlike those you have adopted, whose wives are lawful for you to marry.

﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾ is in the place of the nominative, coordinated with what precedes it of forbidden women. That is: it is forbidden for you to combine two sisters in intercourse, by marriage or by right of possession, whether by blood or by nursing, because of the severing of kinship that it involves. ﴿Except what has already happened﴾ in the Jahiliyyah, for that is pardoned. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾: this is a reason for what the exception implies.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿And all married women, except those whom your right hands possess. This is the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful for you are all others beyond these, that you seek them with your wealth, chaste, not unlawful sexual intercourse. So those with whom you have enjoyed [marriage] – give them their compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree to after the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [24]

﴿And the married women﴾ – i.e., forbidden to you are women who are already married ﴿from among the women﴾, whether free or slave, Muslim or not, lest the waters become mixed and lineage be lost. ﴿Except those whom your right hands possess﴾ – i.e., those among the captives who had husbands in the land of disbelief. They are lawful for the warriors of the Muslims, even if they were married, because being taken captive removes their marriage and makes them lawful after their istibra' (the waiting period to establish that the womb is clear).

Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (p. 1183), al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We captured female captives from the captives of Awtas, and they had husbands. We disliked having intercourse with them while they had husbands, so we asked the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And the married women from among the women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾, so we considered their private parts lawful [to us]."

* *

Note:
Those who said that the transfer of ownership by sale, inheritance or otherwise ends the marriage relied on the general wording of the verse.
From Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When a slave-woman is sold while she has a husband, her master has more right to her body." And from him: "The sale of a slave-woman is her divorce."
This was also narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas – may Allah be pleased with them – who said: "Her sale is her divorce."
Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The divorce of a slave-woman is six [ways]: her sale is her divorce, her manumission is her divorce, her gifting is her divorce, her release is her divorce, and her husband's divorce is her divorce."
Thus I read it in the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir. It is not hidden that the enumerated items are five, and perhaps the sixth is the sale of her husband, since he said after that: "'Awf narrated from al-Hasan: the sale of a slave-woman is her divorce, and the sale of him [her husband] is her divorce." This is the view of these figures from the early generation, and their proof is the generality of the exception in His words: ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾.

The majority hold that the sale of a slave-woman is not a divorce for her. They argued with the hadith of Barirah, recorded in the Two Sahihs and elsewhere, for 'Aishah, the Mother of the Believers, bought her and freed her, yet her marriage to her husband Mughith was not annulled. Rather, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave her the choice between ending it and remaining, and she chose to end it. Her story is well known. Had the sale of a slave-woman been a divorce for her, she would not have been given a choice, and her being given a choice indicates that the intended meaning of the verse is only the captives. In summary, the majority restricted the verse to the cause for which it was revealed.

Al-Razi said: "This amounts to specifying the general wording of the Qur'an by a single report (khabar al-wahid), which is accepted and acted upon in other places, such as the minimum value for theft (nisab al-sariqa). The note that follows adds to this, so reflect on it."

Benefit:
The readers agreed on pronouncing the ṣād in "al-muḥṣanāt" here with a fatḥah. It is read with fatḥah and kasrah in other places, and both are well known. The fatḥah means they were made chaste (uḥṣinna) by husbands or by Islam; the kasrah means they guarded their private parts or their husbands (aḥṣanna). The word is derived from iḥṣān, which means prevention.

﴿Kitāb Allāh﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid), meaning: Allah prescribed the prohibition of these ones as a decree, and made it an obligation. So adhere to His Book and do not go beyond its limits and legislation. ﴿And lawful for you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿forbidden to you﴾ [4:23]. ﴿Beyond these﴾ refers to the prohibited women already mentioned, i.e., marriage to all others is lawful for you.

﴿That you seek﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: it is lawful for you with the intention of seeking; or it is a substitute for "mā," meaning: the seeking of women ﴿with your wealth﴾, i.e., by spending it on their dowries. ﴿Chaste﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "tabtaghū." Iḥṣān is chastity and guarding oneself from falling into what brings blame. ﴿Not unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ means not committing adultery. Sifāh is fornication and debauchery, from safḥ, meaning pouring, because the adulterer has no aim but to pour out his seed. In the Jahiliyyah, when a man proposed to a woman he would say, "Marry me," and when he wanted fornication he would say, "Fornicate with me."

Al-Zajjaj said: Musāfaḥah is a woman remaining with a man in immorality without a valid marriage.

* *

Note:
His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And lawful for you are all others beyond these﴾, are general but specified by other prohibitions established by other evidences. Among them is what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ prohibiting combining a woman with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt. Al-Tirmidhi transmitted the prohibition of this from the entire body of scholars, and said: "We know of no disagreement among them on this."

Among them is marrying a woman in 'iddah. Among them is that whoever has a free wife may not marry a slave-woman. Among them is that one able to marry a free woman may not marry a slave-woman. Among them is that whoever has four wives may not marry a fifth. Among them is the woman who was subject to li'an, who is forbidden to her husband who performed li'an forever. Thus the verse is among those revealed in general, and the Sunnah and passages of revelation indicate that it is specified by other things.

Imam al-Shafi'i said in al-Risalah:
[244] Allah, Mighty and Majestic, obligated people to follow His revelation and the sunan of His Messenger ﷺ.
[245] He said in His Book: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves who recites to them Your verses and teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [2:129].
[250] And He said: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you did not know. And ever has the bounty of Allah been upon you tremendous﴾ [4:113].
in verses similar to these.
Al-Shafi'i said:
[252] Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the Book, which is the Qur'an, and mentioned wisdom. I heard from scholars of the Qur'an whom I trust saying: "Wisdom is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."
[253] This resembles what he said, and Allah knows best.
[254] Because the Qur'an was mentioned and wisdom was followed by it, and Allah, whose praise is great, mentioned His favour upon His creation by teaching them the Book and wisdom. So it is not permissible – and Allah knows best – to say that wisdom here means anything but the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
[255] This is because it is paired with the Book of Allah, and Allah made obedience to His Messenger ﷺ obligatory and made it binding on people to follow his command. So it is not permissible to call any statement "obligatory" except the Book of Allah and then the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.
[256] For what we have described: Allah, whose praise is great, made belief in His Messenger ﷺ paired with belief in Him.
(p. 1186) [257] And the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, explaining from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the meaning of what He intended, is evidence concerning His specific and general [rulings]. Then He paired wisdom with His Book, following it with it, and He did not give this to any of His creation other than His Messenger ﷺ. End of quote.

We cited this only to refute the claim of the Khawarij that the hadith "A woman shall not be married to her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt," narrated in the Two Sahihs and elsewhere, is a single report (khabar wahid), and that specifying the general wording of the Qur'an by a single report is not permissible, as al-Razi transmitted from them. He also cited from their arguments that the general wording of the Book is definitive in text and apparent in meaning, while a single report is probable in text and apparent in meaning; so a single report is weaker than the general wording of the Qur'an, and preferring it over that would be giving precedence to the weaker over the stronger, which is impermissible. End of quote.

Al-Razi here expanded considerably in answering their doubt. Among what was said: the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal or maternal aunt is derived from His words: ﴿And that you combine two sisters [in marriage]﴾ [4:23].

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: This ruling is shared by combining a woman with her paternal aunt and similar relatives, for the basis of the prohibition of combining two sisters is that it leads to severing what Allah commanded to be joined, and this is realized in combining these as well, and even more so. For the paternal aunt and maternal aunt are in the position of a mother. So his words ﷺ, "A woman shall not be married..." etc., are an explanation of the interpretation, not an abrogation. It was also said that it is a well-known report by which it is permissible to add to the Book.

He also said: Perhaps the choice of the demonstrative (meaning in His words "beyond these"), which addresses the described and titled referent, rather than a pronoun which addresses only the essence, is to remind of the title in each of them on which the ruling of prohibition turns, so that the sharing of those with a similar meaning in the prohibition is understood by way of implication, for the prohibition of combining a woman with her paternal aunt, or with her maternal aunt, is not by way of explicit expression but by way of implication, as previously explained. End of quote.

(p. 1187) In "Tanwir al-Iqtibas": It is said regarding His words: ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾ that it means that you seek with your wealth their marriage, which is mut'ah, and it has now been abrogated. End of quote. The discussion of this will come.

﴿So those with whom you have enjoyed﴾ – i.e., whoever of the wives you have enjoyed through intercourse ﴿give them﴾ – give them ﴿their compensation﴾, their dowries in full ﴿as an obligation﴾ – i.e., it is an obligation from Allah upon you that you give the dowry in full. And ﴿as an obligation﴾ is a circumstantial clause from "compensation," meaning obligated; or a qualifier of an omitted infinitive, meaning a giving that is obligated; or an emphatic infinitive, meaning that this was made obligatory as an obligation.

﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾ – no sin upon you ﴿for what you mutually agree to﴾ – you and they ﴿after the obligation﴾ – i.e., by reducing it, or part of it, or adding to it by mutual consent. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ in the rulings He legislated.

* *

Note:
A group interpreted the verse as referring to mut'ah marriage. They said: the meaning of His words ﴿So those with whom you have enjoyed﴾ is: whoever you have had intercourse with from among those you married in mut'ah marriage, then give them their compensation.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: The generality of this verse has been used as evidence for mut'ah marriage, and there is no doubt that it was legislated at the beginning of Islam, then abrogated afterward.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions the view that it is permissible out of necessity, and this is a narration from Imam Ahmad. Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi used to read: "So those with whom you have enjoyed [marriage] for a specified term – give them their compensation as an obligation." Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning mut'ah marriage.

But the majority are of a different view, and the foundation is what is established in the Two Sahihs from the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade mut'ah marriage and the flesh of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar."

In Sahih Muslim, from al-Rabi' ibn Sabrah al-Juhani, from his father: "He was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: 'O people! I had permitted you to enjoy women, but Allah has forbidden that until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever has any of them, let him release her, and do not take back anything of what you have given them.'" End of quote.

In al-Kashshaf: It is said this verse was revealed concerning mut'ah. A man would marry a woman for a set time, a night or two nights or a week, with or without witnesses, and would satisfy his desire from her, then release her. It was called mut'ah because of his enjoyment of her, or because of his providing her with benefit through what he gives her.

Al-Khafaji said: It is narrated that Sa'id ibn Jubayr said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Do you know what you did with your fatwa?" He said: "It travelled with the caravans and poetry was composed about it, such as the saying:
"I said to the shaykh when his sitting dragged on: O friend, do you want the fatwa of Ibn 'Abbas?
Do you want the license of a tender-limbed young woman who will be your lodging until the people depart?"
He said: "We belong to Allah and to Him we return! By Allah, I did not issue fatwa for this, nor did I permit anything except what Allah permitted: carrion and blood."

Imam Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah be pleased with him, said in Zad al-Ma'ad, in discussing the jurisprudence of the Conquest campaign, the following text: Among what occurred in this campaign was the permission of mut'ah with women, then the Prophet ﷺ prohibited it before he left Makkah. Scholars differ on the time at which mut'ah was prohibited, with four views:
The first: that it was on the day of Khaybar. This is the view of a group of scholars, including al-Shafi'i and others.

The second [view]: that it was in the year of the Conquest of Mecca. This is the view of Ibn 'Uyaynah and a group [of scholars].

The third: that it was in the year of Hunayn. In reality this is the second view, because the expedition of Hunayn is connected to the Conquest.

The fourth: that it was in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. This is a mistake made by some of the narrators. The mistake travelled from the Conquest of Mecca to the Farewell Pilgrimage. The travelling of a mistake from one time to another, from one place to another, and from one event to another frequently happens to the memorisers of hadith (huffaz) and to those below them. (p-1189)

The correct view is that mut'ah (temporary marriage) was prohibited only in the year of the Conquest. This is because it is established in Sahih Muslim that "they enjoyed it in the year of the Conquest with the Prophet (ﷺ), with his permission." If the prohibition had been at the time of Khaybar, it would have meant abrogation (naskh) twice, and nothing like this is known in the Shari'ah at all, nor does anything like it occur in it.

Also: there were no Muslim women in Khaybar; they were Jewish women. The permissibility of marrying women of the People of the Book had not yet been established. It was only permitted afterwards in Surah al-Ma'idah, in His saying: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them, and [lawful for you are] chaste women from among the believers and chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] [al-Ma'idah: 5]. This is connected to His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] [al-Ma'idah: 3], and to His saying: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] [al-Ma'idah: 3]. This was at the very end of the matter, after the Farewell Pilgrimage, or during it. So the permissibility of marrying women of the People of the Book was not established from Khaybar. Nor did the Muslims have a desire to enjoy the women of their enemy before the Conquest. After the Conquest, those among them who were taken captive were enslaved and became slave-women of the Muslims. (p-1190)

If it is said: what will you do with what is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the mut'ah of women on the day of Khaybar, and [forbade] eating the flesh of domestic donkeys"? This is authentic and explicit.

It is said: this hadith has been transmitted in two wordings. This is one of them.

The second: [the report] restricting itself to the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of marriage by mut'ah, and of the flesh of domestic donkeys, on the day of Khaybar. This is the transmission of Ibn 'Uyaynah from al-Zuhri.

Qasim ibn Asbagh said: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: meaning that he forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys at the time of Khaybar, not marriage by mut'ah. Abu 'Umar mentioned this in al-Tamhid, then said: most people hold this view. [End of quotation.]

So some narrators imagined that "on the day of Khaybar" was a time-frame for the prohibition of both, and so they narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade mut'ah and domestic donkeys at the time of Khaybar." Some abbreviated part of the hadith and said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade mut'ah at the time of Khaybar," thereby committing a clear error.

If it is said: what is the benefit of combining the two prohibitions if they did not occur at the same time? And what is the connection between mut'ah and the prohibition of donkeys?

It is said: this hadith was transmitted by Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), using it as evidence against his cousin 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas on both matters, for he used to permit mut'ah and the flesh of donkeys. Ali debated him on both matters, transmitted both prohibitions to him, restricted the prohibition of donkeys to the time of Khaybar, and stated the prohibition of mut'ah without restriction, saying: "You are a wanderer (ta'ih). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade mut'ah and forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar," as Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said, and as most people hold. So he related both matters, using them as evidence against him, not restricting them to the day of Khaybar. ... And Allah is the Granter of success.

However, there is another consideration here: did He prohibit it as the prohibition of grave immoralities which are never permitted under any circumstances, or did He prohibit it when one is free from need of it, while permitting it for the one under compulsion? This is what Ibn 'Abbas considered, and he said: "I permitted it for the one under compulsion, like carrion and blood." When those who went to excess in it did so, and did not stop at necessity, Ibn 'Abbas refrained from issuing rulings permitting it, and retracted. Ibn Mas'ud used to hold that it was permitted, and he would recite: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87] [al-Ma'idah: 87]. (p-1191)

In the two Sahihs, on his authority, he said: "We used to go on campaign with the Prophet (ﷺ) and had no women with us. We said: shall we not castrate ourselves? He forbade us from that, then he permitted us afterwards to marry a woman for a garment." Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87] [al-Ma'idah: 87].

Ibn Mas'ud's recitation of the verse immediately after this hadith admits of two meanings:

One: a refutation of those who prohibit it, and that if it were not among the good things, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not have permitted it.

The second: that he intended the end of this verse, which is a refutation of those who permit it absolutely, and that such a person is a transgressor.
