This is because He, Exalted is He, is the Creator, the Provider, the Bestower of blessings, the One who bestows grace upon His creation at all times and in all conditions. Thus He alone deserves that they affirm His oneness and not associate anything with Him, neither the clear nor the hidden shirk, nor (associating with Him) the self and its desires, or what leads to them of wealth and status. And this worship is Allah's right upon us.

As in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim), from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "O Mu'adh, do you know what is the right of Allah upon the servants, and what is the right of the servants upon Allah?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The right of Allah upon the servants is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him, and the right of the servants upon Allah is that He does not punish one who does not associate anything with Him."

Then, Glorified is He, enjoined goodness to parents immediately after mentioning what pertains to the rights of Allah, Mighty and Majestic — which are the most emphatic and greatest of rights — as an alert to the exalted status of parents, by placing them in the same string with it, by His words: ﴿and be good to parents﴾. The occurrences of this arrangement are many in the Mighty Revelation, such as His words: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqman: 14], and ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and goodness to parents﴾ [Al-Isra: 23], meaning: be good to them with a goodness that fulfills the right of their upbringing, for their thankfulness calls to thankfulness to Allah, Who brings one near to Him, along with what it contains of maintaining ties with the closest of relatives, which necessitates Allah's maintaining ties with one, and His severing ties with one who severs them. Then He joined to goodness to the two of them, goodness to relatives, men and women, by His words: ﴿and to relatives﴾, that is, the kin. And there has come in a sound hadith, from Salman ibn Amir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Charity to a needy person is (simply) charity, but to one of the kin it is two: charity and maintaining ties." Narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim and Ibn Majah.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and orphans﴾, because they have lost the one who would manage their affairs and spend upon them. So Allah commanded goodness to them and tenderness toward them, as a descent of His mercy, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And the needy﴾, who are the destitute who do not find what suffices them. So Allah, Glorified is He, commanded helping them with what completes their sufficiency and removes their necessity. ﴿And the neighbor who is near of kin﴾, that is, the one whose neighborhood is close, or the one who, in addition to neighborhood, has nearness and connection by lineage or religion. ﴿And the neighbor who is a stranger﴾, that is, the one whose neighborhood is distant, or the non-relative. Nawf al-Bikali said: "The neighbor who is near of kin" means the Muslim neighbor, and "the neighbor who is a stranger" means the Jew and the Christian.

Many hadiths have come concerning the injunction regarding the neighbor, among them the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Jibril kept enjoining me about the neighbor until I thought he would make him an heir." Related by both Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn Umar.

Among them is what Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The best of companions with Allah is the best of them to his companion, and the best of neighbors with Allah is the best of them to his neighbor."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A man should not be satisfied (with eating) while his neighbor is hungry."

Ibn Kathir said: Ahmad alone narrated it.

And from al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his companions: What do you say about fornication? They said: Allah and His Messenger have forbidden it, so it is forbidden until the Day of Resurrection. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said to his companions: For a man to commit fornication with ten women is easier for him than to commit it with his neighbor's wife."

He said: Then he said: "What do you say about theft?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger have forbidden it, so it is forbidden." He said: "For a man to steal from ten houses is easier for him than to steal from his neighbor."

Ibn Kathir said: Ahmad alone narrated it, and it has a witness in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I asked - or was asked - the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: Which sin is greatest with Allah? He said: That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you. I said: Then which? He said: Then that you kill your child lest it eat with you. I said: Then which? He said: That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbor."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, from a man of the Ansar, who said: "I went out from my family intending to visit the Prophet ﷺ, and there I found him standing, and a man with him facing him, so I thought they had some need. He said: The Ansari said: By Allah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood so long that I began to feel pity for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ because of the length of his standing. When he turned away, I said: O Messenger of Allah! That man stood with you so long that I began to feel pity for you because of the length of your standing. He said: Did you see him? I said: Yes. He said: Do you know who he is? I said: No. He said: That was Jibril, peace be upon him, who kept enjoining me about the neighbor until I thought he would make him an heir. Then he said: Indeed, if you had greeted him with salam, he would have returned your salam."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "A man from al-Awali came while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Jibril, peace be upon him, were praying where prayer is offered over the deceased. When he turned away, the man said: O Messenger of Allah, who is this man whom I saw praying with you? He said: Did you see him? He said: Yes. He said: You have seen much good. This is Jibril, who kept enjoining me about the neighbor until I saw that he would make him an heir."

Ibn Kathir said: He alone narrated it from this route, and it is a witness to the previous one.

Al-Bazzar narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Neighbors are of three kinds: a neighbor who has one right, and he is the lowest of neighbors in right; a neighbor who has two rights; and a neighbor who has three rights, and he is the most excellent of neighbors in right.

As for the neighbor who has one right: he is a polytheist neighbor who has no kinship, having the right of neighborhood.

As for the neighbor who has two rights: he is a Muslim neighbor who has the right of Islam and the right of neighborhood.

As for the one who has three rights: he is a Muslim neighbor who is a kinsman, having the right of neighborhood, the right of Islam, and the right of kinship."

Imam Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated "from Aisha that she asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: I have two neighbors; to which of them shall I send a gift? He said: To the one whose door is nearer to you."

Imam Muslim narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Abu Dharr, when you cook a broth, increase its water, and take care of your neighbors."

In another narration he said: "When you cook broth, increase its water, then look at a household among your neighbors and give them some of it in a good manner."

The two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, he does not believe! By Allah, he does not believe! By Allah, he does not believe!" It was said: "Who, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one whose neighbor is not safe from his harms."

In Muslim's version: "The one who enters Paradise is not one whose neighbor is safe from his harms."

Al-Bawa'iq: the evils and harms.

And both of them narrated from him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O women of the Muslims, let no neighbor belittle her neighbor's gift, even if it were the trotter of a sheep." Its meaning: even if she gives her a sheep's trotter, which is the burnt hoof, and he meant by it a trivial thing.

And both of them narrated from him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him not harm his neighbor."

And His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and the companion at your side﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the righteous companion.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: It is your companion at home and your fellow traveler on a journey, that is, he is like the neighbor.

Al-Zamakhshari clarified it with his words: It is the one who accompanies you by being at your side, whether as a companion on a journey, or as an adjoining neighbor, or as a partner in learning a knowledge or a craft, or as one sitting beside you in a gathering or a mosque or otherwise, from the least companionship that has joined between you and him. So you must observe that right and not forget it, and make it a means to goodness.

It was narrated from Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, who both said: It is the woman, that is, because she is with you and lies down at your side.

﴿And the wayfarer﴾, that is, the son of the road: the stranger traveler who has been cut off from his land and family, who wishes to return to his land and does not find what would suffice him. He is attributed to the road (al-sabil), which is the path, because he passes over it and is connected to it; or it is one who wishes to go to a land other than his own for a necessary matter.

Ibn Arafah said: He is the guest who has been cut off, who is given an amount sufficient for him to reach his homeland.

Ibn Barri said: He is the one whom the road has brought. Thus in "Taj al-Arus," but the early exegetes and lexicographers did not mention "the beggar" (al-sa'il) in the meaning of ibn al-sabil, because it came as a follower of ibn al-sabil in al-Baqarah, in His words: ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 177] - to His words: ﴿and the wayfarer and the beggars﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 177].

Some of them said concerning "ibn al-sabil":

"And one attributed to what he did not beget, thus Allah has revealed in the Book."

﴿And those whom your right hands possess﴾, meaning the slaves, for they are weak in means, captives in the hands of people, like the needy, owning nothing. It is established from Ali, peace be upon him, that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept enjoining his Ummah during his final illness, saying: The prayer, the prayer; fear Allah regarding what your right hands possess." Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah, and this is the wording of Abu Dawud.

Imam Ahmad narrated from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What you feed yourself is charity for you, what you feed your child is charity for you, what you feed your wife is charity for you, and what you feed your servant is charity for you." Also narrated by al-Nasa'i.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: Its chain is sound, and praise be to Allah.

And from Abdullah ibn Amr, that he said to a steward of his: "Have you given the slaves their sustenance? He said: No. He said: Go and give it to them, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: It is enough sin for a person that he withholds from those whose sustenance he owns." Narrated by Muslim.

And from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The slave has his food and his clothing, and he should not be charged with work beyond what he can bear." Also narrated by Muslim.

And from him also, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When one of you is served food by his servant, if he does not seat him with himself, let him give him a morsel or two morsels, or a mouthful or two mouthfuls, for he has taken care of its heat and its preparation." Agreed upon by both, and the wording is that of al-Bukhari.

And from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "They are your brothers, your servants; Allah has placed them under your hands. Whoever has his brother under his hand, let him feed him from what he eats, and clothe him from what he wears, and do not burden them with what overpowers them; but if you burden them, then help them." Agreed upon by both.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love one who is self-deluded﴾, that is, one who is arrogant, disdaining goodness toward those who have been commanded to be dutiful to him, ﴿and boastful﴾, one who counts his virtues out of pride. Allah, Exalted is He, singled out these two attributes for blame in this place, because the self-deluded is the arrogant, and whoever is arrogant rarely undertakes the observance of rights. Then He added to it the blame of the boastful, lest one undertake the observance of these rights for the sake of showing off and reputation, but rather solely for the command of Allah, Exalted is He.

Abu Dawud and al-Hakim narrated with a sound chain from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Raja' al-Harawi, who said: You will not find one of bad ownership (al-mulkah) except that you will find him self-deluded and boastful, and he recited: ﴿and those whom your right hands possess﴾ - the verse; nor will you find one who is undutiful except that you will find him a tyrant and wretched, and he recited: ﴿And dutiful to my mother, and He did not make me a tyrant, wretched﴾ [Maryam: 32]. And there has come, in condemnation of vanity and boasting, what is well known.

**Interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess on people and conceal what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ [37]

﴿Those who are stingy﴾ means: with their wealth, refusing to spend it in what Allah commanded them in the preceding verses. ﴿And enjoin stinginess on people﴾ means: they do not become a cause of goodness, but are stingy with what is in their own hands and with what is in the hands of others. (p. 1235) So they command others to be stingy with it, out of hatred for generosity wherever it is found. Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "More stingy than one who begrudges others the gain of their own gift." The poet said:

*Indeed a man whose hands are withheld from a man who gains a gift from another's hand is truly a miser.*

Al-Zamakhshari, after relating what has preceded, said: "We have seen among those afflicted with the disease of stinginess that when he hears that someone has given generously to someone else, he is startled by it, loosens his sitting posture, becomes agitated, his eyes roll in his head as though his baggage had been plundered and his storehouse broken into, out of distress at that and grief at its existence." End of quotation.

﴿And conceal what Allah has bestowed upon them﴾ means: of wealth and riches, so they give the impression of poverty despite wealth, of indigence despite affluence, and of incapacity despite ability. ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that whoever has this trait is a disbeliever in the blessing of Allah, exalted is He, and whoever is a disbeliever in the blessing of Allah, exalted is He, will have a punishment that humiliates him, just as he humiliated the blessing through stinginess and concealment.

**Benefit:**

Abu al-Baqa' said: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those who are stingy﴾ there are two possibilities:

The first: it is in the accusative as a *badal* (substitution, apposition) for the "man" in His saying ﴿whoever is self-conceited and boastful﴾ [4:36]. It is pluralized according to the meaning of "man." It may also be taken as dependent on His saying ﴿self-conceited and boastful﴾ [4:36], which is the predicate of ﴿kāna﴾ [4:36], and it is pluralized according to meaning as well; or it may be by supposing an implied "I condemn."

The second: it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being "hateful ones," indicated by what preceded in His saying "does not love." It may also be that the predicate is "punished ones," corresponding to His saying ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

(p. 1236) It may also be that the estimate is: "They are those who." It may also be a subject, with ﴿And those who spend﴾ [4:38] coordinated with it, and the predicate being ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong﴾ [4:40], meaning: He does not wrong them.

Then he said: *al-bukhl* and *al-bakhl* are two dialects, and both have been recited. There are two other dialects: *al-bukhul* (with a dammah on the kh and the b) and *al-bakhl* (with a fatha on the b and a sukun on the kh). End of quotation.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever has Satan as a companion, then evil is such a companion.﴾ [38]

﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people﴾ means: intending that creation see them, heedless of the Creator, exalted is He, and blind to Him, so that it may be said, "How generous and how bountiful they are." ﴿And do not believe in Allah﴾ means: the One to Whom worship is drawn near, Who alone is sought, and Whose pleasure is pursued by agreement. ﴿Nor in the Last Day﴾, which is the Day of Recompense. ﴿And whoever has Satan as a companion﴾ meaning a helper in this world, ﴿then evil is such a companion﴾, so the companion and associate Satan is wretched, because he leads him astray from guidance and veils him from the truth. The discourse here has connected with the mention of Satan only as a rebuke to them for obeying him.

The meaning is: whoever's deeds are according to what Satan has embellished for him, then wretched is his deed. It is also permissible that this be a warning to them, that Satan will be joined with them in the Fire.

A subtle point (latifah):

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And those who﴾, are either a conjunction upon "those who withhold" (in the previous verse) or upon "for the disbelievers." They are associated with them in blame and threat because stinginess is like spending for show: they are equal in ugliness and in drawing censure and reproach. It is also permissible that the conjunction is based on treating a difference of attribute as a difference of essence, as in the saying:

"To the lordly king and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded press."

(p-1237) Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, indicated by His words, ﴿and whoever has﴾, etc., meaning: "then their companion is Satan." It was omitted to signal that it is evident and needs no explicit statement. Or the estimate is: their charity is not accepted, because their showing off indicates that they prefer creation over Allah, and their being seen over His reward.

Muslim has related, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: I am the most independent of partners from association. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his association."

Ibn Abi Hatim related, concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The scholars of the Children of Israel used to withhold what they had of knowledge, so Allah revealed: ﴿Those who withhold﴾ [an-Nisa: 37], the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated, through the chain of Ibn Ishaq, from Ibn Abbas, that some Jews (p-1238) used to come to men of the Ansar, advising them sincerely, and would say: "Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you in its loss, and do not hasten in spending, for you do not know what will happen." So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Those who withhold﴾ [an-Nisa: 37], the verse.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And what would it be upon them if they had believed in God and the Last Day and spent from what God has provided them? And God is ever Knowing of them.﴾ [39]

﴿And what would it be upon them if they had believed in God﴾, that is, they would not have preferred the creation over Him. ﴿And the Last Day﴾, with its resurrection and recompense, so that they would not have preferred their glory and their worldly wealth over His reward. ﴿And spent from what God has provided them﴾, what God has given them of wealth, that is, seeking His pleasure and the reward of the Hereafter.

The great scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: The reason it is not stated explicitly is that the preceding detail is relied upon, and the mention of belief in God and the Last Day suffices, for it necessarily implies that spending is for the sake of seeking His Face, exalted is He, and seeking His reward absolutely. That is, "What is upon them?" or "What consequence and harm is upon them in believing in God and spending in His way?!" This is a rebuke to them for their ignorance of the place of benefit and for holding a belief about a thing contrary to what it is, and an exhortation to answer the inquiry; perhaps it will lead them to knowledge of the great benefits and beautiful gains in it. It is also a reminder that one who is called to a matter that carries no harm should respond to it out of caution, so how much more when it contains countless benefits. The mention of belief in these two is given precedence for its importance in itself, and because spending is not considered valid without it. As for the precedence of "their spending to be seen by people" over their non-belief in these two, although the latter is more abominable than the former, it is for the sake of observing the connection between their spending of that kind and what precedes it, namely their stinginess and their enjoining people to it. End of quote.

﴿And God is ever Knowing of them﴾: a warning to them of punishment.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone even] the weight of an atom, and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾ [4:40]

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] the weight of an atom﴾, meaning: He does not deprive anyone of the reward of his deed, nor does He increase his punishment by even the amount of an atom (dharrah), which is (the small ant) according to the linguists.

Tha'lab said: "A hundred dharrah together weigh the same as a grain of barley." This is an example which Allah, Exalted is He, has struck for the smallest of things, and the meaning is: Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, does not wrong anyone in anything, be it little or much, so the statement came concerning the smallest thing people know. ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾, meaning: and if it is a good deed of the weight of an atom, He multiplies its reward. The pronoun referring to "weight" is feminine because "good" (khayr) is feminine, or because it is attached to "atom" (dharrah). ﴿And gives﴾, meaning: in addition to the multiplication, ﴿from Himself﴾, that which befits His greatness, in the manner of bounty, ﴿a great reward﴾, meaning: a lavish gift.

Many hadiths have been transmitted concerning the meaning of this verse. Among them is what is in the two Sahihs from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the long hadith of the intercession (p-1240). In it: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say: Return, and whoever you find in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith, bring him out of the Fire." And in another wording: "Lowest, lowest, lowest, the weight of an atom of faith, bring him out of the Fire." So they bring out a great multitude. Then Abu Sa'id said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the weight of an atom﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning this verse that he said: "As for the polytheist, the punishment will be lightened for him on the Day of Resurrection—meaning: by his good deed—and he will never come out of the Fire."

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: "It may be cited as evidence for this the sound hadith: 'Al-Abbas said: O Messenger of Allah! Did you benefit Abu Talib with anything, for he used to protect you and become angry for your sake? He said: Yes, he is in a shallow part of the Fire, and had it not been for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire.'"

This may be specific to Abu Talib, excluding the disbelievers, based on what Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his Musnad from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not wrong a believer in a good deed; he is rewarded for it with provision in this world and is recompensed for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed with it in this world, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, he will have no good deed." End of quote.

Muslim also narrated it from Anas, likewise traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the wording: "Indeed, Allah does not wrong a believer in a good deed; he is given for it in this world and is recompensed for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed with the good deeds he did for Allah in this world, until, when he arrives at the Hereafter, he has no good deed for which he will be recompensed."

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 4, Verse 41:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words:

﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [4:41]

﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ Al-Razi said: The connection (wajh al-nazm) of the verses is that God, the Exalted, made clear that in the Hereafter no one will be wronged, and that He rewards the doer of good for his good and increases it beyond the measure of his due. So God, the Exalted, explained in this verse that this takes place through the testimony of the Messengers, whom God made the proof against creation, so that the proof against the evildoer would be more emphatic, his rebuke greater, his regret more intense, and the joy of those who accepted that from the Messenger and openly obeyed would be greater. This is also a warning to the disbelievers, concerning whom God said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight﴾ [4:40], and a promise to the obedient, concerning whom God said: ﴿And if it is a good deed, He doubles it﴾ [4:40].

Then he said: It is a habit of the Arabs that they say, about something they expect, "How will you be when such-and-such happens?" or "When so-and-so does such-and-such," or "When the time of such-and-such comes?" So the meaning of this statement is: How will you see the Day of Resurrection when God calls to witness over every nation its Messenger, and calls you to witness over these people, meaning your people addressed by the Qur'an, whom you saw and whose conditions you knew? Then the people of every age bear witness over others whose conditions they saw. On this understanding, Jesus, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them﴾ [5:117]. A parallel to this verse is His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And [mention] the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves﴾ [16:89], and so on.

(The Two Shaykhs, al-Bukhari and Muslim, and others, related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to me: "Recite to me." I said: "O Messenger of God, should I recite to you when it was revealed to you?" He said: "Yes, indeed I love to hear it from someone other than myself." So I recited Surah al-Nisa' until I reached this verse: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ He said: "That is enough for now." And his eyes were shedding tears.

Muslim added: "a witness over them as long as I was among them," or he said, "as long as I was among them" — one of its narrators was uncertain.)

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning this verse that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A witness over them while I am among them; but when You took me up, You were the watcher over them."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 42:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them. And they will not conceal from Allah any statement.﴾ [4:42]

﴿On that Day﴾ i.e., the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Will wish﴾ i.e., will desire. ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ in Allah ﴿and disobeyed the Messenger﴾ by not responding to him. ﴿That the earth were leveled over them﴾ i.e., that they were destroyed within it, meaning that they were buried, so that the earth would be leveled over them as it is leveled over the dead, for that is better for them than the humiliation that will befall them because of their disgraceful deeds. This is like His saying: ﴿The Day when a man will look upon what his hands have sent forth﴾ [78:40], and so on. Thus ﴿tusawwa﴾ (is leveled) means: is made level, and the bāʾ (with) is for accompaniment, i.e., the earth would be leveled while being joined with them.

It was also said: the bāʾ is in the sense of ʿalā (over). In al-Durr al-Masun: "The leveling of the earth with them, or over them, is their burial, or that it splits open and swallows them, or that they remain dust in their original state without being created again."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ is coordinated with (yawaddu) [i.e., "will wish"], meaning: and they will acknowledge all that they did, being unable to conceal it, because their limbs will bear witness against them. Or the wāw is for the circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning: they will wish to be buried in the earth while their state is that they do not conceal from Allah any statement, and they do not deny Him by their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [6:23], as Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak that Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq came to Ibn ʿAbbas and said: "O Ibn ʿAbbas! The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾, and His saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [6:23]?" Ibn ʿAbbas said to him: "I think you have left your companions and said: 'The ambiguous verses of the Qur'an have been thrown at Ibn ʿAbbas. So when you return to them, inform them that Allah, exalted is He, will gather the people on the Day of Resurrection in one plain. The polytheists will say: 'Indeed Allah does not accept anything from anyone except from those who affirmed His oneness.' So they will say: 'Come, let us deny.' Then He will ask them, and they will say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [6:23]." He said: "Then He will seal their mouths and make their limbs speak, and their limbs will bear witness against them that they were polytheists. At that point they will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah any statement."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr something similar to what preceded. Imam Ahmad relied on it in his book "al-Radd ʿala al-Jahmiyya," in the chapter (The explanation of what the heretics (zanadiqa) went astray in regarding the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an), and he cited the like of what was previously mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas. Then he said: "This is the explanation of what the zanadiqa doubted."

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 43 (part 1 of 5):

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:
﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor [while you are] in a state of janabah, except for passing through [a place], until you have washed. And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have contacted women and find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe over your faces and hands. Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ [4:43]

﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾ This verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine, concerning a group who used to drink it and then pray. That is: it is part of the requirement of your faith to feel shame before Allah, and from shame before Him is that you do not stand up for prayer while you are intoxicated, not knowing what you are addressing Him with. So shame before Allah necessitates this. The opening of the address with the two particles of calling and alerting (the particle of vocative and the alerting particle) is for the sake of emphasis in urging them to act upon the requirement of the prohibition. And directing the prohibition to "approaching" prayer, although what is meant is the prohibition of establishing it, is for the sake of emphasis in this matter.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This prohibition was before the prohibition of wine, as indicated by the hadith we mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾ [2:219] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 219], the verse, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it to Umar, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfying explanation regarding wine." When this verse was revealed, he recited it to him, and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfying explanation regarding wine." So they would not drink wine at the times of the prayers, until He revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, indeed wine and gambling and stone altars and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful﴾ [5:90] to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [5:91] [al-Ma'idah: 90-91]. Then Umar said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

The wording of Abu Dawud, from Umar ibn al-Khattab in the account of the prohibition of wine, he mentioned the hadith, and in it: "The verse concerning women was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾ (p-1245) so the caller of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whenever the prayer was established, would call out: 'Let no intoxicated person approach the prayer.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'd (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: Four verses were revealed concerning me. A man from the Ansar prepared food and invited some of the Muhajirun and some of the Ansar. We ate and drank until we became intoxicated, then we boasted, and a man raised the jawbone of a camel and struck with it the nose of Sa'd, so Sa'd's nose was injured. This was before the prohibition of wine, and then there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ the verse.

The hadith in full is in Muslim, and the people of the Sunan narrated it except Ibn Majah.

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he and Abd al-Rahman and another man drank wine, and Abd al-Rahman led them in prayer and recited: ﴿Say, O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1] and garbled it, so there was revealed: ﴿Do not approach﴾ the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf prepared food for us, invited us, and gave us wine to drink. The wine took effect on us, and the prayer time came, so they put forward someone, and he recited: "Say, O disbelievers. I do not worship what you worship. And we do not worship what you worship" — so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer﴾ the verse. Likewise al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: Hasan sahih.

﴿Nor [while you are] in a state of janabah﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾, since the clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The janub is one who has been affected by janabah; the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural are alike in this, because it is a noun that functions in the manner of the verbal noun, which is ijnab.

﴿except for passing through﴾ meaning: passing without staying. ﴿until you have washed﴾ from janabah: that is, do not approach the place of prayer, which is the mosque, while you are in janabah, except as those passing through it, either to leave it or to enter it.

(p-1246) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the meaning of the verse, he said: Do not enter the mosque while you are in janabah, except as those passing through; he said: you pass through it, and do not sit. Then he narrated it from many of the Companions, among them Ibn Mas'ud, and a group of the Successors.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Layth, who said: Yazid ibn Abi Habib narrated to us concerning the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿nor [while you are] in a state of janabah, except for passing through﴾: men from the mosque would be afflicted with janabah, and there was no water with them, so they wanted water and could find no passage except through the mosque, so Allah revealed: ﴿nor [while you are] in a state of janabah, except for passing through﴾.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: What Yazid ibn Abi Habib said is confirmed by what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Block every opening into the mosque except the opening of Abu Bakr."

He ﷺ said this at the end of his life, knowing that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) would assume the affair after him and would need to enter the mosque often for important matters concerning what benefits the Muslims. So he commanded that the doors opening onto the mosque be closed (p-1247) except his door (may Allah be pleased with him). As for the one who narrated "except the door of Ali," as occurs in some of the Sunan, it is an error, and the correct version is what is established in the Sahih.

From this interpretation many of the imams argued that it is forbidden for a junub to remain in the mosque, while passing through it is permitted.

There is another interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except for passing through﴾, namely that what is meant by it is travelers: that is, do not approach prayer in janabah in any state except while you are travelers. Thus this exception is evidence that it is permissible for a junub to proceed to prayer when unable to find water.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ali, regarding this verse, he said: One who is afflicted with janabah should not approach prayer except if he is a traveler and finds no water, then he prays until he finds water. Then he narrated it through another chain from Ali. And it was also narrated from a group of the early generation (salaf) that it refers to travel.

Ibn Kathir said: This view is supported by the hadith narrated by Ahmad and the people of the Sunan (p-1248) from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Clean earth is the purifier of the Muslim, even if he does not find water for ten years; when you find water, then let it touch your skin, for that is better for you." In this interpretation the word "prayer" remains on its literal meaning in both conjoined clauses, whereas in the preceding interpretation the prayer in the second clause is taken to mean its places.

The author of Fath al-Bayan said: In sum, the first state, namely His saying, ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾, strengthens keeping prayer on its literal meaning without supposing an omitted noun; the earlier occasion of revelation strengthens this; and His saying ﴿except for passing through﴾ strengthens the supposition of an omitted noun, that is: do not approach the places of prayer. It is possible to say that some of the qualifiers of the prohibition (namely "do not approach," which is His saying ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾) indicate that the meaning of prayer is its literal meaning, and some qualifiers of the prohibition (namely His saying ﴿except for passing through﴾) indicate that what is meant is the places of prayer. There is no barrier to considering each of them together with its qualifier that indicates it, and this would be like two prohibitions, each restricted by a qualifier: "Do not approach the prayer which consists of the remembrances and the pillars while you are intoxicated," and "Do not approach the places of prayer in a state of janabah except while passing through the mosque from one side to the other." The most that can be said about this is that it is from combining the literal and the figurative, which is permissible under a well-known interpretation.

Ibn Jarir said (after relating the two interpretations): The more preferable of the two interpretations for this is the interpretation of the one who interpreted: (p-1249) ﴿nor [while you are] in a state of janabah, except for passing through﴾ except as those crossing a path through it. That is because He has already stated the ruling for the traveler who lacks water while in janabah in His saying: ﴿And if you are ill or on a journey﴾ to its end. So it was known from that that if His saying ﴿nor [while you are] in a state of janabah, except for passing through, until you have washed﴾ meant the traveler, there would have been no understood purpose in repeating mention of him in His saying ﴿And if you are ill or on a journey﴾, and its ruling had already been mentioned before that.

Since that is so, the interpretation of the verse is: O you who have believed, do not approach the mosques for prayer while praying in them, while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying; and do not approach them either in janabah until you have washed, except as those passing through.

He said: "Passing through a way" (al-'abir al-sabil) is one who crosses it, passing and traversing. It is said of it: I crossed this road, so I cross it, crossing (abr) and crossing (ubur). From it is said: so-and-so crossed the river when he traversed and passed it; and from it is said of a camel strong for journeys: she is 'ubr asfar and 'abr asfar, because of her strength for journeys.

Ibn Kathir said: What Ibn Jarir supported is the view of the majority and is the apparent meaning of the verse. It seems that He, exalted is He, prohibited engaging in prayer in a deficient state that contradicts its purpose, and entering its place in a deficient state, which is janabah, which keeps one away from prayer and from its place as well. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until you have washed﴾ is the limit of the prohibition of approaching prayer and its places while in janabah. The meaning: do not approach them while in janabah until you have washed, except while passing along the way.

* *

Remarks:

The first: In the verse is the prohibition of prayer for the intoxicated person during his intoxication until he becomes sober, and the invalidity of it and the invalidity of following him in prayer; and for one in janabah until he washes, except if he is a traveler, in which case tayammum is permitted for him.

The second: One who held that the divorce of an intoxicated person does not take effect used the verse as evidence, since if he does not know what he is saying, intention is absent. This was the view of Uthman ibn Affan, Ibn Abbas, Tawus, Ata', al-Qasim, Rabi'ah, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, (p-1250) Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and al-Muzani, and al-Tahawi chose it. The matter is discussed at length in Zad al-Ma'ad of the Imam Ibn al-Qayyim.

The third: In the verse there is evidence that the apostasy of an intoxicated person is not apostasy, since reciting Surah al-Kafirun with the negatives dropped is disbelief, yet he was not judged to be a disbeliever until he was addressed by the name of faith; and the Prophet ﷺ did not command separating him from his wife, nor renewing his faith. Also, the community has agreed that one who utters a word of disbelief by mistake is not judged a disbeliever, as stated by al-Nasafi.

The fourth: One of the two earlier interpretations was used as evidence for forbidding entry into the mosque to an intoxicated person, because of the expected defiling and obscene speech from him; so every person with impurity from which defilement or abuse and the like is feared is analogized to him, as stated in al-Iklil.

The fifth: Ibn al-Furs used the addressing of them in the verse as evidence for the obligation of the intoxicated person and his inclusion under the address; but this is open to question, since the address is general to every believer, and even supposing it was aimed at those who prayed in the state of intoxication, it was revealed after they had become sober, as stated in al-Iklil.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until you have washed﴾ is a refutation of those who permitted the junub to sit in general once he has performed wudu', since Allah, exalted is He, made the limit of the prohibition the ghusl, so wudu' does not take its place, as stated in al-Iklil.

I say: This would be a proof only if the verse were a definitive text in one interpretation; but since the possibility of multiple interpretations applies to it, as you have seen, it is not.

The one who permitted it, Imam Ahmad, relied on what he and Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated in his Sunan with a sound chain that the Companions used to do so.

Sa'id ibn Mansur said in his Sunan: Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad, namely al-Darawardi, narrated to us from Hisham ibn Sa'd, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: I saw men of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sitting in the mosque while they were junub, after they had performed wudu' for prayer.

Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain according to the condition of Muslim.

(p-1251) Seventh: Abu al-Su'ud said: Perhaps the placing of the exception before His words, ﴿until you wash yourselves﴾, is to signal from the outset that the ruling of the prohibition in this case is not absolute, as in the case of intoxication; this is to create anticipation for the explanation and to fix it more firmly in minds.

Eighth: He also said: The noble verse contains an indication that the one praying should guard himself against whatever distracts him and occupies his heart, and should purify himself of whatever defiles him, and should not settle for the lowest degree of purification when its higher degrees are possible.

Ninth: The words of the Exalted, ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾, imply a prohibition of prayer while drowsy, as al-Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If one of you feels drowsy while praying, let him leave and sleep until he knows what he is saying." In another narration: "For perhaps he will go to seek forgiveness and will curse himself."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning the verse that he said: "It does not refer to intoxication from wine, but refers to the intoxication of sleep."

Ibn Jarir said: "The correct view is that the intended meaning is intoxication from drink."

(p-1252) al-Razi said: Two things indicate this:

The first: the word "sukr" (intoxication) is literally used for intoxication from drinking wine, and the basic principle in speech is the literal meaning.

The second: all the exegetes agreed that this verse was revealed concerning the drinking of wine, and it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence that when a verse is revealed concerning a specific event and for a specific cause, it is impossible that this cause is not intended by that verse.

Tenth: al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: It may be that the intended meaning of the verse is an allusion to the prohibition of intoxication altogether, because they were commanded to pray at the five times, by night and by day, so a drinker of wine cannot consistently perform the prayer at its times. And Allah knows best.

On this view, it is like His words: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102], which is a command to them to prepare for death in Islam and to persist in obedience for that reason. End quote.

Eleventh: al-Razi said: Some said: this verse, i.e. ﴿do not approach﴾ etc., is abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'idah. I say: The way in which abrogation can be claimed is to say: He forbade approaching prayer while intoxicated, extended to the point where one becomes such that he knows what he says. A ruling extended to a limit implies that the ruling ends at that limit. This implies the permissibility of approaching prayer while intoxicated once one knows what he is saying. It is known that when Allah prohibited wine by the verse of al-Ma'idah, He lifted this permissibility. Thus it is established that the verse of al-Ma'idah abrogates some of the implications of this verse. This is what came to my mind in establishing this abrogation.

The reply to this: We have explained that the essential content of this prohibition returns to a prohibition of drinking that causes intoxication when close to prayer, and singling out a thing by mention does not indicate negation of the ruling for what is other than it, except by way of weak conjecture, and such is not abrogation. End quote.

﴿And if you are sick﴾, i.e. and you do not find (p-1253) water nearby to use, which includes the absence of someone who would hand it to him, or fear of harm from using it. ﴿Or on a journey﴾ where you cannot find it. ﴿Or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾, i.e. or you are in a state of minor impurity. The "ghait" is a low-lying place, so coming from it is a metaphor for impurity, because the customary practice is that one who wishes to relieve himself goes there to hide his person from people's eyes.

al-Khazin said: It was the custom of the Arabs to go to the "ghait" for relieving themselves, so they used it as a euphemism for impurity. This is because a man among them, when he wanted to relieve himself, sought a "ghait" from the land, meaning a low place which screened him from people's eyes, so the impurity was named by this name; it is therefore of the type of naming a thing after its place. End quote.

The attribution of coming to an indefinite one among the addressees, rather than to them all, is to avoid explicitly attributing to them what is shameful or what is disgusting to mention explicitly; so said Abu al-Su'ud.

Then he said: Similarly, the choice of the euphemism in what is coordinated with it, His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿or you have touched women﴾, rather than explicitly mentioning intercourse. Al-Shihab said: In the mention of "one" (aḥad) rather than another word is an indication that a person withdraws when relieving himself, as is his habit and his good manners.

﴿Then you do not find water﴾. al-Mahayimi said: i.e., do not be shy before Allah, but apologize to Him. ﴿Then perform tayammum﴾, i.e. intend: ﴿clean earth﴾, i.e. dust, or the surface of the earth, ﴿pure﴾, i.e. clean. ﴿Then wipe your faces and your hands. Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ This is a justification for the concession and the facilitation, and a confirmation of them, for it is His constant practice to pardon the erring and forgive the sinners; He must be one who facilitates, not one who makes difficult. In this verse there are issues:

First: The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿then you do not find﴾, refer to everything before it, and in that case tayammum is not permitted in any of the cases except when water is absent. As for what has been said, that it refers only to His words, ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself or you have touched women﴾, because the obstacle here is present against restricting travel and illness to the absence of water, namely that each of them is an independent excuse elsewhere, such as fasting, then it is of no benefit; because the absence of water is definitely required in both cases for the permissibility of tayammum, since travel by itself is not permissive, and likewise illness.

(p-1254) As for what is said, that tayammum may be permitted to the sick even when water is present if he fears harm from it, so the absence of water in his case is an unrestricted permission: the reply is that this falls under absence of water, because one for whom its use is impossible is one who lacks it; the intended meaning is not mere existence that is of no benefit. Thus one who sees water at the bottom of a well which he cannot reach by any means is one who lacks it; likewise fear of the road that leads to water; likewise one who needs it for drinking is one who lacks it.

And even if we concede, for argument's sake, that the intended meaning is mere existence, we say: The claim is that He permitted tayammum for the sick when he does not find water, and there is no indication in it of prohibiting him from tayammum when water exists but an obstacle prevents him from it.

If it is said: From where do you derive the permissibility of his tayammum then? We say: From the verification we mentioned, namely that what cannot be used is legally considered nonexistent. Also from His words: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and His words: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and His words: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

Among what Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We set out on a journey, and a stone struck a man among us and wounded him in the head. Then he had a wet dream, so he asked his companions and said: 'Do you find for me a concession for tayammum?' They said: 'We find no concession for you while you are able to use water.' So he washed and died. When we came to the Prophet (ﷺ), he was informed of that, and he said: 'They killed him; may Allah kill them! Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for ignorance is asking. It would have sufficed him to perform tayammum and to bind a cloth over his wound and then wipe over it, and wash the rest of his body.'"

(p-1255) Among what Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and al-Daraqutni narrated from Amr ibn al-As: "I had a wet dream on a cold night during the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, and I feared that if I bathed I would perish, so I performed tayammum, then led my companions in the dawn prayer. They mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'O Amr! You led your companions in prayer while you were in a state of major impurity?' So I informed him of what prevented me from bathing, and I said: 'I heard Allah say: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29].' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed and said nothing." This and what precedes it indicate the permissibility of turning to tayammum out of fear of harm.

Majd al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah said: In the hadith of Amr is the lesson that holding to general expressions is a valid proof. End quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His words, ﴿And if you are sick﴾, that he said: "It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar who was sick and could not stand up to perform wudu', and he had no servant to hand it to him. So he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and Allah revealed this verse."

Ibn Kathir said: This is mursal.

Second: What truly fulfils the concept of the absence of water restricted to standing up for prayer is what is considered the criterion for the permissibility of tayammum, as is apparent from the verse, not absence of water together with a specific search, as has been said: that one must search in each of the four directions in an inclination, or wait until the last part of the time so that only enough time remains to pray after tayammum. There is no evidence for that. So when the prescribed time for prayer enters, and the worshipper intends to stand for it, and then does not find at that moment anything with which to perform wudu', or to bathe at his home or mosque, or what is near them, that is a valid excuse for tayammum. The intended meaning of absence in this case is not that he does not find it after searching, investigating and seeking, but rather that he has no knowledge or assumption of the existence of any of it there, and he could not obtain it in that situation by purchase or the like. This is what is truly called "not finding water" according to the people of language, and it is obligatory to interpret the speech of Allah Most High accordingly, in the absence of any established legal usage.

What he (ﷺ) did indicates what we have mentioned: he performed tayammum from a wall in Medina, as is established in the two Sahihs, without asking or searching; and nothing authentic is reported from him about searching that would establish a proof. So this, while it indicates the obligation of searching, also indicates the non-obligation of waiting until the last part of the time. This is also indicated by the hadith of the two men who performed tayammum on a journey, then found water; one of them repeated the prayer and the other did not. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the one who did not repeat: "You have acted in accordance with the Sunnah." Abu Dawud, al-Hakim and others narrated it from the hadith of Abu Sa'id. This refutes the view of those who say that the one performing tayammum must wait until the end of the time, whether he is traveling or resident; so states al-Rawdah al-Nadiyyah.

Third: The verse indicates that the traveler who does not find water performs tayammum, whether his journey is long or short.

Fourth: In the seven canonical readings it is recited as "lamastum" and "lamastum." Both al-mulamasah and al-lams come in the lexical sense of touching with the hand, and in the sense of intercourse. al-Majd in al-Qamus said: "lamasahu yalmisuhu and yalmusuhu": he touched him with his hand; and "al-jariyah" he had intercourse with her. Then he said: al-mulamasah is contact and intercourse.

Hence the exegetes and imams differed about what is meant here. Some say that lams is literally touching with the hand and figuratively anything else, and the basic principle is to take speech in its literal sense, since that is the preponderant view, especially on the reading "lamastum," since it is not well known for intercourse as "mulamasah" is.

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud by multiple chains that he said: "al-mulamasah is what is less than intercourse." And from him: "The kiss is from touching, and in it is wudu'." Ibn Jarir narrated both.

al-Tabarani narrated with his chain from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud who said: "A man performs wudu' because of physical contact, and because of touching with his hand, and because of a kiss." And he used to say concerning this verse, "or you have touched women": it is caressing.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Nafi' that Ibn Umar used to perform wudu' because of kissing a woman, and held that it requires wudu', and said: "It is of the type of lims (touching)."

Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned that similar views were transmitted from many of the Successors (al-Tabi'un). They said: What supports keeping *al-lams* (touching) in its literal meaning is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a written page on paper, and they had touched it with their hands﴾ [al-An'am: 7], meaning: felt it with their hands.

(ﷺ) said to Ma'iz when he confessed to having committed fornication, alluding to him retracting his confession: "Perhaps you kissed, or touched?"

In the authentic hadith: "The hand's fornication is touching."

'A'isha said: "Hardly a day passed without the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) coming around to us, and he would kiss and touch."

Among this is what is established in the two Sahihs: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the sale of *mulamasa* (a sale by touching)," which refers to feeling with the hand.

They also relied on the hadith narrated by Ahmad from Mu'adh: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! What do you say about a man who met a woman he did not know, and he did everything with her that a man does with his wife except that he did not have intercourse with her?' He said: Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the first hours of the night﴾ [Hud: 114], the verse [to its end]. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Perform ablution, then pray.' Mu'adh said: I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Is this for him specifically or for the believers in general?' He said: 'Rather, it is for the believers in general.'"

At-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: "It is not connected (*muttasil*)." An-Nasa'i narrated it as *mursal*. They said: He ordered him to perform ablution because he had touched the woman without having intercourse with her.

* *

**Section**

Some said: What is meant by touching here is intercourse, because it occurs with this meaning in other verses, which shows that it is among the metaphors (*kinayat*) of the Revelation. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. And He the Exalted says: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. And in the verse of *zihar* He says: ﴿So the freeing of a neck before the two of them touch one another﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3].

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse, ﴿or you have touched women﴾, that he said: "Intercourse."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "Indeed *al-lams*, *al-mass* and *al-mubasharah* mean intercourse, but Allah expresses what He wills by what He wills." It is authentically transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas by more than one route that he said this, and it is established that his interpretation is more preponderant than the interpretation of others, because the Messenger (ﷺ) supplicated for him to be taught the *ta'wil* (deeper interpretation) of the Book, as we previously explained in the introduction to the tafsir.

What supports the view that touching does not nullify ablution is what Muslim and at-Tirmidhi narrated, and he authenticated it, from 'A'isha, who said: "I lost the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night from the bed, so I searched for him, and my hand fell upon the soles of his feet while he was in the mosque, and they were upright, and he was saying: 'O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, and in Your pardon from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You. I cannot count Your praise; You are as You have praised Yourself.'"

An-Nasa'i narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pray while I lay across in front of him like a funeral bier, until when he wanted to perform the witr prayer, he touched me with his foot."

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Talkhis*: "Its chain is authentic." But his statement in *al-Fath*: "It is possible that it was with a barrier, or that it was specific to him (ﷺ)," is an artificial stretch and a contradiction of the apparent meaning.

From Ibrahim al-Taymi, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would kiss some of his wives, then pray without performing ablution." Narrated by Abu Dawud and an-Nasa'i. Abu Dawud said: "It is *mursal*, since Ibrahim al-Taymi did not hear from 'A'isha." An-Nasa'i said: "There is no better hadith on this subject than this one, even though it is *mursal*." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and a group of scholars authenticated it.

It is supported by what was mentioned above and by what at-Tabarani narrated in *al-Mu'jam al-Saghir* from the hadith of 'Amrah from 'A'isha, who said: "I lost the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night, so I said: 'He has gone to his slave-girl Mariyah.' So I got up, feeling for the wall, and I found him standing and praying. I put my hand into his hair to see whether he had performed ritual bathing (*ghusl*) or not. When he finished he said: 'Your devil has seized you, O 'A'isha!'" In its chain is Muhammad ibn Ibrahim from 'A'isha; Ibn Abi Hatim said: "He did not hear from her."

Ibn Jarir said: The most correct of the two views is the view of the one who said that Allah, by His words ﴿or you have touched women﴾, meant intercourse and not any other meaning of touching, because of the authenticity of the report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that "he kissed some of his wives, then prayed and did not perform ablution," which he then traced through several routes. By this it is known that the hadith of 'A'isha is an indicator (*qarinah*) that diverted the intended meaning of touching from its literal sense and necessitated resorting to its metaphorical meaning.

As for what was narrated from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, we do not deny the validity of applying *al-lams* to feeling with the hand; indeed, that is its literal meaning. But we contend that the context is surrounded by indicators that necessitate resorting to the metaphorical meaning.

As for their claim that kissing requires ablution, there is no proof in the statement of a Companion, especially when it contradicts what has come from the Lawgiver (ash-Shari'). This is supported by the statement of the linguists that what is meant by the words of one of the Bedouins to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, his wife does not refuse the hand of one who touches," is a metaphor for her being an adulteress. For this reason he (ﷺ) said to him: "Divorce her."

As for the hadith of Mu'adh, which they relied upon, there is no indication in it that touching nullifies ablution, because it is not established that he had been in a state of ablution before the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to perform ablution, nor is it established that he had been in ablution at the time of touching. So the Prophet (ﷺ) informed him that his ablution had been nullified. Thus it is in *Nayl al-Awtar*.

(p-١٢٦٢) Ibn Kathir said: "It is *munqati'* (broken in its chain), between Ibn Abi Layla and Mu'adh, since he did not meet him. Furthermore, it is possible that he (ﷺ) only ordered him to perform ablution and the obligatory prayer, as mentioned in the hadith of as-Siddiq: 'There is no servant who commits a sin, then perfects his purification, then stands and prays two rak'ahs, then seeks forgiveness from Allah, except that Allah forgives him.'" This is mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran at His words: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Al 'Imran: 135], the verse [to its end].

**The Fifth Issue: Tayammum (dry ablution)**

*Tayammum* linguistically means intending or aiming. It is said: *tayammamtuhu*, *ta'ammamtuhu*, *yammamtuhu*, and *amamtuhu*, meaning: I aimed at him. As for *sa'id*, it is *fa'il* in the sense of *sa'id* (ascending), i.e., that which rises above the surface.

Az-Zajjaj said: "*Sa'id* is the surface of the earth, whether it is dust or other than dust. I know of no disagreement among the linguists about this."

In *al-Misbah*: "In the speech of the Arabs, *sa'id* is used for several things: for the dust that is on the surface of the earth, for the surface of the earth, and for the road."

In *al-Qamus*: "*Sa'id* is dust or the surface of the earth."

Al-Azhari said: "The view of most scholars is that *sa'id* in the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿a pure surface﴾ means dust." End of quote.

They argued with what is in Sahih Muslim from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We were favoured over people in three ways: our rows were made like the rows of the angels, the whole earth was made a mosque for us, and its dust was made a purifier (*tahur*) for us when we do not find water." In another wording: "Its dust was made a purifier for us when we do not find water."

They said: So he specified the purifying quality to dust in a context of favour (*imtinan*). If anything else could take its place, he would have mentioned it along with it.

They also said: The hadith of Jabir, agreed upon: "The earth was made a mosque and a purifier for me," is specified by the preceding hadith, because the general is to be understood in light of the specific.

They also argued that the pure (*tayyib*) can only be dust.

Al-Wahidi said: "In this verse, Allah the Exalted made it obligatory that the *sa'id* be pure (*tayyib*). And the pure land is the one that produces vegetation, by the evidence of His words: ﴿And the good land—its plants come out by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. So it is necessary that land which does not produce vegetation is not pure. Therefore His words ﴿then perform tayammum with pure *sa'id*﴾ are a command to perform tayammum with dust only, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation."

They also argued with the verse of al-Ma'idah. They said: The verse here is absolute (*mutlaq*), but in Surah al-Ma'idah it is restricted (*muqayyad*), namely His words: ﴿and wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. The word *min* ("with it/from it") indicates partiality (*tab'id*), and this cannot apply to bare rock that has no dust on it.

Az-Zamakhshari said: "Their claim that *min* indicates the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghayah*) is a far-fetched view. No one among the Arabs understands from the saying of the speaker, 'I wiped his head with some oil, some water, and some dust,' anything other than the meaning of partiality." Then he said: "Submission to the truth is more deserving than disputation." End of quote.

Those who permit tayammum with the earth and whatever is on it answered these proofs by saying: The apparent meaning of the word *sa'id* is the surface of the earth, because it is that which *sa'ida*, i.e., rises and is elevated over the surface of the earth. This quality is not specific to dust. This is supported by the hadith: "The earth was made a mosque and a purifier for me," which is agreed upon from the hadith of Jabir and others. And what is established in a narration with the wording "its dust (*turbatuha*) is a purifier," as Muslim recorded from the hadith of Hudhayfah, does not necessitate that dust alone has this quality when water is absent. The most that can be said is that the word "dust" indicates by implication (*mafhum*) that other parts of the earth do not share its purifying quality. This is an implication of a *laqab* (a title/name), which is not valid for specifying the generality of the Qur'an and Sunnah. For this reason, no reputable scholar of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul*) has acted upon it. Therefore, the mention of dust in that narration is a case of specifying some individual instances of a general term. The answer regarding the mention of dust in other hadiths is the same. The reason for mentioning it is that it is the most commonly used for this purification. This is supported by the fact that it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed tayammum from a wall.

As for the argument from describing the *sa'id* as *tayyib* (pure), and the claim that the pure can only be dust that is pure and productive, based on His words: ﴿And the good land—its plants come out by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad does not come out except with difficulty﴾ [al-A'raf: 58], this is not useful for the desired conclusion unless it is first shown that *tayyib* is restricted to what was mentioned. And necessity rejects this, because dust mixed with refuse is better for producing vegetation. Thus it is in *al-Rawdah al-Nadiyyah*.

As for the argument from the verse of al-Ma'idah and the apparent partiality in *min*, that applies only if the pronoun refers back to *sa'id*.

An-Nasir said in *al-Intisaf*: "There is another possibility, which is that the pronoun refers to the *hadath* (ritual impurity) implied by His words ﴿and if you are ill﴾ to the end of the verse. For what is understood from it is: 'And if you are in a state of *hadath* in any of these circumstances: travel, illness, coming from the toilet, or touching women, and you do not find water with which to purify yourselves from the *hadath*, then perform tayammum with it (*fa-tayammamu minhu*).' It is said: 'I performed tayammum from the major ritual impurity (*janabah*).' The position of *min* in this sense is common and widely used. In this construction, *min* is either causal (*li-l-ta'lil*) or indicates the starting point, and both are valid for it. And Allah knows best."

**The Sixth Issue**

His words ﴿So wipe your faces and your hands﴾ indicate that what is obligatory in tayammum, whether as a substitute for ablution or for ritual bathing, is wiping only the face and the two hands. This is a consensus. However, the scholars differ regarding the hands. Some say they are to be wiped up to the elbows, because the term "hands" applies to them both when it refers to what reaches the shoulders, and to what reaches the elbows, as in the verse of ablution, and to what reaches the palms, as in the verse of theft: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. They said: Applying what is unrestricted here to what is restricted in the verse of ablution is preferable because of the shared purifying quality.

Ash-Shafi'i narrated from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, from Abu al-Huwayrith, from al-A'raj, from Ibn as-Samma, who said: "I passed by the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was urinating. I greeted him, but he did not return the greeting, until he got up to the wall and scraped it with a stick he had with him. Then he placed his hand on the wall and wiped his face and his forearms, and then he returned the greeting to me."

This hadith is interrupted (munqati'), because al-A'raj, who is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz, did not hear this from Ibn al-Samma. Rather, he heard it from 'Umayr, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn al-Samma. Likewise, it is narrated in the two Sahihs from 'Umayr, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "We entered upon Abu Juhaym ibn al-Harith, and Abu Juhaym said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came from the direction of Bi'r Jamal, and a man met him and greeted him with salam, but the Prophet (ﷺ) did not return the greeting until he turned to a wall, placed his hand on the wall, wiped his face and his hands, and then returned the salam to him."

Abu Dawud has, from Nafi', who said: "I set out with Ibn 'Umar on some need to Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Umar fulfilled his need. Among his narrations that day was that he said: A man passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in one of the alleys, having just come out from defecating or urinating, and he greeted him with salam, but he did not return it. When the man was almost about to disappear into the alley, he struck the wall with his hands and wiped his face with them, then he struck again and wiped his forearms, then he returned the salam to the man, and said: 'Nothing prevented me from returning your salam except that I was not in a state of purity.'"

In another narration: "he wiped his forearms up to the elbows." This is the best that is in this chapter, for al-Bayhaqi indicated its authenticity, as is stated in "Lubab al-Ta'wil."

Ibn Kathir said regarding the hadith of Abu Dawud, verbatim: "But in its chain is Muhammad ibn Thabit al-'Abdi, whom some of the hadith memorizers have declared weak, and others of the trustworthy narrators related it and stopped it at the action of Ibn 'Umar. Al-Bukhari, Abu Zur'a and Ibn 'Adi said: This is the correct version."

Al-Bayhaqi said: "The marfu' (raised) form of this hadith is munkar."

Ibn Kathir said: "Some have mentioned what al-Daraqutni related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Tayammum is two strikes: a strike for the face and a strike for the hands up to the elbows.' But it is not authentic, because in its chain there is a weakness by which the hadith is not established." End of quote. This is because in it is 'Ali ibn Zabyan. The hafiz Ibn Hajar said: He is weak; al-Qattan, Ibn Ma'in and others declared him weak. By this it is known that what was used as evidence for making the two strikes obligatory, from what was mentioned, is open to scrutiny, because all of its routes are not free from criticism, and even if they were authentic, acting upon them would be required because of the additional information they contain.

* *

Section

Al-Zuhri held that one wipes the hands up to the shoulders, and what is narrated from 'Ammar ibn Yasir supports this, who said: "They performed tayammum with the earth with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the dawn prayer. They struck the earth with their palms, then wiped their faces with one wiping, then they returned and struck the earth with their palms a second time, and wiped with all their hands up to the shoulders and the armpits, from the inner surfaces of their hands." Abu Dawud recorded it.

The hafiz said in "al-Fath": As for the narration of the armpits, al-Shafi'i and others said: If that occurred by the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), then every tayammum that was validly performed by the Prophet (ﷺ) after it abrogates it (naskh); and if it occurred without his command, then the evidence is in what he commanded.

* *

Section

The correct position regarding the description of tayammum is to adhere to what is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of 'Ammar, namely limiting it to one strike for the face and the two palms.

"'Ammar said: I became junub and did not find water, so I rolled in the dust and prayed. I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'It would have sufficed you to do just this.' The Prophet (ﷺ) struck the earth with his two palms and blew into them, then wiped with them his face and his two palms." Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim).

In another wording: "It would have sufficed you to strike your palms on the dust, then blow into them, then wipe with them your face and your palms up to the wrists." Narrated by al-Daraqutni.

Al-Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud related from 'Ammar ibn Yasir that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning tayammum: one strike for the face and the hands." 

In another wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him to perform tayammum for the face and the palms." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sahih.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Most of the marfu' reports from 'Ammar mention a single strike, and what is narrated from him regarding two strikes is all idtirab (confused in transmission). As for the answer to the agreed-upon hadith of 'Ammar, that its purpose is to explain the form of the striking and not all that tayammum is accomplished by, it is clear excess and a contradiction of the apparent meaning.

This reached the scholar al-Sindi in his "Hawashi al-Bukhari," where he wrote on the hadith of 'Ammar, verbatim: "The author (i.e., al-Bukhari) used this hadith as evidence that it is not necessary to include the forearms in tayammum in one place, and that the second strike is not obligatory in another place. Likewise, it will come in the narrations of this hadith that he (ﷺ) placed the palms before the face in this incident, so whoever used it as evidence for the non-obligation of order (tartib) ... Perhaps the one who holds otherwise would say: this hadith is not given to explain the number of strikes, nor to explain the limitation of the hand in tayammum, nor to explain the non-obligation of order, but that matter is left to outside evidences. It is only given to refute what 'Ammar supposed, that the junub must cover the whole body, and the restriction in his words 'it would have sufficed you' is relative to him, as the principle is that restriction is considered relative to the claim of the addressee.
