In the *Musnad* of Imam Ahmad: "A man was brought to the Prophet ﷺ who had committed a sin. When he stood before him he said: 'O God, I repent to You, and I do not repent to Muhammad.' He said: 'He has recognized the truth to its people.'"

* *

**Section**

As for *shirk* in wills and intentions, it is that sea without a shore, and few are those who escape it. Whoever intends by his deed other than the face of God, and intends something other than drawing near to Him and seeking His reward, has associated in his intention and will.

*Ikhlas* (sincerity) is to be sincere to God in one's statements, actions, wills and intentions. This is the *hanifiyyah* (uprightness), the religion of Ibrahim, which God commanded to all His servants, and He accepts nothing from anyone other than it. It is the reality of Islam: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 85]. It is the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from which whoever turns away is among the most foolish of fools.

* *

**Section**

When you have understood this introduction, the door to answering the mentioned question is opened. We say (and from God alone we seek help in what is correct): the reality of *shirk* is imitating the Creator and likening the created being to Him. This is the true *tashbih* (likening), not the affirmation of the attributes of perfection with which God described Himself and with which He described His Messenger ﷺ. Thus he who has been overturned by God, whose heart God has reversed, whose sight God has blinded, and whom He has cast down through his confusion of the matter, makes *tawhid* into *tashbih*, and *tashbih* into veneration and obedience. The polytheist likens the created being to the Creator in the specific attributes of divinity. Among the specific attributes of divinity is sole possession of harm and benefit, giving and withholding. This requires attaching supplication, fear, hope and reliance to Him alone. Whoever attaches these to a created being has likened it to the Creator, and has made one who possesses for himself no benefit, no harm, no death, no life and no resurrection superior to others, by likening him to the One to whom the whole matter belongs. The reins of all affairs are in His hand, and to Him they return. What He wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur. None can withhold what He gives, and none can give what He withholds. Rather, if He opens the door of His mercy to His servant, no one can close it, and if He withholds it from him, no one can send it to him. Thus among the most shameful likenings is likening this impotent one, poor in his essence, to the Powerful, Self-sufficient in His essence.

Among the specific attributes of divinity is absolute perfection from all aspects, in which there is no deficiency in any way. This requires that all worship be for Him alone, and veneration, exaltation, fear, supplication, hope, turning in repentance, reliance, seeking help, and utmost humility together with utmost love, all of this is required by reason, by the Law and by natural disposition to be for Him alone, and it is prohibited by reason, the Law and natural disposition to be for another. Whoever gives any of this to another has likened that other to One who has no likeness and no rival. This is the ugliest and most baseless likening. Because of its extreme ugliness and its containing the utmost injustice, God, glorified is He, informed His servants that He does not forgive it, although He has prescribed mercy upon Himself.

Among the specific attributes of divinity is servitude, which stands upon two legs without which it has no foundation: utmost love together with utmost humility. This is the completeness of servitude, and the ranks of creation differ in it according to their differing in these two foundations. Whoever gives his love, his humility and his submission to other than God has likened that other to Him in His exclusive right. This is something that no revealed law could ever bring, and its ugliness is established in every natural disposition and every intellect. But the devils have altered the natural dispositions and intellects of most creatures, corrupted them, and led them astray from them. Whoever God had already granted the best reward remained upon the original natural disposition. God sent His messengers to them and revealed His books to them in accordance with their natural dispositions and intellects, so they increased in light upon light, and God guides whom He wills to His light.

Having understood this: among the specific attributes of divinity is prostration. Whoever prostrates to other than Him has likened the created being to Him. Among them is reliance: whoever relies upon other than Him has likened it to Him. Among them is repentance: whoever repents to other than Him has likened it to Him. Among them is swearing by His name in glorification and exaltation: whoever swears by other than Him has likened it to Him. This is what concerns the side of likening.

[p-1306] As for imitating Him, whoever magnifies himself, shows arrogance, and calls people to praise and exalt him with extravagant praise, to submit to him, to hope in him, to hang his heart on him in fear and hope, to seek refuge with him, and to seek help from him, has imitated Allah and contended with Him in His lordship (rububiyyah) and His divinity (uluhiyyah). He deserves to be humiliated to the utmost degree of humiliation, to be abased to the utmost degree of abasement, and to be placed beneath the feet of His creation.

In the Sahih, from him (ﷺ), it is related that he said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Greatness is My waist-wrapper and majesty is My cloak. Whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will punish him.'" If the image-maker, who makes a picture with his own hand, is among the people who will suffer the most punishment on the Day of Resurrection, because he imitates Allah merely in the act of crafting, then what is the assumption about one who imitates Allah in the specific attributes of lordship and divinity? As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people who will suffer the most punishment on the Day of Resurrection are the image-makers. It will be said to them: 'Give life to what you have created.'"

In the Sahih, from him (ﷺ), that he said: [p-1307] "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Who does greater wrong than one who sets out to create a creation like My creation? Let them create an atom; let them create a grain of barley.'" By mentioning the atom and the grain of barley, he drew attention to what is greater and more significant than them. The point is that this is the state of one who imitates Him in the craft of making an image; so what is the state of one who imitates Him in the exclusive properties of His lordship and divinity? Likewise is one who imitates Him in a name that is fitting for Allah alone, such as "King of kings" (Malik al-Amlak), "Judge of judges" (Hakim al-Hukkam), and the like.

It is established in the Sahih, from him (ﷺ), that he said: "The most despicable of names in the sight of Allah is a man who names himself 'Shahan-shah' (King of kings), and there is no king but Allah." In another wording: "The man most hateful to Allah is a man who is called 'King of the kings' (Malik al-Amlak)." This is the abhorrence and wrath of Allah against one who imitates Him in a name that is fitting for Him alone. He, glory be to Him, alone is King of kings, and He alone is Judge of judges. He is the One who judges all judges and decides over all of them; there is no other.

* *

Note:
Wherever it occurs in a hadith, "Whoever does such-and-such has committed shirk," or "has committed kufr," it does not mean the kufr that expels one from the religion (kufr al-mukhrij min al-millah), nor the greater shirk that expels one from Islam and to which the rulings of apostasy (riddah) apply, and we seek refuge in Allah, Exalted. Al-Bukhari said: "Chapter: On the ingratitude of the spouse, and a kufr that is less than kufr."

Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-Arabi said in his commentary: His intention is to show that just as acts of obedience are called faith (iman), so too sins are called kufr. But wherever kufr is applied to them, it is not meant as the kufr that expels one from the religion. The ignorant and the mistaken among this Ummah, even if they do what amounts to kufr or shirk [p-1308] that would make them a mushrik or a kafir, are excused on account of ignorance and error until the proof is made clear to them. The proof whose rejection constitutes kufr is a clear explanation that is not obscured to someone like them, and denying what is known necessarily from the religion of Islam, that upon which the Muslims have reached a clear and definitive consensus, which every Muslim knows without reflection or deliberation, as will be explained, God willing. Only the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) have disagreed on this.

Shaykh Taqi al-Din said in "Kitab al-Iman": Imam Ahmad did not declare the Khawarij, the Murji'ah, or the Qadariyyah to be disbelievers. What is reported from him and from those like him is the declaring of disbelief against the Jahmiyyah. Yet Ahmad did not declare any specific Jahmiyyah to be a disbeliever, nor did he declare disbelievers everyone who said "I am a Jahmi." Rather, he prayed behind the Jahmiyyah who called people to their doctrine, who tested people and punished with harsh penalties those who did not agree with them. Ahmad and his like did not declare them disbelievers; rather, he believed in their faith and leadership, prayed for them, held it permissible to pray behind them, to perform the Hajj and join the raids with them, and to refrain from rebelling against them, in accordance with what he considered applicable to such rulers. He denied the false doctrine they had introduced, which is great kufr, even though they themselves did not know it to be kufr. He would deny it and strive to refute it as far as he could. Thus he combined obedience to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) in manifesting the Sunnah and the religion and denying the innovations of the Jahmiyyah, the heretics, with safeguarding the rights of the believers among the leaders and the community, even though they were ignorant innovators and unrighteous transgressors. The words of the Shaykh end here. So consider this carefully, free of inclination and injustice.

Shaykh Taqi al-Din also said: Whoever has faith in the Messenger and in what he brought, but has erred in some of the innovations he interpreted, even if he calls to them, is not a disbeliever at all. The Khawarij were among the most manifest of people in innovation, fighting the community and declaring it to be disbelievers. None of the Companions declared them disbelievers, neither Ali nor anyone else. Rather, they ruled concerning them as they ruled concerning the wrongdoing and transgressing Muslims, as the reports from them about this are cited in other places. Likewise with all of the seventy-two sects: whoever among them was a hypocrite is a disbeliever inwardly, and whoever was a believer in Allah and His Messenger inwardly is not a disbeliever inwardly, even if he erred in interpretation, whatever his error may be. Some of them may have a branch of hypocrisy, but not the hypocrisy whose possessor is in the lowest level of the Fire.

Whoever says that each one of the seventy-two sects commits a kufr that removes one from the religion has opposed the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Companions, and indeed the consensus of the four Imams and others than them. None of them declared every one of the seventy-two sects to be disbelievers. The words of the Shaykh end here.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Turuq Ahl al-Bid'ah": Those who agree on the basis of Islam but differ on some fundamentals, such as the Khawarij, the Mu'tazilah, the Qadariyyah, the Rafidah, the Jahmiyyah, and the extreme Murji'ah, are of the following categories:

The first: the ignorant, blind follower (muqallid) who has no insight. He is not declared a disbeliever, nor is he declared a sinner, nor is his testimony rejected, provided he is unable to learn guidance. His ruling is that of the oppressed among men, women, and children.

The second category: one who is able to ask, seek guidance, and know the truth, but who abandons that out of preoccupation with his worldly life, his leadership, his pleasures, and his livelihood. This person is negligent, deserving of the threat, sinful for abandoning what Allah obligated upon him of piety according to his capacity. If the innovation and desire in him outweigh the Sunnah and guidance in him, his testimony is rejected; if the Sunnah and guidance in him outweigh the innovation and desire in him, his testimony is accepted.

The third: one who asks, seeks, and the guidance becomes clear to him, but he abandons it out of partisan zeal or hostility toward his companions. The least of his ranks is that he is a sinner, and declaring him a disbeliever is a matter of scholarly judgment (ijtihad). The words of his statement end here. So look at it and consider it carefully, for he mentioned this detailed classification in most of his books. He also mentioned that the Imams and the people of the Sunnah do not declare them disbelievers, despite his description of them as committing the greater shirk and the greater kufr. In most of his books he showed their disgraceful conduct.

Let us mention a portion of his words to confirm what we have said about him. He, may Allah have mercy on him, said in "al-Madarij": Those who affirm the Creator are of two types.

One of them: the people who associate others with Him in His lordship and divinity, like the Magians and those who resemble them among the Qadariyyah. For they affirm another god alongside Allah. The Magian Qadariyyah affirm a creator of actions alongside Allah, whose actions are not created by Allah nor within His power, and which proceed without His will and power, and He has no power over them. Rather, they are the ones who made themselves agents, willers, and originators. The reality of their doctrine is that Allah is not a Lord who creates the actions of living beings. The words of his statement end here.

He reminded them of this shirk throughout his books, and he compared them to the Magians who say that the world has two creators. Look at how, when he and his Shaykh spoke about declaring disbelief, they both reported the non-declaration of their disbelief from all the people of the Sunnah, even with knowledge of the truth and obstinate opposition. He said: "Their kufr is a matter of scholarly judgment," as his words quoted earlier show.

Ibn Taymiyyah, when he was asked about two men who had spoken on the question of takfir, answered at length, and at the end of the answer he said: If it were assumed that a man repelled takfir against one who believes he is not a disbeliever, in protection of him and in support of his Muslim brother, that would be a legitimate and good Shariah aim. If he strives in that and is correct, he has two rewards; if he strives and errs, he has one reward.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, also said: Takfir occurs only by denying what is known of the religion necessarily, or by denying the widely transmitted rulings upon which there is consensus.

He was also asked, may Allah sanctify his spirit, about the takfir that occurred in this Ummah: who was the first to introduce and innovate it? He answered: The first to introduce it in Islam were the Mu'tazilah, and from them whoever took it received it. Likewise, the Khawarij were the first to make it manifest. People disagreed over this. Some people report two opinions from Malik on it, similarly from al-Shafi'i, and there are two narrations from Ahmad. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and his companions also have two positions. The reality of the matter is that a statement may be kufr, so the statement is declared to be takfir of its speaker, and it is said: "Whoever says such-and-such is a disbeliever." But the specific person who said it is not declared a disbeliever until the proof is established against him, the proof whose rejection makes one a disbeliever, by making known the Shariah ruling, from a ruler or an obeyed authority, as is stated in the books on rulings. When he is informed of the ruling and his ignorance is removed, the proof is established against him. This is the case with the threats in the texts of the Book and the Sunnah, which are very numerous. Affirming what they imply is obligatory in general and absolute terms, without specifying any particular person, so one does not say: "This one is a disbeliever, or a sinner, or cursed, or one who has incurred wrath, or one deserving of the Fire." This is especially so if the person has virtues and good deeds, for everyone other than the prophets may commit minor and major sins, while it is possible that this person is a truthful one (siddiq), a martyr, or a righteous person. As has been fully explained elsewhere, the consequence of sins may be averted by repentance or seeking forgiveness, or by erasing good deeds, or by expiating calamities, or by an accepted intercession, or by the sheer will and mercy of Allah. So when we act upon the implication of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ [al-Nisa': 93] [al-Nisa': from verse 93], up to the end of the verse, and His words: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume into their bellies a fire, and they will enter a Blaze﴾ [al-Nisa': 10] [al-Nisa': 10], and His words: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding eternally therein, and for him is a humiliating punishment﴾ [al-Nisa': 14] [al-Nisa': 14], up to the end of the verse, and His words: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188], to His words: ﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice﴾ [al-Nisa': 30] [al-Nisa': from verse 30], up to the end of the verse, and other verses of the threat; and when we act upon the implication of his words (ﷺ): "Allah has cursed whoever drinks wine," or "whoever disobeys his parents," or "whoever alters the boundary markers of the land," or "whoever slaughters for other than Allah," or "Allah has cursed the thief," or "Allah has cursed the consumer of usury, its payer, its witness, and its scribe," [p-1312] or "Allah has cursed the one who withholds charity and the one who transgresses in it," or "whoever introduces an innovation in Madinah, or gives shelter to an innovator, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels, and all people," and other hadiths of threat, it is not permissible to specify a particular person who committed some of these acts and say: "This specific person has incurred this threat," because repentance and other removers of punishment are possible. He said: The doing of these matters by one who thinks they are permissible, through ijtihad or taqlid or the like, at most means he is excused from the threat falling upon him due to an impediment, just as the threat is prevented from falling upon them due to repentance, good deeds that erase sins, expiating calamities, or other things. This path is the one that must be followed, for whatever is other than it is two corrupt paths.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 48 (part 5 of 5):**

The first position is the claim that the threat (wa'id) applies to each specific individual who commits the act, and the assertion that this is acting in accordance with the textual evidence. This is more repugnant than the view of the Khawarij (al-Khawarij, the early sect that declared grave sinners to be disbelievers), of the Mu'tazila and others who declare people to be disbelievers for sins. Its corruption is known necessarily, and its proofs are known in other places. These texts of threat and its like are true, but the specific person who commits the act cannot be declared to deserve the threat. Thus no specific individual among the People of the Qibla (ahl al-qibla, the Muslims) is to be testified to be in the Fire, because a condition is absent or an impediment is present. Likewise with statements for which the one who says them is declared a disbeliever: the one who says them may not have been reached by the texts that establish knowledge of the truth, or he may have been reached but they were not established for him, or he was unable to know and understand them, or doubts (shubuhat) arose for him for which God will excuse him.

Whoever believes in God and His Messenger, professes Islam, and loves God and His Messenger, God will forgive him if he commits some verbal or practical sins, whether they are called shirk or called acts of disobedience (ma'asi). This is what the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the majority of the Imams of Islam hold. However, the point is that the positions of the Imams are built upon this distinction between the category (nau') and the specific individual (ayn). Indeed, there is no difference in the statements reported from Imam Ahmad and the rest of the Imams of Islam, such as Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, that they did not declare the Murji'a (al-Murji'a, a sect holding that faith is only speech without action) to be disbelievers, even though they say that faith is speech without action. Their texts are explicit in refraining from declaring the Khawarij, the Qadariyya and others to be disbelievers. Imam Ahmad used to state the declaration of disbelief against the Jahmiyya (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan) without qualification, because he was tested by them until he came to know the reality of their affair, that it revolves around ta'til (denial of God's attributes). The declaration of the Jahmiyya as disbelievers is well known from the Salaf and the Imams, but they did not declare their specific individuals to be disbelievers. The one who calls to a view is greater than the one who holds it without calling to it; the one who punishes his opponent is greater than the one who merely calls; and the one who declares his opponent a disbeliever is greater than the one who punishes. Despite this, some of the rulers (wulat al-umur) held the view of the Jahmiyya: that the Qur'an is created, that God will not be seen in the Hereafter, that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an may not be used as evidence for knowledge of God, nor the sound hadiths, and that religion is not complete except with the opinions they embellished, the false imaginings and corrupt intellects; that their imaginings and ignorances are more decisive in the religion of God than the Book of God, the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the consensus of the Companions and the Successors who followed them in excellence (ihsan); and that the statements of the Jahmiyya and the Mu'attila concerning negation and affirmation are more decisive in the religion of God. Because of this they tested the Muslims, imprisoned Imam Ahmad and flogged him, killed a group of people, and crucified others. Yet they would not release a captive or give from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) except to one who agreed with them and affirmed their view. Matters of harm to Islam from them are extensively described elsewhere. Despite this ta'til, which is worse than shirk, Imam Ahmad had mercy upon them and asked forgiveness for them, and he said: "I do not know that they deny the Messenger (ﷺ) or reject what he brought, but they interpreted and erred, and they followed the one who said that."

When Imam al-Shafi'i debated Hafs al-Fard, one of the leaders of the Mu'attila, on the question "the Qur'an is created," al-Shafi'i said to him: "You have disbelieved in God the Mighty." He declared him a disbeliever, but he did not rule his apostasy merely on that basis. Had he believed his apostasy and disbelief, he would have striven to kill him.

The scholars issued fatwas for the killing of their propagandists, such as Ghaylan al-Qadari, al-Ja'd ibn Dirham, Jahm ibn Safwan, the Imam of the Jahmiyya, and others. The people prayed over them and buried them with the Muslims. Their killing became a matter of repelling an aggressor (sa'il) in order to stop their harm, not because of their apostasy. Had they been disbelievers, the Muslims would have treated them as they treat other disbelievers. These matters are extensively described elsewhere.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Sharh al-Manazil": The People of the Sunna agree that a single person may have walaya (friendship) for God and enmity from two different aspects, and may be beloved to God and hated from two aspects. Indeed, faith and hypocrisy (nifaq) may be present in him, and faith and disbelief (kufr) may be present, and he is closer to one of them than to the other, so he is with its people, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167]. And He said: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except while associating others with Him﴾ [Yusuf: 106]. So He affirmed for them, blessed and exalted is He, faith along with committing shirk. If with this shirk there is denial of His messengers, the faith they have will not benefit them. If there is affirmation of His messengers while they commit kinds of shirk that do not remove them from faith in the messengers and the Last Day, then they deserve the threat more than the people of major sins (kaba'ir). On this principle the People of the Sunna affirmed that the people of major sins enter the Fire, then exit from it, and enter Paradise, because of the two causes that exist in them.

He said: Ibn Abbas said concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44], Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "It is not the disbelief that removes one from the religion. When one does it, he has disbelieved by it, but it is not like one who disbelieves in God and the Last Day." Tawus and 'Ata' said the same. End of his words.

Shaykh Taqi al-Din said: The Companions and the Salaf used to say that there is in the servant faith and hypocrisy, and His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, indicates this: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167]. This is abundant in the words of the Salaf, who clarify that the heart may contain faith and hypocrisy, and the Book and the Sunna indicate this.

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has in his heart an atom's weight of faith will come out of the Fire."

So it is known that whoever has with him the least amount of faith will not remain forever in the Fire, even if he has much hypocrisy with him. Such a person is punished in the Fire according to the measure of what he has, then he comes out. He continued: The completion of this is that a person may have in him a branch of the branches of faith, a branch of the branches of disbelief, and a branch of the branches of hypocrisy. He may be a Muslim while having in him a disbelief that is less than the disbelief which removes one from Islam entirely, as the Companions said, Ibn Abbas and others: "A disbelief that is less than disbelief." This is the general view of the Salaf. End of his words.

So reflect on this section, and consider how they related the consensus (ijma') of the Salaf. Do not think this applies only to the one who errs, for his sin of error is lifted from him, as was mentioned repeatedly before.

Shaykh Taqi al-Din said in "Kitab al-Iman": Outward faith, upon which the rulings of this world are applied, does not necessarily entail inward faith. The hypocrites who said: ﴿We believe in God and the Last Day,' but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqara: 8] were outwardly believers. They prayed with the Muslims, married them, and inherited from them, just as the hypocrites were in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) did not rule concerning them with the ruling of the disbelievers who openly show disbelief, neither in marriage, nor in inheritance, nor the like. Rather, when 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy died, who was among the best known people for hypocrisy, his son 'Abdullah inherited from him, and he was one of the best of the believers. Likewise, every one of them who died was inherited from by his believing heirs. If an heir died to them, they inherited from him along with the Muslims, even if it was known that he was a hypocrite inwardly. Likewise, they were under the hudud (prescribed punishments) and rights like the rest of the Muslims. They fought alongside the Prophet (ﷺ), and among them was one who intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) at the battle of Tabuk. Despite this, outwardly the rulings of the people of faith applied to them. He continued: Their blood and their property are protected, and what is lawful to take from the disbelievers is not lawful to take from them.

As for those who profess that they are believers, or who openly show disbelief rather than faith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but God and that I am the Messenger of God. If they say it, they have protected their blood and property from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with God."

And as he said to Usama: "Did you kill him after he said there is no god but God?" He said: I said, "He only said it to seek refuge." He said: "Did you split open his heart?" And he said: "I was not commanded to search the hearts of the people or split open their bellies."

"When he was asked for permission to kill a man, he would say: 'Does he not pray? Does he not testify?' When it was said to him that he is a hypocrite, he would say that."

So his ruling concerning their blood and property was like his ruling concerning the blood of others, and he did not make lawful anything of them, even though he knew the hypocrisy of many of them. End of the words of the Shaykh.

Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may God be pleased with him, clarified in "Fayṣal al-Tafriqa bayn al-Islam wa al-Zandaqa" the disbelief that removes one from the religion, may God protect us, after his astonishing introduction, with his words: "Perhaps you desire to know the limit of disbelief after the boundaries of the categories of the imitators (muqallidun) have become confused for you. Know that the explanation of that is long and its ground is obscure, but I will give you a sound sign which you may apply and reverse, so that you take it as the aim of your inquiry, and by it you refrain from declaring sects to be disbelievers and from lengthening the tongue against the People of Islam, even if their paths differ, so long as they hold firmly to the statement: 'There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God,' affirming it truthfully and not contradicting it. I say: Disbelief is denying the Messenger, peace be upon him, in anything of what he brought, and faith is affirming him in all that he brought. So the Jew and the Christian are disbelievers because they deny the Messenger, peace be upon him. The Brahmin is a disbeliever a fortiori, because he denies all the messengers along with our Messenger. The materialist (dahri) is a disbeliever a fortiori, because he denies all the messengers along with our sent Messenger. This is because disbelief is a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), like slavery and freedom, for example. Its meaning is the permissibility of blood and the ruling of eternal abiding in the Fire, and its basis is legal, so it is known either by a text or by analogy to a text. The texts have come concerning the Jews and the Christians, and by a fortiori reasoning the Brahmins, the Dualists (thanawiyya), the zanadiqa and the materialists have been joined to them, and all of them are polytheists, for they deny the Messenger. So every disbeliever denies the Messenger, and every one who denies the Messenger is a disbeliever. This is the consistent and reversible sign."

The completion of this discussion is in this book, which no scholar can dispense with. Return to it, and hold on to it with your molars. God guides whom He wills to a straight path.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 49:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged a [thread of a] date-fiber.﴾ [49]

﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their self-praise through *tazkiyah* (claiming purity), which means cleansing and clearing oneself of what is ugly in deed and word. It contradicts what they actually are, namely the transgression and polytheism that Allah related about them earlier. The intended people are the Jews. Allah has related of them that they say: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones﴾ [al-Ma'idah: part of 18] [al-Ma'idah: part of verse 18]. He also related of them that they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: part of 80] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 80], and that they said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: part of 111] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 111].

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Ibn 'Abbas (p-1320), who said: The Jews used to bring their children forward to lead them in prayer and to offer their sacrifices, and they claimed that they had no sins or wrongdoings. They lied. Allah said: "I do not purify one burdened with a sin by means of another who has no sin." And Allah revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ That is: look at them and be amazed at their claim that they are pure before Allah, despite what they are in of disbelief and great sin; or [be amazed] at their claim that their sins are expiated, while it is impossible for anything of a disbeliever's disbelief or disobedience to be forgiven.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾, it is a reminder that His purification is the one that counts, not the purification of anyone else, for He is the One who knows what a person harbours of good and evil. He condemned them and purified the chosen believers among His servants.

* *

A note:

Al-Zamakhshari said: Everyone who claims purity for himself and describes himself as pure in deed, and as having increased in obedience, piety and nearness to Allah, falls under this verse. If you say: Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not say: "By Allah, I am trustworthy in the heavens and trustworthy on the earth"? I say: He said that when the hypocrites said to him: "Be just in the distribution," as a refutation of them, since they described him in a way contrary to how his Lord described him. And how far apart is the one for whom Allah testifies to purity from the one who testifies for himself, or for whom someone who does not know testifies.

Many hadiths have come down condemning self-praise and the claiming of purity, among them:

From Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man praising another man and extolling him excessively, so he said: "You have destroyed him, or you have cut the man's back." Agreed upon.

From Abu Bakrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and a man praised him well (p-1321), so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you! You have cut the neck of your companion," saying it repeatedly. "If one of you must praise, let him say: I reckon such-and-such, if he thinks that he is so, and his reckoning is with Allah; and let him not claim purity for anyone before Allah." Agreed upon.

From Hammam ibn al-Harith, from al-Miqdad (may Allah be pleased with him), that a man began praising 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), so al-Miqdad went and knelt on his knees and began throwing gravel into his face. 'Uthman said to him: "What is your problem?" He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who praise excessively, throw dust in their faces." Narrated by Muslim.

Imam Ahmad said: Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father, from Nu'aym ibn Abi Hind, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: Whoever says "I am a believer," then he is a disbeliever; whoever says "he is a scholar," then he is ignorant; and whoever says "he is in Paradise," then he is in the Fire.

It was narrated by Ibn Mardawayh through the route of Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Kurayz, from 'Umar, that he said: The thing I fear most for you is a person's admiration for his own opinion. Whoever says he is a believer is a disbeliever; whoever says he is a scholar is ignorant; and whoever says he is in Paradise is in the Fire.

Imam Ahmad related from Ma'bad al-Juhani, who said: "Mu'awiyah rarely narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ)," he said, "and he rarely left these words on a Friday without narrating them from the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: 'Whoever Allah intends good for, He grants him understanding of the religion. This wealth is sweet and green, so whoever takes it with its right, it will be blessed for him in it. Beware of excessive praise, for it is slaughter.'"

Ibn Majah related from him: "Beware of excessive praise, for it is slaughter."

Ibn Jarir related with his chain to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: A man goes out in the morning with his religion, then returns with nothing of it remaining (p-1322). He meets a man who has no power to benefit or harm him, and says to him: "By Allah, you are such-and-such and such-and-such!" So he may return without having achieved anything of his need, and he has angered Allah against himself. Then he recited: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾, the verse.

﴿And they will not be wronged a [thread of a] date-fiber﴾ is a conjunction with a sentence that has been omitted, relying on the indication of the context and signalling that it is not in need of mention. That is: they will be punished for that ugly act, and they will not be wronged in that punishment a *fatil*, meaning the least and smallest injustice. The *fatil* is the thread in the split of a date-stone, or the dirt rolled between the fingers, and it is used as a proverb for paucity and insignificance. It was also said that the meaning is: those who purify themselves will be rewarded, and nothing will be reduced from their reward at all. The context of warning does not support this, as Abu al-Su'ud said.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

﴿Look how they invent lies against God; and sufficient is that as a manifest sin.﴾ [50]

﴿Look how they invent lies against God﴾ — that is: in their self-praise and their claim that they are the sons of God and His beloved ones, and their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 111], and their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few countable days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 80], and their reliance on the righteous deeds of their forefathers. God has already decided that the deeds of the fathers do not avail the sons in anything, in His words: ﴿That is a community that has passed away; for it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 134] [al-Baqarah: part of verse 134], and so on.

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: (kayfa) is in the accusative, either as an adverb of manner resembling a circumstantial expression or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and its governing element is (yaftaruna), and (ʿala) is attached to it; that is: in what state, or in whatever state, they invent lies against Him, may He be exalted. The purpose is to show the enormity of that state and the completeness of its atrociousness. The clause is in the accusative position after the removal of the preposition, and (al-naẓar) is connected to both of them. This is an expression of wonder upon wonder, and an alert that what they committed includes two grave matters that both necessitate wonder: their claim to possess attributes whose opposite is actually theirs, and their fabrication against God, glorified is He. Their claim of purity before Him includes their claim of His nearness to them and His approval of them—exalted is He far above that, greatly exalted. And because this is more heinous in crime than the first, and more abhorrent in ugliness, since it involves attributing to Him, glorified and exalted is He, what is utterly impossible for Him, namely a word of disbelief, and His approval of it for His servants, and the forgiveness of a disbeliever's disbelief and all his other sins—He directed the gaze to its manner, to intensify the reproach and to emphasize the wonder. The explicit mention of "lying," although fabrication is only lying, serves to exaggerate the ugliness of their condition.

﴿And sufficient is that﴾ — that is: their this fabrication, insofar as it is a fabrication against Him, may He be exalted, setting aside its accompaniment of their self-purification and all their other great sins. ﴿as a manifest sin﴾ — clear and evident that it is a sin. The meaning: that alone suffices for them to be more sinful than every sinful disbeliever, or for their deserving the severest punishments. Then God, may He be exalted, relates of the Jews another kind of deceit, namely that they used to prefer the idol-worshippers over the believers, out of bigotry and obstinacy, in His words, glorified is He:

The Explanation of His Words, may He be exalted:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in jibt and taghut, and they say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided in the way than those who believe."﴾ [51]

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ That is: knowledge of the Torah, which calls to monotheism and to giving precedence to its people, and to rejecting jibt and taghut. Describing them with what was mentioned, namely being given a portion, is because of its incompatibility with what proceeded from them of ugly deeds (p-1324).

﴿They believe in jibt and taghut.﴾ Linguistically, al-jibt (idol, false deity, the one who is ignored) is applied to the idol, the soothsayer, the sorcerer and sorcery, that which has no good in it, and everything that is worshipped besides Allah the Exalted. Likewise al-taghut is applied to the soothsayer, the devil, every head of misguidance, the idols, everything worshipped besides Allah, and the rebellious ones of the People of the Book, as in al-Qamus.

﴿And they say of those who disbelieve﴾ That is: those who associated partners with Allah, namely the disbelievers of Makkah, meaning: concerning them and about them: ﴿"These"﴾ referring to them, ﴿"are better guided in the way than those who believe"﴾ in Allah alone: ﴿in the way﴾ meaning: more rightly guided in manner. Their mention under the title of belief is not from the side of the speakers, but from the side of Allah the Exalted, to identify them by a beautiful attribute and to censure those who preferred over them those characterized by the ugliest of ugly deeds.

**The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed. And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper.﴾ [52]

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾ means: He has removed them from His mercy and expelled them. ﴿And whoever Allah curses﴾ means: He will distance him from His mercy. ﴿You will not find for him a helper﴾ means: none will ward off punishment from him, whether it is worldly or otherworldly, neither through intercession nor through anything else.

Al-Razi said: They deserved this severe curse because what they said about preferring the idol-worshippers over those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) is tantamount to obstinate denial. How can one who worships other than Allah be better off than one who is not content with any object of worship other than Allah? And how can one whose religion is wholeheartedly devoted to serving the Creator, turning away from this world and turning toward the Hereafter, be lower in standing than one who holds the opposite of all these qualities?

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf came to Makkah, Quraysh said: "Do you see this cut-off stump from his people? He claims that he is better than us, while we are the people of the pilgrimage, the keepers of the Ka'bah, and the providers of water for the pilgrims." He said: "You are better." So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off﴾ [al-Kawthar: 3] [al-Kawthar: 3] (p-1325), and He revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ [an-Nisa': 51] down to: ﴿a helper﴾.

Imam Ibn Ishaq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Those who gathered the confederates (al-Ahzab) from Quraysh, Ghatafan, and Banu Qurayzah were Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Abu Rafi', al-Rabi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Abu Amir, Wahwah ibn Amir, and Hawdhah ibn Qays.

As for Wahwah, Abu Amir, and Hawdhah, they were from Banu Wa'il, while the rest of them were from Banu al-Nadir. When they came to Quraysh, they said: "These are the rabbis of the Jews and the people of knowledge of the first Scripture. Ask them: is your religion better, or the religion of Muhammad?" So they asked them, and they said: "Your religion is better than his, and you are more guided than he and those who follow him." So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ [an-Nisa': 51] down to His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ [an-Nisa': 54]. This is a curse upon them and an announcement that they have no helper, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, because they went seeking support from the polytheists. They only said that to them in order to win them over to their support, and the polytheists responded and came with them on the day of the Confederates, until the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions dug the trench around Madinah. So Allah sufficed them against their evil: ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they did not obtain any good. And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting. And Allah is ever Strong and Exalted in Might﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25] [al-Ahzab: from verse 25].

The commentary on His words, the Exalted:

﴿Or do they have a share of dominion? In that case they would not give the people even a speck (naqir).﴾ [53]

﴿Or do they have a share of dominion? In that case they would not give the people even a speck (naqir).﴾ When Allah, glorified is He, censured the Jews for praising themselves and for preferring the polytheists over the monotheists, He began to detail another part of their defects: their being described as stingy and envious, which are the two worst traits.

"Am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'a). The hamza is for denying that they have a share of dominion. The fa' is causal, consequent to an elided condition, meaning: "If they had a share of dominion, then they would not give anyone even the amount of a naqir, because of their extreme stinginess."

The naqir is the small pit in the back of a date stone, and it is a proverb for smallness and worthlessness, like the fatil and the qitmir. By "dominion" is meant either the dominion of the people of this world or the dominion of Allah, as in His words: ﴿Say: "If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy, you would surely withhold them for fear of spending."﴾ [al-Isra: part of verse 100].

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is the clarifying explanation of the reality of their condition. If this is their attitude while they are kings, then what do you think of them when they are humiliated and quarrelsome?

It is also possible that the hamza is not for denying the occurrence, but for denying what has occurred and rebuking them for it, that is, for regarding it as a disgraceful thing unbefitting to occur. In that case the fa' is for conjunction, and the denial is directed at the two conjoined clauses together, in the sense of: Do they have a great share of dominion, since they are owners of wealth, gardens and lofty palaces like kings, yet they do not give the people even a speck despite that? This is like saying to a rich man who does not honour his father: "Do you have this much wealth, yet you spend nothing on your father?"

The function of "idhan" (in that case) is to emphasise the denial and rebuke, since they make the existence of a share the cause of withholding, while it should be the cause of giving. It is cancelled from governing (ilgha') and does not act, as if it were said: "Then they do not give the people." It was also read as "fa-idhan la yu'tu" (with the verb in the subjunctive), treating it as operative.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom.﴾ [54]

﴿Or do they envy the people﴾: The "am" here is also disjunctive (munqati'a, meaning it introduces a new subject rather than joining to what precedes it). It shifts the rebuke from what came before, namely stinginess (al-bukhl), to rebuke for envy (al-hasad). Both are the worst of the base vices, as we have previously mentioned, and there is a mutual connection and attraction between them. The definite article in "al-nas" (the people) is for a known reference (al-'ahd), pointing to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers.

al-Tabarani narrated with his chain of transmission from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding this verse, that he said: "We are the people, and others than the people." The hamzah (the interrogative particle) is for denouncing what has occurred and considering it shameful.

(p-1327) al-Razi said: The mention of "the people" is appropriate for intending a specific group of people, because the purpose of creation is only to perform worship, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 56]. Since those who fulfil this purpose are none other than Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who follow his religion, he and his companions are as if they were all of mankind. Therefore, the term "the people" is appropriately used while specifically intending them.

﴿on account of what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾: This refers to prophethood, the Book, guidance, and the continual increase in honour and victory, day after day.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿We had already given﴾ are a justification for the denunciation and the reproach, and a binding argument against them based on what is accepted by them, and a cutting off of the root of their envy and their disbelief in the bounty. Their envy and their disbelief are based on the assumption that the one envied does not deserve what he has been given of bounty. This is refuted by demonstrating that he deserves it through inheritance, honour inherited from honour. The speech is conducted in the manner of grandeur through a shift of address (iltifat), to show the complete care regarding the matter. The meaning is: their envy mentioned above is extremely ugly and false, for We had already given, before this, ﴿the family of Abraham﴾, who are the ancestors of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his paternal cousins, ﴿the Book and wisdom﴾, meaning prophethood, ﴿and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ whose extent cannot be measured. So how do they consider his prophethood unlikely and envy him for being given it?! This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud.

al-Razi said: Envy occurs only in the presence of excellence. Thus, the more complete and perfect a person's excellence is, the greater the envy of those who envy him will be. It is well known that prophethood is the greatest of positions in religion. Then He, exalted is He, gave it to Muhammad (ﷺ) and joined to it that He made him, each day, stronger in dominion, greater in power, and more numerous in helpers and supporters. Since these blessings were the cause of these people's envy, He, exalted is He, explained what would remove that, saying: ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾. The meaning is: among the descendants of Abraham there were many groups who combined prophethood and kingship, and you are not astonished by that nor do you envy them. So why are you astonished at the condition of Muhammad (ﷺ), and why do you envy him?!

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

(p-1328) ﴿Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it; and Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire.﴾ [55]

﴿Among them are those who believed in it, and among them are those who turned away from it﴾ is a report of what proceeded from their forefathers. That is: from the same kind as these envious ones and their fathers, there are those who believed in what was given to the family of Ibrahim (Abraham), and among them are those who disbelieved in it, turned away from it, and strove to turn people away from it. He (the disbeliever) is one of them and of their kind, that is, of the Children of Israel, and they differed concerning him. So how will it be with you, O Muhammad, when you are not of the Children of Israel? The disbelievers among them are more intense in denying you and further from what you have brought them of guidance and the manifest truth. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that this is their constant habit.

﴿And Hell is sufficient as a blazing fire﴾ means: a fire kindled, by which they are punished for their disbelief, their obstinacy, and their opposition to the Books of Allah and His messengers. Then Exalted Allah informed of what He punishes with, in the Fire of Hell, those who disbelieve in His signs and turn away from His messengers, saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 56:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our verses — We will drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will exchange them for other skins, that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ [56]

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our verses — We will drive them into a Fire﴾ meaning: a great, terrifying one. ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through﴾ meaning: burned away completely. ﴿We will exchange them for other skins, that they may taste the punishment﴾ meaning: so that it may be continuous for them. This is more intense in punishment for the person, because his sensation of the Fire's effect on the skin that has not burned is more acute than his sensation of its effect on the burned skin.

* *

Note:

There are two views concerning the exchange:

The first: it is a true, material exchange, so other new skins, different from the burned ones, are created in their place.

The second: it is a descriptive exchange, meaning: We restore the skins as new, different from the burned ones in form, although they are the same substance, by removing the burning from them so that their sensation of the punishment returns. Thus only their attribute is changed, not their original substance. This view is remote, since the meaning of exchange (tabdil) rejects it.

Al-Razi said: It may be said that this is a metaphor for permanence and non-cessation, as one says of someone whose continuity is to be described: "Whenever he finishes, he has begun, and whenever he reaches its end, he has begun again from its start." Likewise His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through﴾ and so on, meaning: every time they think they have been roasted, burned, and reached destruction, We give them a new strength of life, so that they think they have now come into being and been created anew. The intended purpose is then to show the permanence of the punishment and its non-cessation. End of quotation.

This is further from the truth than what preceded it, for we have no right to turn away from the literal meaning of the words of Allah, Exalted is He, to the figurative, except out of necessity, especially since it has been transmitted from the early generations — Companions and Successors — that they are exchanged many times within a single day or hour, as Ibn Jarir and others have related in detail.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might﴾, nothing He wills is out of His reach, ﴿and Wise﴾ in what He decrees, and among that is this exchange, for the eternal punishment promised for disbelief cannot be fulfilled through a punishment that ends — those who will not be deterred from it by a punishment that ceases — and a promise must be fulfilled. Then he explained the end of the people of happiness, saying:

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to a shade, ever extending.﴾ [57]

﴿And those who believe﴾ i.e., in Muhammad ﷺ, the Qur'an, and all the Books and Messengers. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ i.e., acts of obedience, between them and their Lord, with sincerity. ﴿We will admit them﴾ i.e., in the Hereafter, ﴿to gardens﴾ i.e., orchards, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ i.e., beneath their trees and palaces, ﴿the rivers﴾ (p-1330) i.e., rivers of wine, milk, honey and water.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ i.e., remaining in the Garden, neither dying nor leaving it. ﴿For them therein﴾ i.e., in the Garden, ﴿are purified spouses﴾ i.e., purified from menstruation, post-natal bleeding, harm, base character traits and deficient attributes. ﴿And We will admit them to a shade, ever extending﴾ i.e., a shelter, a dense shelter that the sun does not dispel, with neither heat nor cold in it. "Ẓalīlan" (ever extending) is a descriptive adjective derived from the word "ẓill" (shade) to emphasize its meaning, as one says: "laylun alyal" (a very dark night) and "yawmun ayyawm" (a very long day).

In the two Sahihs, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri - may Allah be pleased with him - from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree under whose shade a rider on a swift, well-trained horse would travel for a hundred years without crossing it."

Also in the two Sahihs, from the narration of Abu Hurayrah - may Allah be pleased with him - who said: "A rider travels in its shade for a hundred years without crossing it."

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 58 (part 1 of 2):**

[The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:]
﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners. And when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾ [58]

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners.﴾ This verse is one of the foundational verses (ummahat al-ayat), comprising many of the rulings of the Sharia.

(p-1331) Abu al-Su'ud said: The opening of the statement with the word of affirmation (inna), the explicit mention of the Majestic Name (Allah), and the presentation of the command in the form of a report, together add a grandeur and an emphasis on the obligation to comply with it, and an indication of the great concern for its matter, beyond which nothing more can be added. It is an address whose ruling encompasses all the responsible persons (mukallafin) without exception, just as trusts (amanat) encompass all the rights attached to their obligations: the rights of Allah, exalted is He, and the rights of the servants, whether they are actions, statements, or beliefs. Although it was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Talha. End of quote.

That is, because the consideration is given to the generality of the wording and not to the specificity of the occasion of revelation (sabab), as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul). And they agreed (ajma'u) that trusts are to be returned to their owners, whether righteous or wicked, as Ibn al-Mundhir said.

In the hadith of Samura: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you.'" Related by Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: Many of the exegetes have mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Talha ibn Abi Talha. The name of Abu Talha is Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Uthman ibn Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy ibn Kilab al-Qurashi al-Abdari, the guardian (hajib) of the Sacred Ka'ba, and he is the paternal cousin of Shayba ibn Uthman ibn Abi Talha, in whose descendants the office of the key-keeping (hijaba) remains to this day.

This Uthman embraced Islam during the truce between the Treaty of Hudaybiya and the Conquest of Mecca, together with Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As. As for his paternal uncle, Uthman ibn Talha ibn Abi Talha, he carried the standard of the polytheists on the day of Uhud, and he was killed that day as a disbeliever.

We have only pointed out this lineage because many exegetes may confuse this one with that one.

The occasion of its revelation concerning him was when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the key of the Ka'ba from him on the day of (p-1332) the Conquest, then returned it to him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, regarding the expedition of the Conquest: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Thawr related to me, from Safiyya bint Shayba: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Mecca and the people were reassured, he went out until he came to the House, and circumambulated it seven times upon his riding camel, touching the corner with a staff (mihjan) in his hand. When he had completed his circumambulation, he called Uthman ibn Talha and took from him the key of the Ka'ba, and it was opened for him. He entered it and found in it a dove made of wood, which he broke with his hand and then threw away. Then he stood at the door of the Ka'ba while the people in the mosque had made room for him."

Ibn Ishaq said: Some of the people of knowledge related to me: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at the door of the Ka'ba and said: 'There is no god but Allah alone, without partner. He fulfilled His promise, He supported His servant, and He defeated the confederates alone. Behold, every inherited glory, blood, or property claimed is under these two feet of mine, except the custodianship of the House and the provision of water for the pilgrims (siqaya al-hajj).'"

He mentioned the rest of the hadith in the Prophet's sermon on that day, until he said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat in the mosque, and Ali ibn Abi Talib came to him with the key of the Ka'ba in his hand and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, combine for us the custodianship (hijaba) with the provision of water, may Allah bless you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Where is Uthman ibn Talha?' He was called, and [the Prophet] said to him: 'Here is your key, O Uthman. Today is a day of righteousness and fidelity.'"

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: "It was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Abi Talha. The Prophet (ﷺ) took the key of the Ka'ba from him and entered the House with it on the day of the Conquest. He came out reciting this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾, then he summoned Uthman to him and handed him the key."

He said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab said (when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out of the Ka'ba reciting this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾): My father and mother be his ransom, I had not heard him recite it before that."

Al-Suyuti said: The apparent meaning of this is that it was revealed inside the Ka'ba. End of quote.

(p-1333) And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Shahr ibn Hawshab, that this verse was revealed concerning the rulers (umara'), meaning the judges among the people.

Al-Suyuti said in "al-Iklil": In this verse is the obligation to return every trust, whether a deposit (wadi'a), a profit-sharing partnership (qirad), a loan (qard), or other than these. The Malikis used the generality of the verse as evidence that if a combatant from the enemy territory (harbi) enters our territory under safe conduct (aman) and deposits a deposit, then dies or is killed, it is obligatory to return his deposit to his heirs. And that if a Muslim borrows from a harbi in the land of war and then leaves, his repayment is obligatory. And that if a captive is entrusted by the harbi with something, it is not permissible for him to betray it. And that whoever deposits property, and the depositee had previously betrayed him, it is not permissible for him to deny it as the other denied it. Parallel to this issue is the hadith: "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning this verse, he said: "It is general (mubhama) for the righteous and the wicked, meaning in general."

Ibn Jarir and others have related that it was revealed concerning the matter of the key of the Ka'ba, when the Prophet (ﷺ) took it from Uthman ibn Talha. But what Ali and others related is preferred: that it is an address to the rulers of the Muslims, who are commanded to render the trust to those over whom they have been placed. From this, the verse is taken as evidence that it is incumbent upon the rulers, the imams, and the supervisors of endowments (nuzzar al-awqaf) to deliver the rights attached to their obligations, such as the appointment to offices and other matters, to those who deserve them. Just as His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ are a command to them to convey the rights attached to the obligations of others to their owners. Since the command here is specific to the time of litigation, it is restricted by it, unlike the command mentioned first, which, since it is not tied to a particular time, was stated absolutely. The root of justice (adl) is equality in things, so everything that departs from injustice and transgression is called justice.

Imam Muslim related from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the just (muqsitin) are with Allah upon pulpits of light, at the right hand of the Most Merciful, and both His hands are right. Those who are just in their judgment, their families, and what they are entrusted with."

(p-1334) And al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The most beloved of people to Allah on the Day of Resurrection and the nearest of them to Him in station is a just ruler (imam 'adil). And the most hated of people to Allah and the farthest of them from Him in station is a tyrannical ruler (imam ja'ir)."

Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related with a sound chain, from Ibn Abi Awfa, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, is with the judge as long as he does not oppress. But if he oppresses, Allah disassociates Himself from him and binds him to Satan."

Imam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his treatise "al-Siyasa al-Shar'iyya" after the preface: This treatise is founded upon the verse of the rulers in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, which is His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾, the verse.

The scholars said: It was revealed concerning those in charge of affairs: they must render the trusts to their owners, and when they judge between people, they must judge with justice. Then he said: Since the verse has made obligatory the rendering of trusts to their owners and judging with justice, these two are the sum of just governance (siyasa 'adila) and righteous authority (wilaya saliha). Then he said: As for the rendering of trusts, it has two kinds:

The first: the appointments to office (wilayat), and this was the occasion of the revelation of the verse. When the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Mecca and received the keys of the Ka'ba from the Banu Shayba, al-Abbas requested them so that the provision of water for the pilgrims and the custodianship of the House might be combined for him. Then Allah revealed this verse, so he returned the keys of the Ka'ba to the Banu Shayba. Therefore, it is obligatory upon the guardian of the affair to appoint, for every task of the affairs of the Muslims, the most suitable person he finds for that task.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is entrusted with any matter of the Muslims, then appoints a man while he finds someone more suitable for the Muslims than him, has betrayed Allah, His Messenger, and the believers." Related by al-Hakim in his Sahih.

And in another narration: "Whoever appoints a man to a task over a group while he finds in that group someone more pleasing than him, has betrayed Allah, His Messenger, and betrayed the believers."

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever is entrusted with any matter of the Muslims, then appoints a man because of affection or kinship between them, has betrayed Allah, His Messenger, and the Muslims. Therefore, it is obligatory upon him to search for those deserving of the offices among his deputies in the provinces, from the amirs who are the deputies of the holder of authority and of the judiciary, and from the commanders of the troops and the leaders of the large and small armies, and the officials in charge of finances, such as the viziers, scribes, collectors, and those who collect the land tax (kharaj) and the alms (sadaqat), and other than these of the properties belonging to the Muslims. Each of these must appoint and employ the most suitable person he finds. This extends to the prayer leaders (a'immat al-salat), the muezzins, the reciters, the teachers, the commanders of the pilgrims, the postal couriers (buruq), the treasurers of wealth, the chiefs of the large and small armies, and the headmen (urafa') of tribes and markets.

It is incumbent upon everyone entrusted with any of the affairs of the Muslims, whether amirs or others, to employ in whatever is under his hand, in every place, the most suitable person he is able to find. A man is not to be preferred because he sought the post or was quick to seek it; rather, that is a reason for denying it. For in the Sahih, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Some people entered upon him and asked him for an appointment, and he said: 'We do not appoint to this matter of ours anyone who seeks it.'"

And he said to Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura: "O Abd al-Rahman! Do not ask for the emirate. For if you are given it without asking, you will be aided in it, and if you are given it upon asking, you will be left to it." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related it in the two Sahihs.

(p-1336) And he said: "Whoever seeks the judgeship and seeks help in it will be left to it, and whoever does not seek it and does not seek help in it, Allah sends down to him an angel who guides him." Related by the authors of the Sunan.

If he turns away from the most entitled and most suitable to another, because of kinship between them, or appoints him out of manumission (ataqa), friendship, agreement in school of thought, region, method, or ethnic group, such as Arab, Persian, Turkish, or Roman, or for a bribe he takes from him from his property or some benefit, or for other such reasons, or out of spite in his heart against the most entitled, or enmity between them, then he has betrayed Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, and has entered into what is forbidden in His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know [better]﴾ [al-Anfal: 27] [al-Anfal: 27].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward﴾ [al-Anfal: 28] [al-Anfal: 28]. A man, out of love for his son or his freedman, may give him preference in some positions of authority or give him what he does not deserve, and thus he has betrayed his trust. Likewise, he may prefer to increase the protection or wealth of such a person by taking what he does not deserve, or by showing favour to one who flatters him in some positions of authority, and thus he has betrayed Allah and His Messenger and betrayed his trust. Then, indeed, the one who discharges the trust, despite going against his own desires, Allah rewards him by safeguarding his family and wealth after him; and the one who follows his desires, Allah punishes him with the opposite of his intention, so that his family is humiliated and his wealth is lost. On this there is the well-known account: that one of the caliphs of the Banu al-'Abbas asked one of the scholars to relate what he had witnessed, and he said: "I saw 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and it was said to him: 'O Commander of the Faithful! You have left your sons in poverty from this wealth, and you have left them destitute with nothing for themselves.' – and this was during his final illness – so he said: 'Bring them in to me.' They were brought in, and they were about ten boys, none of them adult. When he saw them, his eyes filled with tears, and then he said: 'By Allah, my sons, I have not withheld from you a right that is yours, nor was I one who takes the wealth of people and gives it to you. You are only one of two men: either righteous, and Allah takes charge of the righteous; or not righteous, and I will not leave him anything with which he may seek help in disobeying Allah. Stand up and leave me.'"
He said: "I indeed saw one of his sons give a hundred [mounts] in the way of Allah," meaning he gave them to whoever would go on raids with them.
I say: This was while he was the caliph of the Muslims from the farthest east, in the lands of the Turks, to the farthest west, in al-Andalus and other places, including the island of Cyprus, the frontier regions of al-Sham, and the great cities such as Tarsus and the like, down to the farthest part of Yemen. He only allotted each of his sons a small portion of his estate; it is said: less than twenty dirhams.
He said: "I was present with some caliphs when his sons divided his estate, and each one took six hundred thousand dinars. And I indeed saw some of them begging from people, that is, asking them with his palm." In this matter, there are accounts and events witnessed in our time and heard of from before it, which are a lesson for everyone of understanding.
The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has indicated that authority is a trust which must be discharged in a situation like what has preceded, and like his saying to Abu Dharr – may Allah be pleased with him – concerning leadership: "It is a trust, and on the Day of Resurrection it will be a cause of regret and remorse, except for the one who takes it with its right and discharges what is upon him," as related by Muslim.
Al-Bukhari related in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah – may Allah be pleased with him – that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the trust is lost, then await the Hour." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! And what is its loss?" He said: "When affairs are entrusted to other than their people, then await the Hour."
The Muslims have agreed upon this.
Then Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The second category: trusts of wealth, as Allah the Exalted said concerning debts: ﴿And if one of you trusts another, let him who is trusted discharge his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283] [al-Baqarah: from verse 283]. This category includes specific and general property and debts, such as returning deposits, the property of a partner, of one who appoints an agent, of a mudarib (silent partner in a profit-sharing arrangement), the property of a guardian belonging to an orphan, the people of an endowment (waqf), and the like; and likewise the payment of debts from the prices of goods sold, the substitute of a loan, the dowries of women, the wages for usufruct, and the like. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19] ﴿When evil touches him, impatient﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 20] ﴿And when good touches him, withholding﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 21] ﴿Except for the performers of prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 22] ﴿Who are constant in their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 23] ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24] ﴿For the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 25] – up to His saying: ﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 32] [al-Ma'arij: 32]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [al-Nisa': 105] [al-Nisa': 105], meaning: do not dispute on their behalf.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "The believer is one from whom people feel secure regarding their lives and their property, and the Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, and the emigrant is one who emigrates from what Allah has forbidden, and the mujahid is one who strives against his own self for the sake of Allah." This is a sahih hadith; part of it is in the two Sahihs and part in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever takes the wealth of people intending to repay it, Allah will repay it on his behalf; and whoever takes it intending to destroy it, Allah will destroy him." Related by al-Bukhari.
Since Allah the Exalted has made obligatory the discharge of trusts that were received rightfully, this contains an alert to the obligation of returning what was seized unjustly, stolen, or embezzled, and similar wrongs; likewise the return of a loan (ariyah). The completion of this discussion may be studied in the aforementioned treatise, for consulting it is among the essential matters.
﴿Indeed, Allah is excellent in what He instructs you﴾, meaning: how excellent is what He commands you with of discharging trusts, judging justly among people, and other of His commands and His complete and great laws. The word "ma" (what) is either in the accusative, described by "yaʻizukum" (He instructs you), or in the nominative as a relative pronoun; as if it were said: "an excellent thing with which He instructs you," or "the excellent thing with which He instructs you." The sentence is resumed, confirming what precedes and including additional gentleness toward the addressees and a good manner of inviting them to comply with the command.
﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing﴾ of your statements regarding trusts and judgments, ﴿Seeing﴾ of your deeds in them. So if He hears and sees good, He will reward you with the best reward; and if He hears and sees evil, He will repay you for it. This is a promise and a warning.
Ibn Abi Hatim related with his chain from Abu Yunus who said: "I heard Abu Hurayrah recite this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Hearing and seeing﴾, and he would place his thumb on his ear, and the finger next to it on his eye, and say: 'Thus I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it,' and he would place his finger."
Abu Zakariyya said: "Al-Muqri described it to us, and Abu Zakariyya placed his right thumb on his right eye, and the finger next to it on his right ear, and showed us, and said: 'Thus, and thus.'" Related by Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and Ibn Mardawayh in his Tafsir.
This Abu Yunus was a mawla (freedman) of Abu Hurayrah, and his name was Sulaym ibn Jubayr, as mentioned by Ibn Kathir.
