**The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more suitable in outcome.﴾ [59]

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.﴾ Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the rulers and governors to render trusts to their rightful owners and to judge with justice, He commanded the subjects, including the armies and others, to obey those in authority who act accordingly in their distribution of wealth, their judgments, their military campaigns, and other matters. However, if they command disobedience to Allah, then there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator.

Al-Razi said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is incumbent upon the imam to judge by what Allah has revealed and to render the trust. When he does that, it is incumbent upon the subjects to listen and obey." Al-Tabari also narrated with a sound chain from Abu Hurayrah that the "those in authority" are the rulers.

Al-Shafi'i argued for this, saying that Quraysh and those around them among the Arabs did not recognise leadership and did not submit to a commander. So they were commanded to obey whoever holds authority and to submit to him when he dispatches them on expeditions (sariyyah, a small military detachment), and when he appoints them over lands, they should not rebel against him or resist him, so that the word would not be divided. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me." (Agreed upon.)

In al-Bukhari, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, "from Ibn 'Abbas who said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah ibn Qays ibn 'Adi when the Prophet (ﷺ) dispatched him on a sariyyah."

Ibn Kathir said: Thus it was narrated by the rest of the compilers except Ibn Majah. And al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan gharib hadith, and we do not know it except from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj."

Al-Tabari narrated from al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning an incident that occurred between 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Khalid ibn al-Walid, and Khalid was a commander. 'Ammar granted protection to a man without Khalid's order, so they disputed and brought their case to the Prophet (ﷺ). He upheld 'Ammar's protection and forbade him from compelling the second party to submit to a commander.

Ibn Kathir said: Thus Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it through a chain from al-Suddi as a mursal (a report lacking a companion in its chain), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, mentioning it in similar terms. End quote.

There is no contradiction between the two reports, as we mentioned in the introduction to the tafsir in the discussion of the occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), so reflect on this.

Al-Zamakhshari said: By "those in authority among you" is meant the rulers of truth, because Allah and His Messenger are free of the rulers of oppression. So they are not coupled with Allah and His Messenger in the obligation of obedience to them. Rather, Allah and His Messenger are only joined with those rulers who agree with them in preferring justice, choosing truth, commanding these, and forbidding their opposites, such as the rightly-guided caliphs and those who followed them in excellence. The caliphs used to say: "Obey me as long as I act justly among you; but if I deviate, there is no obedience to me from you."

In the two Sahihs, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "Obedience is only in what is right."

Imam Ahmad narrated from 'Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "There is no obedience in disobedience to Allah."

A subtle point:
Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: The reason for repeating the verb before "the Messenger" but not before "those in authority", although the one truly obeyed is Allah, the Exalted, is that by which the obligations are known are the Qur'an and the Sunnah. So the implied meaning is: "Obey Allah regarding what He has decreed for you in the Qur'an, and obey the Messenger regarding what he has made clear to you from the Qur'an and what he has specified for you from the Sunnah." The meaning is: obey Allah in what He commands you from the revelation recited in worship, and obey the Messenger in what he commands you from the revelation that is not the Qur'an.

An excellent response: a certain Successor (tabi'i) said to one of the Umayyad rulers, when he said to him: "Did not Allah command you to obey us in His words: 'and those in authority among you'?" He replied: "Has not obedience been removed from you when you oppose the truth, by His words: 'And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah'?!"

Al-Tibi said: He repeated the verb in "and obey the Messenger" to indicate that the Messenger is independently to be obeyed, and he did not repeat it for "those in authority", to indicate that among them there are some whose obedience is not obligatory. Then he explained that by His words: "And if you disagree over anything", as if it were said: "If they do not act upon the truth, then do not obey them, and refer what you differ over to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger." End quote. (vol. 13, p. 99).

\* \*

A note:
The general wording of "those in authority" includes the scholars, as narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas that it means the people of jurisprudence (fiqh) and religion. Likewise said Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Hasan al-Basri and Abu al-'Aliyah. This is not a second opinion regarding the verse, but rather something its wording encompasses. So it is general to the rulers and the scholars, even though it was revealed on a specific occasion. Commands to obey scholars are numerous, as they are to obey rulers. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Why do the rabbis and scholars not forbid them from their sayings of sin and their consumption of unlawful gain?﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 63]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance (ahl al-dhikr, those with knowledge) if you do not know.﴾ [Al-Nahl: 43]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who [can] draw correct conclusions from it would have known it.﴾ [Al-Nisa': 83].

In the authentic hadith agreed upon as sound, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah, and whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys my commander has disobeyed me."

Abu Dawud narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "Listening and obeying is incumbent upon the Muslim person in what he loves and in what he dislikes, as long as he is not commanded to disobedience. But if he is commanded to disobedience, there is no listening and no obedience."

Al-Bukhari narrated from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Listen and obey, even if an Abyssinian slave with a head like a raisin is put in charge over you." And the hadiths on this are numerous.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book "al-Hisbah fi al-Islam": Allah, the Exalted, has commanded in His Book obedience to Him, obedience to His Messenger, and obedience to those in authority among the believers. Those in authority are the possessors of command, those who command the people. This involves both the people of power and capacity and the people of knowledge and speech. Therefore, those in authority are of two categories: the scholars and the rulers. If they are righteous, the people are righteous, and if they are corrupt, the people are corrupt, as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said (when al-Ahmasiyyah asked him about our remaining upon this affair): "Your leaders have remained upright for you." It includes kings, shaykhs, and the administrators of the registry (diwan), and everyone who is followed is among those in authority. Each of these must command what Allah has commanded and forbid what He has forbidden, and each person to whom obedience is owed must obey him in obedience to Allah and not obey him in disobedience to Allah, as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said when he assumed the affairs of the Muslims and addressed them in his sermon: "O people! The strong among you is weak in my sight until I take the right from him, and the weak among you is strong in my sight until I secure his right for him. Obey me as long as I obey Allah; but if I disobey Allah, there is no obedience to me from you."

﴿And if you disagree﴾, that is: you and those in authority differ, ﴿over anything﴾ from the rulings, ﴿refer it to Allah﴾, that is: return to His Book regarding it, ﴿and the Messenger﴾ by asking him during his lifetime (ﷺ), and by returning to his Sunnah after him, not to what you desire, nor to what the rulers desire. ﴿If you should believe in Allah﴾, who established the laws of justice, ﴿and the Last Day﴾ on which those who agree with and those who oppose those laws will be recompensed, ﴿that﴾, that is: the referral to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger and returning to them in settling disputes, ﴿is better﴾, that is: for you and for your rulers, ﴿and more suitable﴾, that is: in outcome and final result, as al-Suddi and others said. Mujahid said: "and better in reward," and it is close in meaning.

Ibn Kathir said: This is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that every matter over which people disagree, whether among the foundations of religion or its branches, the dispute should be referred to the Book and the Sunnah, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever you disagree about, its judgment is with Allah﴾ [Al-Shura: 10]. Whatever the Book and the Sunnah judge and testify to be correct is the truth, and what is after the truth but error? For this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you should believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, that is: refer disputes and ignorance to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, so judge between yourselves by them concerning what is in dispute among you, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. This indicates that whoever does not seek judgment in the place of dispute by the Book and the Sunnah, and does not return to them in that matter, is not a believer in Allah nor in the Last Day. End quote.

\* \*

Points of note:

First: Al-Baydawi said: His words, ﴿And if you disagree﴾, support that what is meant by "those in authority" is the rulers and not the scholars. He said: Because it is not permissible for the layman (muqallid) to dispute the mujtahid's ruling in the way a subordinate would. Then he said: Unless it is said that the address to those in authority is in the manner of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). Abu al-Su'ud followed him.

Al-Khafaji said: The basis of the support is that the common people may dispute with rulers over some matters, but they do not have the right to dispute with the scholars, since the intended scholars are the mujtahids, and other people do not dispute with them over their rulings. By "the subordinate" (on the pattern of maf'ul) is meant the common people who follow the leader and the head. So when the address in "you disagreed" is to those in authority by way of iltifat, it is valid to intend the scholars, because the mujtahids may dispute with one another in debate and argument, so the meaning is the command to them to hold to what the evidence requires. End quote.

As for his words, "since it is not permissible for the layman...", there is what you will see.

Second: Many people and also exegetes understood that obedience to those in authority who are scholars means following them blindly (taqlid) in what they give fatwas about, and this is an error. Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in", in:

**A chapter**
On convening a debate session between a muqallid and a person of proof who submits to the truth wherever it is.

The muqallid said: Allah has commanded obedience to Him, obedience to His Messenger (ﷺ), and to those in authority, who are the scholars, or the scholars and rulers. Obedience to them is taqlid to them in what they issue fatwas about, for without taqlid there would be no obedience specific to them. He said: His answer is that it has been said that those in authority are the rulers, and it has been said they are the scholars, and these are two narrations from Imam Ahmad. The verification is that the verse encompasses both groups, and their obedience is from the obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ). But it was hidden from the muqallids that they are obeyed in obedience to Allah when they command what Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) command. So where in the verse is there the preference of the opinions of men over the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the preference of taqlid over it?!

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: This verse is among the greatest proofs against them and the most powerful in refuting taqlid, and that is from several aspects:

The first: the command to obey Allah, which is carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibition.

The second: obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). A servant is not obedient to Allah and His Messenger until he is knowledgeable of the command of Allah and His Messenger. As for one who is a muqallid to the people of knowledge in these matters, it is impossible for him to actually realise obedience to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) at all.

**Part 2 of 2**

Third: The custodians of authority (*ulil-amr*) have themselves forbidden people to follow them blindly (*taqlid*), as is authentically reported from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Abdullah ibn Umar, Abdullah ibn Abbas, and others among the Companions. We have also cited this from the four Imams and others. In that case, if obeying them in this matter were obligatory, *taqlid* would be nullified; and if it were not obligatory, then reasoning from evidence (*istidlal*) would be nullified.

Fourth: In the same verse, He, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger, if you truly believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is an explicit statement nullifying *taqlid* and forbidding the referral of a disputed matter to an opinion, a school of thought, or a *taqlid*. If it is said: What, then, is the obedience that is specific to them?

If the obedience is in what they report from Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger ﷺ, then obedience is to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, not to them. It is said: This is the truth, and their obedience is only a follower's obedience, not an independent one. For this reason He joined it with obedience to the Messenger and repeated the governing verb (*'amil*), lest it be supposed that he is obeyed only derivatively, as the custodians of authority are obeyed derivatively. That is not the case. Rather, his obedience is obligatory in its own right, whether he commanded or forbade something in the Qur'an or not. End.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, said before this: The sect of *taqlid* has committed a violation of the command of Allah the Exalted, the command of His Messenger ﷺ, the guidance of his Companions, and the states of their Imams, and they have taken the opposite path to that of the people of knowledge. As for the command of Allah the Exalted, He commanded that what the Muslims dispute be referred to Him and to His Messenger, whereas the *muqallidun* say: We refer it only to the one we follow.

As for the command of His Messenger ﷺ, he ordered, at times of disagreement, that one hold to his Sunnah and the Sunnah of his rightly guided successors, the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and that one cling to it and bite upon it with the molars. The *muqallidun* say: Rather, at times of disagreement we cling to the statement of the one we follow and give it precedence over everything else.

As for the guidance of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, it is known by necessity that no single person used to follow one man in all his statements while opposing all the other Companions, so that he rejects none of his statements and accepts none of theirs. This is among the greatest innovations and the most reprehensible novelties.

As for their opposition to their Imams, the Imams forbade following them and warned against it, as some of this has already been mentioned from them. Their statements are to be examined, scrutinized, and presented to the Qur'an, the established Sunnahs of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the statements of his rightly guided successors. Whatever agrees with these they accept, adopt as their religion, act upon, and issue legal opinions based on. Whatever contradicts these they disregard and reject. As for matters that have not become clear to them, they regard them as among the matters of *ijtihad*, whose ultimate status is that they are permissible to follow, not obligatory to follow, without imposing them on anyone or saying that they are the truth to the exclusion of whatever opposes them. This is the way of the people of knowledge, earlier and later.

But these later people reversed the path and inverted the order of the religion. They have discredited the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, the statements of his successors, and all his Companions, presenting them to the statements of those whom they follow. Whatever agrees with those statements they say: "This is ours," and submit to it in acceptance. Whatever contradicts the statements of their school's authority they say: "The opponent has argued with such-and-such" (*p. 1350*), and they do not accept it or adopt it. Their scholars strive by every possible means to reject it, seeking out every stratagem they can think of. Then, when the same arguments are present in a text that agrees with their school, they denounce their opponents for rejecting it by those very same arguments, and they say: "Texts are not to be rejected on this basis!" Whoever has an aspiration that rises toward Allah and His pleasure, and toward supporting the truth with which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, wherever it is and with whomever it is, would not be content for himself with this vile course and this blameworthy disposition. End.

Third: If it is said: Why could the meaning of His words ﴿then refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ not be: entrust its knowledge to Allah and remain silent about it, not engaging with it? And why could it not be that the meaning is: refer these rulings to the original state of non-obligation (*al-bara'ah al-asliyyah*)?

We say: As for the first, it is refuted, because this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, divided events into two categories. One category is those whose ruling is explicitly stated, and the other is those whose ruling is not explicitly stated. In the first category He commanded obedience and submission, and in the second category He commanded striving (*ijtihad*) in it, and that is referring it back to Allah and to the Messenger. It is not permissible that the meaning of this referral be silence, because the event, whatever it is, cannot tolerate that. Rather, there must be an end to the contention and dispute concerning it, by negation or affirmation. And since this is so, it is impossible to interpret the referral to Allah as silence about that event.

As for the second question, its answer is that the original state of non-obligation is known by the dictates of reason. Therefore, referring the event to it is not a referral to Allah in any sense. But when we refer the ruling on the event to the explicitly stated rulings, this is a referral of the event to the rulings of Allah the Exalted. So interpreting the expression in this way is preferable. Transmitted by al-Razi.

Fourth: Those who affirm analogy (*qiyas*) have used as evidence His words: ﴿then refer it back to Allah﴾, etc. They said: The meaning of the verse is: If you dispute over something whose ruling is not mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah, then refer its ruling to the explicitly stated rulings concerning similar events, and that is analogy. They said: If the meaning of His words ﴿refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ were seeking its ruling from the texts of the Book and the Sunnah, it would fall under His words ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, and that would be a repetition of the same thing as what preceded (*sic*), which is impermissible.

Al-Razi expanded considerably on this argument here, just as he expanded on the claim that His words ﴿and those in authority﴾ point to consensus (*ijma'*). Thus, according to his claim, the verse indicates the four foundations (of jurisprudence). The depth of such inference, in his view, is not hidden.

Fifth: We previously cited al-Bukhari's report concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, that Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Hudhafah.

Al-Dawudi (commentator on the Sahih) said: This is an error on the part of Ibn Abbas. Abdullah ibn Hudhafah went out in command of an army and became angry with them, so he ordered them to light a fire and plunge into it. Some of them refused, and some were about to do it.

He said: If the verse was revealed before this, how is Abdullah ibn Hudhafah singled out for obedience over others? And if it was revealed after, then they were only told: "Obedience is only in what is good," and they were not told: "Why did you not obey him?" End.

Ibn Hajar al-Hafiz answered: That is, the point of the story is His words ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it back to﴾, because they disagreed about carrying out what he had commanded them. The cause is that those who were about to comply stopped at the point of obeying the command, while those who refused were moved by the desire to flee from the fire. So it was fitting that there be revealed what guides them to what they should do when they dispute, namely referring back to Allah and to His Messenger. That is: if you dispute over whether a thing is permissible or not, then return to the Book and the Sunnah. And Allah knows best.

Since the Exalted made obedience to Allah and His Messenger obligatory upon all the responsible, He gave preference to them by saying that the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease do not obey the Messenger and are not content with his judgment, but seek the judgment of others. So He said:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to take their disputes to the false deity (ṭāghūt)? And they were commanded to reject it, while Satan desires to lead them far astray.﴾ [60]

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾ meaning the Torah. Describing them with the claim of believing in the Qur'an and in what was revealed before it serves to emphasize the wonder at their state and to intensify the rebuke and condemnation, by showing the complete contradiction between their claim, which necessarily requires referring judgment to the Messenger, and what proceeded from them of opposing the binding command.

﴿They desire to take their disputes to the ṭāghūt﴾ the one who calls to transgression by judging contrary to what has been revealed to you and what was revealed to those before you. The meanings of ṭāghūt (the transgressor, that which is worshipped or obeyed beyond God) were mentioned shortly before, and what is meant here is whatever other than the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger, of falsehood.

﴿And they were commanded﴾ in all those books ﴿to reject it﴾, that is, to disavow it, because it is judging by other than what God has revealed in His books; so they disobey Him and obey Satan. ﴿While Satan desires﴾, that is, from among the jinn and mankind, ﴿to lead them far astray﴾ from the truth and guidance.

His words ﴿while [Satan] desires﴾ etc. are a conjunction with (they desire), falling under the same ruling of wonder, for their following of the one who desires their misguidance, and their turning away from the One who desires their guidance, is more wondrous than any wonder.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with [complete] aversion.﴾ [4:61]

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed"﴾ i.e., to the ruling of what Allah has revealed in the Qur'an, which you claim to believe in. ﴿And to the Messenger﴾ i.e., to his ruling. ﴿You see the hypocrites turning away﴾ i.e., they prevent (their adversaries) and keep them away, ﴿from you with [complete] aversion﴾, emphatically, (p-1353) so that they may accomplish what they want through bribery.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when it is said﴾, etc., completes the subject of wonder by explaining their explicit aversion to seeking judgment by the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, following the explanation of their aversion to that within the seeking of judgment by the taghut. The mention of (the hypocrites) in the place of a pronoun serves to record hypocrisy against them, to censure them for it, and to indicate the reason for the ruling.

* *

Note: on the occasion of its revelation

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Barzah al-Aslami used to be a soothsayer who judged between the Jews in what they disputed, so some Muslims went to him to dispute, and Allah revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they have believed﴾ [4:60] to His saying: ﴿except for good and conciliation﴾ [4:62].

I say: Then Abu Barzah embraced Islam and accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ); his name was Nadlah ibn 'Ubayd.

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Taqrib: A companion well known by his kunya, he embraced Islam before the Conquest, fought seven campaigns, then settled in Basra, campaigned in Khurasan, and died there in the year 65 [AH], according to the most correct opinion. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim related through the route of 'Ikrimah, or Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Al-Jallas ibn al-Samit, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, Rafi' ibn Zayd, and Bishr — they claimed Islam. Men of their people from the Muslims invited them to dispute between them before the Messenger (ﷺ), but they invited them to the soothsayers, the judges of the Jahiliyyah, so Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim﴾ [4:60], the verse.

Ibn Jarir related, from al-Sha'bi, who said: There was a dispute between a Jew and a hypocrite. The Jew said: "Let me judge you by people of your religion," or he said: "by the Prophet (ﷺ), for he knows that he does not take bribery in judgment." They disagreed and agreed to go to a soothsayer in Juhaynah, and so it was revealed. There is no contradiction with what we preceded in the introduction in the discussion of the occasion of revelation, so reflect on it.

(p-1354) Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that he was a hypocrite from the People of the Book, such as that he was a Jew who outwardly professed Islam in the manner of hypocrisy, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾ [4:60], is only fitting for such a hypocrite. End of quote.

I say: What he deduced contradicts what we have preceded of what has been related about its revelation. Moreover, describing them as believing in ﴿what was revealed before you﴾ does not support what he mentioned, because this is often mentioned as a commendation of it, an affirmation of its being a pillar of faith, and a reminder of it, as is not hidden from one who has examined the principle of revelation in such cases, so understand it.

Discussions

First: The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: This verse is a denunciation from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of one who claims to believe in what Allah revealed to His Messenger and to the earlier Prophets, yet at the same time wants to seek judgment in settling disputes from other than the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation of this verse. Then he cited what we have presented and said: The verse is more general than all of that, for it censures whoever turns away from the Book and the Sunnah and seeks judgment by what is other than them of falsehood; this is what is meant here by (the taghut), and they turn away arrogantly, as He, exalted is He, said concerning the polytheists: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has revealed," they say, "Rather, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers."﴾ [2:170] [Al-Baqarah: part of verse 170]. These are unlike the believers, concerning whom Allah said: ﴿The only statement of the believers when they are invited to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them is that they say, "We hear and we obey."﴾ [24:51] [Al-Nur: part of verse 51], the verse.

Second: The Qadi said: Seeking judgment by this taghut must be like disbelief, and not being content with the ruling of Muhammad (ﷺ) is disbelief, and this is indicated by several points:

The first: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They desire to seek judgment before the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it﴾ [4:60], so He made seeking judgment before the taghut (p-1355) a form of belief in it, and there is no doubt that belief in the taghut is disbelief in Allah, just as rejecting the taghut is belief in Allah.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that which is disputed among them﴾ [4:65], to His saying: ﴿and submit in full submission﴾ [4:65] [An-Nisa: part of verse 65]. This is explicit in declaring disbelief of whoever is not content with the ruling of the Messenger (ﷺ).

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let those beware who oppose his order, lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment* [24:63] [Al-Nur: part of verse 63]. This indicates that opposing him is a great disobedience.

In these verses there are evidences that whoever rejects any of the commands of Allah, or the commands of the Messenger (ﷺ), is outside Islam, whether he rejects it out of doubt or out of rebellion, and this necessitates the correctness of what the Companions held regarding the apostasy of those who withheld zakat, and their killing, and the taking captive of their offspring, as al-Razi related.

The fourth: Some exegetes said: In this verse is the obligation of contentment with the decree of Allah, glory be to Him, and contentment with what He legislated, and it indicates that it is not permissible to seek judgment by other than the law of Islam.

Al-Hakim said: It also indicates that whoever is not content with His ruling has disbelieved, and what was related of the action of 'Umar and his killing of the hypocrite indicates that his blood is forfeited, with no retaliation or blood-money owed for it.

Here is a branch: it may be said that if two men dispute a matter and one of them is content with the ruling of the Muslims while the other refuses and demands judgment by the ruler of the atheists, then he disbelieves, because in that there is contentment with the symbol of the disbelievers. End of quote.

The fourth: In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They desire to seek judgment﴾ [4:60] there is a subtle and wondrous point. Abu al-Su'ud said: (p-1356) Limiting, in the context of wonder and reprobation, the mention to the desire to seek judgment, rather than the act itself, even though the act also occurs, is to draw attention to the fact that even the desire for it is something that warrants wonder and should not be allowed to reach the point of actuality; so what then is your opinion of the act itself?!

The fifth: The exegetes said: The hypocrites only turned away from the ruling of the Messenger (ﷺ) because they were wrongdoers, and they knew that he does not take bribes and that he judges only with the bitter judgment. It was also said: that aversion was due to their enmity toward religion.

And His saying, exalted is He:

**The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿So how will it be when a calamity strikes them because of what their hands have sent ahead, and then they come to you swearing by Allah, "We intended nothing but good and reconciliation"?﴾ [62]

﴿So how will it be when a calamity strikes them because of what their hands have sent ahead﴾ is connected to what precedes it. It explains the harmful outcome of their transgressions that were related above and the severity of their consequences. That is: how will their condition be when destiny drives them to you, amid calamities that befall them because of their sins, among which are their seeking judgment from the false deity (al-taghut) and their aversion to your ruling, and they will need you in that matter?

﴿Then they come to you﴾ to make excuses for the ugly deeds they committed. ﴿Swearing by Allah﴾ falsely, ﴿"We intended nothing"﴾, that is, by that seeking of judgment, ﴿"but good"﴾, that is, a decision in the fair manner, ﴿"and reconciliation"﴾ by settling between the two disputants. ﴿"We did not intend to oppose you, nor to show displeasure at your ruling. So do not hold us accountable for what we did."﴾ This is a warning to them for what they did, and that they will regret it, but regret will not benefit them, and excuses will not avail them.

Al-Razi said: The commentators mentioned several views concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿a calamity strikes them﴾:

The first: it refers to the killing of their companion by ʿUmar, who had affirmed that he would not accept the ruling of the Messenger (peace be upon him). They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and demanded ʿUmar's blood, and they swore that they had intended, by going to someone other than the Messenger, only what was in the public interest. This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj.

(p-1357) I say: His choice is not a preferred one, because the story of ʿUmar killing him has not been transmitted through any sound or fair chain. It is therefore discarded according to the verifying scholars. The argument of al-Hakim (the judge), which we mentioned earlier, is accepted if the story were authentic.

The second: Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i said: What is meant by this calamity is what Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger (peace be upon him) concerning them: that he should not take them along on the military campaigns, and that he should single them out for greater humiliation and expulsion from his presence. This is His saying: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease and the agitators in the city do not desist, We will surely incite you against them. Then they will not remain your neighbors therein except briefly. Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and killed with intense slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60–61], and His saying: ﴿Say, "You will never go out with me, ever"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83]. In sum, verses like these entail for them great humiliation, so they were counted among their calamities, and it strikes them only because of their hypocrisy.

The third: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: When Allah, exalted is He, informed about the hypocrites that they desired the judgment of the false deity and disliked the judgment of the Messenger, He gave good news to the Messenger (ﷺ) that calamities would strike them which would compel them to come to him, to show him their faith in him, and to swear that their intention was good and reconciliation. He said: It is a custom of the Arabs, when giving good tidings or warning, to say, "How will you be when such-and-such happens?" An example of this is His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [al-Nisa': 41], and His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al ʿImran: 25]. Then, when that happens to them, Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to turn away from them and admonish them. End quote.

(p-1358) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts, so turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves.﴾ [63]

﴿Those﴾ refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun), ﴿whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ of hypocrisy and inclination toward falsehood, even though they display their Islam and their excuse through their oaths. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning: do not punish them, for the sake of an interest in preserving them, and do not go beyond restraining them with admonition and advice concerning what they are upon. ﴿And admonish them﴾, meaning: restrain them from the hypocrisy and the hidden evils in their hearts. ﴿And speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves﴾, meaning: an effective word that reaches the essence of the intended meaning.

If it is asked: with what does His saying, exalted is He, ﴿concerning themselves﴾ connect? The answer: it connects with His saying ﴿far-reaching﴾, according to the view of those who permit placing the complement of an adjective before the modified noun, meaning: speak to them a far-reaching word concerning themselves, effective upon their hearts, which causes them to be distressed with grief and to sense fear, namely the threat of killing and extermination should hypocrisy sprout among them and raise its head. And inform them that what is in their souls of corruption and hypocrisy is known to Allah, that there is no difference between you and the polytheists, and that this outward reconciliation is only for your display of faith and concealment and concealing of disbelief; so if you do what reveals your covering, nothing will remain but the sword.

Or it connects with His saying ﴿And speak to them﴾, meaning: speak to them, in the sense of their wicked souls and their hearts folded upon hypocrisy, a far-reaching word, and that Allah knows what is in your hearts, nothing is hidden from Him, so your concealing it will not avail you. So amend your souls, purify your hearts, and cure them from the disease of hypocrisy, or else Allah will bring upon you what He brought upon those who openly associated partners with Him, of His vengeance, and worse than that and more severe. Or: speak to them concerning themselves, privately, being alone with them, with no one else present, confidentially giving them counsel, for it is more effective in secret and more penetrating in sincere counsel: ﴿a far-reaching word﴾ that reaches them and affects them. Thus is it derived from al-Kashshaf.

Al-Nasir said in "al-Insaf": Each of these interpretations has evidence for its soundness.

As for the first: its essence is commanding him to threaten them in a way that reaches the core of their hearts, and the context of the threat in His saying (p-1359) ﴿How then, when a disaster strikes them for what their hands have sent forth, and then they come to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 62] bears witness to it, for He informed of what would befall them by way of threat.

As for the second: the context supports it through His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾, meaning what they harbor of wickedness, deceit and stratagems. Then He commanded him to admonish them and turn away from their offenses, so that punishing them for these should not prevent him from advising and admonishing them. Then came His saying: ﴿And speak to them concerning themselves a far-reaching word﴾ as an explanation of the admonition and a mention of the most important matter in which he admonishes them, namely their souls, which Allah knows harbor the blameworthy qualities. On this view, the intended meaning is admonition and what relates to it.

As for the third: his conduct, peace and blessings be upon him, bears witness to it, in concealing the obstinacy of the hypocrites, overlooking their open expression, and covering over them, to the point that Huthayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, was counted as the keeper of his secret, peace and blessings be upon him, because he singled him out with knowledge of their identities and his naming them by their names; and reports on this meaning are numerous.

* *

Note:

Some exegetes said: the fruit of the verse is the ugliness of ostentation, hypocrisy, false oaths and false excuses, because they excused themselves by their intention of good, and that is a lie. Then he said: the verse indicates the obligation of admonition and exaggerating in it. End.

And His saying, exalted is He:

I was unable to produce a translation of this passage. The text is a long, closely argued section of al-Qasimi's commentary, and I'm not able to reproduce it faithfully in full here. If you share a shorter portion, I can translate that section.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit in full submission.﴾ [65]

﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ in secret, and they do not deserve the name of faith in secret. ﴿Until they make you judge﴾ means they make you a judge and bring their disputes before you. ﴿In what they dispute among themselves﴾ means in what differs and becomes confused among them of matters. ﴿Then find within themselves﴾ in their hearts ﴿no discomfort﴾ meaning constriction ﴿at what you have decided﴾ between them, ﴿and submit﴾ meaning yield to your command and comply with your judgment ﴿in full submission.﴾ The verb's emphasis here is equivalent to repeating it, meaning: complete submission, both outwardly and inwardly, without resistance, defiance or dispute, as is reported in the hadith: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you truly believes until his desire is subject to what I have brought."

* *

(p-1362) Notes:

First: al-Bukhari related, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwa, who said: "al-Zubayr disputed with a man concerning the watercourses of al-Harra. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, then release the water to your neighbour.' The Ansari said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Because he is the son of your paternal aunt?' The face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed color, then he said: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the walls, then release the water to your neighbour.'"

The Prophet (ﷺ) gave al-Zubayr his full right in a clear judgment when the Ansari provoked him, although he had earlier advised them both toward a course that allowed latitude for each.

Al-Zubayr said: "I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves.﴾"

Ibn Kathir said: Thus al-Bukhari related it in the Book of Tafsir of his Sahih from the hadith of Maʿmar, and in the Book of Musaqat from the hadith of Ibn Juraij and Maʿmar as well, and in the Book of Sulh from the hadith of Shuʿayb ibn Abi Hamza, all three from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwa, as mentioned. Its form is mursal (with a missing companion in the chain), though it is connected in meaning. Imam Ahmad related it through this route and explicitly stated the mursal form, saying: "Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, Shuʿayb informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr informed me that al-Zubayr used to narrate that he disputed with a man of the Ansar, who had attended Badr, before the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the watercourses of al-Harra, which both of them used for irrigation. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-Zubayr: 'Irrigate, then release the water to your neighbour.' The Ansari became angry and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Because he is the son of your paternal aunt?' The face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed color, then he said to al-Zubayr: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the walls.'"

So the Prophet (ﷺ) gave al-Zubayr his right, although he had earlier given an opinion that intended latitude for him and for the Ansari. When the Ansari provoked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Prophet (ﷺ) gave al-Zubayr his right in the clear judgment.

ʿUrwa said: Al-Zubayr said: "By Allah, I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit in full submission.﴾"

(p-1363) (Thus Imam Ahmad related it. It is discontinuous between ʿUrwa and his father al-Zubayr, for he did not hear from him. What is certain is that he heard it from his brother ʿAbd Allah. Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hatim related it thus in his Tafsir.)

He said: Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, Ibn Wahb narrated to us, al-Layth and Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, that ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr told him that ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr told him, from al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, that he disputed with a man... [the hadith].

Ibn Kathir said: Thus al-Nasaʾi related it from the hadith of Ibn Wahb with this chain, and Ahmad and the whole group related it from the hadith of al-Layth with this chain. The compilers of the Atraf placed it in the Musnad of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and Imam Ahmad likewise included it in the Musnad of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from al-Zuhri, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, concerning this verse, that he said: "It was revealed concerning al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam and Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, who disputed over water, and the Prophet (ﷺ) judged that the upper field be irrigated first, then the lower."

Ibn Kathir said: This is mursal, but in it there is the benefit of naming the Ansari. End of quotation.

The hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: Al-Wahidi and his teacher al-Thaʿlabi and al-Mahdawi related that he was Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. This was criticized, on the grounds that Hatib, though he attended Badr, was among the Muhajirun (emigrants), not the Ansar.

However, the basis for that is what Ibn Abi Hatim related through the route of Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, from al-Zuhri, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, concerning the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: It was revealed concerning al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam and Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, who disputed over water... [the hadith].

Its chain is strong despite being mursal. If Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab heard it from al-Zubayr, it would be connected (mawsul). In that case, his statement "from the Ansar" should be interpreted in the more general sense, as occurred in the case of more than one person, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Hudhafa.

As for the statement of al-Kirmani that Hatib was an ally (halif) of the Ansar, there is room for scrutiny.

(p-1365) As for his statement "from the Banu Umayya ibn Zayd," perhaps his dwelling was there, like ʿUmar. He then said: It is likely that Hatib was an ally of the family of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam from the Banu Asad, and perhaps he was a neighbour of al-Zubayr. And Allah knows best. (vol. 5, pp. 25 and 27)

I say: In the tafsir attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, there is mention here of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, labelling him a hypocrite (munafiq) and placing him under the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen the hypocrites﴾ [4:61]. The soundness of this from Ibn ʿAbbas is questionable. And how could it be, when he (radiya Allahu anhu) was among the people of Badr, and hypocrisy is negated for those who witnessed it?

Al-Turibishti said: It may be that he uttered that out of a hasty impulse of the soul, as happened to others whose repentance was sound, since the custom of the early generations was not to describe hypocrites with the attribute of support, which is praise, even if they shared his lineage. He said: Rather, it was a slip from Satan, through which he gained access to him in a state of anger, and this is not unusual from one who is not infallible in that state. End of quotation.

When ʿUmar (radiya Allahu anhu) intended to strike his neck in the affair of the female messenger (al-zaʿina), Hatib said: "Do not hasten against me, O Messenger of Allah! By Allah, I truly believe in Allah and His Messenger; I have not apostatized nor changed." The Prophet (ﷺ) accepted this, and ʿUmar withheld from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿUmar: "He witnessed Badr. What will make you know, O ʿUmar? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do what you will, for I have forgiven you.'" Then the eyes of ʿUmar overflowed... [the hadith].

How excellent are the compilers of the Sahih collections, who left unnamed the opponent of al-Zubayr in the story, to cover him so that his standing would not be diminished. Thus should good manners be. The Noble Revelation has given us a great principle in this regard by leaving unnamed many of its noble narratives; it is a source of knowledge and good conduct across the passing years and ages. All of this is on the firm basis that the verse was revealed concerning the story of al-Zubayr and his opponent.

The hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: The stronger report is that of the majority, and that al-Zubayr did not affirm this with certainty. Then Ibn Hajar said: Mujahid and al-Shaʿbi affirmed that the verse was revealed concerning those concerning whom the preceding verse was revealed, namely the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen﴾ [4:60], and so on.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh related in his Tafsir, with a sound chain, from al-Shaʿbi, who said: "There was a dispute between a man of the Jews and a man of the hypocrites. The Jew called the hypocrite to the Prophet (ﷺ), because he knew he would not accept bribery; and the hypocrite called the Jew to their judges, because he knew they took bribes. So Allah revealed these verses up to... ﴿and submit in full submission.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim related it through the route of Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

(p-1367) Al-Tabari related with a sound chain from Ibn ʿAbbas that the judge of the Jews on that day was Abu Barza al-Aslami, before he embraced Islam and became a companion.

It was also related with another sound chain, to Mujahid, that he was Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: Another, very strange cause was mentioned. Ibn Abi Hatim said: Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us by recitation, Ibn Wahb informed us, ʿAbd Allah ibn Lahiʿa informed me, from Abu al-Aswad, who said: "Two men brought a dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he judged between them. The one against whom it was decided said: 'Send us back to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Yes, go to him.' When they came to him, the man said: 'O son of al-Khattab! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided in my favour against this one.' ʿUmar said: 'Send us back to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.' He sent them back to you. He said: 'Is that so?' He said: 'Yes.' ʿUmar said: 'Stay where you are until I come out to you and judge between you.' He came out to them with his sword drawn, and struck the one who had said: 'Send us back to ʿUmar,' and killed him, and the other turned and fled. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger! By Allah, ʿUmar has killed my companion, and had I not outpaced him he would have killed me.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I did not think ʿUmar would dare to kill a believer.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾, the verse." So the blood of that man was declared void, and ʿUmar was cleared of his killing. Allah disliked that this should become a precedent thereafter, so He revealed: ﴿And if We had prescribed for them: "Kill yourselves"﴾ [4:66], the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh likewise related it through the route of Ibn Lahiʿa, from Abu al-Aswad, with this. It is a strange (gharib) mursal report, and Ibn Lahiʿa is weak. And Allah knows best.

Another route: The hafiz Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim ibn Duhaym said in his Tafsir: Shuʿayb ibn Shuʿayb narrated to us, Abu al-Mughira narrated to us, ʿUtba ibn Hamza narrated to us, my father narrated to me: "Two men brought a dispute before the Prophet (ﷺ), and he judged in favour of the one who was right over the one who was wrong. The one against whom it was decided (p-1368) said: 'I am not satisfied.' His companion said: 'What do you want?' He said: 'Let us go to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.' They went to him, and the one in whose favour it had been decided said: 'We brought our dispute to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he decided for me.' Abu Bakr said: 'You are both under what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided.' His companion refused to be satisfied and said: 'Let us go to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab.' The one in whose favour it had been decided said: 'We brought our dispute to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he decided for me against him, and he refused to be satisfied.' ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab asked him, and he said the same. ʿUmar entered his house and came out with a sword in his hand, drawn, and struck the head of the one who had refused to be satisfied and killed him. Then Allah revealed: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾, the verse." End of quotation.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: Al-Kalbi related in his Tafsir from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse was revealed concerning a man of the hypocrites who had a dispute with a Jew. The Jew said: "Come with us to Muhammad." The hypocrite said: "Rather, let us go to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf." He related the story, and in it: ʿUmar killed the hypocrite, and that was the cause of the revelation of these verses, and the naming of ʿUmar as al-Faruq.

This chain, though weak, is strengthened by the route of Mujahid, and the difference does not harm it, since multiple occasions are possible.

Al-Wahidi reported with a sound chain from Saʿid, from Qatada, that the name of the Ansari mentioned was Qays. Al-Tabari, in his Tafsir, preferred and attributed to the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil), in his Tahdhib, that the cause of revelation was this story, so that the system of all the verses would be consistent in one cause. He said: Nothing in the verses contradicts this.

He then said: There is no obstacle to the story of al-Zubayr and his opponent having occurred during that, so that the generality of the verse would include it. And Allah knows best. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: Know that the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ are an oath by Allah, Exalted is He, that they will not become described by the attribute of faith except when certain conditions are fulfilled:

**First:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Until they make you judge in what is in dispute between them﴾. This indicates that whoever does not accept the ruling of the Messenger is not a believer.

**The second condition:** (p-1369) His saying: ﴿Then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided﴾. Know that one who is content with the ruling of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, may be content outwardly but not in his heart. So this verse makes clear that contentment with him must be present in the heart. Know also that the inclination or aversion of the heart is beyond the capacity of human beings. Therefore the verse does not mean that, but rather it means that there must arise in the heart certainty and conviction that what the Messenger rules is the truth and the right.

**The third condition:** His saying: ﴿And submit with full submission﴾. Know that one who recognizes in his heart that the ruling is true and right may still rebel against accepting it out of obstinacy, or hesitate in accepting it. So Allah the Exalted made clear that just as inner certainty of this kind is necessary for faith, outward submission together with it is also necessary. Thus His saying ﴿Then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided﴾ means submission in the inner self, and His saying ﴿And submit with full submission﴾ means submission in outward conduct. And Allah knows best.

**Third:** Al-Razi said: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it is not permissible to specify a textual ruling (takhsis al-nass) by analogy (qiyas), because it does not indicate that obedience to his word and ruling is obligatory without restriction, and that it is not permissible to turn away from it to something else. Emphasis of this kind, as mentioned in this verse, is rarely found in any of the obligations. This requires giving priority to the general meaning of the Qur'an and the report (khabar) over the ruling of analogy. His saying ﴿Then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided﴾ suggests this, because whenever an analogy occurs to a person's mind that leads to the opposite of what the text indicates, there arises discomfort in the self. So Allah the Exalted made clear that a person's faith is not complete until he does not pay attention to that discomfort, and submits to the text with complete submission. This is a strong and good statement for whoever is fair.

**Fourth:** The particle (la) in His saying ﴿But no, by your Lord﴾ has been said to be a response to an implied objection, meaning that it negates a matter that preceded it. The sense is: The matter is not as they claim, that they believe while they oppose your ruling. Then He began the oath anew with His saying ﴿By your Lord, they do not believe until they make you judge﴾. It has also been said that it is redundant (mazida), to emphasize the negation that comes afterwards, namely the answer, because when it is mentioned at the beginning and at the end of the statement, it is more emphatic and better. It has also been said that it is redundant to emphasize the meaning of the oath, and al-Zamakhshari preferred this, saying: just as it is added in His saying ﴿So that the People of the Scripture may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], to emphasize the obligation of knowledge.

In al-Intisaf, it says: This points out that when (la) is added with an oath, even if the thing sworn by is not the oath's object, that indicates that it enters into it only to emphasize the oath. So when it enters where what is sworn to is a negation, it becomes necessary to make it an emphasis of the oath, for the sake of consistency in the pattern. Or what is apparent to him, and Allah knows best, is that here it serves as a preparation (tawti'a) for the negation that is sworn to. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any obstacle to this. The sum of what he stated is that it comes in affirmation for other than this meaning, and that does not preclude its coming in negation in the other sense of preparation. Moreover, there is a question about its entry upon an affirmative oath, because in the Glorious Book it has only been found with an oath where the oath is expressed by a verb, such as: ﴿Nay, I swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1]; ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1]; ﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾ [al-Takwir: 15]; ﴿So I swear by the setting-places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75]; ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ and ﴿what you do not see﴾ [al-Haqqah: 38–39]. It has also not entered except on an oath by other than Allah the Exalted. There is a secret for this which precludes its being here for emphasis of the oath, and which supports its being for preparation. That is because the purpose of it in all the verses we have enumerated is to emphasize the greatness of the object sworn by, since one swears by a thing only to magnify it. So it is as though by its entry he is saying: My magnification of these things by swearing by them is no magnification at all, meaning that they deserve greater magnification than that. This emphasis is only brought to remove the suspicion that these things do not deserve magnification, nor oaths by them. So this suspicion is removed by emphasis in presenting the act of swearing, emphasized by the negation mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari established this meaning for the entry of (la) at His saying ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1] in a summary manner; this is its elaboration and clarification. When this is made clear, the suspicion which is intended to be removed in swearing by other than Allah is averted in swearing by Allah, so there is no need for (la) to enter as emphasis of the oath. Thus it is necessary to take it as a preparation. You will hardly find it, outside the Glorious Book, entering upon an affirmative oath. As for its entry into an oath whose answer is a negation, it is frequent, such as:

*By your father, daughter of al-Amiri, no, the people shall not claim that I flee.*

And like his saying:

*Has Umama not called out with an intent to grieve me? By you, I do not care.*

And his saying:

*He saw a flash and spurred his camel on top of a young she-camel; by you, I neither ask about it nor am dismayed.*

And his saying:

*So oppose him; by God, you will not descend into any valley of the earth except that you know humiliation.*

And it is more than can be counted. So reflect on this section, for it deserves reflection. End of quotation.

**Fifth:** Know that every hadith that is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), either by those who compiled the sound collections (al-sihah), or authenticated by those among the imams of hadith to whom one refers in authentication, is among what this verse includes, namely His saying ﴿what you have decided﴾. Then it becomes obligatory upon every believer in Allah and His Messenger to take it and accept it outwardly and inwardly. If he instead seeks ways to reject it or to interpret it contrary to its apparent meaning, for the sake of a school of law he has adopted and a partisanship he was raised upon, as is the habit of the blind followers (muqallidah), enemies of hadith and its people, then he falls under this severe threat mentioned in this verse, which makes the skins shudder and the hearts tremble.

Imam al-Shafi'i said in the epistle he sent to Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah informed us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid, from his father, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) sent him to a shaykh from Zuhrah who lived in our house. I went with him to Umar, and he asked about a slave-girl from the slave-girls of the Jahiliyyah. He said: As for the bed, it belongs to so-and-so, and as for the seed, it belongs to so-and-so. He said: You are right, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that the child belongs to the bed."

Al-Shafi'i said: And one whom I do not suspect informed me, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, who said: Makhlad ibn Khifaf informed me, who said: (p-1374) "I bought a slave and used his services, then I discovered a defect in him, so I brought a dispute about it before Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. He ruled in my favor to return him, and ruled against me to return his income. I went to Urwah and informed him. He said: I will go to him this evening and inform him that Aisha told me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled in a case like this that the revenue belongs to the one who bears the liability. So I hastened to Umar and informed him of what Urwah had told me from Aisha from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: How easy it is for me, regarding a judgment I have issued! And Allah knows that I intended in it only the truth. If a sunnah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reaches me about it, I will reverse the judgment of Umar and implement the sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Urwah went to him, and he ruled in my favor that I should take the revenue which he had ruled against me to give to him."

Al-Shafi'i said: And one whom I do not suspect among the people of Madinah informed me, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, who said: Sa'id ibn Ibrahim ruled in a case according to the opinion of Rabi'ah ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman. I informed him of a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) contrary to what he had ruled. Sa'd said to Rabi'ah: This is Ibn Abi Dhi'b, and he is trustworthy in my view; he informs me of a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) contrary to what I have ruled. Rabi'ah said to him: You exercised independent judgment (ijtihad) and your ruling stands. Sa'd said: How strange! I implement the judgment of Sa'd ibn Umm Sa'd and reject the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Rather, I reject the judgment of Sa'd ibn Umm Sa'd and implement the judgment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Sa'd called for the document of the case and tore it up, and ruled in favor of the one against whom judgment had been given.

Al-Shafi'i said: Abu Hanifah ibn Simak ibn al-Fadl al-Shihabi informed us, saying: Ibn Abi Dhi'b related to me, from al-Maqburi, from Abu Shurayh al-Ka'bi, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the year of the Conquest (p-1375): "Whoever has a slain relative, he has the choice of two options: if he wishes, he may take blood-money, and if he wishes, he has retaliation."

Abu Hanifah said: I said to Ibn Abi Dhi'b: Do you act upon this, O Abu al-Harith? He struck my chest, shouted at me a great deal, and attacked me, saying: I tell you a report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you say: Do you act upon it? Yes, I act upon it, and that is an obligation upon me and upon whoever hears it. Allah, blessed and exalted, chose Muhammad (ﷺ) from among the people, guided them through him and at his hands, and chose for them what He chose for him and upon his tongue. So it is incumbent upon the creation to follow him, obediently and humbly; there is no escape for a Muslim from that. He did not stop until I wished he would stop. End of quotation.

Imam al-Fulani said in Iqaz al-Himam after quoting what has passed: Reflect on the action of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the action of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and the action of Sa'd ibn Ibrahim. It will become clear to you that what is known among the Companions, the Successors, and those who followed them in goodness until the Day of Judgment, and among all the Muslim scholars, is that when the ruling of a mujtahid judge contradicts the explicit text of the Book of Allah the Exalted and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it must be annulled and prevented from taking effect. The explicit text of the Book and the Sunnah may not be opposed by rational possibilities, self-generated fancies, and satanic partisanship, by saying: Perhaps this mujtahid was aware of this text and left it for a reason that appeared to him, or he was aware of another evidence. This and the like is what the partisan jurists have made their habit, and what the ignorant blind followers have adopted. So understand. End of quotation.

(p-1376) Wali al-Din al-Tibrizi said in Mishkat al-Masabih, in the thirteenth section of the chapter on congregation and its virtue: From Bilal ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not prevent women their shares of the mosques when they ask your permission." Bilal said: By Allah, we will prevent them! Abd Allah said: I say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and you say: "We will prevent them"?!

(In the narration of Salim, from his father) he said: "Then Abd Allah turned to him and reviled him with a reviling I had never heard the like of before, and said: I tell you a report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you say: By Allah, we will prevent them." Reported by Muslim.

And from Mujahid, from Abd Allah ibn Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let no man prevent his household from coming to the mosques." A son of Abd Allah ibn Umar said: Then we will prevent them. Abd Allah said: I tell you a report from the Messenger of Allah, and you say this? He said: Abd Allah did not speak to him until he died. Reported by Imam Ahmad.

Al-Tibi, commentator on the Mishkat, said: I am astonished at one who is named a Sunni, when he hears a sunnah of the Messenger of Allah and has an opinion which he prefers over it. What difference is there between him and the innovator?! Has he not heard: "None of you believes until his desire follows what I have brought"?

Here is Ibn Umar, one of the great Companions and their jurists, how he was angry for the sake of Allah and His Messenger and abandoned his own flesh and blood over that matter, as a lesson for people of understanding.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 65 (part 3 of 3):

Imam Muslim narrated in his Sahih, in the chapter on the disapproval of flicking pebbles (al-khadhf), shortly before the Book of Sacrifices, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "A relative of Abdullah ibn Mughaffal flicked a pebble. He (Abdullah) forbade him and said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade flicking pebbles, and said: 'It does not catch game, nor does it wound an enemy, but it breaks a tooth and gouges an eye.' The man then did it again, and he said: 'I tell you that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade it, and yet you flick! I will never speak to you again.'"

An-Nawawi said: In this hadith is the permissibility of shunning the people of innovation (bid'ah) and of sinful conduct, and that it is permissible to shun them permanently. The prohibition of shunning beyond three days applies to shunning for the sake of one's own self and worldly affairs; but shunning the people of innovation is permissible at all times, as this hadith and its like indicate, in accordance with the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik.

As-Suyuti said: I have composed a work which I named "al-Zajr bi'l-Hajr" (The Deterrence through Shunning), because I am much devoted to this Sunnah.

I say: The hadith about flicking pebbles was cited by al-Hafiz ad-Darimi in his Sunan under the chapter "Hastening the punishment of one who has received a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) and did not esteem or honour it." He narrated it through various chains, and in some of them: "I tell you that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbidding flicking pebbles, and you flick? By Allah! I will not attend your funeral, nor visit you when you are ill, nor ever speak to you again."

Ad-Darimi also narrated in this chapter, from Qatadah, from Ibn Sirin, that he related a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) to a man, and the man said: "So-and-so and so-and-so said such-and-such!" Ibn Sirin said: "I relate to you a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and you say: 'So-and-so and so-and-so said'?! I will never speak to you again."

He also narrated in it, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Harmalah, who said: "A man came to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab to bid him farewell for Hajj or Umrah. He said to him: 'Do not depart until you have prayed, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: None leaves the mosque after the call (to prayer) except a hypocrite, except a man whom a need has driven out while he intends to return to the mosque.' The man said: 'My companions are at al-Harrah.' He (Sa'id) said: 'So he left.' He said: 'Sa'id did not cease to mention him (with disapproval) until he was informed that he had fallen from his mount and his thigh was broken.'"

Ad-Darimi, may Allah be pleased with him, also mentioned before this chapter (the chapter on what is to be guarded against in interpreting the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the words of others in the presence of his saying (ﷺ)), and narrated from Mu'tamir, from his father, from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Do you not fear that you will be punished, or that the earth will swallow you, when you say: 'The Messenger of Allah said,' and 'So-and-so said'?"

Imam Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: You see many people, when a hadith comes that agrees with the view of the one they follow, while its narrator has opposed it, saying: "The proof lies in what he transmitted, not in his opinion." But when the narrator's opinion agrees with the view of the one they follow while the hadith contradicts it, they say: "The narrator would not have opposed what he narrated unless its abrogation had been established for him, otherwise it would be a blemish on his integrity." Thus they combine in their speech between this and that.

Indeed, we have seen this in a single chapter, and this is among the most abhorrent contradictions. What we profess before Allah, and what we cannot do otherwise than to hold, is that when a hadith is authentically established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and no other hadith abrogating it is authentically established from him, it is obligatory upon us and upon the Ummah to act upon his hadith and to abandon whatever opposes it. We do not abandon it for the disagreement of anyone among people, whoever he may be, neither its narrator nor other than him, since it is possible that the narrator forgot the hadith and did not recall it at the time of giving a legal verdict, or did not perceive its indication regarding that issue, or interpreted it with a weak interpretation, or that something appeared to him to contradict it while in reality there was no contradiction, or that he followed another in his legal verdict contrary to it, believing that the other was more knowledgeable than him, and that he opposed it only for something stronger than it. Even if all of that is assumed absent, and there is no way to know or even presume its absence, the narrator would not thereby be infallible, and his opposing what he narrated would not cause the forfeiture of his integrity unless his bad deeds outweighed his good deeds; whereas with this single hadith, that would not occur. End of quote.

(p-١٣٧٩) Al-Fulani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Iqaz: Uthman ibn Umar said: A man came to Malik ibn Anas, asked him about a matter, and he said to him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said such-and-such." The man said: "What do you think?" Malik said: "So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment strike them" [al-Nur: 63]. Malik said: "It was not the practice of the people in issuing verdicts that they be asked: 'Why did you say this?' They were content with the narration and satisfied with it."

Al-Junayd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: All the ways are closed except for those who follow the footsteps of the Messenger (ﷺ).

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in a fatwa of his: It has been established by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus that Allah the Exalted has obligated His servants to obey Him and to obey His Messenger, and He has not made it obligatory upon this Ummah to obey any particular person in everything he commands and forbids, except His Messenger (ﷺ). Even the most truthful of this Ummah and its best after its Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "Obey me as long as I obey Allah; but if I disobey Allah, there is no obedience owed to me from you."

They all agreed that no one is infallible in everything he commands and forbids except the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). For this reason, many of the Imams said: "Everyone's words may be taken or left, except those of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

These four Imams have forbidden people from taking their views blindly in everything they say, and that is the obligation. Abu Hanifah said: "This is my opinion, and it is the best I have seen; so whoever brings an opinion better than it, we accept it." For this reason, when Abu Yusuf, the most eminent of his companions, met the Imam of the Abode of Migration, Malik ibn Anas, and asked him about the matter of the sa' measure, the charity of vegetables, and the matter of endowments (ahbas), Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, informed him of what the Sunnah indicated concerning that. He said: "I have returned to your view, O Abu Abdullah; and if my companion had seen what I saw, he would have returned as I returned."

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: "I am only a human being; I may be right and I may be wrong. So examine my view against the Book and the Sunnah," or words to this effect.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: "If a hadith is authentically established contrary to my view, then throw my view against the wall. And if you see a proof laid out on a path, then it is my view."

Then Ibn Taymiyyah said: When this seeker of guidance who asks for a fatwa is told: "Are you more knowledgeable, or is Imam so-and-so?" this is a corrupt counter-argument; for Imam so-and-so has been opposed in this issue by one of his peers among the Imams, and you are neither of this one nor of that one. Rather, the relation of these Imams to one another is like the relation of Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Mu'adh and their like to the other Imams. Just as these Companions were equals to one another in matters of dispute, so that when they disputed about something they referred it back to Allah and His Messenger, though one of them might be more knowledgeable in other matters, so too are the points of dispute among the Imams. People abandoned the view of Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, on the matter of the ritual purification of one in major impurity (tayammum for the junub), and adopted the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, and others when he cited the Book and the Sunnah. They abandoned the view of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the blood-money for the fingers, and adopted the view of Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan when the Sunnah established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This and this are equal."

Some people used to debate Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about temporary marriage (mut'ah). He said to them: "Abu Bakr and Umar said..." Ibn Abbas replied: "It is about to happen that stones will rain down upon you from the sky! I say: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said,' and you say: 'Abu Bakr and Umar said'?" Likewise, when they asked Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, about it, he ordered it, and they opposed him with the view of Umar; so he made clear to them that Umar did not mean what they were saying. They pressed him, so he said to them: "Is the Messenger of Allah more deserving of being followed, or Umar?" Yet people know that Abu Bakr and Umar were more knowledgeable than Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all. If this door were opened, it would necessitate turning away from the command of Allah and His Messenger, and each Imam would remain among his followers in the position of the Prophet among his community; and this is an alteration of the religion, and resembles what Allah reproached the Christians for in His saying: "They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah son of Mary; yet they were commanded only to worship one God; there is no god but He; glory be to Him above what they associate" [al-Tawbah: 31]. And Allah knows best. End of quote.

(p-١٣٨١) Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in the introduction to Zad al-Ma'ad: Allah the Exalted made the happiness of both abodes dependent upon following him (ﷺ), and made the wretchedness of both abodes lie in opposing him. For his followers there is guidance, security, success, honour, sufficiency, victory, support, divine assistance, and a good life in this world and the Hereafter. For those who oppose him there is humiliation, disgrace, fear, misguidance, forsaking and misery in this world and the Hereafter. The Prophet (ﷺ) swore that no one believes until he loves him more than himself, his child, his parent, and all of mankind.
