We left there the joints of 'Utbah and his son, and 'Amr, Abu Jahl, whom we left lying dead.

You disobeyed the Messenger of God. Fie upon your religion and your wretched affair, which was misguided.

Though you rebuke me, I will still say: may my family and my wealth be a ransom for the Messenger of God.

We obeyed him, and we did not exchange him for anything else among us, a lamp for us in the darkness of night, a guide.

﴿And God is stronger in might﴾: that is, in greater strength and power than Quraysh. ﴿And stronger in punishment﴾: that is, in torment and retribution.

Ibn Kathir said: That is, He is able to overcome them in this world and in the Hereafter, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is so. Had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them, but He tests some of you by means of others.﴾ [Muhammad: 4] End of the quotation.

Al-Khafaji said: The purpose is either a threat or encouragement. Then God, exalted is He, indicated that urging the fighting is an intercession for the expiation of major sins and the raising of ranks, so He said:

(p-1419) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of its burden. And ever is Allah, over all things, Keeper.﴾ [85]

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession﴾ means: one who mediates in a matter, so that good results from it, whether by averting harm or bringing benefit, seeking the Face of Allah, Exalted is He. Among this is urging the believers to fight the disbelievers. ﴿will have a share in it﴾ means the reward of the intercession and the causing of the good that results from it.

﴿And whoever intercedes with an evil intercession﴾ is that which is contrary to the good one, by being in a matter that is not lawful. ﴿will bear a portion of its burden﴾ means: a share of the sin that results from his effort, equal to it in measure without any of it being diminished.

Benefits:

The first: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: The verse praises intercession and censures "si'aya" (tale-bearing/mischief-making), which is the evil intercession, and mentioning people badly before the ruler, and it is counted among the major sins.

The second: Many hadiths have been related concerning the virtue of intercession, among them:

What al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When a person in need came to the Prophet ﷺ, he would turn to his companions and say: 'Intercede, and you will be rewarded, and Allah will decree through the tongue of His Prophet what He loves.'"

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in (p-1420) "the story of Barirah and her husband: the Prophet ﷺ said to her: 'If only you would take him back!' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, are you commanding me?' He said: 'I am only interceding.' She said: 'I have no need of him.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari.

The third: Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd said: this verse was revealed concerning people's intercessions for one another. Whatever is permissible in the religion to intercede for is a good intercession, and whatever is not permissible to intercede for is an evil intercession.

Then al-Hasan said: whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a reward for it, even if he is not himself interceded for, because Allah says "whoever intercedes" (man yashfa'), and did not say "whoever is interceded for" (man yushaffa'). This is supported by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Intercede, and you will be rewarded." Related by al-Razi.

The fourth: al-Zamakhshari said: The good intercession is that by which the right of a Muslim is observed, by which harm is averted from him or good is brought to him, sought for the Face of Allah, no bribe is taken for it, and it concerns a permissible matter, not a legal limit (hadd) of the limits of Allah, nor one of the rights, meaning obligatory ones upon him. The evil intercession is the contrary of that. And from Masruq: he interceded for someone, and the one interceded for gave him a female slave as a gift, so he became angry and returned her, and said: "Had I known what was in your heart, I would not have spoken regarding your need, nor will I speak regarding what remains of it." End.

(p-1421) Abu Dawud related: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Whoever interceded for his brother with an intercession, and he gave him a gift for it, and he accepted it, then he has come to a great door of the doors of usury."

This hadith was also cited by al-Mundhiri in his book al-Targhib wa'l-Tarhib, under the chapter heading "Encouragement to fulfilling the needs of the Muslims and bringing joy to them, and what has come concerning one who interceded and was then given a gift." Then he related the hadith of the two Shaykhs and others, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, nor abandon him. Whoever is in the need of his brother, Allah is in his need. Whoever relieves a Muslim of a distress, Allah will relieve him of a distress of the distresses of this world on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever conceals a Muslim, Allah will conceal him on the Day of Resurrection."

Al-Tabarani related with a good chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no servant whom Allah has blessed with a blessing and perfected it for him, then made of the needs of people toward him, and he becomes weary, but he has exposed that blessing to removal."

Something similar has been related from 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Umar, and Ibn 'Amr.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih related from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever is a means for his Muslim brother to reach a person of authority regarding a matter of righteousness or the facilitation of hardship, Allah will help him across the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection when feet slip."

In a narration of al-Tabarani from Abu al-Darda': "Allah will raise him to the high ranks of Paradise."

Al-Tabarani related, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Among the things that necessitate forgiveness is your bringing joy to your Muslim brother."

He also related it from 'Umar as a marfu' hadith with the wording: "The best of deeds is bringing joy to a believer."

He related something similar from Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah and others; see al-Targhib.

(p-1422) The fifth: The reason for choosing "nasib" (share) for the good and "kifl" (portion) for the evil is what we have pointed to: the nasib includes increase, since the reward of good deeds is multiplied. As for kifl, its origin is a difficult mount, then it was borrowed for an equal matching amount. Therefore it was chosen, as an indication of His gentleness toward His servants, since He did not multiply evil deeds as He multiplies good ones. It is said that although its meaning is "the equal," it became predominant in evil and is rare in other than it, as in His saying: ﴿He will give you two portions of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28]. Therefore it was specifically applied to the evil deed as a softening and to avoid repetition.

"Min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah) or initial (ibtida'iyyah), as al-Khafaji stated.

﴿And ever is Allah, over all things, Keeper﴾ means: Capable (muqtadir), from "aqata 'ala al-shay'" when one is capable of it, as he said:

*And many an enemy whom I restrained myself from, while I was capable of his harm*

That is: many a one who bears grudge against me, I restrained evil from him while having power over him. Or it means: a witness, guardian. Its derivation is from "al-qut" (sustenance), for it strengthens the body and preserves it. And His saying, Exalted is He:

(p-1423) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, respond with one better than it, or return it. Indeed, Allah is ever a Reckoner of all things.﴾ [86]

﴿When you are greeted with a greeting﴾ means: when someone greets you with a salutation that invokes safety for your lives and for those attributes by which life is complete, saying "as-salamu alaykum" (peace be upon you). ﴿Then respond﴾ means: fulfilling the right of the Muslim over you. ﴿with one better than it﴾ means: with a greeting better than it, such as saying "wa alaykumu as-salam wa rahmatullah" (and upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah). If the one greeting says this, one adds "wa barakatuhu" (and His blessings).

Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: The origin of tahiyyah (greeting) is the invocation of life and its prolongation. It was then used for every kind of supplication. When the Arabs met one another, one would say, "hayyaka Allah" (may Allah give you life). Then the Sharia adopted it for the salam, and this is the greeting of Islam. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their greeting therein is "peace"﴾ [Ibrahim: 23], and He said: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him is "peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44], and He said: ﴿Then greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

(p-1424) They said: The salam has a distinction over "hayyaka" (may Allah give you life), because it is an invocation for safety from religious and worldly afflictions, and this safety necessarily entails a long life, whereas the invocation for a long life does not contain that. Also, al-Salam is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, so beginning with the mention of it is something whose excellence and distinction are beyond doubt.

﴿Or return it﴾ means: answer it with its like. The return of the salam (radd al-salam) is its reply with the like of it, because the one replying returns the words of the greeter and repeats them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever a Reckoner of all things﴾ means: He will hold you to account for everything of your deeds, among which is what you have been commanded regarding greeting. So be careful to observe it as you have been commanded. There are various benefits in this verse:

The first: The subtle point of its placement alongside the verses on jihad is a preparation for preventing the believers from killing those who offer them peace in the war that is coming soon, by clarifying that every Muslim has a right that must be rendered to him. This is because the salam is a kind of honour, and one who is honoured is met with the like of his honour or more.

Al-Razi said: In jihad, a man would meet another man in the land of war or near it, and he would greet him with the salam, but he might not pay attention to his greeting and kill him, and perhaps it would become clear that he was a Muslim. So Allah forbade the believers from this, and commanded them that whoever greets them and honours them with some kind of honour, they should meet him with the like of that honour or more. For if he is a disbeliever, it does no harm to the Muslim if he responds to the honour of that disbeliever with some kind of honour. But if he is a Muslim and he kills him, there is in that the greatest harm and corruption.

For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever a Reckoner of all things﴾, meaning: He will hold you to account for all your deeds, and He is sufficient to bring the recompense of your deeds to you. So be wary of contravening this obligation. This indicates the great concern with preserving lives and preventing their being wasted.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: (p-1425) "Whoever greets you from among Allah's creatures, return it to him, even if he is a Magian. That is because Allah says: ﴿then respond with one better than it, or return it﴾."

Qatadah said: "Then respond with one better than it" means to Muslims, and "or return it" means to the people of dhimmah (non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection). From here al-Mawardi reported an opinion that when the people of dhimmah initiate the greeting, one says in reply: "Wa alaykum as-salam," and does not say "wa rahmatullah." Al-Nawawi quoted this from him.

Al-Zamakhshari narrated from al-Hasan that it is permissible to say to a disbeliever: "Wa alayka as-salam," but do not say "wa rahmatullah," for that is a form of seeking forgiveness.

It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he said to a Christian who had greeted him: "Wa alayka as-salam wa rahmatullah." He was asked about this, and he said: "Does one not live by the mercy of Allah?" End of quotation.

It appears that he had in mind the reports and did not intend the content of the greeting. Nevertheless, what is established in the two Sahihs from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), is: "When the People of the Book greet you, then say: 'Wa alaykum'," as will come.

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: In this verse is the legislation of the salam and the obligation of returning it. The majority (of scholars) cited it as evidence for returning the salam to every greeter, whether Muslim or disbeliever, but they differ regarding the wording of the return.

The second: Many hadiths have come concerning the spreading of the salam, among them:

The saying of al-Bara' ibn Azib, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us with seven things, among them: spreading the salam." Narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

From Abu Hurairah (p-1426), may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not direct you to something which, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the salam among yourselves." Narrated by Muslim.

From Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O people! Spread the salam, feed the food, maintain the ties of kinship, and pray while people are sleeping, and you will enter Paradise in peace." al-Tirmidhi said: It is a sound hadith.

The third: On the manner of the salam. al-Razi said: If he wishes, he says: "Salamun alaykum," and if he wishes, he says: "As-salamu alaykum."

Allah the Exalted said concerning Nuh: ﴿O Nuh, descend with peace from Us﴾ [Hud: 48], and He said concerning the Friend (Ibrahim): ﴿He said: "Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾ [Maryam: 47], and He said in the story of Lut: ﴿They said: "Peace." He said: "Peace"﴾ [Hud: 69]. (p-1427) And He said concerning Yahya: ﴿And peace be upon him﴾ [Maryam: 15], and He said concerning Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen"﴾ [al-Naml: 59], and He said concerning the angels: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate. "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24], and He said concerning His own sacred self: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58], and He said: ﴿Then say: "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-An'am: 54].

As for with the definite article (al-salam), there is His saying concerning Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47], and He said concerning Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 33]. Thus it is established that all forms are permissible. End of quotation.

(p-1428) Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Wahidi said: You have the choice regarding the definite and indefinite forms of salam. End of quotation.

Because the indefinite form occurs frequently in the Qur'an, as we have shown, some scholars preferred it over the definite form.

The fourth: On its excellence.

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Darimi narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'As-salamu alaykum.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Ten.' Then another came and said: 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Twenty.' Then another came and said: 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Thirty.'" al-Tirmidhi said: It is a hasan hadith. On this topic there are also reports from Abu Sa'id, Ali and Sahl ibn Hunayf.

al-Bazzar said: This has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) through many routes, and this is the best of them in chain.

In a narration of Abu Dawud from the narration of Mu'adh ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, there is an addition to this. He said: "Then another came and said: 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuhu wa maghfiratuh.' He said: 'Forty.' He said: 'Thus are the virtues.'"

In this there is a refutation of those who claim that nothing may be added beyond "wa barakatuh." It is not said that the narration "wa maghfiratuh" in Abu Dawud is from the route of Abu Marhum, whose name is Abd al-Rahim ibn Maymun, from Sahl ibn Mu'adh, from his father. Abu Marhum was declared weak by Yahya, and Abu Hatim said: his hadith is written down but not used as evidence. We say: al-Tirmidhi has rated his narration from Sahl ibn Mu'adh as hasan, and he, along with Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim and others, graded it sahih.

al-Nasa'i said: The hadith of a man is not abandoned until all of them agree on abandoning it.

Return to the subject:

al-Tabarani narrated from Sahl ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says 'as-salamu alaykum,' ten good deeds are recorded for him, and whoever says 'as-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah' (p-1429) twenty good deeds are recorded, and whoever says 'as-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh,' thirty good deeds are recorded for him."

Ibn Hibban narrated in his Sahih from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a man passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in a gathering and said: 'Salamun alaykum.' He said: 'Ten good deeds.' Then another passed and said: 'Salamun alaykum wa rahmatullah.' He said: 'Twenty good deeds.' Then another passed and said: 'Salamun alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.' He said: 'Thirty good deeds.' Then a man rose from the gathering without greeting. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'How quickly your companion forgot! When one of you comes to a gathering, let him greet; if he wishes to sit, let him sit; and if he rises, let him greet. The first is no more deserving than the last.'"

al-Tabarani narrated with a good chain from Abdullah ibn Mughaffal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The stingiest of people is one who is stingy with the salam." He also narrated it from Abu Hurairah, and Ahmad and al-Bazzar have something similar from Jabir.

al-Tabarani narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When a believer meets a believer, greets him and takes his hand, their sins fall away like the leaves of a tree shed." al-Mundhiri said: I know of no discredited narrator among its transmitters.

al-Bazzar narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When two Muslim men meet and one of them greets the other, the one among them who is most cheerful toward his companion is the most beloved to Allah. When they shake hands, a hundred mercies descend upon them: ninety for the one who initiated, and ten for the one who shook hands."

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people closest to Allah are those who begin them with the salam."

(p-1430) The fifth: On some of its transmitted rulings. Abu Dawud narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It suffices for a group when they pass by that one of them greets, and it suffices for those sitting that one of them returns it."

In the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Aslam, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of the people greets, it suffices for them all." al-Nawawi said: This is a mursal (a report in which the companion is omitted from the chain) with a sound chain.

In the two Sahihs from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O Aisha, this is Jibril, who conveys the salam to you." She said: I said: "And upon him be peace and the mercy of Allah. You see what we do not see" (she meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)).

al-Nawawi said: In some narrations of the two Sahihs the words "wa barakatuh" occur, and in some they do not occur, and the addition of a trustworthy narrator is accepted.

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from Ghalib al-Qattan, from a man who said: My father narrated to me from my grandfather, who said: "My father sent me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Go to him and convey the salam to him.' I came to him and said: 'My father conveys the salam to you.' He said: 'Upon you and upon your father be peace.'"

al-Nawawi said: Although this is a report from an unknown narrator, the scholars are lenient in hadiths of virtues, so it benefits from it the return of the salam to the one who conveys it, just as to the one who greets directly.

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurairah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "When one of you meets his brother, let him greet him. (p-1431) If a tree, a wall or a stone comes between them and then he meets him again, let him greet him." In this is the indication that whoever has been greeted by a person, and then meets him again after a short time, it is recommended to greet him a second and a third time.

The two Shaykhs narrated from Abu Hurairah that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "The rider greets the one walking, the one walking greets the one sitting, and the few greet the many."

The two Shaykhs narrated from Anas: "That he passed by some children and greeted them, and said: 'The Prophet (ﷺ) used to do this.'"

The wording of Abu Dawud: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came upon some boys playing, and he greeted them."

In the version of Ibn al-Sunni in it: "He said: 'As-salamu alaykum, O children.'"

Abu Dawud related from Asma' bint Yazid, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by us while we were among some women, and he greeted us with salam."

At-Tirmidhi related something similar. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the People of the Book greet you with salam, say: 'And upon you.'"

Both of them (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also related from Usama that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a gathering in which there were a mixture of Muslims, polytheists who worshipped idols, Jews, and Muslims, and the Prophet (ﷺ) greeted them with salam."

Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not initiate salam to the Jews or the Christians. When you meet one of them on the road, force him to its narrowest side."

Al-Nawawi said: We have related in the Muwatta' of Malik that he was asked about one who greeted a Jew or a Christian, whether he should retract that greeting. He said: No. Abu Sa'd al-Mutawalli al-Shafi'i said: If he wishes to offer a dhimmi a greeting, he may do so without the word salam, such as by saying: "May Allah guide you," or "May Allah bless your morning."

Al-Nawawi said: What Abu Sa'd said is not objectionable when there is a need for it, so he may say: "May your morning be blessed with goodness, happiness, or well-being," or "May Allah bless your morning with joy, happiness and favour, or with delight, or what is similar to that."

Sixth: Al-Hasan al-Basri said: The greeting (salam) is voluntary (tatawwu') and the return of it is obligatory (fariḍah).

Ibn Kathir said: What he said is the saying of all the scholars without exception: that returning the greeting is obligatory upon the one who is greeted, so he sins if he does not do it, because he has opposed the command of Allah in His saying: ﴿So greet with something better than it, or return it.﴾ End of quote. Abandoning the return of the greeting involves humiliation and contempt, and that is forbidden. For this reason it is recommended that the group greeted should all respond, to show honour and to emphasise it, although the obligation falls away when some of them respond.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you for the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ [87]

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you for the Day of Resurrection﴾ That is: He will surely resurrect you from your graves and assemble you for the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection on one plain, and He will recompense every doer for his deed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-qiyamah (the Resurrection) and al-qiyam are like al-tilabah and al-tilab (both meaning a demand or seeking). It is their rising from the graves or their standing for the reckoning. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6] [al-Mutaffifin: 6].

﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ That is: there is no doubt about the Day of Resurrection, or about the gathering.

﴿And who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ This is a denial that anyone could be more truthful than Him, Exalted is He, in His speech, His reports, His promise and His threat, and an explanation of its impossibility; for it would be a deficiency and an ugliness. Whoever lies does so only because he needs to draw some benefit by his lie or to repel some harm, or else he is ignorant of its ugliness, or he is foolish and does not distinguish between truth and falsehood in his reports and does not care which of them he utters. Thus the impossibility of lying for Him, may His majesty be exalted, is established. As for others—even if the proofs indicate their truthfulness—their lying is possible if one does not consider those proofs.

(p-1434) Benefits:

The first: al-Razi said: Regarding the manner of the composition (al-nazm), there are two aspects:

One of them: We have explained that the purpose of His words: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting, then greet with better than it or return it﴾ [al-Nisa': 86] is that the greeting man should not become one who is killed. Then He, the Exalted, emphasized that with the threat in His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, a Reckoner﴾ [al-Nisa': 86]. Then He exaggerated in emphasizing that threat with this verse, so in this verse He made clear that monotheism and justice are interrelated. So His words ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ are an indication of monotheism, and His words ﴿He will surely gather you for the Day of Resurrection﴾ are an indication of justice. This is like His words: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18] [Al 'Imran: part of 18], and like His words in Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14] [Ta-Ha: 14], which is an indication of monotheism. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming—I almost conceal it—so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15] [Ta-Ha: 15], which is an indication of justice. Likewise in this verse He made clear that it is necessary, by His judgment and wisdom, that He gather the first and the last in the plain of Resurrection, and that He will grant justice to the oppressed against the oppressors. There is no doubt that this is a severe threat.

The second aspect: It is as if He, the Exalted, says: Whoever greets you and salutes you, accept his greeting and honor him and deal with him according to the outward appearance, for the inward matters are known only to Allah, there is no deity except Him. The inward states of creatures are only revealed to creatures on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: His words ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ are either a predicate of the subject, and (la-yajma'annakum) etc. ... is the answer to an omitted oath, and the oath clause is a new sentence with no place in the i'rab, or a second predicate; or it is a parenthetical insertion and the oath clause is the predicate.

The third: The construction of (la-yajma'annakum) with (ila) is either because it carries the meaning of resurrection (al-hashr), as we have explained, or because (ila) carries the meaning of (fi) (in), as the grammarians of Arabic have affirmed. And His words, Exalted is He:

(p-١٤٣٥) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿So what is [wrong] with you that you have become two factions concerning the hypocrites, while Allah has reverted them [to disbelief] for what they have earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And he whom Allah sends astray - never will you find for him a way.﴾ [88]

﴿So what is [wrong] with you concerning the hypocrites﴾ meaning: what is [wrong] with you that you have divided over the matter of the hypocrites ﴿into two factions﴾, meaning two groups, and have not agreed on disassociating yourselves from them. The interrogative is for denunciation, and the negation and address are directed to all the believers, but the sense of reproach in it is directed at some of them. That is because a group of the believers used to incline toward them, defend them and befriend them, while another group among them distanced themselves from them and opposed them. So they were forbidden from that and commanded to be on one course in distancing and disassociating themselves from them, because the indications of their hypocrisy and disbelief are apparent and manifest, so it is not permissible for you to differ regarding their affair. It has been said that the intended ones here are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions who forsook the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the Day of Uhud and turned back with their army after they had set out, as has preceded in Āl ʿImrān. This is clarified by what al-Shaykhān, Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhi related from Zayd ibn Thābit: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to Uhud, and some people who had set out with him turned back. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became two factions concerning them: one faction said, 'Let us kill them,' and another faction said, 'No, [they are not hypocrites, they are] (p-١٤٣٦) believers.' Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿So what is [wrong] with you concerning the hypocrites, two factions?﴾ Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'It is good [Ṭaybah], and it expels impurity as the bellows expels the dross of iron.'" This is the wording of Aḥmad.

Imam Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq mentioned, regarding the battle of Uhud, that ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl turned back that day with a third of the army: he turned back with three hundred, and the Prophet ﷺ remained with seven hundred.

There is another report concerning the revelation of the verse, which Imam Aḥmad related in his Musnad from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf: "A people from among the Arabs came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Madinah and embraced Islam, but the plague and fever of Madinah afflicted them, so they were turned back [from faith], and they left Madinah. A group of his Companions - meaning the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ - met them and said to them, 'What is [wrong] with you that you have returned?' They said, 'The plague of Madinah has afflicted us.' They said, 'Do you not have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example?' Some of them said, 'They have become hypocrites,' and some said, 'They have not become hypocrites.' Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿So what is [wrong] with you concerning the hypocrites, two factions﴾, the verse."

This report is closest to the composition of the verse, as we shall clarify in the second note.

﴿And Allah has reverted them﴾ meaning: He has overturned them and returned them to disbelief ﴿for what they have earned﴾, meaning because of what they earned through their joining the disbelievers. ﴿Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ meaning: do you count them among the guided?

Abū al-Suʿūd said: It is a turning of the address to a specific group and its restriction to those who assert the faith of [one of] the two factions, (p-١٤٣٧) and a reproach for them over their claim, and an indication that it leads to an attempt at the impossible, namely the guidance of one whom Allah has sent astray. That is because judging them to be believers and claiming their guidance - when they are far from that - is an effort toward their guidance and a desire for it. The placing of the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun for the hypocrites serves to intensify the denunciation and affirm the impossibility of guidance by what is mentioned in the clause following it. And directing the denunciation at the desire itself rather than at its object - by saying "Do you guide..." etc. - is for the sake of emphasis in denying it, by showing that it is something whose desire is impossible, let alone its actual occurrence.

﴿And whoever Allah sends astray﴾ from His religion ﴿never will you find for him a way﴾, meaning: a path to guidance.

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, and [then] you would be equal. So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them an ally or a helper.﴾ [89]

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved﴾ is a resumed statement, brought to explain their extremism and persistence in disbelief and their eagerness to lead others astray, following the explanation of their disbelief and misguidance in themselves. That is: they wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved after believing. ﴿and [then] you would be equal﴾, that is, in disbelief and misguidance. ﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾ in support and aid, lest that lead to your disbelief, even if they show you faith, seeking your friendship. ﴿until they emigrate﴾ from the abode of disbelief ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, so that you may verify their faith. ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, from emigration, then they are [as they are]; and even if they show you Islam while they are able to emigrate, then do to them what you do to the disbelievers, for the rule of hypocrisy has been lifted from them by their joining the abode of disbelief.

﴿So seize them﴾, that is, take them captive ﴿and kill them wherever you find them﴾, within the sacred territory and outside it ﴿and do not take from among them an ally or a helper﴾, that is, do not befriend them, nor seek their support against the enemies of Allah, as long as they remain so.

(p-1438) Two points of attention:

The first: al-Razi said: The verse indicates that it is not permissible to befriend polytheists, hypocrites, and those notorious for heresy and atheism. This is further confirmed by the general wording of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1] [al-Mumtahanah: part of 1]. The reason is that the most precious and greatest thing for all creation is religion, for it is the matter by which one draws near to Allah, exalted is He, and by which one seeks the attainment of happiness in the Hereafter. If that is so, then the enmity arising from it is the greatest kind of enmity, and if that is so, then seeking love and allegiance is impermissible in a situation where the greatest cause of enmity exists. And Allah knows best.

The second: It appears to me that the closest account concerning the occasion of revelation of these verses, I mean His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why do you have two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88] etc., is the narration of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, as the course and careful reflection on these verses indicate with honest consideration and thoroughness. Al-Fadil al-Mahayimi was guided to this in his tafsir, and he limited himself to this view, saying: They are those who asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to go out to the desert because of the unsuitability of Madinah, and they kept moving stage after stage until they joined the polytheists. End.

As for al-Suyuti's statement that the chain of the narration of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf in Ahmad contains tadlis (concealment) and inqita' (break in the chain), this does not detract from its hitting the core of the truth, because it has a qarinah (contextual indicator) that connects it to what is accepted, namely its agreement with the wording of the verse without strain. In that case, the saying of Zayd ibn Thabit, "So it was revealed concerning what preceded," means that it includes what occurred from those who withdrew from Uhud and the disagreement of the believers about their situation, not that what occurred was the cause of its revelation. The use of "revelation" in this sense is well known, as we explained in the introduction. Otherwise, His saying, "unless they emigrate," would be problematic, since emigration is only demanded of those far from Madinah, whereas those who withdrew from the Muslims at Uhud were already in it. It would then be necessary to interpret emigration as their going out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers, patient and seeking reward, sincere, as some exegetes have said.

This meaning is not widespread in the sense of emigration. Also, His saying, ﴿So seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾, would be problematic, for it indicates that they are not among the hypocrites of the people of Madinah, and that there is an expectation of gaining mastery over them; otherwise, the hypocrites of Madinah were among them night and day. Thus, in this context, the narration of Ibn Awf is the apparent one, and the end of Zayd's narration hints at it, where he said: "Indeed it is good (ṭaybah) and it expels impurity (al-khabath)," indicating that Madinah expelled those who departed from it after their Islam. And Allah knows best.

Then he made an exception from taking captive and killing the apostates, saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 90:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Except those who seek refuge with a people between whom and you there is a covenant, or who come to you with their hearts constricted from fighting you or fighting their own people. Had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you. So if they keep away from you and do not fight you, and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them.﴾ [90]

﴿Except those who seek refuge﴾ (yasilun): take refuge, take shelter. ﴿with a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾: that is, a treaty of truce or a pledge of safety. So treat their ruling as their ruling, lest it lead to fighting those with whom they have sought refuge, which would lead to the breaking of the covenant.

﴿Or who come to you﴾ is a conjunction with the relative clause, meaning: and those who come to you. ﴿with their hearts constricted﴾ is a circumstantial clause with (qad) understood, meaning: their souls have become tight and withdrawn. ﴿from fighting you﴾ because of their desire for peace. ﴿or fighting their own people﴾, that is, with you, against them, out of kinship to them. So they are neither for you nor against you.

Abu al-Su'ud said: Two groups are excepted from those commanded to be seized and killed:

The first: one who has left the fighters and joined the covenanted.

The second: one who has come to the believers and refrained from fighting both parties.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Hasan that Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji related to them, saying: "When the Prophet ﷺ prevailed over the people of Badr and Uhud, and those around them embraced Islam, he said: 'I have heard that he intends to send Khalid ibn al-Walid to my people, the Banu Mudlij.' So I came to him and said: 'I beseech you by the blessing. I have heard that you intend to send someone to my people, and I want you to make a truce with them. If your people embrace Islam, they will embrace Islam too, and if they do not embrace Islam, it is not fitting to overpower your people over them.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took Khalid's hand and said: 'Go and do what he wants.' (p-1440) So Khalid made peace with them on condition that they would not aid anyone against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that if Quraysh embraced Islam, they would embrace it with them. And Allah revealed: ﴿Except those who seek refuge with a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾. So whoever joined them became with them under their covenant."

In His words, exalted is He: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you﴾, there is an indication of their strength in themselves, and that in targeting them for killing there is a manifestation of their hidden strength in general, functioning as a rationale for excepting them from the seizing and killing.

﴿So if they keep away from you﴾, that is, leave you alone, ﴿and do not fight you﴾ despite what you know of their capacity to do so by the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and offer you peace﴾, that is, submission and surrender, ﴿then Allah has not made for you any way against them﴾, that is, any path by way of capture or killing, since there is no harm from them to Islam, and fighting them would only show the completeness of their strength.

A subtle point:

al-Khafaji said: (al-salam), with two fathas, means submission. It was also read with the lam sukun and the sin either fatha or kasra. The phrase "offering peace" is likely a metaphor, since one who offers something to another casts it down and places it before the one to whom it is offered. And the non-making of a way is an intensification in not confronting them, since how can one confront someone one does not even pass by?

* *

A note:

The apparent sense of the noble text is that the two excepted groups are from the disbelievers. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani attempted to make them Muslims, saying: When He, exalted is He, made migration obligatory upon everyone who embraced Islam, He excepted whoever has an excuse, saying: ﴿Except those who seek refuge﴾, who are a people of the believers who intended the Messenger for migration and support, except that on their route there were disbelievers, and they could find no way to him out of fear of those disbelievers. So they went to a people between whom and the Muslims there was a covenant, and they stayed with them until deliverance became possible for them. He then excepted, after that, those who reached the Messenger and would not fight the Messenger or his companions, because he fears Allah, exalted is He, regarding them; and who would not fight the disbelievers either, because they are his kin, or because he left his children and wives among them, so he fears that if he fought them they would kill his children and companions. These two groups are therefore from the Muslims, and fighting them is not permitted, even if no migration or fighting of the disbelievers has been found from them. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 91:

(p-1441) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people. Whenever they are returned to temptation (fitnah), they are plunged back into it. So if they do not withdraw from you, offer you peace, or restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. Against these We have given you a clear authority.﴾ [91]

﴿You will find﴾ other people ﴿who wish﴾ by showing Islam to you ﴿to be secure from you﴾, meaning for their own selves, ﴿and to be secure from their own people﴾ by showing disbelief. ﴿Whenever they are returned to temptation﴾, meaning they are called to apostasy and polytheism, ﴿they are plunged back into it﴾, meaning they return to it upside down on their heads.

﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾, meaning they do not keep away from you to the side, neither being with you nor against you, ﴿offer you peace﴾, meaning they do not offer submission, ﴿or restrain their hands﴾, meaning from fighting you, ﴿then seize them﴾, meaning take them captive, ﴿and kill them wherever you find them﴾, meaning wherever you come upon them in your territory or theirs. ﴿Against these We have given you a clear authority﴾, meaning a manifest proof to attack them by killing and taking captive, due to the evident enmity of these people, the exposure of their condition in disbelief and treachery, and their harm to the people of Islam; or a manifest dominion, since We have permitted you to seize them and kill them.

Two admonitions:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: These others, in outward appearance, are like those who preceded them, but the intention of these is other than the intention of those. These are hypocrites who show Islam to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions so that they may be secure by this with them regarding their blood, wealth and offspring, and who flatter the disbelievers inwardly, worshipping with them what they worship so that they may be secure by this with them, while in their inner selves they are with those (disbelievers), as He, exalted is He, said: (p-1442) ﴿And when they go alone to their devils, they say: "Indeed we are with you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], and the verse continues.

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that it was revealed concerning a people from Makkah who would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and show Islam out of hypocrisy, then return to Quraysh and relapse into the idols, seeking by that to be secure here and there. So he was commanded to kill them if they did not withdraw and make peace.

The second: al-Razi said: Most scholars said: In the verse is an indication that if they withdraw from fighting us, seek peace from us, and restrain their hands from harming us, it is not permissible for us to fight them or kill them. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not drive you out of your homes, from being kind to them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190]. So the command to fight is restricted to those who fight us, not those who do not fight us.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake (must free) a believing slave and pay blood-money (diyah) to his family, unless they forgo it as charity. If he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, (then he must free) a believing slave. And if he was from a people between you and whom there is a treaty, then blood-money is to be paid to his family and (he must free) a believing slave. And whoever does not find (the means), then (he must fast) two consecutive months, as a repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [92]

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾: that is, it is not permissible, nor valid, nor befitting for a believer to kill his believing brother, for faith restrains one from that. The exception is by way of error, for that may occur, since it is not entirely possible for humans to guard against it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "With what is *khata'an* (by mistake) in the accusative?" I say: It is a *maf'ul lahu* (object of purpose), meaning: it is not appropriate for him to kill him for any reason except by mistake alone. It may also be a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier), meaning he does not kill him in any state except in the state of error. And it may be an adjective of the verbal noun: "except a killing by mistake."

The meaning: it is inherent in the believer that the occurrence of killing a believer should be entirely negated from him from the outset, except when it occurs from him by mistake, without intent, such as when he shoots at an unbeliever and hits a Muslim, or shoots a person thinking he is an unbeliever and it turns out he is a Muslim. End of quotation.

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake﴾: that is, in the manner we have mentioned. Such a person, although he is pardoned, is not free of shortcoming in regard to the right of Allah, and the blood of the believer is not entirely wasted. ﴿Then (he must free) a believing slave﴾: that is, it is obligatory upon him, as a right of Allah, to free a soul adjudged to be a believer, even if it is a young child, so that Allah may free for him, for each part of it, a part of the Fire.

Imam Ahmad narrated, from ʿAbd al-Razzaq, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah, from a man of the Ansar: that he came with a black female slave and said: "O Messenger of Allah, upon me is the freeing of a believing slave. If you consider this one a believer, I will free her." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her: "Do you bear witness that there is no god but Allah?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Do you bear witness that I am the Messenger of Allah?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Do you believe in resurrection after death?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Free her." This is a sound chain, and the ignorance of the Companion (in the chain) does not harm it.

In the Muwatta' of Malik, the Musnad of al-Shafiʿi and Ahmad, the Sahih of Muslim, and the Sunan of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, from Muʿawiya ibn al-Hakam: that when he brought that black slave-girl, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Who am I?" She said: "You are the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer." Related by Ibn Kathir.

Two subtleties:

The first: Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-tahrir* means manumission (*al-i'taq*). *Al-hurr* (free) and *al-ʿatiq* (noble) mean generous, because nobility is found in free people, just as baseness is found in slaves. From this come *ʿitaq al-khayl* (noble horses) and *ʿitaq al-tayr* (noble birds) for their nobility. *Hurr al-wajh* (the free part of the face) is the most honourable place of it. And their saying of a base person, "slave," and "so-and-so is a slave of deeds," meaning base in deeds. *Raqaba* (neck) is an expression for the person, just as it is expressed by "head" in their saying, "so-and-so owns such-and-such a head of slaves."

The second: It has been said regarding the wisdom of manumission: when he removed a believing soul from the number of the living, it became incumbent upon him to bring into the number of the free another soul like it, for freeing her from the bondage of slavery is like giving her life, since the slave is counted among the dead, slavery being a consequence of disbelief, and disbelief is death in judgement. ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life?﴾ [al-Anʿam: 122] [al-Anʿam: part of verse 122]. For this reason he is prevented from the free person's dispositions. This is problematic, for if it were so, it would also be obligatory in intentional killing. But it may be said: this was obligatory upon him because Allah, Exalted, preserved for combat a believing soul by not prescribing retaliation (*qisas*), so He prescribed upon him a believing slave as its equivalent. Related by al-Nasafi.

﴿And blood-money paid to his family﴾: that is, the obligation upon him, also, as a right of the heirs of the slain, is a compensation to them for what they lost of their slain relative: a blood-money paid to his heirs, who divide it according to the division of inheritance.

The Sunnah has explained its amount. This is in what al-Nasa'i, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and others narrated, from Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Hazm, from his father, from his grandfather: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote a letter to the people of Yemen, in which it stated: "For a soul, the blood-money is one hundred camels." And in it: "And upon the people of gold, one thousand dinars."

Abu Dawud narrated, from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he: "imposed the blood-money upon the people of camels as one hundred camels, upon the people of cattle two hundred cows, upon the people of sheep two thousand sheep, and upon the people of garments two hundred garments."

In the Muwatta', that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab assessed the blood-money upon the people of the towns, making it upon the people of gold one thousand dinars, and upon the people of silver twelve thousand dirhams. This blood-money is obligatory only upon the *ʿaqila* (paternal kin) of the killer, not on his own property.

Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I know of no dissenter that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed the blood-money upon the *ʿaqila*.

In the Two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "Two women of Hudhayl fought, and one of them struck the other with a stone and killed her and what was in her womb. They brought the matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he decreed that the blood-money for her fetus was a *ghurra* (a slave or slave-girl), and decreed the blood-money of the woman upon her *ʿaqila*."

Abu Dawud narrated it from Jabir with the wording: "Two women of Hudhayl, one of them killed the other, and each of them had a husband and a child. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made the blood-money of the slain woman upon the *ʿaqila* of the killer woman, and he exonerated her husband and her child." He said: "The *ʿaqila* of the slain woman said: 'Her inheritance is for us.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'No, her inheritance is for her husband and her child.'"

The *ʿaqila* (agnatic kin): the relatives from the father's side, and they are his *ʿasaba* (agnates). They are the ones who used to tie camels at the door of the guardian of the slain (*yaʿqilun*), and the blood-money was named *ʿaql* by way of naming by the verbal noun, because camels were tied at the courtyard of the guardian of the slain. Then usage became common until *ʿaql* was applied to blood-money even when it was not camels. The imposing of the blood-money on the *ʿaqila* appears to contradict the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir: 18] [Fatir: part of verse 18]. Thus the hadiths that decree the imposing upon the *ʿaqila* specify the generality of the verse, because of the benefit in that: for if the killer were taken for the blood-money alone, it would nearly consume all his property, since a succession of mistakes cannot be guarded against; and if he were left without any fine, the blood of the slain would be wasted. Thus in *Nayl al-Awtar*.

Al-Mahayimi said: The blood-money is obligatory upon all the *ʿaqila* of the killer, who are his agnates other than the ascendants and descendants, because once the killer is pardoned, there is no basis for taking from him, and his ascendants and descendants are parts of him, so taking from them is taking from him. And there is no basis for wasting the blood of a believer, so it is taken from his *ʿaqila* who inherit from him by the strongest of the categories, which is agnation, since liability follows benefit. If he has no *ʿaqila*, or they are poor, then it falls upon the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*). End of quotation.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm and the majority of the Kharijites differed, and they obligated the blood-money upon the killer and not upon his *ʿaqila*. They argued with five rational arguments, which al-Fakhr al-Razi set forth here, and all of them are not worth a fils, since they are opposing a prophetic text with pure personal opinion. O Allah, we disavow ourselves to You from that. They overlooked the wisdom of the legislation regarding the *ʿaqila*, which we have explained.

*You must abandon every saying in the presence of the words of Muhammad, for no one who trusts in his religion is like one who gambles with it.* [a verse]

* *

Note: His words ﴿blood-money paid﴾ (*diyatun musallamatun*) include its delivery, whether immediate or deferred. However, consensus has been reached that the blood-money for mistaken killing is deferred upon the *ʿaqila*. But they differed regarding the length of the term. The majority held that the term is three years, and Rabiʿa said: five years.

In *al-Bahr*, it is related from some people, after mentioning the earlier consensus, that it is immediate, since nothing has been transmitted from him ﷺ about its deferment. In *al-Bahr* it is said: We reply that it was transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he decreed the blood-money upon the *ʿaqila* over three years, and ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas said so, and it was not disputed. End of quotation.

Al-Shafiʿi said in *al-Mukhtasar*: I know of no dissenter that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ decreed the blood-money upon the *ʿaqila* over three years.

Al-Rafiʿi said: Our companions spoke about whether a report with this was transmitted. Some of them said it was transmitted, and attributed it to the narration of ʿAli, peace be upon him. Others said it was transmitted that "he ﷺ decreed the blood-money upon the *ʿaqila*," but as for the deferment, no report has come concerning it, and it was taken from the consensus of the Companions.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: What al-Shafiʿi mentioned, we do not know it at all from Book or Sunnah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal was asked about this and said: "We know nothing concerning it." It was said: "Abu ʿAbd Allah (meaning al-Shafiʿi) narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ." He said: "Perhaps he heard it from that Madani," for he had a good opinion of him (meaning Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya). Ibn al-Rif'a responded to this: whoever knows a proof has a proof over one who does not know it.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated through Ibn Lahiʿa, from Yahya ibn Saʿid, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "It is from the Sunnah that the blood-money be paid in installments over three years." Al-Tirmidhi in his *Jami'* and Ibn al-Mundhir agreed with al-Shafiʿi in transmitting the consensus, each of them relating the consensus. Thus in *Nayl al-Awtar*.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿unless they forgo it as charity﴾: that is, unless the guardians of the slain give up the blood-money to the killer, so it is not obligatory upon him. The forgoing of it is called *sadaqa* (charity), urging toward it and drawing attention to its excellence.

Al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: In it (that is, this verse) is the magnifying of the killing of a believer and the sin in it, and the negating of it from mistake; that in killing by mistake there is an expiation (*kaffara*) and blood-money, not retaliation; that the blood-money is delivered to the family of the slain, unless they forgo it as charity, that is, they absolve themselves of it. In it is the permissibility of acquittal from the blood-money's recipients, even though it is unknown. And in His words "*musallama*" (delivered) rather than "*yusallimuha*" (they deliver it) is an indication that it is upon the *ʿaqila* of the killer. This was mentioned by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, related by Ibn Abi Hatim, and he used His words "*ila ahlihi*" (to his family) as evidence that the wife inherits from it, since she is among the family, contrary to the Literalists (*al-Zahiriyya*). It was used as evidence by one who permitted the killer to inherit from it, since he is of his family. The Literalists used His words "unless they forgo it as charity" as evidence that the slain has no right to pardon the blood-money, since Allah made that exclusively for his family. The generality of the verse includes the ruler (*imam*) if he kills by mistake, contrary to one who said there is nothing upon him nor upon his *ʿaqila*. Its generality was also used as evidence by one who said that in killing a slave there is blood-money and expiation, that upon a child and a madman who kill there is expiation, and that a partner in the killing bears a complete expiation. End of quotation.

﴿If he was from a people hostile to you﴾: that is, the slain, by mistake, ﴿and he is a believer﴾ but the killer did not know of him because he was among his people, by having embraced Islam among them without leaving them, or by having come to them after leaving them for some important matter.

﴿Then (he must free) a believing slave﴾: that is, upon his killer is the expiation, as a right of Allah, not the blood-money, for it is void, since there is no inheritance between him and his family, because they are combatants.

Imam Zayd ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, peace be upon them, said: The blood-money is not to be paid to them, because they would strengthen themselves by it. It is known that the forfeiture of the blood-money for one in this condition is derived from Allah's obligating upon his killer only the expiation, and He did not mention the blood-money as He mentioned it at the beginning and end of the verse.

Al-Hakim and others narrated, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding this verse, that he said: "A man used to come to the Prophet ﷺ and then return to his people, who were polytheists. Then the Muslims would strike him in a military detachment or a raid, and the one who struck him would free a slave."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 92 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if he was﴾, i.e., the one slain by mistake, ﴿from a people﴾, i.e., disbelievers, ﴿between you and whom there is a covenant﴾, i.e., a treaty of truce or safe-conduct, meaning he was upon their religion and creed, ﴿then [there is] a compensation﴾, i.e., upon his slayer is a blood-money (diyah) ﴿delivered to his family﴾, since they are, in matters of rights, like the Muslims.

﴿And the freeing of a believing slave﴾ is for the right of Allah, the Exalted. The mention of the blood-money here, with its being deferred in what preceded, is to indicate hastening to deliver the blood-money, to avoid the suspicion of breaking the covenant.

Al-Suyuti said: al-Hakim and others narrated, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if he was from a people between you﴾ etc.: "He is the man who is a mu'ahad (one under covenant), and whose people are people of a covenant, so the blood-money is delivered to them, and the one who caused the death frees a slave."

Al-Suyuti said: In it is that if the slain is from the people of dhimmah and covenant, then there is a blood-money delivered to his family along with the expiation (kaffarah). In it is also a refutation of those who said: there is no expiation for killing a dhimmi. Those who said that said: the verse concerns a believer whose family are people of a covenant, and they said: they have more right to his blood-money because of their covenant. Ibn 'Abbas's explanation mentioned above refutes this, and also that He, the Exalted, did not say in it "and he is a believer," as He said in the preceding verse. End.

* *

Note:
Whoever held that the blood-money of the mu'ahad, whether a combatant or a People of the Book, is equal to that of a Muslim, took evidence from the verse, because He, the Exalted, mentioned both the expiation and the blood-money for each of them, so their blood-money must be equal, just as the expiation for both is equal, since the unqualified "blood-money" indicates the known blood-money, which is the blood-money of a Muslim.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated, from Ibn 'Abbas, and said: it is gharib, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) paid the blood-money of the two men of 'Amir whom 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri killed, and they had a covenant from the Prophet (ﷺ) which 'Amr was not aware of, with the blood-money of the Muslims."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated, from al-Zuhri, that the blood-money of the Jew and the Christian in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) was like the blood-money of a Muslim, and in the time of Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman; then when Mu'awiyah came, he gave the family of the slain half and cast half into the public treasury. He said: then 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ruled with half, and cancelled what Mu'awiyah had imposed.

He also narrated from Ibn 'Umar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) paid a dhimmi the blood-money of a Muslim."

There is discussion regarding the two reports of al-Bayhaqi mentioned: the first is faulted for being mursal, and the second because its chain includes Abu Karaz, who is matruk (abandoned).

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi narrated, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The blood-money of a disbeliever is half the blood-money of a Muslim."

Abu Dawud narrated from him with the wording: "The blood-money of a mu'ahad is half the blood-money of a free man." And in another wording: "He decreed that the blood-money of the two People of the Book is half the blood-money of the Muslims," and they are the Jews and the Christians. Narrated by Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

In my view, there is no contradiction between these narrations mentioned: the apparent meaning is that the obligation in the blood-money of the disbeliever is only half, and there is no harm in increasing it beyond that until it reaches the blood-money of a Muslim, as a voluntary gift and favour. By this the narrations are reconciled. The inference from the verse to the equality of the blood-money of the Muslim and the disbeliever mentioned earlier is not clear, because of the generality (ijmal) in the blood-money, whose explanation is referred to the Sunnah. The Sunnah has explained it, and it is authentically established in it that the obligatory amount is half. And Allah knows best.

﴿So whoever does not find﴾, i.e., a slave to free, meaning he does not possess one nor what would lead him to one, ﴿then [he must fast] two consecutive months﴾, i.e., he must fast two months in succession without breaking the fast between them, such that if he fasts fifty-nine [days] and deliberately breaks a day, he must begin all of them anew, because the mistake arose from the turbidity of the soul, and this amount removes it and brings purification.

Al-Mahayimi said: ﴿A repentance from Allah﴾, i.e., an acceptance from Allah and mercy from Him, from (tāba 'alayhi) when He accepts his repentance. ﴿A repentance﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose, i.e., He prescribed that for you as a repentance from Him, or it is an emphatic infinitive for an omitted verb, i.e., He turned to you in repentance from Him.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of all things, among which is the measure of the turbidity of this great mistake, ﴿Wise﴾ in the remedy for its removal.

Al-Mahayimi said: If the mistake has this turbidity, along with His pardon for it, then where is the turbidity of the intentional killing?! I.e., which is the one mentioned in His saying, the Exalted:

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 93 (part 1 of 4):

On the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾ [93]

﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ for killing him. ﴿His recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him﴾ because he killed his own guardian (waliyy) intentionally. ﴿And curse him﴾ i.e., He removes him far from mercy. ﴿And prepare for him﴾ beyond that ﴿a great punishment﴾ i.e., greater than the punishment for the rest of the major sins, apart from polytheism (shirk).

Imam Ibn Kathir said: This is a severe threat and a firm promise for one who engages in this grave sin, which is linked with associating partners with Allah in more than one verse of the Book of Allah, where He, glorified is He, says in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] [al-Furqan: from verse 68] to the end of the verse. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him"﴾ [al-An'am: 151] [al-An'am: from verse 151] to the end of the verse. The verses and hadiths on the prohibition of killing are very numerous.

Among them is what is established in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn: the two authentic collections of Bukhari and Muslim), from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The first matter to be judged among people on the Day of Resurrection is concerning blood."

In the other hadith narrated by Abu Dawud, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The believer continues in a wide latitude of his religion (mu'nieqan salihan) so long as he has not shed unlawful blood. When he sheds unlawful blood, he is brought to a standstill (balah)."

In another hadith: "The passing away of the world is less significant to Allah than the killing of a Muslim man." I say: It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i from Ibn 'Amr.

In another hadith: "If the people of the heavens and the earth were to join together in killing a Muslim man, Allah would overturn them into the Fire." I say: It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, with the wording: "If the people of the heaven and the earth shared in the blood of a believer, Allah, mighty and majestic, would overturn them into the Fire."

In another hadith: "Whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim, even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with written between his eyes: 'Despairing of the mercy of Allah.'" I say: It was narrated by Ibn Majah from Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn 'Abbas used to hold that there is no repentance for one who deliberately kills a believer.

Al-Bukhari said: Adam narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, al-Mughirah ibn al-Nu'man narrated to us, who said: I heard Ibn Jubayr say: The people of Kufa differed concerning it, so I travelled to Ibn 'Abbas and asked him about it. He said: This verse was revealed: ﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell﴾, it is the last thing revealed, and nothing abrogated it.

Likewise, he (al-Bukhari) narrated it, and Muslim and al-Nasa'i, through various chains from Shu'bah with the same wording.

Abu Dawud narrated it from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Ibn Mahdi, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Mughirah ibn al-Nu'man, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell﴾, and he said: Nothing abrogated it.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza said to me: Ibn 'Abbas was asked about His saying: ﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: Nothing abrogated it. And concerning this verse: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] to its end, he said: It was revealed concerning the people of polytheism.

Ibn Jarir also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell﴾. He said: If a man knows Islam and the laws of Islam, and then kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, and there is no repentance for him. I mentioned that to Mujahid, and he said: Except for one who regrets.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, that "a man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: What do you say about a man who killed a man deliberately? He said: ﴿Then his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: It was revealed among the last of what was revealed, and nothing abrogated it until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was taken (in death), and no revelation came after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The man said: What do you say if he repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then is guided? He said: How would he have repentance? I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'May his mother be bereaved! A man who kills a man deliberately comes on the Day of Resurrection, his killer grasped by his right or left hand, or holding his head in his right or left hand, his veins gushing blood before the Throne, saying: O Lord, ask Your servant why he killed me.'" It was narrated by al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

This hadith has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas through many chains.

Among the early generation (al-Salaf: the righteous predecessors) who held that there is no repentance for him were Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Hurayrah, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim; it was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim.

On this subject there are many hadiths. Among them is what al-Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The one who was killed will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to his killer, holding his head with his other hand, and he will say: O Lord, ask this one why he killed me. He will say: I killed him so that the might would be Yours. He will say: Indeed, it is Mine." He said: "Another will come clinging to his killer and will say: O Lord, ask this one why he killed me. He will say: I killed him so that the might would be for so-and-so. He will say: It is not for him. Bear your sin." He said: "He will be hurled into the Fire for seventy autumns." It was narrated by al-Nasa'i.

Imam Ahmad and al-Nasa'i reported from Mu'awiyah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Every sin, Allah may forgive it, except the man who dies as a disbeliever, or the man who kills a believer deliberately."

Imam Ahmad said: Al-Nadr narrated to us, Sulayman ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, Humayd narrated to us, who said: "Abu al-'Aliyah came to me, myself and a companion of mine, and said to us: Come, you two are younger than me and more retentive of hadith than me. He took us to Bishr ibn 'Asim, and Abu al-'Aliyah said to him: Narrate your hadith to these people. He said: 'Uqbah ibn Malik al-Laythi narrated to us, who said: The Prophet ﷺ sent a expedition (sariyyah) which raided a people, and a man among the people fled, and a man from the expedition pursued him, brandishing his sword. The man from the people said: I am a Muslim. He did not consider what he said, and struck him and killed him. The matter reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said a severe word about it. It reached the killer. While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, was delivering a sermon, the killer said: By Allah, he only said what he said to seek refuge from being killed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned away from him and from those around him among the people, and continued his sermon. Then he (the killer) said again: O Messenger of Allah, he only said what he said to seek refuge from being killed. He turned away from him and from those around him among the people, and continued his sermon. Then he could not wait, and said a third time: By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, he only said what he said to seek refuge from being killed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned toward him, displeasure visible on his face, and said: 'Indeed Allah refuses (to accept) from one who kills a believer,' three times." It was narrated by al-Nasa'i.

Then Ibn Kathir said: What the majority of the early and later generations of this community hold is that the killer has repentance between himself and Allah, mighty and majestic is He. If he repents, turns back, humbles himself and submits, and does righteous deeds, Allah replaces his evil deeds with good deeds, and compensates the slain for his wrong and satisfies him concerning his wrong. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] to His saying: ﴿except those who repent and believe and do righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] [al-Furqan: 68-70] to the end of the verse. This is a report that cannot be abrogated, and applying it to polytheists while applying this verse to believers goes against the apparent meaning, and its application would require proof. And Allah knows best.

He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah"﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] [al-Zumar: from verse 53] to the end of the verse. This is general concerning all sins, of disbelief, polytheism, doubt, hypocrisy, killing, immorality, and other than that. Whoever repents from any of these, Allah accepts his repentance. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116] [al-Nisa': from verse 48 and 116]. This verse is general concerning all sins other than polytheism, and it is mentioned in this noble surah after this verse and before it, to strengthen hope. And Allah knows best.

It is established in the two Sahihs the report of "the Israelite who killed one hundred souls, then asked a scholar: Is there any repentance for me? He said: Who stands between you and repentance? Then he directed him to a land where Allah is worshipped, so he migrated to it, but died on the way, and the angels of mercy took him."

If this is the case among the Children of Israel, then repentance being accepted in this community is all the more so, by way of greater priority, because Allah has removed from us the burdens and the shackles that were upon them, and sent our Prophet with the tolerant, easy monotheism (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah). As for the noble verse, which is His saying: ﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately﴾ to the end of the verse, Abu Hurayrah and a group of the early generation said: This is his recompense, if he is recompensed.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it with his chain as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ), but it is not authentic. The meaning of this formulation is that this is his recompense if he is requited for it, and likewise every threat upon a sin. However, there may be no obstacle to that from righteous deeds that prevent that punishment from reaching him, according to the view of the proponents of balancing (al-muwazanah) and nullification (al-ihbat) of deeds. This is the best course to take in the matter of threats. And Allah knows best what is correct.

Even if the killer enters the Fire, either according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas and those who agree with him that there is no repentance for him, or according to the view of the majority where he has no righteous deed by which he may be saved, he is still not abiding therein forever, for "khulud" (abiding) means a long stay, and the hadiths have been transmitted in a widely reported way from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that "whoever has in his heart even an atom's weight of faith will leave the Fire."

Then Ibn Kathir said: As for the slain man demanding (his right from) the killer on the Day of Resurrection, it is among the rights of human beings, and it is not dropped by repentance. But it is necessary to restore it to them. There is no difference between the slain, the one from whom something was stolen, the one from whom something was seized, the one defrauded, the one slandered, and the rest of the rights of human beings, for the consensus (ijma') is established that these are not dropped by repentance, but restoring them to their owners is necessary for the validity of repentance. If that is impossible, then the demand (for them) on the Day of Resurrection is necessary. However, the occurrence of the demand does not necessarily entail the occurrence of requital, since the killer may have righteous deeds that are transferred to the slain, or some of them, and then a surplus of reward remains for him by which he enters Paradise, or Allah compensates the slain with whatever He wills of His bounty, such as palaces of Paradise, its delights, the raising of his rank therein, and the like. And Allah knows best. End of quotation.
