Al-Nawawi said in his "Sharh Muslim" in explaining the hadith of the Israelite who killed one hundred souls: It is cited as evidence for the acceptance of the repentance of one who kills deliberately, and this is the position of the scholars and their consensus; no one among them opposed it except Ibn 'Abbas. As for what has been reported from some of the early generation of severity regarding this, the intention of its speaker is deterrence and repentance, not that he believes his repentance is invalid.

Although this hadith concerns the law of those before us (shar' man qablana: the earlier revealed laws), and there is disagreement over using it as evidence, this is not the place of the disagreement. Its place of disagreement is when our law has not come with its agreement and confirmation. If it has come, it is indisputably a law for us. And this has come with our law, namely His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, and do not kill the soul﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] to His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] [al-Furqan: 68] to the end of the verse.

It is said regarding the verse, "And whoever kills a believer intentionally..." (﴿ومَن يَقْتُلْ مُؤْمِنًا مُتَعَمِّدًا﴾), that the correct meaning is: his recompense is Jahannam. He may be repaid with it, he may be repaid with something else, or he may not be repaid at all but pardoned. If he kills intentionally while deeming it lawful, without any right and without any interpretation (ta'wil), then he is an apostate unbeliever who will abide in Jahannam by consensus (ijma'). If he does not deem it lawful but believes it to be forbidden, then he is a sinful disobedient, one who has committed a major sin (kabirah), whose recompense is Jahannam, abiding therein. However, God the Exalted has shown favour and informed that whoever dies professing God's oneness (muwahhid) will not abide in it. So this one will not abide in it. Rather, he may be pardoned and not enter the Fire at all, or he may not be pardoned but be punished like the other sinning monotheists (u gaṣat al-muwahhidin), then he will leave with them for Paradise and will not abide in the Fire.

He (al-Qasimi) said: This is the correct meaning of the verse. That he deserves to be repaid with a specific punishment does not necessitate that this recompense be certain. The verse does not inform that he will abide in Jahannam; rather, it says that this is his recompense, i.e., he deserves to be repaid with it. It is also said: the verse was revealed concerning a specific man. It is also said: what is meant by abiding (khulud) is a long duration, not perpetuity. It is also said: its meaning is, "This is his recompense if He repays him." All these opinions are weak or corrupt, because they contradict the literal reality of the verse's wording. So the correct view is what we have put forward. End of quotation.

 'Ala' al-Din al-Khazin said: The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse: is it abrogated (mansukhah) or not? And is there repentance for one who kills intentionally or not? It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Is there repentance for one who intentionally kills a believer?" He said: "No." So I recited to him the verse in al-Furqan: ﴿And those who do not invoke with God another god, and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], to the end of the verse. He said: "This is a Meccan verse, abrogated by a Medinan verse: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Jahannam﴾."

In another narration he said: The people of Kufa differed concerning the killing of a believer, so I travelled to Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: "It was revealed among the last of what was revealed, and nothing abrogated it."

In another narration Ibn 'Abbas said: This verse was revealed at Medina: ﴿And those who do not invoke with God another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], to His saying: ﴿humiliated﴾ [al-Furqan: 69]. The polytheists said: "What does Islam avail us, when we have made equals to God, have killed the soul God forbade, and committed indecencies?" So God the Exalted revealed: ﴿Except one who repents and believes and does righteous deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], to the end of the verse.

It is added in one narration: As for one who entered Islam and understood it, then killed, there is no repentance for him. Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) reported it in the two Sahihs.

It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, that he debated Ibn 'Abbas over this verse, saying: "From where do you have that it is muhkam (not abrogated)?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "The accumulation of threats (takaththuf al-wa'id) in it."

Ibn Mas'ud said: It is muhkam, and it only increases in severity.

From Kharijah ibn Zayd, who said: I heard Zayd ibn Thabit say: "This verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Jahannam, abiding therein﴾, after the one in al-Furqan: ﴿And those who do not invoke with God another god and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], by six months." (Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i reported it.) Al-Nasa'i added in one narration: "by eight months."

Zayd ibn Thabit also said: When this verse in al-Furqan was revealed, ﴿And those who do not invoke with God another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], we wondered at its leniency. We remained seven months, then the stern verse came after the lenient one and abrogated it. By the stern one he meant this verse in Surat al-Nisa', and by the lenient one the verse of al-Furqan.

Most of the scholars of the earlier and later generations went to the view that this verse is abrogated, but they differed about its abrogating verse. Some said: it was abrogated by the one in al-Furqan, but this is not strong, because the verse of al-Furqan was revealed before the verse of al-Nisa', and what comes earlier does not abrogate what comes later. The majority of those who held abrogation said that its abrogating verse is also the one in al-Nisa', namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48].

Those who held that it is abrogated answered the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier, reported in the Two Sahihs, by saying: this verse is a report about the occurrence of punishment upon the one who does that act mentioned in the verse, and abrogation does not enter reports. And even if we concede that abrogation enters reports, reconciling the two verses is possible in such a way that no contradiction exists between them: by taking the unrestricted (mutlaq) wording of the verse of al-Nisa' as qualified by the verse of al-Furqan, so the meaning becomes: "His recompense is Jahannam, except one who repents."

Some said: what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas is only meant as emphasis and exaggeration in deterring from killing. It is like what was narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, that he said: "If he has not killed, it is said to him: there is no repentance for you; and if he killed, then regretted and came repentant, it is said to him: there is repentance for you."

It was said: something similar has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also narrated from him that his repentance is accepted, and this is the view of the People of the Sunnah. The Book and the Sunnah indicate it. As for the Book, there is His saying: ﴿And indeed, I am the Forgiving for whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then is guided﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53].

As for the Sunnah, there is what was narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "A Bedouin man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, what are the two things that necessitate?' He said: 'Whoever dies not associating anything with God enters Paradise, and whoever dies associating something with Him enters the Fire.'" (Muslim reported it.)

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from 'Ubada ibn al-Samit who said: "We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in a gathering, and he said: 'Pledge to me that you will not associate anything with God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right.'"

In another narration: "...nor kill your children, nor bring a slander which you fabricate between your hands and feet, nor disobey me in what is good. Whoever among you fulfils it, his reward is upon God; whoever incurs any of that and God conceals it for him, his affair is with God: if He wills, He pardons him, and if He wills, He punishes him. So we pledged to him upon that." End of quotation.

Al-'Allama Abu al-Su'ud said: The Kharijites and the Mu'tazilites held by this verse to the eternal abiding of one who intentionally kills a believer in the Fire, but there is no proof for them in it. Not because it is said that it concerns one who deems it lawful, as is the opinion of 'Ikrimah and his like, on the evidence that it was revealed concerning Maqis ibn Subaba al-Kinani the apostate, for the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause. Rather, because what is meant by abiding (khulud) is a long stay, not perpetuity, since the texts clearly state that the punishment of sinning believers does not endure.

As for what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that there is no repentance for one who intentionally kills a believer, and likewise what was narrated from Sufyan, that the people of knowledge, when asked, said: "There is no repentance for him" — it is to be understood as following God's way of severity and harshness. On this is also to be understood what was narrated from Anas, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, said: "God refused to make repentance for the killer of a believer." 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah and Abu Salih said: the meaning is "that is his recompense if He repays him." They said: one may say to someone whom he is warning against a matter: "If you do it, your recompense is death or beating," and then if he does not repay him with that, it is not a lie on his part.

Al-Wahidi said: The principle in this is that God, Mighty and Majestic, may fail to carry out a threat, though it is impossible for Him to fail to carry out a promise. The verification is that there is no necessity to base what we are discussing on the aforementioned principle, because this is a report from Him, exalted, that his recompense is that, not that He will repay him with it. How not? God has said: ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. And if this were a report that He, exalted, repays every evil with its like, it would conflict with His saying: ﴿And He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. End of quotation.

Al-'Allama al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: As for explaining the reconciliation between this verse and what opposes it, we say: there is no dispute that His saying, ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾, is among the forms of generality that include the repentant and the non-repentant, indeed the Muslim and the disbeliever. The exception mentioned in the verse of al-Furqan, namely His saying: ﴿except one who repents﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], after His saying: ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], is specific to the repentant, and so it specifies the generality of His saying: ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾.

As for the view that is the correct doctrine, that the general is built upon the specific unconditionally, whether the specific came earlier, later or concurrently, it is evident. As for the view of those who say that a later general abrogates an earlier specific, then even if we concede that His saying, ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾, is later than the verse of al-Furqan, we do not concede that it is later than the general texts which indicate that killing with repentance is among what God forgives, such as His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God; indeed God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116].

Among that is what Muslim reported from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever repents before the sun rises from its west, God will accept his repentance."

And what al-Tirmidhi reported and graded sound from the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A gate from the direction of the west, a rider could travel across its width for forty or seventy years — God created it on the day He created the heavens and the earth — is open for repentance; it will not be closed until the sun rises from its west."

Al-Tirmidhi also reported from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not begun the death rattle."

Muslim reported from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, extends His hand by night so that the wrongdoer of the day may repent, and extends His hand by day so that the wrongdoer of the night may repent, until the sun rises from its west." And other hadiths like these, too many to enumerate.

It cannot be said that these general texts are specified by His saying: "And whoever kills a believer intentionally," to the end of the verse. For we say: the verse is more general in one respect, namely that it includes the repentant and others, and more specific in another respect, namely that it concerns the killer. These general texts are more general in one respect, namely that they include one whose sin is killing and one whose sin is other than killing, and more specific in another respect, namely that they concern the repentant. When two generals conflict, there remains nothing but recourse to preponderance (tarjih). And there is no doubt that the proofs indicating the acceptance of repentance unconditionally are preponderant, due to their number.

And likewise it is said: the hadiths about the emergence of the monotheists (al-muwahhidun) from the Fire, whose meaning is mass-transmitted (mutawatir al-ma'na), as anyone well versed in the books of hadith knows, indicate the emergence of every monotheist, whether his sin was killing or something else. The verse that mandates the emergence of one who killed a soul is more general than whether the killer is a monotheist or not. So two generalities conflict, and both are probabilistic in their indication (zanni al-dalalah). However, the generality of the verse on killing has been qualified by what you have heard, unlike the hadiths on the emergence of the monotheists, which have been qualified only by what is more general than them in absolute terms, such as the verses of threat against the disobedient that indicate eternity (al-khulud), which include both the disbeliever and the Muslim, and this qualification has no effect. Or by what is more specific than them in absolute terms, such as the hadiths that mandate the eternal punishment of some people who commit sins, like: "Whoever kills himself..." And the general is built upon the specific. From what we have established, the view that the killer's repentance is accepted if he repents becomes clear to you, [p. 1465] and that he does not remain eternally in the Fire if he does not repent. It also becomes clear to you that there is no proof in what Ibn 'Abbas argued, that the verse of al-Furqan is Meccan and abrogated (mansukhah) by the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ and so on, as al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated this from him. Likewise, there is no proof for him in what al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi narrated from him: that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The one who was killed will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to the killer, his forelock and head in his hand, and his veins gushing blood, saying: 'O Lord, this one killed me,' until He brings him close to the Throne." And in a narration of al-Nasa'i: "He will say: 'Ask this one why he killed me.'" Because the most that this entails is the occurrence of a dispute before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that does not necessitate taking the repentant one to account for that sin, nor his eternal abiding in the Fire, on the supposition that he did not repent.

The beneficial repentance here is the confession of the killing before the heir, if he has an heir, or before the ruler if he has no heir; regret for that deed; resolve not to return to the like of it; and not merely regret and resolve without confession; and surrendering oneself or the blood money (diyah) if its rightful recipient chooses it, because the right of the human being (haqq al-adami) requires an additional matter beyond the rights of Allah, namely handing it over, or handing over its equivalent, after confessing to it.

If you say: then how do you interpret the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and the hadith of Mu'awiyah mentioned at the beginning of the chapter? For the first indicates that the killer or the one who aids in killing will meet Allah with written between his eyes: "Despair of mercy," and the second indicates that the sin of killing is not forgiven by Allah?

I say: both are to be understood as referring to the killer not having made repentance. The evidence for this interpretation is what is in the chapter of the general and specific proofs that mandate acceptance, and if there were nothing of that except the hadith of the man who killed one hundred, over whom the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment disputed, and the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit mentioned before it, they would compel us to adopt that interpretation. Especially with what we have presented of the later date of the hadith of 'Ubadah, [p. 1466] and with the fact that the two hadiths are in the Two Sahihs, unlike the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Mu'awiyah. Also, within the hadith of Mu'awiyah itself there is what points to this interpretation, for he linked the man who kills intentionally with the man who dies as a disbeliever. There is no doubt that one who dies as a disbeliever, persisting in his sin and not repenting of it, is among those who abide eternally in the Fire. From this qualification it is derived that repentance erases the sin of disbelief, so that this companion, which is killing, is more deserving of its acceptance.

The great scholar al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: this verse contains a great deal of threat, distancing, flashing and thundering, and a grave matter and a severe affair. He said: For this reason there has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas what has been narrated, that the repentance of one who intentionally kills a believer is not accepted. And from Sufyan: "The scholars, when asked, used to say: there is no repentance for him." And this is understood from them as following the Sunnah of Allah in severity and harshness. Otherwise, every sin is erased by repentance, and it suffices as proof that shirk is erased.

Then he mentioned the hadith: "The disappearance of this world is less significant to Allah than the killing of a Muslim man," which is in al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Ibn 'Amr, and al-Tirmidhi also narrated it. The words of al-Shawkani end here.

And Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in al-Jawab al-Kafi: Since injustice and transgression are contrary to the justice upon which the heavens and the earth stand, and Allah, Glorified is He, sent His messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, and revealed His books so that people might establish justice, [injustice] was among the greatest of major sins (al-kaba'ir) in the sight of Allah, and its rank in grievousness was according to its corruption in itself. And the killing of a believing human being was among the most ugly and severe of injustices. Then he said: And since [p. 1467] the corruption of killing was of this magnitude, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Because of that, We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32].

Then he said: In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Samurah ibn Jundub, he said: The first part of a person to rot is his belly; so whoever among you is able not to eat except what is good, let him do so; and whoever is able that there not come between him and Paradise a handful of blood that he has spilled, let him do so.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from Nafi', he said: 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar looked one day at the Ka'bah and said: "How great you are, and how great your sanctity, yet the believer has greater sanctity than you." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan hadith.

Also in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believer remains in latitude in his religion so long as he does not shed unlawful blood." Al-Bukhari also mentioned from Ibn 'Umar, he said: Among the ruinous affairs from which there is no escape for one who casts himself into them is the shedding of unlawful blood without its lawful basis.

In the Two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Abusing a believer is wickedness (fusuq), and fighting him is disbelief (kufr)."

And in the same two, also from him (ﷺ): "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks."

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from him (ﷺ): "Whoever kills a mu'ahid (one under a covenant) will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance is found from a distance of forty years."

This is the punishment for the killer of an enemy of Allah when he is a mu'ahid within his covenant and his safe-conduct. So how much more is the punishment of the killer of His believing servant?!

And if a woman entered the Fire because of a cat that she confined until it died of hunger and thirst, and the Prophet (ﷺ) saw her in the Fire while the cat was scratching her face and chest, then how much greater is the punishment of one who imprisons a believer until he dies without any crime?!

In some of the Sunan from him (ﷺ): "The disappearance of this world is less significant to Allah than the killing of a believer without right."

And Ibn al-Qayyim also said before that: Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, has made the recompense for the intentional killing of a believing soul to be eternal abiding in the Fire, the wrath and curse of the Almighty, and the preparation of a great punishment for him. This is the consequence of intentionally killing a believer, so long as no preventing factor intervenes.

There is no disagreement that Islam occurring after the killing, voluntarily and by choice, is a preventing factor against the implementation of that recompense. But does the repentance of the Muslim from it after it has occurred prevent it? On this there are two opinions among the early and later scholars, and these are two narrations from Ahmad.

Those who said: repentance does not prevent its implementation, saw that it is a right of a human being which he did not receive in this world, and the one who was wronged departed with his grievance, so it must be satisfied for him in the abode of justice. They said: What the heir has taken is only the pure right that Allah gave him the choice of exacting or pardoning. And what benefit does the murdered man gain from his heir's retaliation? And what compensation for his grievance has he obtained by his heir's exaction? This is the more correct of the two opinions on the matter: that the right of the one killed is not extinguished by the heir's exaction. These are two views of the companions of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and others. But a group held that it is extinguished by repentance and the heir's exaction, for repentance wipes out what came before it, and the sin he committed has had its penalty applied to it.

They said: If repentance erases the effect of disbelief and sorcery, which are greater in sin than killing, then how could it fall short of erasing the effect of killing? Allah has accepted the repentance of disbelievers who killed their allies, and made them among His chosen servants, and He called those who burned His friends and tempted them away from their religion to repentance.

[p. 1470] And Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. This applies to the killer, and it encompasses disbelief and what is less than it. They said: How can a servant repent from a sin and be punished for it after repentance? This is known to be impossible in the law and recompense of Allah. They said: The repentance of this sinner is the surrender of himself, and it is not possible to surrender it to the one killed, so the Lawgiver established his guardian (waliyy) in his place, and made surrendering the self to him like surrendering it to the one killed, just as the surrender of the property owed to the heir is equivalent to surrendering it to the deceased.

The verified position on the matter is that three rights are connected with killing: a right of Allah, a right of the wronged one who was killed, and a right of the guardian (waliyy). So if the killer surrenders himself voluntarily and by choice to the guardian, out of regret for what he did and fear of Allah, with sincere repentance, then he has settled the right of Allah through repentance, and the right of the guardian through exaction, pardon, or reconciliation. The right of the one killed remains, which Allah compensates for on the Day of Resurrection on behalf of His repentant, virtuous servant, and He reconciles between them. So this one's right is not nullified, nor is this one's repentance nullified.

Section

Some scholars chose to suspend judgment in this matter, among them the Imam Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Murtada al-Yamani, for he said in his book Ithar al-Haqq, in the section on promise and threat, the following text: There is no doubt that exception from promise and threat, and the specification of general statements by connected and disconnected evidences, is acceptable, either by way of harmonization (al-jam')—and there is no doubt about its permissibility, soundness and goodness—and there is consensus on this and its frequent occurrence among the early and later generations of the Ummah. Indeed, there is no doubt that it takes precedence in rank and in beginning before preference (al-tarjih). If harmonization is impossible, then preference applies. If it is clarified, it is acted upon. If it is not clarified, suspension is obligatory, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra': 36].

For this reason I chose suspension regarding the ruling on the killer of a believer after the wronged one has been vindicated against him, and [I chose not to hold] the certainty that he is a wicked accursed one, whose killing is obligatory and from whom one must disassociate, and the certainty that his recompense is Jahannam, abiding in it forever, as He, Exalted is He, said according to what He intended. Rather, I suspended judgment in the place of conflict that I clarified in al-'Awasim, not in accordance with what has been said about whether Allah, Exalted is He, in this verse, has stated His recompense which He may enact if He wills, or has stated the recompense which He chose for him in its execution when nothing remains but His right after the right of the wronged killed one has been satisfied. And Allah, Glorified is He, knows best.

So whoever prefers harmonizing the threat against the killer with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], and with all verses and hadiths of hope, holds the first. Whoever prefers the threat against the killer in this verse and in the hadiths that specify the killing of a believer for cutting off hope, as I have clarified in al-'Awasim, prefers the threat against the killer. And whoever faces conflicts and does not see in the execution of a belief any benefit, nor any requirement for it, nor any necessity for it, prefers suspension. Allah is the one present in the tongue of every speaker and in his intention. There is no doubt in preferring the specific text over the general and giving it precedence, and on this is the practice of the scholars of Islam regarding the evidences of the Shari'ah. Whoever does not give it precedence in some places will not be able to fulfill that in every place, and will be compelled to arbitrariness and inconsistency without a clear proof.

Al-Qasimi's commentary (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 93 (part 4 of 4):

Those among the Muslims whose agreement counts (man yu'tadd bihi) have reached consensus on restricting the minor sins from among the general threat verses that apply to all sins, whenever those who commit minor sins are Muslims. No contradiction arises from this for the threat verses, nor is there any falsehood, nor any denial of any part of them. Likewise, every hadith of hope (ahadith al-raja') that is authentically transmitted contains no contradiction with the general wording of the threat verses, and does not entail permitting a breach of promise (khulf) on the part of Allah, the Exalted. This is one single chapter.

For this reason, the hadiths of hope became widely known in the era of the Companions and the Successors (al-tabi'un), and no one denounced them. Rather, their narrators were their greatest figures and their imams. In al-'Awasim there are, on this subject, some ten-odd reports from 'Ali, peace be upon him. Moreover, the specifying factors (al-mukhassisat) for the general statements on this matter are Qur'anic. And the general statements of promise (umumat al-wa'd), prior to the specification of the threat, prevent a definite judgment that the general threat applies without exception, in preference to the general promise. Furthermore, according to many groups, khulf occurs only in failing to fulfil a promise of good; as for a threat of evil, there is disagreement over whether leaving it unfulfilled counts. They agreed that it is called 'pardon' ('afw), as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"I have been informed that the Messenger of Allah threatened me, yet pardon from the Messenger of Allah is hoped for."

They differed, despite its being called pardon, over whether it is called khulf or not. Whoever prohibited that (i.e., calling it khulf) prohibited the soundness of its linguistic transmission, and argued for its impermissibility by saying that it is not valid for a praise term and a dispraise term to be combined on one referent. End of quotation.

* *

Section

Expiation (kaffarah) is prescribed for intentional killing, on the basis of what Imam Ahmad narrated from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa', who said: "A group from Banu Sulaym came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'A companion of ours has incurred the obligation (awjaba).' He said: 'Let him free a slave; Allah will ransom with each of its limbs a limb of his from the Fire.'"

He also narrated it through another chain from him, who said: "We came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning a companion of ours who had incurred the obligation. He said: 'Free [a slave] on his behalf; Allah will free with each of its limbs a limb of his from the Fire.'"

This was narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, and the wording of Abu Dawud is: "He has incurred the obligation (i.e., the Fire) by killing."

al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: "The hadith of Wathilah is evidence for the establishment of expiation for intentional killing. This applies when the killer is pardoned or the heir accepts blood money (diyah). As for when retaliation (qisas) is carried out against him, there is no expiation for him; rather, the killing itself is his expiation, based on the hadith of 'Ubadah mentioned in the chapter, and on what Abu Nu'aym narrated in al-Ma'rifah: 'The Prophet ﷺ said: The killing is an expiation (kaffarah).' It is from the hadith of Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, and its chain includes Ibn Lahi'ah."

The Hafiz said: "However, it comes from the hadith of Ibn Wahb from him, so it is hasan. al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali as a mawquf report."

Then Allah, the Exalted, warned against what leads to intentional killing, namely carelessness in affairs, with His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 94 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth [to fight] in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life. But with Allah are many acquisitions. Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you. So investigate carefully. Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ [4:94]

(p-1474) ﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth﴾, i.e., you set out, ﴿in the cause of Allah﴾, to the land of the enemy for the raid, ﴿investigate carefully﴾, i.e., seek clarity regarding everything you do and everything you leave undone, and do not hasten in it without reflection and deliberation.

﴿And do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ is a prohibition against what is the result of neglecting the commanded act, and a specification of an important matter among those in which clarification is required. That is: do not say (to one who shows submission to your call, saying, "There is no deity but Allah," or who greets you with peace, the greeting of Islam): "You are not a believer" inwardly; he only said it with his tongue to seek safety. Rather, accept from him what he displays and deal with him according to its requirement.

﴿Seeking﴾, i.e., you seek by killing him, ﴿the goods of worldly life﴾, i.e., his wealth, which is quickly exhausted. The clause is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "do not say," indicating what drives them to haste and to abandoning deliberation.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But with Allah are many acquisitions﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against seeking his wealth, through the implicit promise contained in it, as if it were said: Do not seek his wealth, for with Allah are many spoils which He will grant you, thereby sparing you from committing what you have committed. Abu al-Su'ud conveyed this.

Then he said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you﴾ is a reason for the prohibition against the aforementioned saying. That is: Like that one who gave you the greeting of peace, you too were at the beginning of your Islam, displaying to people nothing other than what he displayed to you, of the greeting of Islam and the like. Then Allah conferred His favor upon you by accepting from you that status, and by it He protected your blood and your property, and did not command an inquiry into your inner hearts.

The "fa" in His saying, ﴿So investigate carefully﴾ is the eloquent (faṣīḥa) fa, meaning: if the matter is so, then seek clarification of this clear matter, measure his state by yours, and do to him what was done to you at the beginning of your affairs, namely accepting the apparent state without pausing to examine whether the outward and inward agree. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ — so do not rush into killing, and be cautious and careful in that.

Ibn Kathir said (regarding its occasion of revelation):

Imam Ahmad narrated from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A man from the Banu Sulaym passed by a group of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ while tending his sheep. He greeted them with peace. They said, 'He only greeted us with peace so that he might seek refuge from us.' So they went to him and killed him, and brought his sheep to the Prophet ﷺ. (p-1475) Then this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ to its end."

al-Tirmidhi narrated it and then said: "This is a hasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith, and in the chapter there is also a report from Usama ibn Zayd."

al-Hakim narrated it and declared it authentic. al-Bukhari narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding this verse, that he said: "There was a man with a small flock of his own, and the Muslims overtook him. He said, 'Peace be upon you,' but they killed him and took his small flock." So Allah revealed concerning that ... to His saying: "the goods of worldly life": "that small flock."

al-Bukhari also said: Habib ibn Abi ʿAmra narrated from Saʿid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to al-Miqdad: 'If a believing man conceals his faith among a disbelieving people, then he manifests his faith, and you kill him, then likewise you used to conceal your faith in Makkah before.'" Thus al-Bukhari narrated it in mu'allaq form, abridged.

al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated it at length, in a connected chain, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent a expedition in which was al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. When they reached the people, they found that they had dispersed, but one man remained who had much wealth and did not leave. He said, 'I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah,' and al-Miqdad moved toward him and killed him. A man from among their companions said to him, 'Did you kill a man who bore witness that there is no deity but Allah? By Allah, I will mention that to the Prophet ﷺ.' When they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ they said, 'O Messenger of Allah! A man bore witness that there is no deity but Allah, and al-Miqdad killed him.' He said, 'Call al-Miqdad to me. O al-Miqdad! Did you kill a man who says, "There is no deity but Allah"?! How will you deal with "There is no deity but Allah" tomorrow?' He said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ to His saying: ﴿Thus were you before﴾, the verse. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to al-Miqdad: 'A believing man was concealing his faith among a disbelieving people, then he manifested his faith, and you killed him. Likewise you used to conceal your faith in Makkah before.'"

Ibn Kathir said: So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you﴾ means: you were before this state like this one who conceals and hides his faith from his people, as mentioned in the raised (marfuʿ) hadith, and as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land﴾ [8:26], the verse. This is another interpretation regarding the referent of the demonstrative, different from what has preceded, and it is the more precise, and the more deserving of acceptance.

al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": It is derived from this narration (i.e., the narration of al-Bazzar) that the killer is named. As for the slain man, al-Tha'labi narrated through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated through the route of Qatada something similar, and the wording is that of al-Kalbi: that the name of the slain man was Mirdas ibn Nahik, from the people of Fadak, and that the name of the killer was Usama ibn Zayd, and that the name of the commander of the expedition was Ghalib ibn Fadala al-Laythi. When the people of Mirdas were routed, he alone remained, having driven his sheep to a mountain. When they overtook him, he said, "There is no deity but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon you," but Usama ibn Zayd killed him. When they returned, the verse was revealed.

Likewise al-Tabari narrated through the route of al-Suddi something similar, and in the final part of the narration from Qatada: because the greeting of the Muslims is peace, by which they recognize one another.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of Ibn Lahi'a, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Mirdas." This is a fine supporting report (shahid hasan). Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted with a chain that Usama swore never to kill a man who says, "There is no deity but Allah," after that man, and because of what he encountered from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding it.

Some of the Zaydi exegetes, from among their imams, said: With this he excused himself to ʿAli, upon him be peace, to the point that he stayed behind from him, although it was an unacceptable excuse, since fighting alongside the Imam is obligatory when the rebels rise, and he must expiate his oath.

al-Hakim said: Except that the Commander of the Faithful permitted him. End of quotation.

Al-Imam Ahmad narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Hadrad, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent us to Idam. I set out with a group of Muslims, among them Abu Qatada al-Harith ibn Ribʿi and Muhallim ibn Jaththama ibn Qays. We set out until, when we were in the valley of Idam, ʿAmir ibn al-Adbat al-Ashja'i passed by us on his riding camel, with a bundle of goods (mutayyiʿ, diminutive of matāʿ, meaning merchandise) and a waterskin of milk. When he passed us he greeted us with peace, but we refrained from him. Muhallim ibn Jaththama charged at him and killed him, for something that was between them, and he took his camel and his goods. When we came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him of the news, the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah﴾ to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿expert﴾."

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Ibn ʿUmar and added: "Muhallim came wearing two garments, and sat before the Prophet ﷺ so that he might ask forgiveness for him. The Messenger of Allah said, 'May Allah not forgive you.' He rose while catching his tears with his two garments. Not a seventh day had passed for him before he died. They buried him in the earth, but the earth expelled him. They came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him. He said, 'Indeed the earth accepts one who is worse than your companion, but Allah wished to admonish you.' Then they threw him between the two sides of a mountain and cast stones upon him," and the verse was revealed.

The historians of the biographies (aʾimmat al-siyar) narrated: "When the year of Khaybar came, ʿUyayna ibn Badr came seeking the blood of ʿAmir, who was the chief of Qays, while al-Aqra' ibn Habis was defending Muhallim, who was the chief of Khindif. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the people of ʿAmir: 'Will you take from us now fifty camels, and fifty more when we return to Madina?' ʿUyayna ibn Badr said: 'By Allah! I will not leave him until I make his women taste the heat as he made my women taste it.' He kept at it until he agreed to the blood-money."

Ibn Ishaq said: Salim ibn al-Nadr narrated to me, who said: "They did not accept the blood-money until al-Aqra' ibn Habis stood up and withdrew with them, and said: 'O assembly of Qays! The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked you for a slain man that you would leave so that he might reconcile between the people, and you refused him. Are you secure that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will become angry with you, so that Allah becomes angry with you because of his anger? Or that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will curse you, so that Allah curses you with his curse? By Allah! You will either hand him over to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or I will bring fifty men from the Banu Tamim, all of whom will testify that the slain man never prayed at all, and I will thus nullify his blood.' When he said that, they accepted the blood-money."

Ibn Mandah narrated from Juz ibn al-Hidrijan, who said: "My brother Qiddad came to the Prophet ﷺ from Yemen, and the detachment of the Prophet ﷺ met him. He said to them, 'I am a believer,' but they did not accept from him and killed him. This reached me, so I went out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth﴾, the verse. So the Prophet ﷺ gave me the blood-money of my brother."

al-Qaffal said: There is no contradiction between these narrations; it may be that the verse was revealed at the time of all these events together, so each party thought it was revealed concerning their own incident. End of quotation.

Earlier in our introduction to the tafsir, in the section on occasions of revelation, there is what removes the apparent conflict in cases like this, so refer back to it.

* *

A note:

al-Razi said: Know that the purpose of this verse is to emphasize the prohibition of killing believers, and to command those who fight in God's cause to be certain in it, lest they shed unlawful blood on the basis of a weak interpretation.

In "al-Iklil": It has been used as evidence (p-1479) from its apparent meaning for accepting the repentance of the zindiq if he displays submission, and that the unbeliever is judged to be Muslim if he displays what contradicts his belief, according to the reading "al-salam." The verse also indicates the obligation of verification in matters, especially killing, and the obligation of calling to Islam before fighting. End of quotation.

al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": The verse is evidence that whoever displays some of the signs of Islam, his blood is not made lawful until his situation is tested, because "al-salam" is the greeting of the Muslims, whereas their greeting in the Jahiliyya was otherwise, so this was a sign.

As for the reading "al-sallam" with two fathas, or with a kasra then a sukun, the meaning is submission, which is a sign of Islam. End of quotation.

Some of the Zaydi exegetes said: The fruit of this noble verse is the obligation of verification and deliberation in what may be either forbidden or permitted, due to His saying: "fa-tabayyanū" (with a nun), which is the reading of most, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-tathabbatū" from "al-thabat."

This includes many rulings concerning beliefs, reports, deeds, and the rest of the rulings and other actions. So this is one ruling. The second ruling is that the apparent must be acted upon: whoever displays Islam or some of its rituals is not to be called a liar, but is accepted from him. This includes the atheist and the hypocrite, and this is our school's position and that of most scholars. It also includes accepting the repentance of the apostate, contrary to Ahmad, and accepting the repentance of the zindiq, and this is the view of the majority of imams.

Malik said: It is not accepted, because this is precisely their doctrine, that they display the opposite of what they conceal.

Al-Radi billah and Imam Yahya said: If they display what they habitually conceal, their repentance is accepted; otherwise, it is not.

Ali Khalil said: His repentance is accepted, even if we know from their inner state that it differs from what they displayed, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) accepted [the profession of faith] from the hypocrites, although God, exalted is He, had informed us of their disbelief.

Abu Mudar said: [Their profession] is accepted so long as its falsehood is not known. This disagreement concerns the outward judgment. As for with God, if they are sincere, then it is accepted by consensus.

Al-Hakim said: This indicates that reaching wealth through a forbidden means is not permissible. The scholars have mentioned various cases of reaching a permissible end through a forbidden means, which are mentioned in other places than this one. The proof here is from His saying, ﴿You seek the goods of the worldly life﴾, because what is intended here for seizure is forbidden, since the declaration of Islam protects the life and property [of the one who declares it]. Thus this is reaching a forbidden end through a forbidden means.

As for His saying, ﴿to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾, it has been recited as (al-Sallam) [with the lām vowelled with a fatha and without an alif]. This is the reading of Nafi', Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir, without an alif, and it means submission (al-istislam). It has also been said that it means the outward declaration of Islam. The rest [of the readers] recited (al-Salam) with an alif, which means greeting (al-tahiyyah). End of quote.

Abu Mansur said in "al-Ta'wilat": In it is the command to verify when there is doubt, and the prohibition against proceeding when there is doubt. Likewise, it is obligatory upon the believer to pause when a doubt arises in every action and every report, because God, exalted is He, commanded verification of deeds with His saying, ﴿So verify, and do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾, and He said regarding reports, ﴿If a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 6], commanding verification of reports when there is doubt, just as He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) regarding actions: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [Al-Isra: 36]. End of quote.

In the verse is evidence of the corruption of the view of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology), because He forbade them to say to one who says "I am a Muslim": "You are not a believer," while they say that the one who commits a major sin (kabirah) is not a believer, and he says a thousand times, by way of example: "I am a Muslim." So when He prohibited them from saying, "He is not a believer," He commanded them to say, "He is a believer." It is said to them: "Do you know better, or God?" as was said to those [who argued this way] previously. End of quote.

Al-Razi said: Most jurists said: If a Jew or a Christian says, "I am a believer," or says, "I am a Muslim," he is not judged to have become Muslim by this alone, because his creed is that what he holds is Islam and faith. If he says, "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God," then according to some people he is not judged to be Muslim, because among them are those who say that he is the Messenger of God to the Arabs only, not to all [people]; and among them are those who say that Muhammad, who is the true Messenger, [has come] after what has come [before], and [another] will come after that. Rather, he must acknowledge that the religion he was upon is false, and that the religion present among the Muslims is the truth. And God knows best. End of quote.

I say: Whoever among the combatants says, "I am a believer" or "I am a Muslim," displaying submission to us and that he is of our community, he is judged to be Muslim, and is restrained from being killed and from having his property taken, whether he is a People of the Book or a polytheist. This is the intended meaning of the verse.

As for the question of one who wishes to enter Islam while holding a corrupt creed, and that it is necessary for the validity of his Islam that he disavow it and cast it behind his back, and that it is not sufficient for him to say, "I am a Muslim," that is a separate question, and it is an established one. But it is not something the verse covers. Likewise, one who displays Islam and utters the two testimonies but does not adhere to the laws of Islam or establish its rites, like some of the rough, uncivilized desert tribes, it is obligatory upon the ruler to fight them. It is not said that the verse includes them, for the reason we have mentioned. It is evident that the focus of the prohibition in the verse is only on shedding blood in pursuit of the goods of worldly life, as shown by His saying, ﴿you seek﴾, which is a circumstantial clause (hal), as we have previously stated, and a circumstantial clause is a restriction on its governing element. Therefore what al-Razi related from the jurists is not something the verse covers, because the discussion is not about the minimum by which a disbeliever becomes a Muslim, but about refraining from killing one who submits to us. So understand. And His, exalted is He, saying:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their selves over those who sit at home by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the good reward, and Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit at home with a great reward.﴾ [95]

﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm, are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah﴾ is an explanation of the differing ranks of the believers according to the differing degrees of their efforts in jihad, after the command to it and the exhortation of the believers to it had preceded. This is so that the one who sits at home may feel disdain (ya'naf) for it, and raise himself above the lowering of his station, so that he is stirred (yahtazz) toward it, desiring the elevation of his rank. Abu al-Su'ud said this.

Its origin is from al-Zamakhshari, where he said: "If you say: it is known that the one who sits without an excuse and the one who strives are not equal, so what is the benefit of negating equality? I say: its meaning is a reminder of the great difference and the vast distance between them, so that the one who sits may feel disdain and raise himself above the lowering of his rank, so that he is stirred toward jihad and desires it, and desires the elevation of his rank. Similar to it is: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9], which is intended to move the ignorant by his zeal and disdain, so that he is driven toward learning and rises with himself from the attribute of ignorance to the nobility of knowledge." End.

Those meant at the time of revelation were those who stayed back from the battle of Badr and those who went out to it, as al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas.

His saying ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ excludes those with the excuses that permit leaving jihad, such as blindness, lameness and illness, from being equal to those who sit at home. For they are equal to the strivers in intention, and the added reward of action is not counted for them, because of the greatness of the matter of intention.

As Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud narrated from Anas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, in Medina there are people. You do not travel any journey nor cross any valley except that they are with you in it.' They said: 'And they are in Medina, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes, the excuse has held them back.'" And in this meaning the poet said:

O you who journey to the Ancient House, you have travelled in bodies, and we have travelled in spirits.

We have remained upon an excuse and by decree, and whoever remains upon an excuse is like one who has journeyed.

(p-1483) Al-Bukhari narrated from al-Bara' who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Zayd and he wrote it down. Then Ibn Umm Maktum came and complained of his blindness, so Allah revealed: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾."

In a narration of al-Bukhari from Zayd: "Ibn Umm Maktum came to him while he was dictating it to me, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah! By Allah, if I were able to do jihad I would have done jihad,' and he was blind. So Allah revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his thigh was upon my thigh, and it became heavy upon me until I feared that my thigh would be crushed. Then the revelation was lifted from him, and Allah revealed: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿with their wealth﴾ means: those which they spend upon themselves in jihad, or upon another striver. ﴿And their selves﴾ means: those which are dearer to them than anything, even if others spend upon them when they have no wealth.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The mention of them, meaning the fighters, under the title "strivers" (al-mujahidin), rather than with "going out" (al-khuruj), which corresponds to the attribute of the item coordinated with it, as occurred in the wording of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and likewise the restriction of striving to being "in the way of Allah, with their wealth and their selves", is for praising them with that, and indicating the cause of their deserving the high rank, along with what there is in it of the fine placement of "the way" in contrast to "sitting". End.

It is evident that negating equality implies preference, but because of giving it importance, and so that it may be firmly established most firmly, it did not suffice with what was understood implicitly; rather it stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿Allah has preferred the strivers﴾, because they gave precedence to its side ﴿with their wealth and their selves over those who sit at home﴾, meaning: other than those with a harm, ﴿by a degree﴾ in nearness to the one whose side they gave precedence to. ﴿And to each﴾, meaning: each one of the sitters and the strivers, ﴿Allah has promised the good reward﴾, meaning: the good recompense, which is Paradise, because of the goodness of their creed and the sincerity of their intention. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD), brought as a remedy (tadarruk) for what the preference of one of the two groups over the other might suggest, of the deprivation of the one who is preferred less (p-1484), ﴿and Allah has preferred the strivers﴾ through the jihad ﴿over those who sit at home﴾, meaning: without an excuse, ﴿with a great reward﴾, meaning: abundant recompense in Paradise.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [96]

﴿Degrees from Him﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿a reward﴾ — a substitution of the whole (badal al-kull), clarifying the quantity of the excellence. And ﴿from Him﴾ is attached to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of ﴿degrees﴾, indicating their grandeur and the magnitude of their rank. So said Abu al-Su'ud.

It is established in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in Paradise there are one hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for those who strive in His cause; the distance between every two degrees is like the distance between the heaven and the earth."

And al-A'mash said, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu 'Ubaydah, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever shoots an arrow, for him is a reward of one degree." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah! And what is the degree?" He said: "Indeed, it is not the threshold of your mother; the distance between the two degrees is a hundred years." ﴿And forgiveness﴾, i.e., for their sins; ﴿and mercy﴾ (p-1485) beyond the reward and its degrees.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming what He promised of forgiveness and mercy. Here are several benefits:

The first: The verse indicates that jihad is not an individual obligation (fard 'ayn), for if it were an obligation of individual duties, the one who stays behind would have no excellence; rather, the excellence varies between him and the one who strives. And He said: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾.

The second: It also indicates that jihad is superior to the acts of worship that the one who stays behind performs, because He preferred it over the one who stays behind absolutely. This is supported by his (ﷺ) saying: "Jihad is the summit of the religion."

The scholars have derived from this that if a man endowed his wealth for the best of the ways of righteousness, or bequeathed that it be spent in the best of the ways of righteousness, it is spent on jihad — contrary to what Abu 'Ali mentioned, that it is spent on the pursuit of knowledge. So it is mentioned in some tafsir works.

The third: al-Suyuti said in "al-Iklil": The verse contains the preference of the mujahidin over others, and that those excused are in the rank of the mujahidin. It was derived as evidence from His words ﴿with their wealth﴾ that the mujahid who strives with his own wealth is preferred over the mujahid who strives with wealth given to him from debts or the like.

The fourth: al-Razi said: One may say: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], mentioning the self before the property. And in the verse we are discussing, which is His saying: ﴿those who strive with their wealth and their lives﴾ [al-Nisa': 95], He mentioned the property before the self. What is the reason? The answer: The self is more noble than property. The buyer mentioned the self first, to alert that the desire for it is stronger, while the seller delayed mentioning it, to alert that reluctance regarding it is stronger, so he does not consent to give it except at the last of the stages.

The fifth: Abu al-Su'ud said: Perhaps the repetition of the preference by way of conjunction (al-'atf), which indicates difference, and its restriction at one time to "a degree" and at another to "degrees," while the preferred and the preferred-over are the same — as the context requires and as the excellence of arrangement demands — is either: to treat the difference in description between the two preferences and between "a degree" and "degrees" as if it were an essential difference, as a preparation for the method of vagueness followed by explanation, in order to increase verification and affirmation, as in His saying: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and saved them from a harsh punishment﴾ [Hud: 58]. It is as if it were said: He preferred the mujahidin over those who stay behind by a degree whose measure cannot be estimated and whose reality cannot be reached. And since the realization of this great gap between them would give the impression of the deprivation of those who stay behind, it was said: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]. Then it was intended to explain what the indefinite form conveyed by way of vagueness, in such a way that the possibility of its being for unity is cut off, so what was said was said. How excellent is the manner of the Revelation!

Or: because of an essential difference between the two preferences and between "a degree" and "degrees," with the intent of the first preference being what Allah granted them swiftly in this world of spoils, victory, and good remembrance, which is fitting to be called one degree, and of the second preference being what He bestowed in the Hereafter of lofty degrees that cannot be counted, as is indicated by the placing of the first before and the second after, and by the placement of the promise of Paradise between them. Between them in mention has been placed what is intermediate between them in existence, namely the promise of Paradise, to clarify their state and to hasten the consolation of the one who is preferred-under. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves—the angels will say, "In what condition were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." The angels will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious that you could have emigrated therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and evil it is as a destination.﴾ [97]

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (p-1487) that some Muslims were with the polytheists, increasing the numbers of the polytheists against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. An arrow would be shot and strike one of them and kill him, or he would be struck and killed. So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom [the angels take in death]...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh also related it, and in his narration he named some of them: Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Qays ibn al-Faakih ibn al-Mughirah, al-Walid ibn 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Amr ibn Umayyah ibn Sufyan, and 'Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf. He mentioned concerning them that they went out to Badr, and when they saw the small number of the Muslims, doubt entered them and they said, "These people have been deceived by their religion." So they were killed at Badr.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related it and added: among them al-Harith ibn Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, and al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj.

Al-Tabarani related, "from Ibn 'Abbas who said: There were people in Makkah who had embraced Islam. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated, they disliked to migrate and feared, so Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ up to His words: ﴿except the oppressed﴾ [An-Nisa: 98]."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir related, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: There were people from the people of Makkah who had embraced Islam, and they used to conceal Islam. The polytheists took them out with them on the Day of Badr, and some of them were struck. The Muslims said, "These were Muslims, but they were compelled, so seek forgiveness for them." So the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death...﴾ the verse. They wrote with it to those who remained among them, and that there was no excuse for them. So they went out, and the polytheists caught up with them and tempted them, and they returned. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 10]. The Muslims wrote to them with that, and they grieved. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried...﴾ [An-Nahl: 110] the verse. They wrote to them with that, and they went out, and they caught up with them; some were saved and some were killed.

(p-1488) Ibn Jarir related it through many chains similar to it, as is mentioned in "Lubab al-Nuqul."

Al-Mahayimi said: Since what was understood from what preceded, namely the equality of those who sit back who have a harm and the strivers, could give the impression that whoever stays away from jihad because he is in the land of disbelief is counted among them, even if he is unable to manifest his religion—then if he is not counted among them, at least he should be counted among the sitters other than those with a harm, for whom the good reward is promised—that impression is removed by the fact that by leaving emigration from a place where it is not possible for them to manifest their religion, while emigration from it is possible, they become wrongdoers deserving the reproach of the angels, rather the punishment of Hell. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾, that is, in a state of wronging themselves by leaving emigration from a place where they cannot manifest their religion, while they are able to do so, and by agreeing with the disbelievers.

The word (tawaffahum) may be past, as in the reading of one who reads (tawaffathum), or present with the meaning of (tatawaffahum), meaning that Allah causes the angels to take their souls so they take them, that is, enables them to complete their taking, so they complete it. Thus in "al-Kashshaf."

The word (al-zulm, wronging) may mean disbelief, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], and it may mean disobedience, as in His words: ﴿So among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir: 32]. It is valid to intend both meanings here, as we have indicated.

Abu Dawud related from Samurah ibn Jundub who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever associates with a polytheist and lives with him, then he is like him."

﴿They will say﴾, that is, the angels to those who are taken: establishing their shortcoming and reproaching them. ﴿In what condition were you?﴾ that is, in what matter of your religion were you? ﴿They will say, "We were oppressed in the land,"﴾ that is, the land of the enemies.

Al-Zamakhshari said: How is it correct that His words ﴿We were oppressed in the land﴾ come as an answer to their words ﴿In what condition were you?﴾, when the answer should have been: "We were in such-and-such," or "We were in nothing"? I say: The meaning of ﴿In what condition were you?﴾ is reproach, that they were in nothing of the religion since they were able to emigrate and did not emigrate. So they said, "We were oppressed," as an excuse for what they were reproached with, and a pretext of weakness, and that they were not able to emigrate so as to be in something. Then the angels rebuked them by their saying: ﴿The angels will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious that you could have emigrated therein?"﴾ meaning: you were able to leave Makkah for some of the lands where you would not be prevented from manifesting your religion, and to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as the emigrants did to the land of Abyssinia. This is evidence that when a man is in a land where he cannot establish the matter of his religion as is obligatory, for some reasons—and the obstacles to establishing religion are not limited—or he knows that he is more upright in the right of Allah and more constant in worship in another land than his own, emigration becomes obligatory upon him. End of quote.

﴿For those﴾, that is, that group mentioned, ﴿their refuge is﴾, that is, their destination ﴿Hell﴾, because they are those who weakened themselves, since the enemies did not compel them to dwell in their homes. ﴿And evil it is as a destination﴾, that is, Hell, in place of the destination to the abode of emigration. Then He, glorified is He, excepted from the people of the threat what He explained by His words, Exalted is He:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Except the oppressed among men, women and children, who have no power to devise a plan, nor are they guided to a way﴾ [98]

﴿Except the oppressed among men﴾ — due to blindness, lameness, sickness, old age, or poverty. ﴿And women and children﴾ — that is, the young boys, for they are excused from abandoning the emigration (hijrah), because they: ﴿have no power to devise a plan﴾ to depart, since they have no strength to leave and no provision (nafaqah).

﴿Nor are they guided to a way﴾ — that is, they do not know a path to the abode of emigration (dar al-hijrah).

**The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 4, Verse 99**

**On the interpretation of His statement, exalted is He:**

﴿So those, it may be that Allah will pardon them. And ever is Allah Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ [99]

﴿It may be that Allah will pardon them﴾ means: He will overlook them by their abandoning emigration (hijra).

Al-Razi said: [p. 1490] Here there is a question. The people, since they were unable to emigrate, and one who is unable to do something is not obligated to do it, and if he is not obligated to it, there is no punishment upon him for leaving it. So why did He say, "It may be that Allah will pardon them"? Pardon can only be conceived where there is a sin. Also, "ʿasā" (it may be) is a word of hope, and this implies that the pardon for them is not certain. The answer to the first point is that the one who is oppressed may be able to do something with a degree of hardship. Distinguishing the weakness that gives rise to the dispensation (rukhsa) from the limit at which the dispensation does not arise is difficult and ambiguous. A person may think himself unable to emigrate when he is not so, especially in emigrating from one's homeland, for it is hard on the soul, and due to the intensity of aversion, a person may think himself unable when in fact he is not. For this reason, the need for pardon is especially strong in this context. The answer to the second point is that the benefit of "ʿasā" is to indicate that abandoning emigration is a matter of constraint with no latitude in it. Even the one who is clearly compelled should say, "It may be that Allah will pardon me," so what of others? This is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned.

The preferable answer is what we have previously presented: that due to the intensity of a person's aversion to leaving his homeland, he may think himself unable to do so, when in reality he is not. For this reason, the pardon was mentioned with the word "ʿasā" and not with a word that indicates certainty. End of quote.

Abu al-Suʿud said: The word of hope ("it may be") and the term "pardon" were used to indicate that emigration is of such emphatic obligation that abandoning it, for one who has been established as not being obligated to it, should be regarded as a sin for which pardon must be sought, with hope and yearning, but not with certainty and conviction.

Al-Mahayimi said: In it is an indication that abandoning emigration is a grave matter, to the extent that the one who is compelled should be watchful for the opportunity and attach his heart to it. And if a child is able, there is no escape for him from it, and their guardians are obliged to emigrate with them. Then He emphasized the word of hope so that they would not despair, and said: ﴿And ever is Allah Pardoning and Forgiving﴾.

The insertion of "ever" (kāna) indicates His attributes with this quality before the creation of creatures, or that this is His habit, exalted is He, which He applies to His creatures. And His promise of pardon and forgiveness, absolutely, indicates that He, exalted is He, may pardon a sin before repentance.

* *

[p. 1491] Note:

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: The verse has been cited as evidence for the obligation of emigrating from the abode of disbelief (dar al-kufr), except for the one who cannot bear it. From Malik: The verse requires that everyone who is in a land where the sunnas (practices) are changed should leave it. End of quote.

Some of the commentators of the Zaydiyya said: The fruit of the verse is the obligation of emigrating from the abode of disbelief, and there is no disagreement that it was obligatory before the Conquest (of Mecca). For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, said in Surah al-Anfal: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship over them whatsoever﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. It was said that it was abrogated (naskh) after the Conquest. The correct view is that there is no abrogation, and his saying (ﷺ): "There is no emigration after the Conquest" means from Mecca.

Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said: This indicates that a man who is in a land where he cannot establish the matters of his religion as is obligatory, due to some reasons, and he knows that he is more able to fulfill the right of Allah in another land, emigration becomes obligatory upon him.

Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He said in al-Tahdhib: From al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim: When corruption (fisq) appears in a dwelling and one is unable to enjoin good, then emigration is obligatory. This is based on the view that the abodes are three: the abode of Islam, the abode of corruption, and the abode of war. This division is the doctrine of al-Hadi, al-Qasim, and Ibn Abi al-Najm in the book "al-Hijra wal-Duur" [p. 1492], from al-Radi billah, Jaʿfar ibn Mubashshir, and Abu ʿAli.

The Ikhwan (Mu'tazilite-associated group) and the general body of jurists and most of the Mu'tazila went to the negation of the abode of corruption. Know that whoever is compelled to an act of disobedience, or to abandoning an obligation, or whom the Imam demands to do so, the accepted doctrine is that emigration is obligatory when the valid conditions are met. Al-Radi billah said: Whoever resides in the abode of war while deeming it permissible has disbelieved, because that is a rejection of the explicit Qur'an, and he argued with this (verse).

The jurist Husam al-Din Humayd ibn Ahmad related, from al-Qasim, al-Hadi, and al-Radi billah, the declaration of disbelief (takfir) upon one who dwells among the disbelievers in their lands.

And in the doctrine of al-Radi billah, one becomes a disbeliever if he dwells with them for a year.

The jurist Sharaf al-Din Muhammad ibn Yahya said, relating from al-Radi billah: He becomes a disbeliever by residing in the abode of war even if he does not deem it permissible, because that is for him a manifestation of disbelief upon himself, and the ruling of disbelief is possible here. Then he said: Allah, exalted is He, only excepted the children, though they are not included in the obligation, to clarify their lack of means, and emigration is only obligatory upon one who has means. End of quote.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: Hijra is abandonment, and hijra to something is moving to it from something else. In the Sharia, it is abandoning what Allah has forbidden. It has occurred in Islam in two ways:

The first: moving from the abode of fear to the abode of safety, as in the two emigrations to Abyssinia and the beginning of the emigration from Mecca to Medina.

The second: emigration from the abode of disbelief to the abode of faith. This was after the Prophet (ﷺ) settled in Medina, and whichever Muslims were able to, emigrated to him. At that time, emigration was specific to moving to Medina, until Mecca was conquered, and the specificity ended, and the general obligation of moving away from the abode of disbelief remained for whoever is able to do it. End of quote.

Ibn ʿUmar clearly expressed the intended meaning in what al-Isma'ili transmitted with the wording: "Emigration to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ended after the Conquest, and emigration does not end as long as the disbelievers are fought," meaning: as long as there is an abode of disbelief in the world.

So emigration from it is obligatory upon the one who has embraced Islam and fears being tempted away from his religion.

Many hadiths have been related regarding the meaning of the verse, which Majd al-Din ibn Taymiyya cited in "Muntaqa al-Akhbar" under the chapter heading: "The continuation of emigration from the abode of war to the abode of Islam, and that there is no emigration from a dwelling [p. 1493] whose people have embraced Islam." Then he said: From Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever associates with the polytheist and dwells with him, then he is like him." Related by Abu Dawud.

And from Jarir ibn ʿAbd Allah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment to Khath'am, and some people among them sought refuge in prostration, but killing hastened upon them. The news reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he ordered for them half the blood money (ʿaql), and said: 'I am free of every Muslim who dwells among the polytheists.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Why?' He said: 'Do not let their fires see each other.'" Related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi.

And from Muʿawiya, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Emigration does not end until repentance ends, and repentance does not end until the sun rises from its west." Related by Ahmad and Abu Dawud.

And from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Saʿdi: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Emigration does not end as long as the enemy is fought.'" Related by Ahmad and al-Nasa'i.

[p. 1494] And from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no emigration after the Conquest, but there is jihad and intention." Related by the group except Ibn Majah.

And from ʿAʾisha, when she was asked about emigration, she said: "There is no emigration today. The believer used to flee with his religion to Allah and His Messenger, fearing that he would be tempted. But today Allah has made Islam manifest, and the believer worships his Lord wherever he wishes." Related by al-Bukhari.
