And from Mujashi' ibn Masʿud: "He brought his brother Mujalid ibn Masʿud to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'This is Mujalid, who has come to pledge allegiance to you for emigration.' He said: 'There is no emigration after the Conquest of Mecca, but I accept his pledge for Islam, faith, and jihad.'" Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim).

Since the chapter heading of Majd (may Allah have mercy on him) contained two parts [p. 1495], he cited hadiths for each. From his words: "There is no emigration after the Conquest..." etc., all of it is for the second part, which is his words: "and that there is no emigration from a dwelling whose people have embraced Islam," as an indication of reconciling these hadiths, which is evident. Then He, exalted is He, encouraged emigration by His saying:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Whoever emigrates in the way of God will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to God and His Messenger, and then death overtakes him, his reward has indeed become due from God. God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ [100]

﴿Whoever emigrates in the way of God﴾ in obedience to Him, ﴿will find on the earth many a refuge﴾ that is, a path by which he humbles the noses of his enemies who seek to overtake him, ﴿and abundance﴾ that is, in provision, or in the manifestation of the religion, or in the breast, since fear is replaced by security.

﴿And whoever leaves his home﴾ in Mecca ﴿as an emigrant to God﴾ to His obedience, or to the place of God's command, and [reading] "to His Messenger" [as] in Medina ﴿and then death overtakes him﴾ that is, on the way, before he reaches the destination ﴿his reward has become due﴾ that is, it is established ﴿from God﴾ that is, he need not fear the loss of his full reward, because he intended it together with the beginning of the act, and there was no shortcoming on his part in not completing it.

﴿God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ so He forgives him what he had neglected of sins, the sum of which is remaining seated from emigration until the time of departure, and He shows him mercy by completing the reward of his emigration.

* *

Remarks:

The first: concerning what has been related about the occasion of revelation of the verse:

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Ya'la related, with a good chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Damrah ibn Jundub went out from his home as an emigrant, and he said to his family: "Carry me and take me out of the land of the polytheists to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." He died on the way before he reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and the revelation descended: ﴿And whoever leaves his home…﴾ the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Abu Damrah al-Zuraqi, who had lost his sight and was in Mecca: when the verse ﴿except the oppressed men, women and children who have no means﴾ [An-Nisa 4:98] was revealed, he said: "Indeed I am wealthy and I have means," so he prepared himself, intending the Prophet (ﷺ), but death overtook him at al-Tan'im, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever leaves his home…﴾ to its end.

Ibn Jarir related something similar through several routes, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and others. In some of these he is named Damrah ibn al-'Is, or al-'Is ibn Damrah; in some, Jundub ibn Damrah al-Jundu'i; in some, al-Damri; in some, a man from the Banu Damrah; in some, a man from Khuza'ah; in some, a man from the Banu Layth; in some, from the Banu Kinanah; and in some, from the Banu Bakr.

Ibn Sa'd related in al-Tabaqat, from Yazid ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Qusayt, that Jundu' ibn Damrah al-Damri was in Mecca, and fell ill, and said to his sons: "Take me out of Mecca, for its distress has killed me." They said: "To where?" He pointed with his hand toward Medina, intending emigration. They took him out, and when they reached the pond of the Banu Ghifar, he died. God revealed concerning him: ﴿And whoever leaves…﴾ the verse.

Al-Umawi related in his Maghazi, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, who said: "When news of the emergence of the Prophet (ﷺ) reached Akthan ibn Sayfi, he wished to come to him, but his people refused to let him go. He said: 'Then let him send someone who will convey [his message] to him for me and convey [his reply] to me.' Two men were appointed, and they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We are the envoys of Akthan ibn Sayfi, and he asks you: Who are you? What are you? And why have you come?' He said: 'I am Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, and I am the servant of God (ﷺ) and His Messenger.' Then he recited to them: ﴿Indeed God commands justice and beneficence﴾ [An-Nahl 16:90], [An-Nahl: part of verse 90], the verse. The two came to Akthan and told him this. He said: 'O people! Indeed he commands the noble qualities of character and forbids what is contrary to them. So be leaders in this matter and do not be followers in it.' He mounted his camel, heading for Medina, but he died on the way, and this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿And whoever leaves his home…﴾ the verse." Al-Suyuti said: it is mursal (its chain is broken), and its isnad is weak.

Abu Hatim related in the book al-Mu'ammarin by two routes from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about this verse, and he said: "It was revealed concerning Akthan ibn Sayfi." It was said: "Then where is al-Laythi?" He said: "This was before al-Laythi by a time; it is specific and general."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mandah and al-Bawardi in al-Sahabah related from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, that al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: "Khalid ibn Haram emigrated to the land of Abyssinia, and a snake bit him on the way, and he died. This verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿And whoever leaves…﴾ the verse."

Al-Zubayr said: "I was expecting him and waiting for his arrival while I was in the land of Abyssinia. Nothing grieved me more than the grief of his death when news reached me; for few from Quraysh emigrated without some of their family or relatives with them, and no one from the Banu Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza was with me, nor did I hope for anyone other than him."

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: "This report is very strange, for this story is Meccan, while the revelation of the verse is Medinan. Perhaps he meant that it includes its ruling along with others, even if that was not the occasion of revelation. And God knows best."

The second: the fruit of the verse:

That whoever goes out for emigration and dies on the way, his reward has become due from God. Al-Hakim said: "However, the scholars have differed. It was said: the reward of his intention. It was said: the reward of his action, but not the reward of emigration. It was said: rather, he has the reward of emigration, and this is apparent in the occasion of revelation of the verse."

Al-Hakim said: "Some scholars have used this as evidence that the warrior deserves a share [of the spoils] even if he dies on the way." He said: "This is far-fetched, because what is meant by the verse is the reward of merit."

Al-Zamakhshari, relating from the exegetes, said: "Every emigration for a religious purpose, such as seeking knowledge, or pilgrimage, or jihad, or fleeing to a land where one increases in obedience, or contentment, or asceticism in this world, and seeking lawful provision, is an emigration to God and His Messenger, and if death overtakes him on his way, his reward is due from God."

In al-Zamakhshari's words on the preceding verse occurs this supplication: "O God! If You know that my emigration to You was only for the sake of fleeing with my religion, then make it a cause for a good end, and for attaining what is hoped for of Your bounty, and what is sought of Your mercy, and join my neighborhood with You, by my devotion at Your House, with Your neighborhood in the abode of Your honor, O Vast in forgiveness."

His words, may God have mercy on him, are based on the premise that it is recommended for a person to call upon God by his righteous deeds.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim mentioned the hadith of the three men who entered the cave and a boulder sealed them in, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approved of them, and each of them supplicated by his righteous deed, and the rock was moved away from them.

The verse necessitates the obligation of emigration, even by spending wealth, as in pilgrimage. And in what preceded, the hadith of the one who was carried out of Mecca, and he said: "Carry me, for I am not among the oppressed" indicates that emigration is obligatory when one is able to ride, even lying down in the litter, because he was carried on a stretcher. The later scholars have mentioned (regarding the pilgrimage) that the correct position, which is binding, is that one must be able to remain steady on the litter sitting upright, not lying down, because no one is unable to do that. It may be that the two matters are equated, and that pilgrimage is obligatory even lying down, (and that the two are not obligatory with lying down), and the act of Damrah was an anomaly. It may also be that a distinction is made between them, and emigration is considered more serious, because committing a prohibited act, which is remaining [in Mecca], is more serious than abandoning an obligation. This requires verification. Thus [it is stated] in the exegesis of some of the Zaydis.

The third: numerous hadiths have been related with the meaning of this verse, among them what is in the Two Sahihs, the Sunan and the Musnads, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended. Whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was to worldly gain he would obtain, or to a woman he would marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is general regarding emigration and all actions."

From it is the established hadith in the Two Sahihs about the man who killed ninety-nine souls, then completed the hundred by [killing] that devotee, then asked a scholar: "Is there repentance for me?" He said to him: "Who stands between you and repentance?" Then he guided him to move from his land to another land where God is worshipped. When he set out from his land as an emigrant to the other land, death overtook him on the way. The angels of mercy and the angels of punishment disputed concerning him: these said, "He came repentant," and those said, "He has not yet prayed." So they were commanded to measure the distance between the two lands; to whichever of them he was nearer, he belongs to it. God commanded this land to draw near and that land to recede, and they found him nearer by a span to the land to which he had emigrated, so the angels of mercy took him.

In another narration: when death came to him, he leaned his chest toward the land to which he had emigrated.

Imam Ahmad related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Atik (may God be pleased with him), who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever leaves his home as an emigrant in the way of God, and falls from his mount and dies, his reward has become due from God; or he dies of his natural death, his reward has become due from God.'"

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 101 (part 1 of 3):

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy.﴾ [101]
His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when you travel through the land﴾, meaning: you journey. ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, meaning: no sin (p-1502) ﴿for shortening﴾, meaning: reducing something ﴿from the prayer. If you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾, meaning: may fight you ﴿in the prayer. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy﴾, of manifest enmity, so they do not observe the sanctity of the prayer because of their hostility.
* *
A notice regarding issues related to the verse:
The first issue: The majority (al-Jumhur) held that the verse concerns the legislation of the travel prayer (salat al-safar), and that the meaning of His words, exalted is He, ﴿that you shorten from the prayer﴾ is shortening in quantity (qasr al-kammiyyah), namely that the four-rak'ah prayer is made two rak'ahs. They said: its ruling for the traveller in a state of safety is the same as its ruling in a state of fear, because the Sunnah clearly establishes its legislation absolutely.
Al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) left Madinah for Makkah fearing none but the Lord of the worlds, and he prayed two rak'ahs.
Al-Bukhari and the rest of the group (al-Jama'ah) related from Haritha ibn Wahb, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer at Mina, when it was the safest it had ever been, two rak'ahs."
Al-Bukhari and the rest related from Anas, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Madinah to Makkah, and he prayed two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, until we returned to Madinah." I said: "Did you stay in Makkah for any time?" He said: "We stayed there ten days."
In that case, His words, exalted is He, ﴿if you fear﴾ came out in the manner of what is usual (kharaja makhraja al-ghalib) at the time the verse was revealed, since their journeys after the Hijrah, in its beginning, were dangerous. Indeed, they did not set out except for a general campaign (ghazw 'amm) or a specific detachment (sariyyah khassah), and the rest of the tribes were at war with Islam and its people. And an explicit statement that comes out in the manner of what is usual has no implicit meaning (mafhum), like His words: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity﴾ [an-Nur: 33] and like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives﴾ [an-Nisa: 23], and the rest of the verse.
They said: What indicates that the intended meaning of the verse is the travel prayer is what Imam Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan related from Ya'la ibn Umayyah, who said: "I asked 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, I said to him: 'His words, exalted is He: ﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾, while people are now secure?' 'Umar said to me, may Allah be pleased with him: 'I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he said: "It is a charity which Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity."'"
Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Hanzalah al-Hadhdha', who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about the travel prayer? He said: 'Two rak'ahs.' I said: 'Where is His words: ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾, and we are secure?' He said: 'It is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"
Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu al-Waddak, who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about two rak'ahs in travel? He said: 'It is a concession (rukhsah) that came down from the heavens; if you wish, then reject it.'"
They said: This indicates that the shortening mentioned in the verse is shortening in the number of rak'ahs, and that this was understood by them from the meaning of the verse. They said: What also indicates that the term (al-qasr) was specific in their usage to reducing the number of rak'ahs, and for this meaning, "when the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the noon prayer two rak'ahs, Dhu al-Yadayn said to him: 'Has the prayer been shortened, or have you forgotten?'"
Moreover, many of the early generations (al-Salaf), among them Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, held that this verse was revealed concerning the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), and that what is meant by shortening is shortening in manner (qasr al-kayfiyyah), not in quantity, because in their view the quantity of the traveller's prayer is two rak'ahs, so it is complete, not shortened, as 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them all, said. They said: For this reason He said: ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve may tempt you﴾, and He said after it: ﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them﴾ [an-Nisa: 102], and the rest of the verse. So He clarified the intended meaning of shortening here, and mentioned its description and manner. For this reason, when al-Bukhari entitled a chapter "The Book of the Prayer of Fear," he began it with His words: ﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾, up to His words: ﴿He has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ [an-Nisa: 102].
Likewise Juwaybir said, from al-Dahhak, concerning His words: ﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾: "That is at the time of fighting, the rider prays two takbirs wherever his face is directed."
Asbat said, from al-Suddi, concerning this verse: "When the prayer is prayed two rak'ahs in travel, it is complete, not shortened. It is not permitted except if one fears from those who disbelieve that they will tempt him away from the prayer, and then the shortening is one rak'ah."
Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid: "﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾ was on the day when the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions were at 'Usfan, and the polytheists were at Dajnan, and they agreed, so the Prophet (ﷺ) led his companions in the noon prayer, four rak'ahs, with their bowing, prostrating and standing together all at once. Then the polytheists resolved to raid their goods and baggage." Ibn Abi Hatim related this.
Ibn Jarir related it from Mujahid and al-Suddi, and from Jabir and Ibn 'Umar, and he also chose this view, for he said, after mentioning the opinions on this matter: "And this is the correct view."
Then it was related "from Umayyah that he said to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar: 'We find in the Book of Allah the shortening of the prayer of fear, but we do not find the shortening of the traveller's prayer.' 'Abd Allah said: 'We found our Prophet (ﷺ) doing an action, and we acted upon it.'" So he named the prayer of fear "shortened" and applied the verse to it, not to the shortening of the traveller's prayer. Ibn 'Umar approved of this, and he argued for the shortening of the prayer in travel by the action of the Lawgiver, not by the text of the Qur'an.
More explicit than this is what he also related from Simak al-Hanafi, who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about the travel prayer? He said: 'Two rak'ahs, complete, not shortened. Shortening is only in the prayer of danger.' I said: 'And what is the prayer of danger?' He said: 'The imam prays with one group one rak'ah, then these come to the place of those, and those come to the place of these, and he prays with them one rak'ah. So the imam has two rak'ahs, and each group has one rak'ah, one rak'ah.'"
This is what Ibn Kathir related, and it agrees with what some of the commentators of the Zaydiyyah related from the Hadawiyyah and the Qasimiyyah, that the verse concerns the prayer of fear, and that what is meant by shortening in the verse is shortening of the description (qasr al-sifah), in the sense that the follower shortens his following (i'timan) so that he follows the imam in one rak'ah and prays alone for one rak'ah. End of quotation.
(p-1506) The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: This noble verse is general (mujmalah) concerning the measure of the shortening and its manner, and concerning what is connected with it of the prayers, and concerning the measure of the duration of travel upon which the shortening is contingent. So everything that came from him (ﷺ) of shortening in a state of safety, and its restriction to the four-rak'ah prayers by way of halving, and to travel of a specified duration, is an explanation (bayan) of the general statement of the Book.
The second issue: If the shortening is taken to mean shortening in number, and the four-rak'ah prayer becomes two rak'ahs, what is the ruling on this shortening? We say: On this there are four positions:
The first: that shortening is a concession (rukhsah), and completing is better.
The second: that it is obligatory (hatm).
The third: that it is a sunnah, not obligatory.
The fourth: that it is optional (mukhayyar), as one has a choice in expiations (kaffarat), and that both of them, that is shortening and completing, are obligatory.
There is an explanation connected to these positions:
Those who held the first view relied on His words, exalted is He: ﴿there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾. This expression is used of what is permissible and lawful, not of what is obligatory, like: ﴿So there is no blame upon them both if they return to one another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], and ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], and ﴿There is no blame upon them both concerning what she gives up﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. If it is said: This expression is also used of what is obligatory (p-1507), like: ﴿So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'Umrah, there is no blame upon him to go around between them both﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], they answered that this is by way of metaphor (majaz).
From the Sunnah: what is related from 'A'ishah, who said: "I performed 'Umrah with the Prophet (ﷺ) from Madinah to Makkah, until when I arrived at Makkah, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, I shortened and you completed, I fasted and you broke the fast?' He said: 'You have done well, O 'A'ishah, and he did not reproach me.' And 'Uthman used to shorten and complete."
From the perspective of meaning: what is understood and grasped from the term "shortening" is only a concession because of the hardship of the traveller, just as he is granted a concession to break the fast. And in the hadith: "That is a charity which Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity."
Those who held the second view argued: We took the term "blame" (junah) to mean obligation, although it is metaphorical, because of what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The prayer was prescribed in residence as four, and in travel as two rak'ahs."
And from 'Umar: "The Friday prayer is two rak'ahs, and the travel prayer is two rak'ahs, complete and not shortened, upon the tongue of your Prophet. The Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer during his journeys was two rak'ahs, and he stayed in Makkah eighteen days, shortening, and he said: 'Complete, O people of Makkah, for we are a travelling people.'"
And from al-Sha'bi: "Whoever completes the prayer in travel has turned away from the religion of Ibrahim."
It is related "that 'Uthman completed the prayer at Mina, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud denounced him, and said: 'I prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) two rak'ahs, and behind Abu Bakr two rak'ahs, separately,' and 'Uthman excused himself with various excuses," among them that he had taken a wife in the place; and it was said: He completed because his school held that shortening is for one who has no provision and no mount, and this is the view of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. So our saying "the prayer was shortened" would be metaphorical, since it is complete when four is reduced from. They say: These reports contradict what is understood from the rationale of ease.
The argument of those who held the third and fourth views is the reconciliation of the reports, and the rest of the aspects by which those who held the first two views argued. So it was obligatory and optional. As for him who said it is a sunnah, it is because what is well known from the Prophet (ﷺ) is shortening during journeys. Thus in the tafsir of some of the Zaydiyyah.
I say: The hadith of 'A'ishah mentioned above was related by al-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, and al-Daraqutni's statements about it differ. In the Sunan he said: "Its isnad is good (hasan)." In al-'Ilal he said: "The mursal (version) is more similar." Ibn Hazm said: "This hadith contains nothing good," and he criticised it. Ibn al-Nahwi, in al-Badr al-Munir, said: "In the wording of this hadith there is an oddity (nakarah), namely that 'A'ishah went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on an 'Umrah in Ramadan, while it is well known that all his 'Umrahs were in Dhu al-Qa'dah." He elaborated on this at length.
Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to shorten the four-rak'ah prayer, praying it two rak'ahs from the time he set out as a traveller until he returned to Madinah. It is not established from him at all that he completed the four-rak'ah prayer during his journey. As for the hadith of 'A'ishah that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to shorten during travel and complete, and break the fast and fast, it is not sound. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah say: 'It is a lie upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" End of quotation.
It has been related "(kana yaqsuru wa tutimm)" with the first verb in the third person with the letter ya', and the second with the letter ta' above, and likewise "(yuftiru wa tasum)", meaning: she herself took the stricter course (al-'azimah) in both places.
Our shaykh Ibn Taymiyyah said: "This is false. The Mother of the Believers would not oppose the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and all his companions, so that she prays contrary to their prayer. How so, when the established report from her is that Allah prescribed the prayer as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs; then when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah, the residence prayer was increased and the travel prayer was kept? So how could it be supposed of her, with all that, that she would pray contrary to the prayer of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims with him?"

(p-1509) Ibn al-Qayyim then said: I say: Aisha too completed the prayer after the death of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Abbas and others said: she interpreted it as Uthman did. And the Prophet ﷺ always shortened the prayer, but some narrators combined two hadiths into one and said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would shorten, and she would complete," and some narrators erred and said: "He would shorten and complete," meaning he himself did so.

The interpretation she adopted has been disputed. It was said: she thought that shortening was conditional upon fear and travel, so when the cause of fear ceased, the cause of shortening ceased. This interpretation is not sound, for the Prophet ﷺ travelled while secure, and he would shorten the prayer. The verse had become unclear to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, so they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he answered them with the healing, and that this was a charity from Allah and a law He prescribed for the Ummah. This was an explanation that the ruling of the implied meaning (mafhum) is not intended, and that there is no blame in shortening the prayer whether one is secure or fearful. Its ultimate outcome is that it is a kind of specification (takhsis) of the implied meaning, or its abrogation (raf').

It may be said: the verse implied a shortening that covers the pillars (arkan) by lightening them, and the shortening of the number (qasr al-'adad) by reducing two rak'ahs. This was restricted by two matters: journeying on the earth and fear. When both matters exist, shortening is permitted, so they pray a complete, full prayer. If one of the two causes exists, its shortening is established alone. When fear and residence exist together, the pillars are shortened and the number is kept complete. This is a kind of shortening, but not absolute shortening. This prayer may be called "shortened" with regard to the reduction in number, and it may be called "complete" with regard to the completion of its pillars, and it did not enter into the shortening of the verse. The first is the terminology of many later jurists, and the second is indicated by the statements of the Companions, such as Aisha, Ibn Abbas and others.

Aisha said: "The prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs; when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Madinah, it was increased for the prayer of residence (hadar) and the prayer of travel was confirmed." This indicates that the prayer of travel, in her view, was not shortened from four, but was itself prescribed thus, and that the obligation upon the Muslim is two rak'ahs.

Ibn Abbas said: "Allah prescribed the prayer through the tongue of your Prophet: four in residence, two in travel, and one in fear." Agreed upon with the hadith of Aisha, and Muslim alone narrated the hadith of Ibn Abbas.

Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "The prayer of travel is two rak'ahs, the Friday prayer is two rak'ahs, and the Eid is two rak'ahs, a completion not a shortening, upon the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ, and he who fabricates has failed." This is established from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he is the one who asked the Prophet ﷺ: "Why do we shorten while we are secure?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "It is a charity which Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity." There is no contradiction between his two hadiths; when the Prophet ﷺ answered him that this is Allah's charity upon you, and His religion is ease and tolerance, Umar knew that the intent of the verse is not the shortening of the number, as many people understood it, so he said: "The prayer of travel is two rak'ahs, a completion not a shortening." Based on this, there is no evidence in the verse that shortening of the number is permissible, with blame removed from it; rather, if the worshipper wishes he does it, and if he wishes he completes. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to persist in travel with two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, and never prayed four except for something he did in part of the prayer of fear, as we shall mention there, and we shall clarify what is in it, God willing.

Anas said: "I went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from Madinah to Makkah, and he prayed two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, until we returned to Madinah." Agreed upon.

When it reached Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that Uthman ibn Affan had prayed four rak'ahs at Mina, he said: "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return. I prayed two rak'ahs with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Mina, and I prayed two rak'ahs with Abu Bakr at Mina, and I prayed two rak'ahs with Umar; would that my share of four rak'ahs were two accepted rak'ahs." Agreed upon.

Ibn Mas'ud would not have said "istirja'" (the formula of return) over an act of Uthman that was one of two permitted options between which one may choose; rather, the first is preferred according to one view. He only said it because of what he witnessed of the constant practice of the Prophet ﷺ and his caliphs with two rak'ahs.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I accompanied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and in travel he did not exceed two rak'ahs; and Abu Bakr and Umar and Uthman, meaning at the beginning of Uthman's caliphate; otherwise Uthman completed in the latter part of his caliphate." That was one of the matters for which he was criticised, and interpretations have been given for his act:

First: that the Bedouins had performed Hajj that year, so he wished to inform them that the obligatory prayer is four, lest they suppose it is two in residence and travel alike. This interpretation was refuted by the fact that they were more fitting for this during the Hajj of the Prophet ﷺ, when they were newer to Islam and their acquaintance with the prayer was recent, and yet the Prophet did not complete it four for them.

Second: that he was the imam of the people, and the imam wherever he alights, that is his work and the place of his authority, so it is as his homeland. This was refuted by the fact that the imam of all creation absolutely, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, was more entitled to this, and he was the absolute imam, yet he did not complete it four.

Third interpretation: that Mina had been built up and had become a village in which many dwellings existed in his time, whereas in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ it was open land. For this reason it was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we not build for you a house at Mina to shade you from the heat?" He said: "No. Mina is the resting place of whoever arrives first." So Uthman interpreted that shortening is only in the state of travel. This was refuted by the fact that "the Prophet ﷺ stayed in Makkah for ten days shortening the prayer."

Fourth interpretation: that he stayed there three days, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "The emigrant may stay three days after his rites," calling him a resident, and the resident is not a traveller. This was refuted by the fact that this is a restricted stay during the course of travel, not the residence which is the opposite of travel; and the Prophet ﷺ stayed in Makkah for ten days shortening the prayer, and he stayed at Mina after his rites during the three days of the stoning, shortening the prayer.

Fifth interpretation: that he had resolved to settle and establish residence at Mina, making it the seat of the caliphate, and for this reason he completed; then it became apparent to him to return to Madinah. This interpretation also does not stand firm, for Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, was one of the first emigrants, and the Prophet ﷺ prohibited the emigrant from residing in Makkah after his rites, permitting him only three days. Uthman would not have stayed there when the Prophet ﷺ had forbidden it; he only permitted three days there, because they had left it for Allah's sake, and what is left for Allah is not returned to or reclaimed. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ forbade the giver of charity from buying back his charity, and said to Umar: "Do not buy it, and do not return to your charity," so he made him one who returns to his charity even while taking it back for a price.

Sixth interpretation: that he had married at Mina, and a traveller who stays in a place and marries there, or has a wife there, completes the prayer. A hadith marfu' from the Prophet ﷺ is related about this: Ikrimah related from Ibrahim al-Azdi, from Abu Dhi'ab, from his father, who said: "Uthman led the people of Mina in four rak'ahs and said: 'O people! When I came, I married here, and I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: When a man marries in a town, he prays there the prayer of a resident.'" Imam Ahmad narrated it in his Musnad, and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr al-Humaydi also in his Musnad. Al-Bayhaqi criticised it for its disconnection (inqita') and for the weakness of Ikrimah.

Abu al-Barakat Ibn Taymiyyah said: It is possible to dispute the weakness, for al-Bukhari mentioned him in his Tarikh and did not attack him, and his habit is to mention the discredited and those who are criticised. Ahmad and Ibn Abbas before him stated that if a traveller marries he is bound to complete, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, Malik and their companions. This is the best excuse offered for Uthman.

An excuse has also been offered for Aisha: that she was the Mother of the Believers, so wherever she alighted that was her homeland. This too is a weak excuse, for the Prophet ﷺ is the father of the believers, and the motherhood of his wives is a branch of his fatherhood, and he did not complete for this reason. Hisham ibn Urwah related from his father that she used to pray four rak'ahs in travel. I said to her: "Why not pray two rak'ahs?" She said: "O son of my sister! It does not burden me."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If the obligation upon the traveller were two rak'ahs, Uthman, Aisha and Ibn Mas'ud would not have completed it, and it would not be permissible for a traveller to complete it behind a resident. Aisha herself said: "All of that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did: he completed and he shortened."

Then he related from Ibrahim, from Muhammad, from Talhah ibn Umar, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Aisha who said: "The Prophet ﷺ did all of that: he shortened the prayer in travel and he completed it."

Al-Bayhaqi said: Likewise Mughirah related it from Ziyad, from Ata'. The most authentic chain in this is what Abu Bakr al-Hazimi informed us, from al-Daraqutni, from al-Mahamili: Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Ayyub related to us, Abu 'Asim related to us, Umar ibn Sa'id related to us, from Ata', from Aisha, "that the Prophet ﷺ used to shorten the prayer in travel and complete it, and break the fast and fast."

Al-Daraqutni said: This is a sahih chain. Then he transmitted through the route of Abu Bakr al-Naysaburi, from Abbas al-Duri, who said: Abu Nu'aym related to us, al-Ala' ibn Zuhayr related to us, Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad related to me, "from Aisha, that she performed the umrah with the Prophet ﷺ from Madinah to Makkah, until when she arrived at Makkah she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be ransomed for you, I shortened and you completed, I fasted and you broke the fast.' He said: 'You did well, O Aisha!'"

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah say: This hadith is a lie upon Aisha. Aisha would not have prayed contrary to the prayer of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and of the rest of the Companions, while she saw them shortening and then completing alone without any reason. How could it be thought that she exceeded what Allah prescribed and opposed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, when she is the one who said: "The prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs; it was increased for the prayer of residence and the prayer of travel was confirmed"?

Al-Zuhri said to Urwah (when he related to him from his father, from her, this matter): "Then what of her? She used to complete the prayer." He said: "She interpreted as Uthman interpreted." If the Prophet ﷺ approved her act and confirmed it, then interpretation has no basis at that point, and it is not sound to attribute her completing it to interpretation on this assumption. Ibn Umar reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not exceed two rak'ahs in travel, nor did Abu Bakr or Umar. Is it then thought of Aisha, the Mother of the Believers, that she opposed them while she saw them shortening?!

As for after his death ﷺ, she completed, as Uthman completed, and each of them interpreted, and the proof lies in their narration, not in the interpretation of one of them, especially when others opposed him, and Allah knows best.

Umayyah ibn Khalid said to Abdullah ibn Umar: "We find the prayer of residence and the prayer of fear in the Qur'an, but we do not find the prayer of travel in the Qur'an." Ibn Umar said to him: "O my brother! Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ and we knew nothing; so we do only as we saw Muhammad ﷺ doing."

Anas also said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to Makkah, and he prayed two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, until we returned to Madinah." Ibn Umar said: "I accompanied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he did not exceed two rak'ahs in travel, nor Abu Bakr, nor Umar, nor Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them all." All these are sahih hadiths. End of the words of Ibn al-Qayyim.

Imam al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: Those who hold that shortening (qasr) is a concession (rukhsa) have relied on the two hadiths of ʿAʾisha. It is answered that the second hadith provides them no proof, because of what has preceded, that the wording (tutimmu wa-tasum), with the letter taʾ above the line (i.e., the verb in the feminine form, meaning "she completes and fasts"), refers to her own action. Even supposing it were not opposed to his ﷺ saying and doing, her action is no proof, so how much less when it opposes what is established from him ﷺ through her channel and the channels of other Companions!? As for the first hadith (p-1515), if it were sound it would be a proof, because of his ﷺ saying in answer to her: "You did well" (aḥsanti). But it cannot stand against what is in the Two Sahihs and others through the channel of a group of Companions. This is after granting that it is good (ḥasan), as al-Daraqutni said. How then? It has been criticized with those criticisms mentioned earlier, for these alone necessitate the dropping of using it as evidence when there is no opposing report. End of quote.

The third issue: Those who permit shortening on any journey, long or short, have used the generality of the verse. Its basis is that the words of the Most High, ﴿And when you travel through the land﴾, apply to every kind of traveling. However, the "travel" (ḍarb), i.e., walking, for other than a journey was excluded, because of what the Prophet ﷺ used to do, such as going out to the Baqiʿ al-Gharqad and the like, and he did not shorten prayer on those occasions.

No text has come specifying the distance of the journey in which the traveler shortens prayer, so it is necessary to return to what is called a journey (safar) linguistically and legally. Whoever leaves his town heading to a destination, and during his going there is considered a traveler, shortens the prayer, even if that destination is less than a barid (postal distance). Those who considered the barid, or a day, two days, three days, or more than that, have not brought a clear proof. The most they have brought is the hadith: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to travel three days without a mahram," and in another narration: "a day and a night," and in another: "a barid."

This hadith does not mention shortening, nor is it in its context, and using it as evidence is mere conjecture. The best that has been transmitted regarding the measure is what Shuʿba related from Yahya ibn Zayd al-Hunai, who said: "I asked Anas about shortening the prayer. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he set out a distance of three miles or three farsakh, would pray two rakʿas." The doubt is from Shuʿba. Related by Muslim and others.

If you say: The point of evidence in the prohibition on a woman traveling that distance without a mahram is that he ﷺ called that a journey, I say: calling it a journey does not negate calling what is less than it a journey. The Prophet ﷺ called the distance of three days a journey, just as he called the distance of a barid a journey in that hadith, according to the difference of narrations. And calling a barid a journey does not negate calling what is less than it a journey.

If you say: al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he ﷺ said: "O people of Makka! Do not shorten for less than four barids from Makka to ʿUsfan," I say: It is weak and does not establish proof, for its chain includes ʿAbd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid ibn Jabr, who is abandoned (matruk). On this question there are various positions, and this is the most preferred of them. The conclusion is that what is obligatory is to return to what truly bears the name of journey, legally or linguistically, as stated in al-Rawda al-Nadiyya.

In al-Misbah: "safara al-rajul safaran" (like talaba) means he went out for travel.

In al-Qamus: "qawm safr, and safira, and asfar, and sufar" means those who are on a journey, as opposed to residents (hadar).

This is the matter, and there are established discussions on shortening in the explanations of the Sunna.

Since the preceding text that came concerning the legislation of shortening was general (mujmal), it explained its manner in a form where it was most needed, and for the rest it suffices to rely on the explanation of the Sunna. Thus the Most High said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons. Then when they have prostrated, let them go behind you, and let another group who have not prayed come forward and pray with you, taking their precaution and their weapons. The disbelievers wish that you would be heedless of your weapons and your belongings, so they could charge at you in one single charge. And there is no blame upon you if rain has caused you discomfort or if you are ill, for you to lay down your weapons; but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

﴿And when you are among them﴾, i.e., with your companions, as a witness, while you fear the enemy (p. 1517). ﴿and establish the prayer for them﴾, i.e., you intend to lead them in the prayer in congregation, whose great reward makes its hardships bearable. ﴿let a group of them stand with you﴾ in the prayer, i.e., after you have been divided into two groups, and let the other group stand facing the enemy to guard you from them. The reason it was not stated explicitly is that it is evident.

﴿And let them take their weapons﴾, i.e., the group that stands with you, ﴿their weapons with them﴾, because that is closer to caution. ﴿Then when they have prostrated﴾, i.e., those standing with you have completed the two prostrations of the first rak'ah and finished the rak'ah, they leave you and complete their prayer, while you remain standing, waiting for them. ﴿Then when they have finished, let them go behind you﴾, i.e., let them turn to face the enemy to keep watch.

﴿And let another group who have not prayed come forward﴾, namely the group that is facing the enemy, ﴿and pray with you﴾, their first rak'ah, ﴿with you﴾ while you are in the second rak'ah. When you sit waiting, they stand up to their second rak'ah and complete it, then they sit so that they may give the salutation with you. The noble verse does not clarify the state of the fourth rak'ah remaining for each of the two groups, being content with the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of it to them, as will come.

﴿And let them take their precaution﴾, i.e., their vigilance, because the enemy imagines in the first rak'ah that the Muslims are standing in battle. When they stand up for the second rak'ah, it becomes apparent to the enemy that they are in prayer, so here the enemy seizes the opportunity to attack them. Therefore this position was singled out for additional warning, and He said: ﴿and let them take their precaution﴾, treating it as an instrument, so He commanded its taking and joined to it ﴿and their weapons﴾. Al-Wahidi said: In this there is a concession for the one who fears during prayer, that he may direct part of his attention to matters other than the prayer.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The obligation on each of the two groups to do what has been mentioned is because occupation with prayer is a likely cause of laying down weapons and turning away from other things, and a cause of the enemy's assault, as the saying of the Exalted indicates: ﴿The disbelievers wish﴾, i.e., they desire ﴿that you would be heedless of your weapons﴾, so that you would lay them down ﴿and your belongings﴾, i.e., your necessities by which you are sustained, ﴿so they could charge at you in one single charge﴾, i.e., they would attack in one assault and kill you. This is the reason for the command to take up weapons, and the command to do so is obligatory, as shown by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾, i.e., there is no hardship or sin upon you ﴿if rain has caused you discomfort﴾ that makes carrying weapons burdensome ﴿or if you are ill﴾ and carrying them is burdensome for you ﴿to lay down your weapons﴾.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The verse ﴿if rain has caused you discomfort or if you are ill﴾ was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who was wounded. Then they were nevertheless commanded to be vigilant and cautious, so it was said: ﴿and take your precaution﴾, lest the enemy attack you by surprise.

﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾, i.e., they will be humiliated by it. It is also said: a severe punishment.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is the reason for the command to take precaution, i.e., He has prepared for them a humiliating punishment by forsaking them and granting you victory over them. So be attentive to your affairs and do not neglect taking the means, so that His punishment may befall them at your hands.

It is also said: Since the command to be cautious of the enemy might give the impression of expecting their dominance and power, that impression is negated by the statement that Allah, exalted is He, will grant them victory and humiliate their enemy, to strengthen their hearts.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 4, Verse 103 (Part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:
﴿And when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. And when you are secure, then establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾ [103]

﴿And when you have completed﴾, i.e., you have finished, ﴿the prayer﴾, i.e., the prayer of fear, as has been detailed. ﴿Then remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾, i.e., persist in remembering Him, exalted is He, in all circumstances, for what you are in, of fear and caution in the face of the enemy, is deserving of constancy in the remembrance of Allah and humble supplication to Him. So said al-Razi.

Ibn Kathir said: He, exalted is He, commanded abundant remembrance after the prayer of fear. Although remembrance is also prescribed and encouraged after other prayers, it is more emphatic here because of the relief granted in its pillars, the permission to walk and to ride during it, and other matters not found in other prayers, just as He, exalted is He, said (concerning the sacred months): ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36] [al-Tawbah: 36]. Although this is forbidden at other times too, it is more emphatic in them because of their great sanctity and magnitude.

﴿And when you are secure﴾, i.e., your hearts are at rest with safety, ﴿then establish the prayer﴾, i.e., in the state you knew it, so do not change anything of its forms. ﴿Indeed, the prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾, i.e., an obligation with fixed times, which may not be delayed beyond its times, even if deficiencies occur in observing it.

* *

**Section**
On rulings related to this verse:

**First:** In this verse is the legislation of the prayer of fear and its description. It is not obligatory to make it up later, and it is required to carry weapons during it, except for a valid excuse.

**Second:** Those who hold to the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿And when you are among them﴾ [al-Nisa': 102], deny that the prayer of fear continues after his death (ﷺ), claiming it was specific to his time, since the verse stipulates that he be among them. But it is not hidden that the imams after him are his deputies, standing in what he used to do, so the ruling of the address addressed to him (ﷺ) applies to them, as in His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103] [al-Tawbah: 103]. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Pray as you have seen me praying."

The general wording of this hadith takes precedence over that implied meaning. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and others narrated that Sa'id ibn al-'As said, during a military campaign, and with him was Hudhayfah: "Which of you witnessed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" Hudhayfah said, "I did." So Hudhayfah commanded them, and they put on their weapons. Then he said: "If an assault comes upon you, then fighting is permitted for you." He led one of the two groups in one rak'ah while the other faced the enemy. Then those ones withdrew and took the place of the others, and the others came, and he led them in another rak'ah. Then he gave the salam to them. The campaign was in Tabaristan. Some of them said: This took place in the presence of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and no one denied it, so it stands in the place of consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement).

Abu Dawud narrated that 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah led the prayer of fear at Kabul.

**Third:** Imam Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated, concerning the occasion of the revelation of the verse, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at 'Usfan, and the polytheists confronted us, led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, and they were between us and the qiblah. The Prophet (ﷺ) led us in the Dhuhr prayer. They said, 'They were in a state where, if we had attacked, we would have caught them off guard.' Then they said, 'Now a prayer will come upon them which is dearer to them than their children and themselves.' So Jibril descended with these verses between Dhuhr and 'Asr: ﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]. The prayer came due, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded them to take up their weapons. We lined up behind him in two rows. Then he bowed and we all bowed; then he rose and we all rose. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated with the row nearest him while the others stood guarding them. When they sat, the others sat and prostrated. Then he gave the salam to them."

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated, from al-Thawri, from Hisham, something similar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), except that he said: "The front row withdrew backward when they raised their heads from prostration, and the rear row advanced and prostrated in the places of the first."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Jarir narrated, from Ibn Abi Najih, who said: Mujahid said, concerning His saying, ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will harm you﴾ [al-Nisa': 101]: It was revealed on the day the Prophet (ﷺ) was at 'Usfan and the polytheists were at Dajnan, and they faced each other. The Prophet (ﷺ) led his Companions in the Dhuhr prayer, four rak'ahs, with them all bowing, prostrating, and standing together. The polytheists resolved to raid their belongings and fight them. So Allah sent down: ﴿Let a group of them stand﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]. The Prophet (ﷺ) then prayed 'Asr, and his Companions formed two rows, and he said takbir with them all together. The first row prostrated with his prostration, while the others stood and did not prostrate, until the Prophet (ﷺ) and the first row rose. Then he said takbir with them and they all bowed together. The rear row then moved forward and the front row withdrew, and they alternated the prostration as they had done the first time. The Prophet (ﷺ) shortened the 'Asr prayer to two rak'ahs.

In these hadiths: the prayer of both groups was with the imam together; they shared in the guarding; they followed him in all the pillars of the prayer except prostration. One group prostrates with him while the other waits until the first group finishes, then it prostrates. When they finish the first rak'ah, the group that was behind advances to the place of the group that was in front, and the group in front withdraws.

(If you say): What is in the verse does not fit these narrations that relate its occasion of revelation, because it says in the verse: ﴿Let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons. And when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group come which has not prayed﴾ [al-Nisa': 102], and the verse, while in these narrations they all stood with him (ﷺ) in the prayer. What fits what is in them is only what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the prayer of fear with one of the two groups for one rak'ah, while the other group faced the enemy. Then they withdrew and took the places of their companions, facing the enemy. The others came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed with them one rak'ah, then gave the salam. Then these completed one rak'ah and those completed one rak'ah."

And what they both narrated from Salih ibn Khawwat, from one who prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Dhat al-Riqa': "The group lined up with him and another group faced the enemy. He completed one rak'ah with those who were with him, then he remained standing. They completed for themselves, then they withdrew facing the enemy. The other group came, and he prayed with them the remaining rak'ah of his prayer. They completed for themselves, and he gave the salam with them."

(I say): By reference to what we set forth in the introduction regarding the principle of sabab al-nuzul (occasion of revelation), the difficulty is removed.

From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) camped between Dajnan and 'Usfan. The polytheists said: 'For these people there is a prayer dearer to them than their fathers and mothers, which is the 'Asr. So unite your decision and fall upon them in one swoop.' Jibril, peace be upon him, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and commanded him to divide his Companions into two halves, so that he would lead one and another group would stand behind them, and they should take their caution and their weapons. Thus one group would have one rak'ah and the Prophet (ﷺ) would have two rak'ahs." Narrated by the authors of the Sunan.

Then I found that al-Qurtubi discussed in his Tafsir something similar to what I had set forth. He said: What we mentioned of the occasion of revelation in the story of Khalid ibn al-Walid is not compatible with dividing the people into two groups. Then he said (after narrating the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned above): I say: There is no contradiction between these narrations. Perhaps he (ﷺ) prayed with them another prayer, with them separated. End of quotation.

**Fourth:** The apparent meaning of the noble verse is a concession for each group to pray one rak'ah only, because it does not specify the status of the remaining rak'ah. Al-Nasa'i narrated, from Ibn 'Abbas, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed at Dhi Qarad, and he arranged the people behind him in two rows: a row behind him and a row facing the enemy. He prayed with those behind him one rak'ah, then those ones withdrew to the place of these, and those ones came, and he prayed with them one rak'ah, and they did not make up any rak'ah."

Likewise Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i also narrated, from Hudhayfah, that he prayed at Tabaristan with these one rak'ah and with those one rak'ah, and they did not make it up.

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i narrated, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "Allah prescribed the prayer upon your Prophet (ﷺ): four rak'ahs in residence, two rak'ahs while traveling, and one rak'ah in fear." These hadiths indicate that among the description of the prayer of fear is limiting it to one rak'ah for each group.

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: Al-Thawri, Ishaq, and those who followed them held the view of limiting it to one rak'ah in fear. Abu Hurayrah, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and more than one of the Successors (tabi'un) also held it, and among them are those who restricted it to severe fear.

The majority said: The shortening in fear is a shortening of form, not of number. They interpreted these hadiths to mean one rak'ah with the imam, and there is no negation of the second in them. This is refuted by his saying in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and Hudhayfah: "and they did not make it up one rak'ah," and likewise his saying in the second hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "and in fear one rak'ah."

As for their interpretation of the phrase "they did not make it up" as meaning that they did not repeat the prayer after the safety, that is very far-fetched. Thus said Nayl al-Awtar. Yes.

In the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, agreed upon, which we have already cited, occurs: "Then these completed one rak'ah and those completed one rak'ah." And in Abu Dawud, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "Then he gave the salam, and these stood and prayed one rak'ah for themselves, then they gave the salam and departed, and those returned to their place and prayed one rak'ah for themselves, then they gave the salam."

In truth, everything that has been narrated is among its permissible forms. When Imam Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in Zad al-Ma'ad the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) in performing it, he said at the end of one form: "Sometimes he would pray one rak'ah with one of the two groups, and they would depart without making up anything, and the other group would come, and he would pray one rak'ah with them, and they would make up nothing. Thus he would have two rak'ahs, and they would have one rak'ah each. All these forms are permissible for the prayer."

Imam Ahmad said: "Every hadith narrated in the chapter on the prayer of fear, acting upon it is permissible." End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: The prayer of fear has many types, for the enemy is sometimes in the direction of the qiblah and sometimes not in its direction. Then sometimes they pray in congregation, and sometimes the fighting is so close that they cannot gather in congregation, but pray individually, facing the qiblah or not facing it, on foot or mounted. In that state they may walk and strike successive blows during the prayer. Among the scholars is one who said: In that state they pray one rak'ah, based on the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal held this view.

Al-Mundhiri said: Atā', Jabir, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Hakam, Qatadah, and Hammad held this view, and Tawus and al-Dahhak also went to it.

Abu 'Asim al-'Abbadi narrated from Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi that he held that the dawn prayer is reduced to one rak'ah in fear, and Ibn Hazm also went to this. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: As for when the fighting is at close quarters, one rak'ah suffices for you, which you perform by gesture; if you cannot, then one prostration, because it is a remembrance of Allah.

Others said: One takbir suffices, so perhaps he meant one rak'ah, as Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and his companions said. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Ka'b, and more than one of the Companions, and al-Suddi, also held this view.

Ibn Jarir narrated it, but those who reported it understood it literally, as permitting the performance of the prayer with a single takbir. This is the view of Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and Amir Abd al-Wahhab ibn Bukht al-Makki also held it, to the point that he said: "If one is unable to say the takbir, he should not abandon it in his heart," meaning by intention. Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated this in his *Sunan* from Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from Shu'ayb ibn Dinar, from him. And Allah knows best.

Among the scholars there are those who permitted delaying the prayer because of the excuse of fighting and engaging the enemy, just as the Prophet ﷺ delayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). He prayed them after sunset, then prayed the Maghrib and then the 'Isha' after them. He also said, on the day of Banu Qurayza, when he dispatched the army to them: "None of you should pray 'Asr except in Banu Qurayza." Then the prayer time came upon them while they were on the road. Some of them said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ only intended that we hasten the march, not that we delay the prayer beyond its time," so they prayed at its proper time on the road. Others among them delayed the 'Asr prayer and prayed it in Banu Qurayza after sunset. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not rebuke either of the two groups. Thus he accepted their excuse for delaying the prayer for the sake of jihad and for hastening to besiege the treacherous breakers of the covenant from the cursed sect, the Jews.

As for the majority, they said: "All of this has been abrogated (naskh) by the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), for it had not yet been revealed. When it was revealed, the delaying of the prayer for this reason was abrogated." This is clearest in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, which al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and the authors of the *Sunan* narrated. However, what al-Bukhari recorded in his *Sahih* is problematic for this view, where he said: "Chapter: Prayer at the assault on fortresses and the encounter with the enemy."

Al-Awza'i said: "If the conquest is imminent and they are unable to pray, they should pray by gesture, each person for himself. If they are unable to gesture, they should delay the prayer until the fighting ends, or until they are safe, and then pray two rak'ahs. If they are unable to do that, they pray one rak'ah and two prostrations. If they are unable to do even that, then the takbir does not suffice for them, and they should delay it until they are safe." Makhul also said this.

Anas ibn Malik said: "I was present at the assault on the fortress of Tustar at the break of dawn, and the fighting intensified so that they were unable to pray. We did not pray until the day had risen high. Then we prayed while we were with Abu Musa, and it was opened to us." Anas also said: "I would not be pleased with that prayer in exchange for this world and all that is in it." End of quotation.

Then he (al-Shafi'i or the author of the cited work) followed this with the hadith of delaying the prayer on the day of the Confederates, then with the hadith of his command that they should not pray 'Asr except in Banu Qurayza, and it seems that he favoured this. And Allah knows best.

For those inclined to this view, there is the practice of Abu Musa and his companions on the day of the conquest of Tustar, which is widely known, and that was during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is not reported that he or any of the Companions denounced them. And Allah knows best.

These scholars said: The prayer of fear was legislated at the Trench (al-Khandaq), because the Expedition of Dhat al-Riqa' came before the Trench according to the majority of scholars of the biographies and campaigns (al-siyar wa al-maghazi). Among those who explicitly stated this were Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Musa ibn 'Uqba, al-Waqidi, Muhammad ibn Sa'd, his scribe, Khalifa ibn al-Khayyat, and others.

Al-Bukhari and others said: Dhat al-Riqa' came after the Trench, based on the hadith of Abu Musa, and it was not advanced except to Khaybar. And Allah knows best.

(p-1527) Fifth ruling: Allah's words ﴿a group﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] have been cited as evidence that it is not required for the two groups to be equal in number. However, it is necessary that the group which guards be one in which trust is achieved for this purpose.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: The term *ta'ifah* (group) is applied to the few and the many, even to one individual. So if they were three and the fear befell them, it is permissible for one of them to lead the prayer with one (companion), while one guards, and then the other prays. This is the least that can be imagined for the prayer of fear in congregation.

Sixth: The verse has been cited as evidence for the great importance of congregation, indeed for preferring the view that it is obligatory, since many things are excused in this situation that would not be excused otherwise. Had each person prayed alone, the need for most of that would not have arisen. This was stated by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar in *al-Fath*.

Ibn Kathir said: How excellent is the evidence used by those who hold that congregation is obligatory from this noble verse, since many actions were excused for the sake of congregation. Had it not been obligatory, that would not have been permissible.

Seventh: Some exegetes said: There is disagreement about who is meant by the command to take up arms in Allah's words ﴿and let them take their weapons﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]. It was said: They are the group who face the enemy, and this is apparent. It was also said: Rather, they are the group who are praying, and what is meant is what does not distract from the prayer, such as a coat of mail, a dagger, a sword, and the like. It was also said: It refers to both groups, and this is the view of al-Qasim. End of quotation.

Al-Nasir said in *al-Intisaf*: The apparent meaning is that the one addressed with taking up weapons is the praying group, since whoever does not pray is prepared for guarding, so it is apparent that there is no need to command them to this and alert them to it, for they only delayed the prayer for this reason. As for those who pray, they are liable to set down their weapons, since they are not accustomed to carrying them during prayer. So they were alerted that they should not set down their weapons, even while praying, because of the necessity of fear and the fear of being caught off guard. Also, the structure of the verse indicates this, for He said: ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa': 102], and followed it with: ﴿and let them take their weapons﴾ [al-Nisa': 102]. So the apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to them, and where it returns to those who are not praying, it requires some strain to justify returning it to them, since the strength of the discourse points to them even though they were not mentioned.

Al-Nasir also disputed with al-Zamakhshari his interpretation of Allah's words ﴿So when they have prostrated, let them be﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] as referring to those who are not praying. He said: The apparent meaning of prostration here is prayer, and it is often expressed by prostration, and what is meant is: "When the group has prayed (i.e., completed its prayer), let them be behind you." End of quotation.

Eighth: Abu Ali al-Jurjani, the author of *al-Nazm*, said: Allah's words ﴿and take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 71] indicate that it was permissible for the Prophet ﷺ to perform the prayer of fear in a manner by which he would be cautious, not heedless of the enemy's plotting. What the Qur'an revealed in this passage is the form of precaution, because on that day at Dhat al-Riqa' the enemy was facing the qiblah, while the Muslims had their backs to the qiblah. Whenever they faced the qiblah, they would have their backs to their enemy. Therefore they were commanded to form two groups: one group facing the enemy, and another group with the Prophet ﷺ facing the qiblah. As for when the Prophet ﷺ was at 'Usfan and at Batn Nakhl, he did not divide his companions into two groups. That was because the enemy had their backs to the qiblah, and the Muslims were facing it. So they could see the enemy while they were in prayer, and they only needed to take precaution during prostration. Therefore, when the first row prostrated, the second row remained guarding them. When they had finished prostrating and stood up, they withdrew, and the second row advanced and prostrated, while the first row, while standing, guarded the second row. From what we have mentioned, it is established that Allah's words ﴿take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 71] indicate the permissibility of all these forms.

What shows that the intended meaning of this verse is what we have mentioned is that if we did not interpret it this way, it would become pure repetition without benefit, and the Messenger's action at 'Usfan and Batn Nakhl would contradict the text of the Qur'an, which is impermissible. This was related by al-Razi.

Al-Khattabi said: The prayer of fear has several forms, which the Prophet ﷺ performed on different days and in different manners. In all of them, what is most cautious for the prayer and most effective for guarding is sought. Despite the differences in their forms, they are unified in meaning. End of quotation.

Its forms are explained in the commentaries on the Sunnah. Then Allah urged them to jihad with His words:

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the people. If you are suffering, then indeed they are suffering as you are suffering, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [104]

﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the people﴾ meaning: do not be feeble in pursuing your enemy with fighting. Rather, exert yourselves against them and lie in wait for them at every passage. Then He established the proof against them with His words, glorified be He: ﴿If you are suffering, then indeed they are suffering as you are suffering﴾, meaning: the pain you find from wounding and killing is not specific to you; rather it is shared between you and them, as He, exalted, said: ﴿If a wound touches you, a wound has certainly touched the people like it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]. Then He increased the establishing of the proof, and made clear that the believers are more deserving of steadfastness in fighting than the polytheists, with His words, exalted be He: ﴿but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for﴾, meaning: you aspire from Allah to nearness to Him, to deserving the ranks in His gardens, and to the manifestation of His religion, as He promised you in His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ, what they do not aspire to. Therefore you are more deserving of jihad than they are, and more worthy of establishing the word of Allah.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, meaning: He does not impose upon you except what He knows to be a cause of your righteousness in your religion and your worldly affairs. So exert yourselves in complying with that, for in it are praiseworthy outcomes.

Some of the exegetes of the Zaydiyyah (Zaydi) said: The fruit of the verse is: the obligation of jihad, and that it does not lapse because of the harm that results from wounds and the like; that endurance and seeking what strengthens (oneself) are required; and that what causes weakness is not permissible to do. It also indicates the permissibility of argumentation and debate, by His words: ﴿for indeed they suffer﴾. And it indicates that the fighter may fight seeking reward, by His words: ﴿but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for﴾, so He made this a motivating cause for jihad. This is the meaning of the words of al-Hakim.

A parallel to this: if one prays seeking reward or safety from punishment, there is a difference of opinion regarding that. From al-Radi billah: it is accepted (as valid) (yujza). Al-Faqih Yahya ibn Ahmad strengthened this. From Abu Mudar: it is not accepted, because he did not intend the aspect for which the obligatory act was prescribed. End of quotation.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 4, verses 105–109 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-1530) On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous.﴾ [105]

﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [An-Nisa: 106] [106]

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is treacherous and sinful.﴾ [An-Nisa: 107] [107]

﴿They conceal themselves from the people, but they cannot conceal themselves from Allah, and He is with them when they plot at night in speech that does not please Him. And ever is Allah, of what they do, encompassing.﴾ [An-Nisa: 108] [108]

﴿There you are, those who argued on their behalf in this worldly life, but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ [An-Nisa: 109] [109]

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between the people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous.﴾

﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [An-Nisa: 106]

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is treacherous and sinful.﴾ [An-Nisa: 107]

﴿They conceal themselves from the people, but they cannot conceal themselves from Allah, and He is with them when they plot at night in speech that does not please Him. And ever is Allah, of what they do, encompassing.﴾ [An-Nisa: 108]

﴿There you are, those who argued on their behalf in this worldly life, but who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be their guardian?﴾ [An-Nisa: 109]

(p-1531) Al-Hafiz Ibn Mardawayh narrated, through al-Awfi, from Ibn Abbas: "A group of the Ansar went out on one of the expeditions with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a coat of mail (dir') belonging to one of them was stolen. A man from the Ansar was suspected of it (*fa-uzinna*, i.e., he was accused). The owner of the coat of mail came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Indeed, Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq stole my coat of mail.' When the thief saw that, he went to it and threw it into the house of an innocent man, and said to a group of his tribe: 'I have hidden the coat of mail and thrown it into the house of so-and-so, and it will be found with him.'

They went to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) at night and said: 'O Prophet of Allah! Our companion is innocent, and the owner of the coat of mail is so-and-so, and we have knowledge of this matter. So excuse our companion before the people and argue on his behalf, for if Allah does not protect him through you, he will be destroyed.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, declared him innocent, and excused him before the people. So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down﴾, the verse." Then He, Exalted, said to those who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concealing themselves with falsehood: ﴿They conceal themselves from the people, but they cannot conceal themselves from Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 108], meaning those who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concealing themselves and argued on behalf of the treacherous.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whoever does wrong﴾ [An-Nisa: 110], the verse, meaning those who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concealing themselves with falsehood. Then He said: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or transgression and then attributes it to an innocent person has borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾ [An-Nisa: 112], meaning the thief and those who argued on behalf of the thief.

Ibn Kathir said: "This context is unusual. Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others mentioned (concerning this verse) that it was revealed about the thief of the Banu Ubayriq, with differing contexts, though they are close in meaning."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated this story at length, and Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi narrated it from him, through his route, in his "Jami'" in the Book of Tafsir, from Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: (p-1532) "There was a household among us called the Banu Ubayriq: Bishr, Bushayr (Abu Dharr al-Khushani said: 'Bashir ibn Ubayriq'; thus it occurs here as *Bashir* with a fatha on the ba'; al-Daraqutni said: it is only *Bushayr* with a damma on the ba'), and Mubashshir. Bushayr was a hypocrite, and he used to compose poetry satirizing the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then he would attribute it to some of the Arabs, saying: 'So-and-so said such-and-such, or so-and-so said such-and-such.' When the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard that poetry, they said: 'By Allah, no one composes this poetry except the wicked one.' He said:

*Do men compose a poem, and they are accused, and they say: 'The son of al-Ubayriq composed it'?*

He said: They were a household of poverty and need, in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. The people's food in Medina was dates and barley. When a man had means, a caravan (*dafitah*) would come from Syria with fine flour (*al-darmak*), and the man would buy from it and reserve it for himself, while his dependents had only dates and barley. A caravan came from Syria, and my uncle Rifa'ah ibn Zayd bought a load of fine flour, and placed it in a storeroom (*mashrubah*) of his, in which he had weapons: two coats of mail, two swords, and what was needed for them. Someone attacked him from beneath the house, the storeroom was breached, and the food and weapons were taken. When morning came, my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said: 'O nephew! You know that we were attacked during this night; our storeroom was breached, and our food and weapons were taken away.'

(p-1533) He said: I searched the house and asked, and it was said to us: 'We saw the Banu Ubayriq kindle a fire this night, and we do not think, as far as we can see, that it was except on some of your food.'
