And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom, and taught you what you did not know. And the grace of Allah upon you has been ever great.﴾ [113]

﴿Had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy﴾ by informing you, through revelation, of what they were upon, and by alerting you to the truth. ﴿a group of them would have resolved to mislead you﴾ by casting blame on the innocent and by pleading on behalf of the treacherous, referring to Usayr ibn Urwah and his companions. He means by this that they praised the Banu Ubayriq and blamed Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man for accusing them, when they were righteous and innocent. The matter was not as they had reported it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿But they mislead none except themselves﴾ because its evil falls upon them. ﴿and they cannot harm you at all﴾ because you acted only on the apparent state of affairs, and it did not occur to you that the reality was contrary to that.

When the Exalted had sent down the decisive judgment of the matter and made it clear to His Messenger (ﷺ), He bestowed favour upon him by supporting him in all circumstances, saying: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom﴾, that is, the Qur'an and the Sunnah. ﴿and taught you﴾ concerning matters of the religion and the laws ﴿what you did not know﴾, that is, before that was sent down to you, as in His saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and the verse continues, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 86]. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been ever great﴾, that is, in what He taught you and bestowed upon you.

Al-Razi said: This is one of the greatest proofs that knowledge is the most noble of virtues and merits. Then the Exalted pointed to what they used to confer about in secret when they plotted what He does not approve of in speech, with His statement, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 114:

(p-1542) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward.﴾ [114]

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾, i.e., their whispering. The context, although it indicates the private conversation of some of the people of that thief with one another, is general in meaning. The intent is: there is no good in what people confer about and engage in of speech. Then He, glorified and exalted, made an exception for secret talk in acts of good with His saying: ﴿except for one who enjoins charity﴾, i.e., except in the secret talk of one who enjoins charity, in secret from those present, so that he may give it privately, concealing thereby the shame of the one who receives the charity.

﴿Or what is right﴾, i.e., by obedience to Allah, and all acts of righteousness are "what is right" (ma'ruf). The secret of conferring in it is that the one commanded does not feel too proud to accept it, were it announced openly.

﴿Or reconciliation between people﴾, meaning reconciling two opposing parties who are in dispute, so that they return to the harmony and unity they had, in accordance with what Allah has permitted and commanded. The secret of conferring in it is that if it were made known at first, it might perhaps not be completed.

Al-Mahayimi said: It has been said regarding the restriction: good is either a material benefit, which is in enjoining charity; or a spiritual one, which is in enjoining what is right; or a repelling (of harm), which is in reconciliation.

It may be said: good is either a benefit transferred from the one commanded, which is charity; or a benefit that remains with him, which is what is right; or the repelling of harm, transitive or intransitive, which is reconciliation. Its goodness is only complete when it is sought with the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿And whoever does that seeking﴾, i.e., desiring, ﴿the pleasure of Allah, We will give him﴾, meaning in the Hereafter, ﴿a great reward﴾ equal to the reward of the doer or exceeding it.

The verse indicates encouragement toward charity, what is right, and reconciliation between people. Allah, exalted is He, has emphasized the encouragement by His saying: ﴿great﴾, and that intention is a condition for attaining reward, by His saying, exalted is He: (p-1543) ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾; and that a person's speech is against him, not for him, except for what is of this kind and similar to it, as came in the hadith narrated by Ibn Mardawayh with his chain to Muhammad ibn Yazid ibn Khunays, who said: We entered upon Sufyan al-Thawri to visit him, and Sa'id ibn Hassan entered upon us. Al-Thawri said to him: "Repeat to me the hadith you had related to me from Umm Salih." He said: Umm Salih narrated to me, from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, from Umm Habibah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of the speech of the son of Adam is against him, not for him, except the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or enjoining what is right or forbidding what is wrong."

Sufyan said: "Did you not hear Allah say in His Book: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people﴾? That is exactly this. Did you not hear Allah say: ﴿The day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits and who speaks what is correct﴾ [al-Naba: 38]? That is exactly this. Did you not hear Allah say in His Book: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss﴾ [al-Asr: 1-2], and so on? That is exactly this."

At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also narrated this hadith from the hadith of Ibn Khunays, from Sa'id ibn Hassan with it, but did not mention al-Thawri's words to its end.

Then at-Tirmidhi said: "A gharib hadith, not known except through the hadith of Ibn Khunays." I say: He is acceptable (maqbul), as in al-Taqrib of Ibn Hajar, so his hadith is graded hasan.

(p-1544) The group (of compilers) narrated from Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah that she informed him that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The liar is not the one who reconciles between people, so that he conveys good or says good."

She also said: "I did not hear him grant permission in anything that people say except in three: in war, in reconciliation between people, and a man's speech to his wife, and a woman's speech to her husband."

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and at-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of something better than the rank of fasting, prayer, and charity?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Reconciling between people. For the corruption of relations between people is the shaver (destroyer of religion)." At-Tirmidhi said: Hasan sahih.

**The interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):**

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the believers - We will give him what he has turned to, and burn him in Hell, and it is an evil destination.﴾ [115]

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ means: he contravenes him and is hostile towards him. ﴿After guidance has become clear to him﴾ means: the truth has become evident to him. ﴿And follows other than the way of the believers﴾ means: other than that to which they steadfastly adhere in belief and action, which is the upright religion. ﴿We will give him what he has turned to﴾ means: We will leave him in charge of what he has chosen, namely opposition and following other than their way. So We will adorn it for him, as the adornment of disbelief is made attractive to disbelievers, as a means of gradual leading on (istidraj), so that it becomes a sign of the severity of punishment in the Hereafter, as Exalted is He said: ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse; We shall lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ [al-Qalam: 44]. And He Exalted said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-An'am: 110].

﴿And burn him in Hell﴾ means: We will cause him to enter it. ﴿And it is an evil destination﴾: He made the Fire his destination in the Hereafter, because whoever departs from guidance has no path except the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, as Exalted is He said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [al-Saffat: 22]. And Exalted is He said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are about to fall into it, and will not find from it any escape﴾ [al-Kahf: 53].

(p-1546) Imam Ibn Kathir said: His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ is inseparable from the first attribute. However, the opposition may be to the explicit text of the Lawgiver, or it may be to what the Muhammadan community has unanimously agreed upon, in matters whose agreement is known with certainty. For indeed the community has been guaranteed immunity from error in its consensus (ijma'), as an honour for them and a glorification of their Prophet. Numerous hadiths have been related on this, and some scholars claimed that their meaning is mutawatir (widely transmitted). And what al-Shafi'i - may Allah have mercy on him - relied upon in arguing that consensus is a proof whose opposition is forbidden is this noble verse, after long reflection and thought, and it is among the finest and strongest of deductions, although some have found this problematic and considered the implication from it to be remote. End of quotation.

One of the exegetes of the Zaydiyyah said: The verse indicates that opposing the Messenger ﷺ is a major sin, and may reach the level of disbelief. It also indicates that ignorance is an excuse, by His saying: ﴿after guidance has become clear to him﴾. It also indicates that opposing consensus is a major sin, and that it is an evidence like the Book and the Sunnah; but it is only a major sin if its transmission is certain (qat'i) and not solitary (ahad). End of quotation.

Al-Muhayymi said: In the verse there is evidence for the prohibition of opposing consensus, because He, mighty and majestic, attached the severe threat to opposing the Messenger and opposing consensus. So either it is because of the prohibition of one of the two - and this is invalid, since it would be abhorrent to say: "Whoever drinks wine and eats bread deserves the prescribed punishment," as eating bread has no bearing on it - or it is because of the prohibition of combining the two - and this is also invalid, because opposing the Messenger is forbidden even if nothing else is added to it - or it is because of the prohibition of each of them separately, which is what is sought. End of quotation.

Al-Khafaji related the story of al-Shafi'i's deduction from this verse, from Imam al-Muzani, who said: I was with al-Shafi'i one day when an old man came to him wearing woollen clothing and holding a staff. When he saw that he was a man of dignity, he sat up straight - he had been leaning against a pillar - and straightened himself and arranged his clothes. Then the old man said to him: "What is the proof in the religion of Allah?" He said: "His Book." He said: "And what else?" He said: "The Sunnah of His Prophet." He said: "And what else?" He said: "The consensus of the community." He said: "From where is this last one? Is it in the Book of Allah?" Then he (al-Shafi'i) reflected silently for a while. The old man said to him: "I give you three days and their nights. If you bring a verse, well and good; otherwise, withdraw from the people."

(p-1547) He remained three days without going out, and on the third day he came out between the noon and afternoon prayers, his complexion changed. The old man came to him, greeted him and sat down, and said: "My need?" He said: "Yes. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger...﴾ to the end of the verse. He would not cause him to enter Hell for opposing the believers unless following them is obligatory." He said: "You have spoken truly," and he rose and left.

It is related from him that he said: "I recited the Qur'an in one day, and every night three times, until I attained it."

Al-Raghib objected to this, saying that there is no proof in it for what he mentioned: every described subject to which a ruling is attached, the command to follow it lies in the basis of that attribute. So when it is said: "Follow the one who prays," what is meant is his prayer. Likewise, "the way of the believers" means their way in faith only, and so there is no indication in the verse for following them in anything else.

It was answered that this is a restriction by something which the first condition rejects. Furthermore, if the habitual practice of those who fast is seclusion (i'tikaf), the command to follow them includes that as well. Likewise it includes what is required by faith in the matter under discussion. So "the way of the believers," even if interpreted as what they are upon in religion, encompasses the fundamentals and the subsidiaries, the whole and the part. Moreover, the punishment is consequent upon each of the two matters mentioned in the condition, not upon the combination, because it is certain that mere opposition to the Messenger suffices in meriting the threat, in meaning. Furthermore, abandoning the way of the believers is following other than the way of the believers, because the responsible person cannot be free of following some way whatsoever. End of quotation.

I have seen, from Imam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah in his book "al-Furqan Bayn al-Haqq wal-Batil," an excellent treatise on this verse and consensus, in which he ranged his pen with skill and excellence, and extended and was eloquent. He, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "What some people call the subsidiary matters, the Sharia and the jurisprudence (fiqh), the Messenger has clarified in the best of clarifications. Nothing remains of what Allah commanded, forbade, made lawful or made unlawful, except that He clarified it, and Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]."

(p-1548) And Exalted is He said: ﴿It was not a narration invented, but a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾ [Yusuf: 111]. And Exalted is He said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. And Exalted is He said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back﴾ [al-Shura: 10]. And Exalted is He said: ﴿And Allah would not misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should fear﴾ [al-Tawbah: 115]. So He has made clear to the Muslims everything they should fear, as He said: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden you, except what you are compelled to﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. And Exalted is He said: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. That is referral to the Book of Allah, (p-1549) or to the Sunnah of the Messenger after his death.

And His saying: ﴿if you dispute﴾ [al-Nisa': 59] is a condition, and the verb is indefinite in the context of a condition, so whatever they dispute over, refer it to Allah and the Messenger. If the clarification of Allah and the Messenger were not decisive in resolving disputes, they would not have been commanded to refer to it.

And it has come from him ﷺ that he said: "I have left you upon a white (clear) path, its night is like its day, none deviates from it after me except one who is destroyed." And from Umar ibn al-Khattab - may Allah be pleased with him - there is a statement similar to this.

The conclusion is that the Book and the Sunnah suffice for all matters of the religion. As for the consensus of the community, it is in itself true: the community does not agree upon misguidance. Likewise sound analogy (qiyas) is true, for Allah sent His messengers with justice, and sent down (p-1550) the Balance along with the Book. The Balance includes justice and that by which justice is known. They have explained the sending down of this as the inspiring of servants with knowledge of it. Allah and His Messenger equate between like things and distinguish between unlike things, and this is sound analogy. Allah has struck in the Qur'an every kind of parable, and He clarified by sound analogy - which are the parables struck - what He clarified of the truth. However, sound analogy agrees with the text, for the Balance agrees with the Book, and Allah commanded His Prophet to judge with justice. He sent down the Book, and He sent it down only with justice. He said: ﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49], and ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42].

As for the consensus of the community, it is true: the community - and to Allah be praise - does not agree upon misguidance, as Allah described it in the Book and the Sunnah. He said: ﴿You are the best community produced for mankind; you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong and believe in Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. This is a description of them as enjoining every right and forbidding every wrong. So if the community were to say in religion something that is misguidance, they would not have enjoined the right in that, nor forbidden the wrong in it. And He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced community that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The "wasat" (justly balanced) is the just and the best. Allah has made them witnesses over the people (p-1551) and established their testimony in the place of the testimony of the Messenger.

And it is established in the authentic collections that the Prophet ﷺ passed by a funeral procession, and the people praised the deceased with good, so he said: "It is obligatory." Then he passed by another funeral procession, and the people spoke ill of the deceased, so he said: "It is obligatory." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you mean by 'it is obligatory'?" He said: "This one you praised with good, so I say: Paradise is obligatory for him. And this one you spoke ill of, so I say: The Fire is obligatory for him. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth."

If the Lord has made them witnesses, they do not testify to falsehood. So if they testify that Allah has commanded something, then He has commanded it; and if they testify that Allah has forbidden something, then He has forbidden it. Had they been testifying to falsehood or error, they would not be the witnesses of Allah on earth.

And He said: ﴿And follow the way of one who turns back to Me﴾ [Luqman: 15]. The community turns back to its Lord, so it is obligatory to follow its way.

And He said: (p-1552) ﴿And the foremost of the early emigrants and the helpers, and those who followed them in excellence - Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100]. So He is pleased with whoever follows the foremost until the Day of Resurrection. This indicates that their follower acts by what pleases Allah, and Allah is not pleased except with the truth, not with falsehood. And He said: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the believers - We will give him what he has turned to, and burn him in Hell, and it is an evil destination.﴾

Al-Shafi'i - may Allah be pleased with him - when he extensively discussed the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), argued for consensus from this verse, as he and others used to hear from Malik. This has been related from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. The verse indicates that the one who follows other than the way of the believers deserves the threat, just as the one who opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him deserves the threat. It is known that this attribute entails the threat by itself. So if the other attribute were not included in that, there would be no benefit in mentioning it. And here, people have three views:

It is said: following other than the way of the believers is, by itself, the opposition to the Messenger mentioned in the verse.

And it is said: rather, opposition to the Messenger is independently blameworthy, and likewise following other than their way is independently blameworthy.

And it is said: rather, following other than the way of the believers necessitates blame, as the verse indicates.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 115 (part 2 of 3):

However, this does not require that it (the second matter) be separate from the first. Rather, it may necessarily imply it. So every one who follows a path other than the way of the believers is, in reality, opposing the Messenger, and likewise, one who opposes the Messenger is following a path other than the way of the believers. This is like the case of obedience to God and the Messenger: obedience to God is obligatory, obedience to the Messenger is obligatory, and each of disobedience to God and disobedience to the Messenger entails blame. The two are mutually implicative, for whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed God.

In the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) he said: "Whoever obeys me has obeyed God, and whoever obeys my commander has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed God, and whoever disobeys my commander has disobeyed me."

(p. 1553) Then Taqi al-Din (may God have mercy on him) said, after three pages:

Some people say that the verse does not indicate the point of dispute, since the blame in it is directed at one who combines both matters, and there is no dispute about this; or at one who follows a path other than the way of the believers, by which they were believers, which is following the Messenger, and there is no dispute about this; or the way of the believers is the deriving of proofs from the Book and the Sunnah, and there is no dispute about this. So this and similar statements are the view of those who say that it does not indicate the place of dispute.

Others say: rather, it indicates the obligation of following the believers absolutely, and they went to great lengths to support this, as their statements are well known, and they did not answer the objections of those people with satisfactory answers.

The third, middle view is that it indicates the obligation of following the way of the believers and the prohibition of following other than their way, but together with the prohibition of opposing the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him. It indicates the blame of each of these, as has been mentioned, but it does not negate their mutual implication, as was mentioned regarding obedience to God and the Messenger.

Then he says: The blame is either a right owed for opposing the Messenger alone, or for following other than their way alone, or the blame does not attach to either one of them, but to both together when they are combined, or the blame attaches to each of them even when separate from the other, or to each of them because it entails the other. The first two are invalid, because if only one of them were the operative cause, mentioning the other would be wasted and pointless. That the blame does not attach to either of them is clearly false, for opposing the Messenger entails the threat (of punishment) regardless of whether one follows him or not. That the blame attaches to each of them even when separate from the other is not indicated by the verse, for the threat in it is directed only at the combination.

The remaining category is that each of the two descriptions entails the threat because it necessarily implies the other, just as the same is said about disobedience to God and the Messenger, and about contradicting the Qur'an and Islam. One says: whoever contradicts the Qur'an and Islam, or whoever departs from the Qur'an and Islam, is among the people of the Fire. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, has certainly strayed far astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. For disbelief in any one of these foundations entails disbelief in the others. Whoever disbelieves in God has disbelieved in all of them, and whoever disbelieves in the angels has disbelieved in the books and the messengers, and thus he is a disbeliever in God, since he has denied His messengers and His books.

(p. 1554) Likewise, whoever disbelieves in the Last Day has denied the books and the messengers, and so he is a disbeliever. Likewise is His saying: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you mix the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 71]. He blamed them for both descriptions, and each of them entails blame, and the two are mutually implicative. For this reason He forbade both of them together in His saying: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42]. For whoever mixes the truth with falsehood, covering it with it so that he misleads (others) by it, necessarily conceals the truth which has become clear to be that this is falsehood, since if he were to make it clear, the falsehood by which he mixed the truth would disappear. Thus is the case of opposing the Messenger and following other than the way of the believers: whoever opposes him has thereby followed other than their way, and this is evident; and whoever follows other than their way has thereby also opposed him, for He has made it a point of entry into the threat, which shows that it is an operative description in the blame. So whoever departs from their consensus has, beyond doubt, followed other than their way, and the verse requires the blame of that.

If it is said: the verse blamed it only together with opposing the Messenger, we say: because the two are mutually implicative. This is because everything upon which the Muslims agree is necessarily stated by the Messenger, so one who opposes them opposes the Messenger, just as one who opposes the Messenger opposes God. But this entails that everything upon which the Messenger agreed has been explained by the Messenger, and this is the correct view. There is no matter ever agreed upon except that there is an explanation of it from the Messenger. But this may be hidden from some people, and one who knows the consensus derives proof from it, just as one derives proof from the text without knowing the indication of the text. The consensus is a second proof alongside the text, like the parables struck in the Qur'an. Likewise, consensus is another proof, as when one says: this is indicated by the Book and the Sunnah and the consensus, and what is indicated by the Qur'an is taken from the Messenger. So the Book and the Sunnah are both taken from him. And there is no matter upon which consensus is reached except that there is a text regarding it. Some people used to mention consensus without a text in matters such as the mudaraba (profit-sharing partnership), but this is not so. Rather, the mudaraba was well known among them in the Jahiliyyah, especially among the Quraysh, for most of their livelihood was trade, and the owners of wealth used to give their money to workers.

(p. 1555) The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had travelled with the wealth of others before prophethood, just as he travelled with the wealth of Khadijah. The caravan in which Abu Sufyan was had most of its goods in mudaraba with Abu Sufyan and others. When Islam came, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approved of it, and his Companions used to travel with the wealth of others in mudaraba, and he did not forbid this. The Sunnah is his saying, his action, and his tacit approval. Since he approved of it, it was established by the Sunnah.

The well-known report on this from 'Umar, which Malik related in the Muwatta' and on which the jurists rely, is that when Abu Musa sent money which he had lent to his two sons, and they traded with it and profited, 'Umar asked that the entire profit be taken for the Muslims, because he had singled them out with it to the exclusion of the rest of the army. One of them said to him: "If the money had been lost, it would have fallen on us; how then should the profit be ours while the liability is on us?" Then one of the Companions said to him: "Make it a mudaraba," so he made it a mudaraba.

(p. 1556) He only said that because the mudaraba was known among them, and the time of the Messenger was recent, and it had not come into being after him. So it is known that it was known among them in the time of the Messenger, just as farming and other crafts were, such as tailoring and leatherwork. On this basis, matters on which there is consensus may be such that a group of mujtahids did not know a text regarding them, so they gave a view based on personal reasoning that agreed with the text, but the text was known to others.

Ibn Jarir and a group say: consensus is not valid unless it is from a text they transmitted from the Messenger, while they accept the validity of qiyas (analogy). We do not require that all of them knew the text and transmitted it in meaning, as reports are transmitted. Rather, we have surveyed the cases of consensus and found all of them to be textually based.

Many scholars did not know the text and yet agreed with the majority, just as one may argue by analogy while there is a consensus on the matter which he did not know, and so he agrees with the consensus. And there may be a specific text on a matter, yet a scholar derives proof in it from a general wording, as Ibn Mas'ud and others derived proof from His saying: ﴿And the women with children, their term is that they lay down their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. Ibn Mas'ud said: "Surat al-Nisa' al-Qusra (the short Nisa') was revealed after al-Tula (the long one)," meaning after al-Baqarah.

His saying: ﴿their term is that they lay down their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4] (p. 1557) indicates that the term is limited to this. So if one were to obligate her to observe the longer of the two periods, her term would not be that she lay down her burden. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and others included her under the general wording of both verses, and the specific text in the case of Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah came in agreement with the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

Likewise, when they disputed about the mufawwidah (a woman whose marriage was concluded without a fixed dower, and whose husband died), whether she is owed the equivalent dower (mahr al-mithl), Ibn Mas'ud gave a ruling by his personal opinion that she is owed the equivalent dower. Then they related the hadith of Bir'a bint Washiq in agreement with that. But 'Ali, Zayd and others disagreed with him, and they said: she has no dower.

So it is established that some mujtahids may give a ruling based on a general wording or on analogy, while there is in the case a specific text which they did not know, and so their ruling agrees with it. And one does not know of a single matter on which they agreed that there is no text regarding it. Rather, most of what they disputed, some of them derived proof in it from texts, and those others derived proof from a text too. Such as the case of the widow who is pregnant: these scholars argued that both verses include her, while the others said: she is only included in the verse about pregnancy, and the verse about the (waiting) months concerns the non-pregnant woman, just as the verse about the menstrual periods (qur') concerns the non-pregnant woman.

(p. 1558) Likewise, when they disputed about the prohibition (haram, a wife declared unlawful), those who made it an oath argued by His saying: ﴿Why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? And God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1], and ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2].

Likewise, they disputed about the irrevocably divorced woman (mabtutah), whether she is entitled to maintenance (nafaqah) or lodging (sukna). These argued by the hadith of Fatimah, and by the fact that the lodging mentioned in the Qur'an is for the revocably divorced woman. Those others said: rather, it is for both of them. The indications of texts may be obscure, so God singles out some people with understanding of them, as 'Ali said: "Except an understanding which God grants a servant regarding His Book."

(p. 1559) A text may be clear and yet a mujtahid overlooks it, as in the case of tayammum for one in a state of major impurity (junub). It is clearly stated in the Qur'an in two verses, and when Abu Musa argued with Ibn Mas'ud by this, one present said: "'Abd Allah did not understand what he was saying, except that he said: 'If we permitted them this, one of them would soon, when he feels the cold, perform tayammum.'"

Ibn 'Abbas, Fatimah bint Qays and Jabir said: the divorced woman (muttalaqah) in the Qur'an is the revocably divorced one, by the proof of His saying: ﴿You know not, perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. And what matter would He bring about after three (divorces)?

A group argued for the obligation of 'umrah by His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], and whoever prohibited the fasKH (changing an intended hajj into 'umrah) argued by this verse. (p. 1560)

Others say: it only commands completion, and likewise the lawgiver's command is that it be completed. Likewise, regarding fasKH, they said: whoever changes his 'umrah into one not followed by hajj has not completed it; but if he changes it in order to perform hajj in the same year, then he has done what completes what he began, for the Lawgiver (ﷺ) instructed his Companions in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage.

They disputed about the one in whose hand is the marriage contract (the husband), and about His saying: ﴿or you have touched women﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], and similar matters which are not the place to examine thoroughly.

As for a matter alone on which they agreed that no text, clear or hidden, is used as proof, this is something I do not know.

When most of them said that the grandfather is a father, they derived proof for this from the Qur'an by His saying: ﴿As He brought your parents out of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. (p. 1561) Ibn 'Abbas said: "If the jinn thought that humans called the father of the father a grandfather, they would not have said: ﴿And that He, exalted is He, the grandfather of our Lord﴾ [al-Jinn: 3]." We say: it is indeed a father, but a father further removed than a father.

It has been related from 'Ali and Zayd that they both argued by analogy. Whoever claims that they agreed on abandoning reasoning (ra'y) and analogy absolutely has erred, and whoever claims that there is a matter on which none of them spoke except by reasoning and analogy has erred too. Rather, each of them spoke according to the knowledge he had: whoever saw the indication of the Book mentioned it, and whoever saw the indication of the balance (mizan, i.e., rational reasoning) mentioned it. Correct proofs do not contradict one another, but the way in which they agree, or the weakness of one of them, may be hidden from some scholars.

The Companions had an understanding of the Qur'an that is hidden from most later scholars. Likewise, they had knowledge of matters of the Sunnah (the Prophet's practice and sayings) and of the circumstances of the Messenger that most later scholars do not know. They witnessed the revelation, saw the Messenger in person, and knew from his sayings, actions and conditions what they could use as evidence for his intent, which most later scholars who lacked this knowledge did not know. So they sought the ruling from what they believed to be consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) or analogy (qiyas, reasoning by comparison).

As for the later scholar who said that consensus is the basis of most of the Sharia, he was reporting on his own state. Because of his shortfall in knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah, he needed that. This is like their saying that most incidents require analogy because the texts do not indicate them. This is nothing but the words of one who has no knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah and of how they indicate the rulings.

Imam Ahmad (may Allah be pleased with him) said: There is no issue except that the Companions spoke about it or about its equivalent. When the lands were conquered and Islam spread, all kinds of new matters arose, and they spoke about them according to the Book and the Sunnah. Only some of them spoke by personal opinion (ra'y) on a few issues. Consensus was not something most of them relied upon or needed, since they themselves were the people of consensus, and there was no consensus before them. But when the Successors (tabi'un) came, Umar wrote to Shurayh: "Judge by what is in the Book of Allah. If you do not find it, then by what is in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. If you do not find it, then by what the righteous before you judged." In another narration: "then by what the people agreed upon." Thus Umar gave precedence to the Book, then the Sunnah. Likewise Ibn Mas'ud said the same as Umar, giving precedence to the Book, then the Sunnah, then consensus. Likewise Ibn Abbas used to give fatwa according to what is in the Book, then what is in the Sunnah, then the Sunnah of Abu Bakr and Umar, based on his saying: "Follow the two after me: Abu Bakr and Umar."

These reports are established from Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, and they were among the most renowned Companions for issuing fatwas and judging. This is the correct position.

However, a group of later scholars said: the mujtahid (qualified jurist who derives rulings) begins by examining consensus first. If he finds it, he does not turn to anything else. If he finds a text that contradicts it, he believes that the text has been abrogated (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) by a text he has not reached. Some of them said: consensus abrogates it.

The correct position is the way of the early generations (salaf). This is because, if a text contradicts a consensus, there must necessarily be with the consensus a known text indicating that the other text has been abrogated. As for the situation in which the firm (muhkam) text has been lost by the community while it preserved the abrogated text, this never occurs at all. It would amount to attributing to the community the preservation of what it was forbidden to follow and the loss of what it was commanded to follow, and the community is protected from that.

Knowledge of consensus can be very difficult or, most of the time, impossible. For who can encompass the opinions of all the mujtahids? By contrast, knowledge of the texts is possible and accessible. The Companions used to judge by the Book first, because the Sunnah does not abrogate the Book. So there is nothing in the Qur'an abrogated by the Sunnah. Rather, if there is something abrogated in it, its abrogating text is in the Qur'an, and nothing other than the Qur'an is placed before it. Then, if he does not find that, he seeks it in the Sunnah. There is nothing abrogated in the Sunnah except that the Sunnah itself abrogated it; neither consensus nor anything else abrogates the Sunnah, and the Sunnah is not opposed by consensus, and most wordings of the reports are like this. If he does not find it, the seeker may not find what he seeks in the Sunnah even though it is there, and likewise in the Qur'an. So it is permissible for him, if he does not find it in the Qur'an, to seek it in the Sunnah. When the ruling is in the Sunnah, what is in the Sunnah does not conflict with what is in the Qur'an. Likewise, a sound consensus does not conflict with either the Book or the Sunnah. End of his words, may Allah sanctify his soul.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly gone far astray.﴾ [116]

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills.﴾ This noble verse has already been discussed at length at the beginning of this surah. They said: its repetition is either for emphasis and reinforcement, or to complete the story of Ṭu'mah, and his death as a disbeliever has already been mentioned.

Or: it has another occasion of revelation, as narrated by al-Tha'labi, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "An old man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'I am an old man immersed in sins, but I have not associated anything with Allah since I came to know Him and believed in Him, I have not taken any protector besides Him, I have not committed sins out of audacity, and I never imagined for the blink of an eye that I could escape Allah by flight. Indeed, I am regretful and repentant. So what is my state with Allah, glorified and exalted is He?' Then this was revealed."

Some scholars preferred the last opinion, saying: because emphasis, despite the remoteness of its context, does not require the specification of this particular place, so there must be a specifier.

Al-Mahayimi went further, considering it to point to both halves of the noble verse, saying: "Then he indicated that the threat for opposing the Messenger is definite, without contradicting the consensus (ijma'), because opposing the Messenger is evidence of denying him, and this entails associating partners with Allah, since the creation of miracles can only be by one of perfect power, and only by a god. So when one denies them of Allah, he has attributed a partner to Him, and Allah does not forgive that He be associated with. As for opposing the consensus, it may be forgiven, since He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills, as it does not reach the level of association." All these occasions clearly indicate, without any doubt, the implication of this verse, that everything other than association is definitely forgiven, whether repentance has occurred or not.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more beloved to me than this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with…﴾ to ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah has certainly gone far astray.﴾" That is: far from the truth, for association (shirk) is the greatest kind of misguidance and the furthest from correctness and uprightness. In the first verse the phrase ﴿has certainly fabricated﴾ [al-Nisa': 48] was mentioned because it is connected to the story of the People of the Book, and the source of their association was a kind of fabrication, namely their claim of adoption against Allah, by their saying: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18]. Said by al-Qadi.

In (al-Samin): the preceding verse was concluded with His words ﴿has certainly fabricated﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], and this one with His words ﴿has certainly gone astray﴾, because the former concerns the People of the Book, who had knowledge of the validity of his prophethood and that his law abrogates all previous laws, yet despite that they were arrogant about it and fabricated against Allah; while this one concerns a people who were polytheists, who had no scripture and no knowledge, so it was fitting to describe them with misguidance. Also, mention of guidance, which is the opposite of misguidance, has already occurred here. End.

The discussion on the interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:

﴿They call upon, besides Him, none but females; and they call upon none but a rebellious devil.﴾ [117]

﴿They call upon, besides Him﴾ means what the idolaters of Makkah and those like them worship besides God. ﴿None but females﴾ Al-Razi said: "(yad'un) here means (ya'buduna, they worship), because whoever worships something calls upon it when he is in need of it." End of quote.

Al-Imam Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, the authors of the Sunan collections and others narrated on the authority of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir (p-1565) that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is worship." It was also narrated by Abu Ya'la on the authority of al-Bara', and al-Tirmidhi narrated it on the authority of Anas with the wording: "Supplication is the marrow of worship."

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿none but females﴾, there are several views:

The first: what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of A'ishah, who said: "It means idols." Accordingly, the naming of them as females refers to the fact that most of their names were feminine, such as Manat, al-'Uzza, al-Lat and the like. Also, they used to dress them in various kinds of ornaments and adorn them in the forms of women.

It is narrated on the authority of Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, Abu Malik, al-Suddi and Muqatil something similar to what is attributed to A'ishah.

The second view: that it refers to the angels, because some of them worshipped the angels and said of them: "The daughters of God."

Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of al-Dahhak regarding the verse: The idolaters said of the angels, "The daughters of God," and "We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness." He said: "They took them as lords, and fashioned them as young maidens, so they imitated and copied, and said: 'These resemble the daughters of God whom we worship,' meaning the angels."

Ibn Kathir said: "This interpretation is similar to God's saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [An-Najm: 19] [An-Najm: 27] and the verses (that follow), and His saying: ﴿They have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 19] [Az-Zukhruf: 19]... the verse, and He said: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [As-Saffat: 158] [As-Saffat: 137]." End of quote.

And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the name of females﴾ [An-Najm: 27]

(p-1566) The third view: what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding the verse, who said: "With every idol there is a female jinn."

The fourth: 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah and al-Dahhak narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: ﴿females﴾ means dead things. Al-Hasan said: "The females are everything dead which has no spirit in it, whether it is a dry piece of wood or a dry stone." Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir.

In the (Dictionary) al-Qamus and its commentary: "Al-inath is the plural of unthá, which is the opposite of the male of everything. Al-mawat, which is the opposite of living beings, such as trees, stones and wood, [is named so] according to al-Lihyani. According to al-Farra': The Arabs say: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and similar feminine deities." End of quote.

The Imam Abu al-Baqa' said: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿females﴾ is the plural of unthá, on the pattern of (fi'al), and by it is meant everything that has no spirit, such as a rock, the sun and the like.

It is read as (unthá) in the singular, and the singular indicates the plural.

It is read as (unuthan), like rusul (messengers). It may be an adjective in the singular, like "imra'atun junub" (a woman in a state of major ritual impurity), and it may be a plural of anith, like qalib and qulub; and they have said "hadid anith" (a female-like iron) with this meaning.

It is read as (uthunan), and the singular is wathan, which is an idol, and its original form is wathan; in the plural as in the singular, except that the waw was changed into a hamzah when it took a permanent damma, and it is like (asad and usud, lion and lions). It is read with the waw according to the original form in the plural, and it is read with a sukun on the tha' along with the hamzah and the waw. End of quote.

Al-Baydawi said: "Perhaps He, may He be exalted, mentioned them by this name to draw attention to the fact that they worship what they call females, because it is acted upon and does not act, whereas it is due to the one worshipped that he be an agent, not one acted upon, so that this would be a proof of the extreme of their ignorance and the excess of their foolishness."

﴿And they call upon﴾ meaning: what they worship besides God, ﴿none but a rebellious devil﴾, and he is Iblis, may God curse him, due to their obedience to him in their worship of them. When they obey him in what he embellished for them, they have worshipped him, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60] [Ya-Sin: 60] And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them﴾ [Saba': 41] [Saba': 41]. Al-marid is the one who is rebellious, obstinate and tyrannical.

(p-1567) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Allah cursed him, and he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion."﴾ [118]

﴿Allah cursed him﴾ is a second attribute of "a devil" (shaytanan), meaning: Allah removed him far from His mercy, so he wished to remove from the path those who were led astray because of him. ﴿And he said﴾ when he was removed: ﴿"I will surely take from among Your servants"﴾, that is, those for whose sake You removed me, meaning: "I will surely make for myself from among them" ﴿a portion﴾, that is, a share, ﴿appointed﴾, that is, cut off and determined, from their worship, by making them worship other than You, or by making them show off in it, or by making them vain of it, or by squandering it in wrongdoings, or by nullifying it through disbelief after it.

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And he said﴾ etc., is a conjunction upon the preceding sentence: that is, a rebellious devil combining the curse of Allah with this abominable statement issued by him at the time of being cursed.

He established, by way of reasoning, that the worship of idols is the utmost of misguidance, on the ground that those whom they worship are acted upon and do not act with a voluntary act, and this is utterly incompatible with divinity. Then he argued for it by showing that such worship is worship of Satan, which is the most heinous misguidance in three respects:

The first: that he is immersed in error and hardly clings to anything of goodness or guidance, so obeying him is a far-off misguidance from the truth.

The second: that he is cursed for his misguidance, so submitting to him produces nothing but curse and misguidance.

The third: that he is in the utmost pursuit of destroying them and leading them astray, so allying oneself with one of such a nature is the utmost misguidance, let alone worshipping him.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 119:**

[p. 1568] On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿And I will surely mislead them, and I will surely arouse in them false desires, and I will surely command them, so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will surely command them, so they will alter the creation of Allah.² And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss.﴾ [119]

﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾, i.e., away from guidance. ﴿And I will surely arouse in them false desires﴾, i.e., the vain wishes that come from long life and the attainment of hopes. Al-Razi said: When Satan claimed that he would mislead creatures, he said: ﴿And I will surely arouse in them false desires.﴾ [p. 1568] This indicates that he has no stronger means of misleading than the desires in the hearts of creatures and the pursuit of what produces two things: greed (al-hirs) and hope (al-amal). Greed and hope necessitate most of the blameworthy traits, and they are like two matters inseparable from the essence of the human being. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The son of Adam grows old, and two things grow young with him: greed and hope."

Greed necessitates undertaking the dangers of this world and the dangers of religion, for when a person's greed for a thing becomes intense, he may be unable to obtain it except by disobeying Allah and harming people. When his hope lengthens, he forgets the Hereafter and becomes drowned in this world. He then hardly moves toward repentance, and admonition hardly affects him, so his heart becomes like stones or even harder in hardness.

﴿And I will surely command them﴾, i.e., contrary to Your command, leading them astray. ﴿So they will slit the ears of cattle﴾, i.e., they will cut and split them as a mark and sign for the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released, forbidden to be used) and the sa'iba (a freed animal), so that they would forbid them after You had made them lawful.

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Here, al-tabtik (slitting) is cutting the ears of the bahira, by the consensus of the exegetes. This was because they used to slit the ear of a she-camel when she had given birth to five litters and the fifth was a male; then she was released. They forbade themselves to benefit from her, so they left her back free from riding, carrying loads, and slaughter, and did not turn her away from water or pasture. If an exhausted, stranded traveler met her, he would not ride her. Iblis made it seem to them that this was an act of devotion, and this was the bahira.

Ibn Sayyidah said: "Bahara the she-camel or the sheep (yabharuhā)" means he split its ear into two halves, and it was shortened in length by two halves.

﴿And I will surely command them, so they will alter the creation of Allah﴾, i.e., the religion of Allah, exalted and majestic is He. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from Ibn Abbas and many others. This is like His words: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30], according to the view of those who take that as a command, meaning: do not change the natural disposition of Allah, and leave people upon their natural disposition. [p. 1569]

As is established in the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitra (natural disposition). Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you find any mutilation in it?"

In Sahih Muslim, from Iyad ibn Himar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Allah, exalted and majestic, said: "I created My servants as hanifs (upright in monotheism), but the devils came to them and led them away from their religion, and forbade them what I had made lawful for them."

[p. 1570] Imam Ahmad and the two Shaykhs narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I saw Amr ibn Amir al-Khuza'i dragging his intestines in the Fire. He was the first to release the sawa'ib and to split the ear of the bahira."

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The first to change the religion of Ibrahim was Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'a ibn Khindif, the father of Khuza'a."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas that he meant by the verse the castration of animals. Anas said: From it is khisa' (castration).

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade ikhsa' (castration).

Imam Ahmad also narrated it from him with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the castration of horses and beasts."

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that any of the children of Adam be castrated."

[p. 1571] Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade sabr al-ruh (torturing a living creature by confinement or mutilation) and the castration of animals."

Al-Hasan said: By the verse is meant al-washm (tattooing, with the letter shin dotted, i.e., with a shin). Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayra: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade tattooing (al-washm)."

In the Sahih, from Ibn Mas'ud: "Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their eyebrows and those who have them plucked, and those who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah, exalted and majestic." Then he said: "Shall I not curse whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah, exalted and majestic?" meaning His words: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7].

Al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: The verse is thus used as evidence for the prohibition of castration, tattooing, and what is similar to them, such as attaching hair extensions, al-tafalluj (filing or separating the teeth), and al-tanmis (plucking hair from the face). End of quotation.

[p. 1572] Some of the Zaydis said: What is done to the cheek for adornment, such as beauty marks (al-shurat), is added to tattooing (al-washr).

Al-Zajjaj related from some of them regarding the meaning of the verse: Allah, exalted is He, created the cattle to be ridden and eaten, but they forbade them to themselves, like the bahira, the sa'iba, and the wasila. He created the sun, the moon, and the stars subjected to people, from which they benefit, but the polytheists worshipped them, thereby altering the creation of Allah. It is not hidden that the generality of the verse applies to all these meanings, since all of them are alterations of the creation of Allah, so there is no barrier to interpreting the verse accordingly.

Al-Baydawi said: His words ﴿so they will alter the creation of Allah﴾ mean: from its face and form, or its attribute. This includes what has been said about: gouging out the eye of a falcon, castrating slaves, tattooing and al-washr, sodomy, lesbianism, and the like; worshipping the sun and the moon; altering the natural disposition of Allah, exalted is He, which is Islam; and using the limbs and faculties for what does not return to the self as perfection, and does not bring it nearness to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. End of quotation.

These sentences attributed to the accursed one are things his tongue uttered, whether by speech or by state. All the lam-particles in them are for oath, and the object of the command in both places is omitted, relying on the context of the wording to indicate it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, warned against following him, saying: ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of Allah﴾ by preferring what he calls to, exceeding the guardianship of Allah by abandoning what He calls to, ﴿has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾, i.e., evident, clear in its outcome: the entry into the everlasting Fire for him.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

﴿He promises them and arouses their desires, but Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾ [120]

﴿He promises them﴾ that they will be the triumphant ones. ﴿And arouses their desires﴾, that is, with what they will never attain. ﴿But Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾, meaning falsehood and misguidance, and the creation of the illusion of benefit from that which holds nothing but harm.

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted:

﴿Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape.﴾ [121]

﴿Those﴾, i.e., the allies of Satan, ﴿their refuge﴾, their destination and their final end on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape﴾, meaning no place to turn aside to and no place of flight.

The discussion on the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the explanation of meaning) of the words of Allah, the Exalted:

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ [122]

﴿Those who believe﴾, i.e., whose hearts affirm the truth. ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, i.e., whose limbs act upon the good they were commanded to do. ﴿We will admit them into gardens beneath which﴾, i.e., beneath their chambers and dwellings, ﴿rivers flow﴾: rivers of wine, water, milk and honey. ﴿Abiding therein﴾, remaining in the Garden, they will neither die nor be removed from it, ﴿forever. The promise of Allah is true﴾, a truth that will certainly come to pass. And how could the promise of Allah not be true, ﴿and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ in promise and in good tidings. This is a question carrying the sense of negation, meaning: no one is more truthful in speech than Him. There is no god but Him; there is no lord besides Him.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say in his sermon: "Indeed, the most truthful speech is the Book of Allah, the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad (ﷺ), the worst of matters are their innovations, every innovation is a heresy, and every heresy leads to the Fire."

The purpose of the verse is to set against the false satanic promises made to his companions the true promise of Allah to His friends, and to emphasize its affirmation, as an encouragement for the servants to attain it. The word *qil* (القيل) is a verbal noun (*masdar*), like *qal* (القال) and *qawl* (القول).

**The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will find for himself, besides Allah, no protector nor helper.﴾ [123]

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking﴾, that is: the matter does not follow your desires and wishes, O polytheists, that the idols will benefit you. ﴿Nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾, nor does it follow the desires of the Jews and the Christians, when they said: (p. 1574) ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18] [al-Ma'idah: 18] ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days, numbered﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80] [al-Baqarah: 80].

﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾, that is: from among the polytheists and the People of the Book. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿and he will find for himself, besides Allah, no protector nor helper﴾. This is a warning (wa'id) to the disbelievers, because after it He said:

**The discourse on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged even by the size of a naqir.﴾ [124]

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya). The first *min* in *min al-salihat* is superfluous according to al-Akhfash, and a qualifier according to Sibawayh, meaning: "some of the righteous deeds." ﴿Those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged even by the size of a naqir﴾ means that not even the measure of a naqir will be taken from their good deeds. The naqir is the small pit on the back of a date stone. This is a way of emphasizing the negation of injustice, and a promise that the reward of their deeds will be paid in full without any reduction. The pronoun in *wa la yuzlamun* refers to both the doers of evil and the doers of good together, and it is permissible that mention of it with one group implies its mention with the other.

As for His words, ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123], and His words, ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾, after the mention of the wishful thinking of the People of the Book, are like His words, glorified is He: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81] [al-Baqarah: 81], and His words: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 82], following His words: ﴿And they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80].

* *

(p-1575) Note:

What we have previously put forward, that the address in His words ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾ [al-Nisa': 123] is to the polytheists, and that His words ﴿Whoever does evil﴾ [al-Nisa': 123] refer to the People of the Book and the polytheists, is what the context of the verse and its noble arrangement indicate, as we have explained.

al-Tabari narrated from Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Hasan, and the first two said, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The evil (al-su') here is polytheism." al-Hasan said: "﴿Whoever does evil﴾ [al-Nisa': 123] is the disbeliever," then he recited: ﴿And do We recompense except the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba': 17].

Since the generality of this address carries an awesome force, and what an awesome force, many of the Companions were fearful because of it.

Ibn Kathir said: It has been reported that when this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily upon many of the Companions.

Imam Ahmad said: Abdullah ibn Numayr narrated to us, Isma'il narrated to us, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Zuhayr, who said: I was informed that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the prospect of success after this verse: ﴿Not by your wishful thinking, nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]? For every evil we do, we are recompensed for it?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah forgive you, O Abu Bakr. Do you not fall ill? Do you not become weary? Do you not grieve? Do you not suffer hardship?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is what you are recompensed for."

And from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123] was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: 'Be upright and moderate, for in everything that afflicts a Muslim there is an expiation, even the thorn that pricks him and the stumble that makes him fall.'" Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur, (p-1576) Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i.

And Ata' ibn Yasar said, from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra, that they both heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "No fatigue, illness, sickness, or sorrow befalls a Muslim, not even the worry that troubles him, except that Allah expiates his sins for it." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

And Ibn Mardawayh narrated, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾.' He said: 'Yes, and whoever does a good deed will be recompensed for it tenfold.' So he is ruined whose single evil deed outweighs his good deeds."

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf (one who turns away from falsehood toward truth), and God took Abraham as a khalīl (intimate friend)?﴾ [125]

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾: that is, he sincerely devotes himself to Him, Exalted is He, so he does not take any lord other than Him. ﴿while being a doer of good﴾: that is, he brings good deeds and abstains from evil deeds; or, he performs righteous deeds in the proper manner, which is their descriptive excellence (ḥusn al-waṣfī), which entails their intrinsic excellence (ḥusn al-dhātī). The Prophet (ﷺ) explained ihsān (excellence) with his saying: "It is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, [know that] He sees you."

﴿and follows the religion of Abraham﴾: the one agreed upon as correct and accepted, which is in accord with the religion of Islam. ﴿a ḥanīf﴾: that is, inclining away from polytheism deliberately, meaning abandoning it with insight, and turning wholly toward the truth, with no one turning him away from it and no one repelling him from it.

Al-Razi said: Know that when He, Exalted is He, made the attainment of salvation and the winning of Paradise conditional upon a person being a believer, He explained faith and showed its excellence in two respects:

The first: that it is the religion which includes displaying complete servitude, humility and submission to God, Exalted is He.

The second: that it is the religion upon which Abraham (peace be upon him) was. Each of these two aspects is an independent reason for encouraging the religion of Islam.

As for the first aspect: know that the religion of Islam is founded upon two matters: belief and action.

As for belief: it is indicated by His saying: ﴿submits his face to God﴾. This is because submission is surrender and humility, and the face is the most excellent of a person's limbs. So when a person knows his Lord with his heart, and acknowledges His lordship and his own servitude, he has submitted his face to God.

As for action: it is indicated by His saying: ﴿while being a doer of good﴾, and it includes performing good deeds and abstaining from evil deeds. So reflect on this concise expression and how it encompasses all aims and purposes.

Also, His saying ﴿submits his face to God﴾ implies restriction (ḥaṣr), its meaning being that he submitted himself to God and did not submit to other than God. This is an alert that the perfection of faith is not attained except by entrusting all affairs to the Creator and manifesting disavowal of power and might. Also, it contains an alert against the corruption of the method of one who seeks help from other than God, for the polytheists used to seek help from idols and say: "These are our intercessors with God." The Dahriyya (materialists who deny a Creator) and the naturalists seek help from the spheres, the stars, the natures and others.

The Jews used to say, to ward off the punishment of the Hereafter from themselves: "We are the descendants of the prophets." The Christians used to say: "Third of three." So all the sects sought help from other than God.

As for the second aspect in explaining the excellence of Islam: Muhammad (ﷺ) only called people to the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him). It is well known among all people that Abraham called only to God, Exalted is He, as he said: ﴿And indeed I am free from what you associate﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. He did not call to the worship of a sphere, nor to obedience to a star, nor to prostration to an idol, nor to seeking help from nature. Rather, his habit was calling to God and turning away from everything other than God. Likewise is the call of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Furthermore, the law of Abraham is accepted by all. This is because the Arabs take no pride in anything as they take pride in their affiliation to Abraham, and as for the Jews and Christians, there is no doubt that they take pride in him too. If this is established, it follows that the law of Muhammad is accepted by all.

﴿And God took Abraham as a khalīl﴾: that is, a chosen one whose love for Him is pure. The mention of Abraham (peace be upon him) by name in a place where a pronoun would be expected serves to magnify his status and to make explicit that he is the one being praised. The secret of this sentence is to encourage following his religion, upon whom be blessings and peace. For one who has reached such a degree of nearness to God, Exalted is He, as to justify calling him khalīl, is worthy that following his path be the most important thing toward which the necks of resolutions stretch, and the most noble thing toward which the eyes of nations gaze. The rank of khullah (intimate friendship) is the highest station of love, and this is only because of the abundance of his obedience to his Lord, as He described him in His saying: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾ [al-Najm: 37].

Many of the scholars of the early generations said: that is, he carried out everything he was commanded, and in every station of worship, so no great matter occupied him from a trivial one, nor a major one from a minor one. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], to the end of the verse. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to God, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [al-Nahl: 120], to the end of the verse.

Linguistically, khalīl means the close friend who is specially chosen. Ibn al-A'rabi said: the khalīl is the sincere one.

Al-Zajjaj said: He is the lover in whose love there is no defect, and with this he explained the verse, meaning: He loved him with a perfect love with no defect in it.

Ibn Durayd said: the khalīl is of the purest and most sound affection. He said: "I will not add anything to it, because it is in the Qur'an." End.

Al-Razi said: They mentioned several views on the derivation of khalīl:

Among them: the khalīl of a person is the one who enters into the depths of his affairs and secrets, and whose love has penetrated into the interior of his heart. There is no doubt that this is the utmost in love. It was said: When God revealed to Abraham (peace be upon him) the highest and lowest kingdoms, and he called the people time after time to the oneness of God, and prevented them from worshipping the star, the moon and the sun, and prevented them from worshipping idols; then he was thrown into the fires, his son was offered for sacrifice, and his wealth was given to guests, God made him an imam for creation and a messenger to them, and gave him the good news that kingship and prophethood would be among his descendants. Because of these distinctions He named him khalīl, since God's love for His servant is an expression of His will to bring good things and benefits to him. End.

[The phrase "since God's love for His servant ... etc." is a theological rather than a Salafi line of reasoning.]

Then al-Razi said: In my view there is another aspect, which is that when the essence of the soul is luminous, radiant, and lofty, little attached to corporeal being and bodily states, and then to such a noble, sacred essence are added deeds that increase its polish from bodily turbidities, and thoughts that increase its illumination with sacred knowledge and divine manifestations, such a person becomes absorbed in the world of holiness and purity, disengaged from the ties of body and sense. Then this person continues to increase in these noble states until he becomes such that he sees nothing but God, hears nothing but God, moves only by God, rests only by God, and walks only by God. It is as if the light of God's majesty has permeated all his bodily faculties, pervaded them, plunged into their substances, and penetrated their realities. Such a person is truly described as khalīl, because God's love has permeated all his faculties. To this the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his supplication alludes: "O God, place light in my heart, light in my hearing, light in my sight, and light in my nerves." End.

The eminent imam Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim said in his book "al-Jawab al-Kafi": Khullah entails the perfection and ultimate limit of love, such that no room remains in the heart for other than the beloved. It is a station that admits no sharing in any way. This station is specific to the two khalīls, God's blessings and peace be upon them both: Abraham and Muhammad, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God took me as a khalīl just as He took Abraham as a khalīl."

In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "If I were to take a khalīl from among the people of the earth, I would have taken Abu Bakr as a khalīl, but your companion is the khalīl of God."

In another hadith: "I disavow before God any khalīl of his khullah."

When Abraham (peace be upon him) asked for a child, and he was given one, his love became attached to his heart, so he took a portion of it. The Beloved (God) became jealous of His khalīl that there should be in his heart a place for another. So he was commanded to sacrifice him, and the command was given in a dream so that carrying out the command would be a greater trial and test. The aim was not the slaughter of the son, but the slaughter of him from his heart, so that the heart might be purified for the Lord. When the khalīl hastened to comply and preferred the love of God over the love of his son, the aim was achieved: the slaughter was lifted, and he was ransomed with a great sacrifice. Indeed the Lord, Exalted is He, did not command something and then nullify it entirely; rather, He must leave some part of it or a substitute for it, just as He left the law of ransom, just as He left the recommendation of charity before private consultation, and just as He left the five prayers after the fifty were lifted, retaining their reward. He said: ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾ [Qaf: 29]. They are five in action and fifty in reward.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim, may his secret be sanctified, said: As for what some of the suppositious think, that love is more perfect than khullah, and that Abraham is the khalīl of God while Muhammad (ﷺ) is the beloved (ḥabīb) of God, this stems from their ignorance. Love is general and khullah is specific, and khullah is the ultimate limit of love. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that God took Abraham as a khalīl and denied that He has any khalīl other than his Lord, while also informing us of his love for ʿĀʾishah, her father, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and others.

Also, God, Glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, God loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222]; and: ﴿God loves the steadfast﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 146]; and: ﴿God loves the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]; ﴿God loves the righteous﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 76]; and: ﴿God loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8]. Khullah is specific to the two khalīls, upon them be prayer and peace. The young man who repents is a beloved of God. This view arises only from little knowledge and understanding of God and His Messenger (ﷺ). End.

Those who claimed that love is purer than khullah have relied on what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "Some of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were sitting waiting for him. He came out until he approached them, and he heard them discussing. Some of them were saying: 'How strange! God took a khalīl from among His creation: Abraham is His khalīl.' Another said: 'What is more remarkable than that Moses was spoken to directly.' Another said: 'Jesus is the Spirit of God and His Word.' Another said: 'Adam was chosen by God.'

He came out to them, greeted them, and said: 'I have heard your words and your wonder. Indeed Abraham is the khalīl of God, and he is so. Moses is His interlocutor, Jesus is His Spirit and His Word, and Adam was chosen by God, and he is so. Likewise Muhammad (ﷺ) said: Beware, I am the beloved (ḥabīb) of God, and there is no boasting in that. I am the first intercessor and the first whose intercession is accepted, and there is no boasting in that. I am the first who will move the ring of Paradise, and God will open it for me and admit me into it, along with the poor among the believers, and there is no boasting in that. I am the most honoured of the first and the last on the Day of Resurrection, and there is no boasting in that.'"
