It is also possible that the helpers took a bribe from him and released him, and took another in his place, just as Yahudha, despite being his friend and messenger, took a bribe and pointed them to him. It is also possible that God, exalted, sent a devil in his likeness, and they crucified him. It is also possible that the angel who descended upon him to strengthen him, as was mentioned in the Gospel of Luke according to their claim, became a ransom for him. It is also possible that this one who descended only descended to raise him up, for if he had descended to strengthen him, he would have strengthened him. Since we do not see that he strengthened him, this requires that he raised him up to heaven, or that he ransomed himself for him.

Some of the learned said: Among the evidences for his raising and the crucifixion of a likeness is what is in the ninth chapter of the Gospel of Luke, the wording of which is: "The Messiah went up a mountain to pray, and took Butrus, Yuhanna and Ya'qub with him. While he was praying, his appearance and face changed, and his garment became bright and shining..." etc.

So this contains an indication of his raising and of the occurrence of the likeness that we speak of, since there is no meaning to the appearance of Musa and Ilya', the falling of sleep upon his companions, the change of his face and the brightening of his garment, except his raising up... And their seeing him after that is only from the transformation of his spirit, because he, peace be upon him, had the power of transformation, and this is among the rulings of the spirit and the soul.

And even if we say that this does not indicate raising in the complete sense, we still concede and say: since on this occasion his appearance, face and garment changed, and he gathered with the prophets and heard this voice from the cloud, then this is at least a preface to his raising, a measure and a beginning for his strengthening and consolation. The Jews did not verify for themselves that he was the Messiah. Rather they relied on the statement of Yahudha, as was mentioned to you. Yahudha's statement is a single report, and unfit for argument, because of the possibilities and evidences we mentioned to you. So there remains in the statements of the two sects no proof that the one crucified was the Messiah, peace be upon him, and not his likeness. The state of their Gospels is known to you, and the explanation of their confusion as narrated to you in the Qur'an is not hidden from you. End of quotation.

Here is a question that some Christians raise: If Jesus, peace be upon him, was not truly crucified, but a man upon whom his likeness was cast was crucified, and he himself was raised to heaven, then why did he not inform the disciples of that, either before his raising or after it?

The answer: Jesus, peace be upon him, did not inform them of that because he knew that people would fabricate lies about him and claim his divinity. So the matter was left ambiguous, so that this would more clearly indicate that he was a servant of God's servants, who cannot bring benefit or repel harm. This is unlike what would have happened had he said that he would not be crucified, or was not crucified, and that the one crucified was his likeness, for that might have strengthened the doubts of that group. Also, this matter was not originally one of the matters of belief. For if anyone believed, before the sending of our Prophet, peace be upon him, in the crucifixion of Jesus, it would not have harmed him. But when our Prophet, who does not speak from desire, came, he clarified the error of the Christians in two respects:

One of them: believing that Jesus is God.

The other: believing that he was killed and crucified.

And he clarified that he is a servant of God, exalted, whom God entrusted with the message and chose, and protected and guarded from the hands of his enemies. Thus it is in *Muniyat al-Adhkiya fi Qasas al-Anbiya'* (The Wish of the Intelligent in the Stories of the Prophets).

[[The author's words were abridged due to their great length.]]

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the disgraceful conduct of the Jews and the ugliness of their deeds, and explained that they intended to kill Jesus, peace be upon him, and showed that they did not achieve that aim, while Jesus attained the greatest rank and the most exalted station, He then clarified the confirmation of what He had established in the previous verse, namely the certainty of their lying. He affirmed that, in their extreme enmity toward him, they would become among his followers who believe in all of his command, of which is belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), emphasizing this with the strongest emphasis in response to their denial of him, by His saying:

(p-١٧١١) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.﴾ [159]

﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death.﴾ That is: none of the People of the Scripture will live to see the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, at the end of time, except that he will surely believe in him before his death, meaning the death of Jesus, peace be upon him. That is: he will not die until he descends at the end of time, by whom Allah strengthens the religion of Islam, so that all the people of the religions enter into it. This is an indication that Moses, peace be upon him, although Allah, exalted is He, supported him with prophets who renewed his religion for a long period, the prophet who abrogates the law of Moses, who is Jesus, peace be upon them both, is the one by whom Allah strengthens this Arab Prophet in renewing his law, preparing his affair, and defending his religion. He will be from his community after having been a bearer of an independent law, and of followers in great number. This is a matter that Allah, exalted is He, decreed from eternity, so refrain, O Jews.

The meaning of the verse, then, and Allah knows best, is: there is none among the People of the Scripture who differ concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, who is in doubt, except that he will be certain of Jesus, peace be upon him, before his death, after his descent from the heaven, that he was neither killed nor crucified, and he will believe in him when the doubt is removed. This was stated by al-Biqa'i.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, the son of Mary will surely soon descend among you as a just judge, and he will break the cross, kill the pig, abolish the jizyah (poll tax), and wealth will overflow until no one accepts it, until a single prostration will be better for him than the world and whatever is in it." Then Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.﴾"

(p-١٧١٢) Muslim also narrated it, and Ibn Mardawayh, and he added after his saying "before his death": "the death of Jesus, son of Mary." Then Abu Hurayrah repeated it three times.

Imam Ahmad also narrated it, from Hanzalah, from Abu Hurayrah, also as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report, and its wording is: "Jesus, son of Mary, will descend, and he will kill the pig and erase the cross, prayer will be gathered for him, wealth will be given until it is not accepted, and he will abolish the kharaj (land tax), and he will descend at al-Rawha', and perform Hajj from there, or 'Umrah, or both."

He said: Abu Hurayrah recited: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.﴾ Hanzalah claimed that Abu Hurayrah said: "He will believe in him before the death of Jesus." I do not know whether all of this is the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) or something Abu Hurayrah said.

Ahmad also narrated it, from 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayrah, and in it: "Allah will destroy in his time all the religions except Islam, and he will remain forty years, then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him."

(p-١٧١٣) In the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an in Muslim: "He will descend at the minaret east of Damascus."

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir has mentioned here the mutawatir (widely transmitted) hadiths concerning his descent, peace be upon him, from the narrations of Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, Abu Umamah, al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, Mujammi' ibn Jariyah, and Abu Sarihah Hudhayfah ibn Usayd, may Allah be pleased with them all. In them is evidence of the manner of his descent and his place, that it is in al-Sham, indeed in Damascus, at the eastern minaret, and that this will occur at the time of the dawn prayer.

Ibn Kathir said: In these times, in the year 741 AH, a minaret was built for the Umayyad Mosque, white, of carved stone, in place of the minaret that was destroyed by the fire attributed to the handiwork of the Christians, may the continuous curses of Allah be upon them until the Day of Resurrection. Most of its construction was from their wealth, and the assumptions strengthened that it is the one upon which the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon them both, will descend, and this is a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning that. End of quote.

I say: This minaret has become well known as the "Minaret of Jesus."

The Hafiz Abu al-Qasim ibn 'Asakir mentioned in his "Tarikh" from some of the early scholars (al-salaf) that Jesus, peace be upon him, after his descent will be buried with the Prophet (ﷺ) in his chamber. And Allah knows best.

The interpretation mentioned in the verse was narrated by Ibn Jarir from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-'Awfi, both from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-١٧١٤) Ibn Abi Hatim narrated with his chain, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: "It means the Jews specifically." And with his chain to al-Hasan: "It means al-Najashi (the Negus) and his companions."

And with his chain to him (al-Hasan), he said: "Indeed Allah raised Jesus to Himself, and He will send him back before the Day of Resurrection, to a station in which the righteous and the wicked will believe in him."

Likewise said Qatadah, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and others than one.

Ibn Kathir said: This view is the truth.

It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Muhammad ibn Sirin, al-Dahhak, and Juwaybir, that the meaning is: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in Jesus before the death of that Scripturist at the time of the death throes (al-gharghara), when faith will not benefit him, going on the view that when he sees (the reality), he knows the truth from falsehood; for everyone to whom death comes, his soul does not leave until the truth becomes clear to him from falsehood in his religion."

'Ikrimah said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "A Jew does not die until he testifies that Jesus is the servant of Allah and His Messenger, even if he is struck with a sword."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: What is the benefit of informing about their belief in Jesus before their death? I say: Its benefit is the warning, and that they may know that they must believe in him soon at the moment of witnessing it, and that this will not benefit them; it is an incitement for them and an alert to hastening belief in him at the time when it benefits, and to establish the proof against them. End of quote.

Al-Asbahani said: What indicates the soundness of this interpretation is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him: "(illa layu'minunna bihi qabla mawtihim)" (إلّا لَيُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِمْ), with a damma on the nun and the attachment of the plural mim, meaning "before their death" (in the plural, referring to the People of the Scripture).

The chains to Ibn 'Abbas in this interpretation are all sound, as Ibn Kathir said.

There is another view: that the first pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the second to the Scripturist. This was narrated by Ibn Jarir from 'Ikrimah, who said: "No Christian and no Jew dies until he believes in Muhammad (ﷺ)," and he recited the verse.

(p-١٧١٥) Ibn Jarir said: The most correct of these views is the first view, namely that none of the People of the Scripture will remain, after the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, except that he will believe in him before his death, that is, before the death of Jesus, peace be upon him.

Ibn Kathir said: There is no doubt that what Ibn Jarir said is the correct view, because it is the aim of the context of the verses in establishing the falsehood of what the Jews claimed of killing Jesus and crucifying him, and the acceptance of those ignorant Christians who accepted that from them. So Allah, exalted is He, informed that the matter was not so, but rather it was made to appear to them, so they killed the one resembling him, while they did not realize it. Then He raised him to Himself, and he is still alive, and he will descend before the Day of Resurrection, as the mutawatir hadiths indicate, and he will kill the Dajjal (the false messiah), break the cross, kill the pig, and abolish the jizyah (that is, he will not accept it from anyone of the religions; rather he will accept only Islam or the sword).

So this noble verse informs that all of the People of the Scripture will believe in him at that time, and not one of them will hold back from affirming him.

Then he said: As for the one who interprets this verse as meaning that every Scripturist does not die until he believes in Jesus or Muhammad, peace be upon them both, this is what actually occurs, for at his dying moment everyone sees clearly what he was ignorant of and believes in it, but that will not be a faith beneficial to him, when he has witnessed the angel, as Allah, exalted is He, said at the beginning of this surah: ﴿And repentance is not accepted from those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now."﴾ [An-Nisa': 18], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in Allah alone."﴾ [Ghafir: 84], and the verse.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them﴾, that is, Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿against them﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], that is, against the People of the Scripture: ﴿a witness﴾, that is, concerning their deeds, which he witnessed from them before his being raised to heaven, (p-١٧١٦) and after his descent to the earth.

Qatadah said: He will testify against them that he had conveyed the message to them from Allah, and that he acknowledged his servitude to Allah, mighty and majestic. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people..."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], up to His saying: ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118] [al-Ma'idah: 116].

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of Allah﴾ [160]

﴿So for wrongdoing﴾ means: because of a great wrongdoing. The tanwin here is for magnification (tafkhim), and it encompasses the detailed account of their breaking the covenant and what follows it, of things they made lawful after the Torah had made them unlawful.

﴿Of those who were Jews﴾ means: those who adopted Judaism (talabbasu bil-yahudiyyah). This also magnifies their wrongdoing, since it proceeded from them after they had claimed that they were people of the Torah and of returning to the truth.

﴿We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ Ibn Kathir said: this prohibition may be qadari (decreed), meaning that He, exalted is He, subjected them to distorting and altering in their Book the things that had been lawful for them, so they made them unlawful for themselves through excessive strictness and extremism. It may also be shar'i (legislated), meaning that He, exalted is He, prohibited for them in the Torah things that had been lawful for them before that, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: Bring the Torah and recite it﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 93]. That is: other than what Israel had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed, namely the flesh and milk of camels. Then He, exalted is He, prohibited many things in the Torah, as He said in Surat al-An'am: (p-1717) ﴿And to those who were Jews We made unlawful every animal with claws, and from cattle and sheep We made unlawful to them their fat, except what their backs or entrails carry, or what is mixed with bone. That We repaid them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful﴾ [al-An'am: 146]. That is: We only made that unlawful for them because of their transgression, their opposition to their messenger, and their disputing with him.

When He mentioned their wrongdoing, He mentioned a comprehensive part of its particulars in His words: ﴿and for their hindering from the way of Allah﴾, that is, the way that is neither clearer, easier, nor greater, ﴿many﴾, meaning many people, or many instances of hindering. They hindered people and hindered themselves from following the truth. This is a disposition characteristic of them, from ancient times until recent ones. For this reason they were enemies of the messengers, killed a multitude of the prophets, and disbelieved in Jesus and Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon them both.

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾ [161]

﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it﴾ i.e., in the Torah. ﴿And their consuming of people's wealth unjustly﴾ through bribery (rishwa) and all the other forbidden means.

﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them﴾ i.e., among the Jews who persisted in disbelief, not for those among them who repented and believed. ﴿A painful punishment﴾, a grievous torment that reaches into their hearts.

[p. 1718]

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you. And those who establish prayer, and those who give zakah, and those who believe in God and the Last Day, those We will give a great reward.﴾ [162]

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ means: those who are steadfast in knowledge and insightful in it, such as Abdullah ibn Salam.

Al-Razi said: "Those firm in knowledge (al-rasikhun) are those who are steadfast in it. In reality they are those who reason from evidence (al-mustadillun), because the muqallid (one who follows authority without independent verification) is such that if doubt is cast on him, he doubts. But the one who reasons from evidence never doubts at all. So those firm in knowledge are those who reason from evidence."

﴿And the believers﴾ means: among the unlettered who join them in firmness through companionship with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ of the Qur'an, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾ to the other prophets, because they have understood the perfections of what was revealed to you and that it confirms what was revealed before you, so belief in it too is necessary.

﴿And those who establish prayer﴾: Ibn Kathir said: "This is how it stands in the codices (masahif) of the Imams, and it is likewise in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b."

al-Zamakhshari said: The nominative of (al-rasikhun) is by way of the inchoative (mubtada', subject), and ﴿believe﴾ is its predicate (khabar). ﴿And those who establish prayer﴾ is in the accusative by way of praise (al-madh), to show the excellence of prayer. This is a broad topic, which Sibawayh has elucidated with examples and evidences. Nor should one heed what they claim, that its occurrence is a grammatical error (lahn) in the orthography of the codex. Some who have not studied the Book and do not know the methods of the Arabs may be drawn to this, and they are unaware of the variety of usages in the accusative of specification (al-nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas). They fail to realize that the foremost early ones, whose likeness is in the Torah and whose likeness is in the Gospel, were far too zealous in guarding Islam and in repelling attacks upon it to leave in the Book of God a gap for later generations to fill, or a tear for those who come after them to mend.

[p. 1719] It has also been said: it is in conjunction with ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning: they believe in the Book and in those who establish prayer, and these are the prophets.

In the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it reads (wal-muqimuna) with a waw, and this is the reading of Malik ibn Dinar, al-Jahdari, and Isa al-Thaqafi.

It is also permitted to take (al-muqimin) as conjoined to the pronoun in (minhum), or to the pronoun in (ilayka), since the Book was revealed to the Prophet and to his followers. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ [Yunus: 57]. So it is stated in the marginal notes of al-Shudhur.

By his words "were far too zealous", al-Zamakhshari alluded to a refutation of what is reported: that when Uthman, may God be pleased with him, had finished the codex, it was brought to him, and he said: "You have done well and beautifully. I see some lahn which the Arabs will correct with their tongues. Had the dictator been from Hudhayl and the scribe from Quraysh, this would not have been found in it."

al-Hafiz al-Sakhawi said: This report is weak, and its chain (isnad) has irregularity (idtirab) and disconnection (inqita'). For Uthman, may God be pleased with him, was made an imam for the people to follow. How then would he see a lahn in it and leave it for the Arabs to correct with their tongues? He wrote seven codices, and there is never any disagreement among them except in matters of the modes of recitation (wujuh al-qira'at). If he and those who directly oversaw the collection did not correct it, how could others correct it?

[p. 1720] Some people interpreted the lahn in his speech (on the assumption that it is authentic from him) as meaning symbolism and allusion, as in the verse:

*"A splendid speech, and at times you commit lahn; yet the best of speech is that which is lahn."*

[p. 1721] That is, what is meant by it is symbolism, by omitting some letters in the writing, as with the alif of (al-sabirin), which the reciters recognize when they see it; and likewise adding some letters. So it is stated in 'Inayat al-Radi.

﴿And those who give zakah﴾: its nominative is by conjunction to ﴿those firm in knowledge﴾, or to the pronoun in ﴿believe﴾, or it is a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being ﴿those, We will give them﴾. The aforementioned possibilities apply to ﴿those who establish prayer﴾ on the reading of the nominative.

﴿And those who believe in God and the Last Day﴾ means: those who affirm the oneness of God, exalted is He, and the resurrection after death, and reward and punishment. Belief in the prophets, the books, and what they confirm, namely following the laws, was mentioned first because it is the aim in this context, since this is to explain the state of the People of the Book and to guide them. They used to believe in some of these matters and abandon others, so He made clear to them what binds them and what is obligatory upon them.

﴿Those, We will give them a great reward﴾ means Paradise, because they combined true belief with righteous deeds.

**A subtle point:**

There are several grammatical analyses (i'rab) of the verse. The best of them is what Abu al-Su'ud adopted: that the clause ﴿those, We will give them﴾ etc. is the predicate of the subject which is ﴿those firm in knowledge﴾ and what is conjoined to it; and that the clause ﴿believe in what has been revealed﴾ etc. is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the believers," explaining the manner of their belief, or a parenthetical emphatic clause (i'tiraḍ) relating to what precedes it.

He said: This is more fitting to the correspondence of the two sides of the contrast (istidrak), since the first group were threatened with a painful punishment, and the latter were promised a great reward. It is as though it was said, after His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment﴾ [al-Nisa': 161]: "But the believers among them, We will give them a great reward."

As for what the majority inclined to, making His words, exalted is He, ﴿believe in what has been revealed﴾ etc., the predicate of the subject, it is sound in full, except that it does not address the correspondence of the two sides.

(p-1722)

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying:

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the al-Asbat (the tribes, the descendants of Jacob), and to Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ Know that when He, Exalted is He, related that the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to send down to them a Book from the heavens, and He, Exalted is He, mentioned after that that they do not ask for guidance but out of obstinacy and contentiousness, and He clarified kinds of their disgraceful conduct, He alluded to refuting their doubt. He argued against them that he (ﷺ) is not an innovation among the messengers, and his matter regarding revelation is like that of the other prophets whose prophethood they agree upon. A book was not sent down to each one of them in its entirety as was sent down to Moses. When this is not a condition of prophethood, it becomes clear that their request was pure obstinacy.

* *

Note:

It was said: He began with Noah because he was the first prophet on whose tongue Allah, Exalted is He, legislated the rulings, the lawful and the unlawful. In al-'Inayah (a commentary), it is said that He began with him as a warning to them, because he was the first prophet whose people were punished, not because he was the first lawgiver, as is wrongly assumed.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those before Noah were not given revelation in the manner in which it was given to our Prophet (ﷺ), not that they were not revealed to at all, as has been said. End of quote.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the al-Asbat,﴾ who are the sons of Jacob, peace be upon them.

﴿and Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms.﴾

**[p. 1723]** The discussion of the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His words, exalted is He:

﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ [164]

﴿And messengers We have related to you before﴾: that is, in the Meccan surahs.

﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾: that is, We did not name them for you in the Qur'an. Some careful scholars have counted the prophets and messengers of the Jews and Christians and found that their number does not exceed fifty.

Traditions have been related concerning their number, and their chains of transmission have been criticised. Among them is the hadith of Abu Dhar: "Indeed, the prophets are one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the messengers are three hundred and thirteen." Ibn Hibban authenticated it, but Ibn al-Jawzi disagreed, listed it in his *Mawdu'at* (fabricated traditions), and accused Ibrahim ibn Hashim of fabricating it. More than one scholar has spoken critically of it.

﴿And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech﴾: that is, He addressed him directly, without an intermediary. The emphasis of (*kallama*, "spoke") with the verbal noun (*masdar*), *taklimah*, indicates the reality of the speech. Moses, peace be upon him, heard the speech of Allah without doubt, because verbs used in a figurative sense (*majaz*) are not emphasised with verbal nouns. One does not say, "The wall wanted to fall, a wanting," and this is a refutation of those who say that Allah created speech in a locus, and Moses heard that speech.

Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call everything that reaches a person "speech," by whatever means it reaches him, but they do not affirm it with a verbal noun. When it is affirmed with a verbal noun, it is nothing but the true reality of speech. So His words, exalted is He, "(*taklimah*) [direct speech]," indicate that Moses truly heard the speech of Allah without an intermediary.

Some scholars said: Just as Allah, exalted is He, singled out Moses, peace be upon him, for speaking directly and honoured him with it, and this did not undermine the prophethood of other prophets, so too the revelation of the Torah to him all at once did not undermine the prophethood of those prophets to whom His Book was revealed in parts. So it is mentioned in *al-Lubab*.

* * *

**A note:**

It is fitting in this place to set out the creed of the noble predecessors (*salaf*) on the question of speech (*kalam*), for it is among the greatest matters of religion. Opinions on it have been bewildered among the people of desires, both earlier and later; views on it have been confused; great calamities have arisen because of it; it has stirred up trials, brought about afflictions, imprisoned imams, and brought distress upon peoples. Doctrines on it have branched out, and paths on it have diverged. Only the saying of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah*), who follow the traces of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his noble Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), has been established.

So we say: Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may the mercy of the Most Merciful and peace be upon him, said in his letter to the group of the gnostic ('Arif) 'Adi ibn Musafir, the following text:

**Chapter**

Among this is moderation in the Sunnah and following it as it came, without addition or deficiency, like the discussion of the Qur'an and all the attributes. The doctrine of the early generations of the Ummah and the People of the Sunnah is that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, sent down, uncreated; from Him it originated and to Him it returns. This is what more than one of the predecessors said.

It is related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who was one of the notable Successors, that he said: "I always heard people say that the Qur'an which Allah sent down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is this Qur'an which Muslims recite and write in their codices, and it is the speech of Allah, not the speech of anyone else, even if servants recite it and convey it with their movements and voices. For speech belongs to the one who first said it, not to the one who said it as a conveyor and transmitter." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection until he hears the speech of Allah﴾ (9:6). This Qur'an is in the codices, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ (85:21–22). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is a Qur'an that is honoured, in a Book that is guarded﴾ (56:77–78) and ﴿reciting pages that are purified, containing upright scriptures﴾ (98:2–3).

The Qur'an is the speech of Allah with its letters, its arrangement, and its meanings. All of that enters into the Qur'an and into the speech of Allah. The inflection (*i'rab*) of the letters is part of the completeness of the letters, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an and observes its inflection, for him is a reward of ten good deeds for every letter."

Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Memorising the inflection of the Qur'an is dearer to us than memorising some of its letters."

Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Affirming what has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah speaks with a voice and calls Adam, peace be upon him, with a voice," and similar hadiths, this is the position that the predecessors of the Ummah and the imams of the Sunnah held.

The imams of the Sunnah said: The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, the Exalted, uncreated, wherever it is recited and wherever it is written. So it is not said of the recitation of a servant of the Qur'an that it is created, because that would include the Qur'an that was sent down; nor is it said that it is uncreated, because that would include the actions of servants. None of the imams of the predecessors ever said that the voices of servants in reciting the Qur'an are eternal; rather, they denounced those who said, "The utterance of the servant with the Qur'an is created."

As for those who say that the ink is eternal, this is among the most ignorant of people and the furthest from the Sunnah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ (18:109). So He informed that the ink is that with which His words are written.

Likewise, whoever says, "The Qur'an is not in the codex; rather, in the codex there is only ink, paper, narration, and expression," is an innovator and misguided. Rather, the Qur'an that Allah sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) is what lies between the two covers, and speech in the codex, in the manner people know it, has a particular quality by which it is distinguished from all other things.

Likewise, whoever goes beyond the Sunnah and says that the words and voices of servants are eternal is an innovator and misguided, just as whoever says that Allah does not speak with a letter or a voice is misguided too, for he is also an innovator who rejects the Sunnah. Likewise, whoever goes further and says that the ink is eternal is misguided, just as whoever says that there is no speech of Allah in the codices.

As for those ignorant people who go further than this, saying that the paper, the leather, the peg, and a piece of the wall are the speech of Allah, they are in the same position as one who says, "Allah has not spoken with the Qur'an, nor is it His speech." This extremism on the side of affirmation confronts denial on the side of negation, and both are outside the Sunnah and the Community.

Likewise, treating speech as separate from the diacritical dots and vowel marks is an innovation, whether by negation or affirmation, and this innovation arose about one hundred years or a little more ago.

Whoever says that the ink with which the letters are dotted and vowelled is eternal is misguided and ignorant. Whoever says that the inflection of the letters of the Qur'an is not part of the Qur'an is misguided and an innovator.

Rather, it is obligatory to say: This Arabic Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and its letters with their inflection have entered into that, just as its meanings have. It is said: Everything between the two covers is the speech of Allah. If the codex is dotted and vowelled, it is applied to everything between its two covers that it is the speech of Allah. If it is not dotted or vowelled, like the ancient codices that the Companions wrote, then what lies between the two covers is also the speech of Allah. It is not permissible to cast strife among the Muslims over a newly invented matter and a verbal dispute that has no reality, nor is it permissible to introduce into religion what is not part of it.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about two men who debated. One of them said: "The Qur'an is letter and sound." The other said: "It is neither letter nor sound." One of them said: "The dots in the codex and the vowel marks are part of the Qur'an." The other said: "That is not part of the Qur'an." What is the correct view on this?

He answered, may Allah be pleased with him: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. This question is one over which many people dispute, and they mix truth with falsehood. As for the one who said that the Qur'an is letter and sound: if he meant that this Qur'an which is recited by Muslims is the speech of Allah, which the Trustworthy Spirit brought down upon Muhammad, seal of the prophets and messengers, and that Gabriel heard it from Allah, the Prophet (ﷺ) heard it from Gabriel, and the Muslims heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth﴾ (16:102), and He said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ (6:114), then he is correct in this.

**[p. 1727]** This is the doctrine of the predecessors of the Ummah and its imams, and the evidences for it from the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus are many.

As for the one who says that the Arabic Qur'an was not spoken by Allah, and that it is only the speech of Gabriel or someone else, which expressed the meaning subsisting in the Essence of Allah, as Ibn Kullab, al-Ash'ari, and those who agree with them say, this is a false statement in many respects.

For these people say that it is one meaning subsisting in the Essence, that the meaning of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an is one, that it does not multiply or divide, and that if it is expressed in Arabic it is the Qur'an, in Hebrew it is the Torah, and in Syriac it is the Gospel. Thus they make the meaning of the Verse of the Throne, the Verse of Debt, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (112:1), ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ (111:1), the Torah, the Gospel, and others one meaning. This is a corrupt claim by reason and by law, and it is a doctrine invented by Ibn Kullab, which no one among the predecessors preceded him in.

If someone who affirms letter and sound means that the audible voices of the reciters and the ink in the codices are eternal and without beginning, he has erred, innovated, and said what contradicts reason and law. For the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Adorn the Qur'an with your voices." He made clear that the voice is the voice of the reciter, and the speech is the speech of the Creator, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection until he hears the speech of Allah﴾ (9:6).

So the Qur'an that Muslims recite is **[p. 1728]** the speech of Allah, not the speech of anyone else, as Allah has stated.

In the Sunan it is related from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to present himself to the people at the gatherings, saying, 'Is there not a man who will carry me to his people? For the Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.'"

When Abu Bakr al-Siddiq recited to them, "Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated" (30:1–2), they said: "Is this your speech or the speech of your companion?" He said: "It is neither my speech nor the speech of my companion, but it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He."

When people convey the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as his saying, "Actions are only by intentions," they know that the hadith they hear is the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ), spoken by him with his voice, letters, and meanings, and the narrator conveyed it from him with his own voice, not with the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ). The Qur'an is therefore more fitting to be the speech of Allah, when the messengers convey it from Him and people recite it with their voices. Allah spoke the Qur'an with its letters and meanings with His own voice, and He called out to Moses with His own voice, as has been established by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the predecessors. The voice of the servant is not the voice of the Lord, nor like His voice, for Allah, there is nothing like Him, neither in His Essence, nor in His attributes, nor in His actions.

The imams of Islam, Ahmad and those before him among the imams, have explicitly stated what the Book and the Sunnah have expressed: that Allah calls out with a voice, that the Qur'an is His speech, spoken with letters and voice, none of it being the speech of anyone else, neither Gabriel nor anyone other than him, and that servants recite it with the voices of their own selves and their actions. So the audible voice of the servant is the voice of the reciter, and the speech is the speech of the Creator.

And many of those who delve into this question do not distinguish between the voice of the servant and the voice of the Lord. Rather, they treat this as that, so they negate both of them together and affirm both of them together. When one negates the letter and the sound, one negates that the Arabic Qur'an is the speech of God, that He calls out to His servants with His voice, and that the Qur'an which Muslims recite is the speech of God. Likewise, one negates that the voice of the servant is an attribute of God. Then one makes the speech of God, which takes many forms, a single thing, with no distinction between the eternal (qadim) and the originated (hadith). This [position] is correct regarding this distinction but not regarding the second [point], which contains a kind of atheism (ilhad) and divesting God of His attributes (ta'til). By making the varied speech of God one thing that has no reality upon close examination, and when he does affirm [speech], he makes the voice of the Lord the voice of the servant, or he remains silent about distinguishing between them, along with his statement that the letters succeed one another in existence, are conjoined in essence, and are eternal in their individual existence. Thus he makes the very attribute of the Lord indwell in the servant and become unified with his attribute. He speaks of a kind of indwelling (hulul) and unification (ittihad) that leads to a kind of divesting [of God's attributes].

It is known that negating the distinction and separation between the Creator and His attributes and the created and its attributes is an error and misguidance, which none of the early predecessors (salaf) of the Community and its Imams adopted. Rather, they all agree on distinguishing between the voice of the Lord and the voice of the servant. They agree that God spoke the Qur'an that He sent down to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), both its letters and its meanings, that He calls out to His servants with His voice, and they agree that the audible sounds of the reciters are the voices of the servants, and that it is not any part of the voices of the servants, nor the ink of the copies (masahif), in eternity. Rather, the Qur'an is written in the copies of the Muslims, recited with their tongues, and preserved in their hearts, and it is the speech of God. The Companions wrote the copies when they wrote them without shakl (vowel marks, i.e., the short vowels) or naqt (diacritical dots), because they were Arabs who did not commit grammatical errors (lahn). Then, when grammatical errors arose, people added dots to the copies and vocalized them.

If [the Qur'an] is written without shakl or naqt, it is permissible; if it is written with naqt and shakl, it is permissible, and it is not disliked according to the more evident of the two opinions of the scholars, and it is one of the two narrations from Ahmad [ibn Hanbal]. The ruling on naqt and shakl is the ruling on the letters, for shakl clarifies the i'rab (grammatical case endings) of the Qur'an, just as naqt clarifies the letters. The ink with which the letters are written, and with which the shakl and naqt are written, is created. The Arabic speech of God which He sent down and which is written in the copies, with shakl and naqt or without shakl and naqt, is not created. The ruling on i'rab is the ruling on the letters. However, i'rab does not stand on its own; rather, it follows the dotted letters. Likewise, shakl and naqt do not stand on their own; rather, they follow the written letters. Therefore, there is no need to isolate them and separate them in speech. Rather, the Qur'an which Muslims recite is the speech of God: its meanings, its letters, and its i'rab.

God spoke the Arabic Qur'an which He sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), and people recite it with their actions and their voices. What is written in the copies of the Muslims is the speech of God, and it is the Arabic Qur'an that was sent down to His Prophet, whether it is written with shakl and naqt or without shakl and naqt. The ink with which the Qur'an is written is not eternal; rather, it is created. The Qur'an that is written in the copy with ink is the speech of God, sent down, uncreated. The copies must be honored by the consensus of the Muslims, because the speech of God is written in them. Honoring the naqt and shakl, when the copy is written vocalized and dotted, is like honoring the letters, by the consensus of the scholars of the Muslims. Just as the sanctity of the i'rab of the Qur'an is like the sanctity of its dotted letters, by the consensus of the Muslims.

For this reason Abu Bakr and Umar said: "Memorizing the i'rab of the Qur'an is more beloved to us than memorizing some of its letters." God spoke the Qur'an with its letters and its meanings, so all of it is the speech of God.

Thus it is not said: "Some of it is the speech of God and some of it is not the speech of God." He, glory be to Him, called out to Musa with a voice that Musa heard, for He has informed that He called out to Musa in more than one place in the Qur'an, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has there come to you the story of Musa?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 15] ﴿When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 16] [al-Nazi'at: 15-16]. And calling (nida') is only a voice, by the consensus of the people of language (ahl al-lugha). He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you just as We revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, the Tribes, Isa, Ayyub, Yunus, Harun, and Sulayman, and We gave Dawud the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisa': 163] ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And God spoke to Musa with direct speech﴾ [al-Nisa': 163-164]. Thus God distinguished between His revelation (iha') to the prophets and His speaking (taklim) to Musa. So whoever says that Musa did not hear a voice but was inspired with its meaning has not distinguished between Musa and others. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and He raised some of them in degrees﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253] [al-Baqarah: 253]. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿It is not for a human that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, Most Wise﴾ [al-Shura: 51] [al-Shura: 51]. Thus He distinguished between revelation (iha') and speaking from behind a veil, as God spoke to Musa. Whoever equates this with that is astray.

Imam Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, and others said: "God has never ceased to be speaking whenever He wills, and He speaks by His will and His power. He speaks one thing after another." As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when he came to it, he was called: O Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 11] [Ta-Ha: 11]. So He called to him when he came to it, and He had not called to him before that. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿So he led them on by deception. Then when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves from the leaves of Paradise. And their Lord called to them: Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?﴾ [al-A'raf: 22] [al-A'raf: 22]. So He, glory be to Him, called to them when they tasted the tree, and He had not called to them before that. Likewise, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 11] [al-A'raf: 11], after He had created Adam and fashioned him, and He had not commanded them before that. Likewise His statement: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Isa with God is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him: Be, and he is﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] [Al 'Imran: 59]. So He informed that He said to him: ﴿Be, and he is﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] [Al 'Imran: 59], after He had created him from dust.

Similar reports are numerous in the Qur'an, informing that He spoke at a specific time and called out at a specific time. It is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he went out to al-Safa, he recited His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158] [al-Baqarah: 158], and said: "We begin with what God began with." So he informed that God began with al-Safa before al-Marwa.

The early predecessors (salaf) agreed that the speech of God is sent down, uncreated, from Him it began and to Him it returns. Some people thought that what they meant was that it is eternal in its individual existence (qadim al-'ayn).

Then a group said: it is one meaning, namely the command to everything commanded, the prohibition of everything prohibited, and the report of everything reported. If it is expressed in Arabic, it is the Qur'an; if it is expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; if it is expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel. This view contradicts the Sharia and reason.

Another group said: it is letters and sounds that are eternal in their individual existence, inseparable from the essence of God, always inseparable from His essence. The ba', the sin, and the mim exist, conjoined with one another together, eternally and forever. None of them has ever preceded another. This too contradicts the Sharia and reason.

Another group said: God does not speak by His will and His power, and in eternity He was speaking with the call that Musa heard. What was renewed was Musa's hearing, not that He called to him when he came to the sacred valley. Rather, He had called to him before that without end, but at that hour Musa heard the call. These agreed with those who said that the Qur'an is created in the root of their doctrine. The root of their doctrine is that the Lord is not the subject of voluntary (ikhtiyariyya) matters, so no speech or act occurs in Him by His choice and will. They said: these are originated events, and the Lord is not the subject of originated events. Thus they contradicted authentic transmission and clear reason.

They believed that by this they refute the philosophers and prove the origination of the world, but they erred in that. They did not support Islam, nor did they defeat the philosophers. They claimed that the Lord was not able in eternity to speak a speech or perform an act, and that He became able after He had not been able, without a new event occurring. Or they alter the expression and say: He has always been able, but the object of power (maqdur) was impossible, and the act became possible for Him after it had been impossible for Him, without anything new occurring. Sometimes they express this by saying: He was able in eternity to do what is possible, regarding what is still impossible in eternity. Thus they combine two contradictories, since they affirm Him as able while the object of His power is impossible according to them. They did not distinguish between the type of speech and act, and between the two of them, just as the philosophers did not distinguish between this and that. Rather, the philosophers claimed that His specific effect is eternal with His eternity. Thus they went astray in that and contradicted clear reason and authentic transmission.

The proofs do not indicate the eternity of any specific thing in the world. Rather, they indicate that whatever is other than God is created and originated, after it was not, since He acts by His power and will, as clear decisive proofs also indicate. The agent who acts by will does not have any part of his effect necessarily attached to him, by clear reason and the agreement of all rational people. Indeed, every agent has no part of its effect necessarily attached to its essence, and it is not conceivable that its specific effect is concurrent with it. Even if one supposes that He acts without will, how much more so the agent by will? As for what is said, that the effect is concurrent with its cause, this is only valid regarding causes that function as conditions (shurut). A condition does not have to precede what it conditions; rather, it may be concurrent with it, just as life is concurrent with knowledge. But whatever is an agent, whether called a cause or not, must precede the specific act. The specific act may not be concurrent with any of its effects, and rational people do not know of any agent that is ever bound to a specific effect. The saying of one who says, "I moved my hand and the ring moved," belongs to the category of conditions, not to the category of agents.

[p-1734] For if the world were eternal, its Agent would necessarily be an originator by His essence from eternity, and its effect and requirement would not be delayed from Him. And if that were so, He would never have brought about any of the temporal events. This contradicts observation. Yet He, glorified be He, has never ceased to be capable of speech and action; indeed He has never ceased to be a speaker whenever He wills, a doer of whatever He wills. He has never ceased to be described with attributes of perfection and characterized by the descriptions of majesty and generosity. The world contains such precision and mastery that it indicates the knowledge of the Lord; it contains such particularity that it indicates His will; it contains such benevolence that it indicates His mercy; it contains such praiseworthy outcomes that it indicates His wisdom; and it contains such temporal events that it indicates the power of the Lord, exalted is He. Yet the Lord deserves the attributes of perfection by His very essence. He deserves every perfection that is possible for existence, with no deficiency in Him, exempt from every deficiency. He, glorified be He, has no equal in any of His affairs. So He is described with the attributes of perfection in detail, exempt in them from likeness and comparison, and exempt from imperfections absolutely, for to describe Him with them is among the greatest falsehoods. His perfection is among the necessary qualities of His holy essence; it is not acquired from anything else. Rather, He is the One who bestows favor upon His creation by creating and bringing into being, and by placing in them the attributes of living beings. The Creator of the attributes of perfection is more deserving of them than the one who has no equal in them.

The root of people's confusion over the question of the speech of Allah is this: when the Jahmiyya (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan) and the Mu'tazila debated the philosophers (falasifa) on the question of the createdness of the world, they believed that what subsists in Him of attributes and successive actions can only be temporal, on the basis that what is infinite cannot exist. They committed themselves to the view that the Lord, from eternity, was not capable of action and speech; rather, that was impossible for Him, and He was idle in respect of it. Sometimes they express this by saying that He was capable from eternity of acting in what is ever-continuing, while acting was impossible for Him from eternity. Thus they combine two contradictories, describing Him with power while the object of power is impossible in His essence. For action entails that it has a beginning, and eternity has no beginning; combining the affirmation of a beginning with its negation is combining two contradictories. They did not discern the difference between what entails a beginning and temporality, which is a particular act and a particular effect, and what does not entail that, which is the type of act and speech. Rather, this (the type) is always present, even though each of its individual instances is temporal, just as it will always be present in the future, and even though each of its individual instances is perishable. This differs from a Creator whose particular creation necessarily remains with Him always. The latter is the falsehood that is refuted by clear reason and sound transmitted proof. For this reason, the natural dispositions of intelligent people agree in rejecting it, and only a small group of philosophizers disputed it, such as Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and others like him, who claimed that the possible thing that is made may be eternal and necessarily existent through something other than itself. In this they opposed the majority of intelligent people, and they also opposed their predecessors, Aristotle and his followers, for they did not say this, even though they held the eternity of the celestial spheres. Aristotle was the first of the Peripatetic philosophers to hold the eternity of the spheres, on the basis of affirming a final cause for the motion of the sphere, through the sphere's movement for the sake of attaining a relation with it. They did not affirm an originating agent for it, nor did they affirm an eternal possible thing necessary through something other than itself.

These people, though they were more ignorant of God and more unbelieving than their later successors, still concede to the majority of intelligent people that whatever is possible in its essence can only be originated, preceded by non-existence. So they were compelled to say: His speech is created and separate from Him.

A sect agreed with them about the impossibility of an infinite existence, but they said: voluntary matters subsist in Him. So they said: He was not speaking from eternity; indeed, speech was not even within His power. Then He became a speaker without any event occurring, by a speech subsisting in Him. This is the doctrine of the Hashimiyya, the Karramiyya, and others.

Another sect said: if the Qur'an is uncreated, then it can only be eternal in its very substance, necessarily belonging to the essence of the Lord. Thus He does not speak by His will and power. Then some of them said: it is one meaning that is not multiplied and not divided into parts. Some of them said: it is letters and sounds, eternally conjoined and necessarily attached to the essences. These also agreed with the Jahmiyya and the Mu'tazila in the root of their doctrine that He speaks with a speech that does not subsist in Himself and by His will and power, and that voluntary matters do not subsist in Him; that He did not settle upon His Throne after He created the heavens and the earth; that He will not come on the Day of Resurrection; that He did not call out to Musa when He called to him; that sins do not anger Him, nor do acts of obedience please Him, nor does the repentance of the repentant gladden Him. They said, regarding His words: ﴿And say, "Work; Allah will see your work, and His Messenger and the believers."﴾ [al-Tawba: 105] and similar verses, that He does not see them when they come into existence. Rather, either He has always been seeing them, or no existent thing has newly come into being; rather, a non-existent thing has become the object of His knowledge.

These are among the doctrines by which they opposed the texts of the Book and the Sunna, along with opposing clear reason. What drove them to this was their agreement with the Jahmiyya on the root of their doctrine, that He, glorified be He, is not able from eternity to act or to speak. They also opposed the Salaf (the early generations) and the Imams in their saying: Allah has never ceased to be a speaker whenever He wills. Then they split into four factions, as was previously mentioned: the Khalqiyya (those who say the Qur'an is created), the Hadathiyya (those who say it is temporal), the Ittihadiyya (those who hold unity of existence), and the Iqtiraniyya (those who hold conjunction).

Worse than these are the Sabians and the philosophers, who say that Allah did not speak, neither with a speech subsisting in His essence, nor with a speech He utters by His will and power, neither of eternal type nor eternal individual, neither temporal nor created. Rather, His speech for them is what overflows upon the souls of the prophets. They say that He spoke to Musa from the heaven of His intellect.

They sometimes say that He, exalted is He, knows universals but not particulars, for He only knows them in a universal way. Yet they also say that He knows His own essence and knows what He does. Their statement "He knows His essence and His creatures" is true, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Should not He know who created? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted.﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]. But their further statement that "He does not know specific individual entities" is ignorance and contradiction. For His holy essence is a specific individual, the spheres are specific individuals, and every existent is a specific individual. If He does not know specific individuals, He does not know any of the existents, since universals exist only in minds, not in external reality. Whoever knows only universals does not know any of the existents. Exalted is Allah far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

Their adherence to this heresy was driven by their flight from the Exalted Creator's states undergoing change. These people say: temporal events subsist in the eternal, and temporal events have no beginning. But they negated this of the Creator, because they believed He has no attribute; rather, He is pure existence. They said: knowledge is the very essence of the knower, power is the very essence of the powerful, knowledge and the knower are one thing, and the willer and the will are one thing. Thus they made this attribute to be the other, and they made the attributes to be the described.

Some of them say: rather, knowledge is the entirety of the known, as al-Tusi, author of "Sharh al-Isharat" (the Commentary on the Pointers), says. He denied Ibn Sina's affirmation of his knowledge of himself and of what proceeds from his essence. Ibn Sina was closer to the truth, but he contradicted himself in this, since he denied that attributes subsist in Him and made the attribute identical with the described, each attribute identical with the other. For this reason, these people were more deeply immersed in unity of existence and heresy than those who say that the meanings of speech are one thing.

But (p-1737) those people imposed their doctrine upon the others, and said: if it is permissible for multiple meanings to be one thing, then it is permissible for knowledge to be power, and power to be will. The shrewd among those people admitted that this objection has no answer. Then they said: and if it is permissible for this attribute to be the other, then it is permissible for the attribute to be the described.

Then came Ibn 'Arabi, Ibn Sab'in, al-Qunawi and their like, and said: if it is permissible for this attribute to be the other, and the attribute to be the described, then it is permissible for the existent that is necessary, eternal, and creating to be the existent that is possible, originated, and created.

They said: the existence of every created thing is identical with the existence of the Creator. They said: existence is one. They did not distinguish between one in kind and one in individual, just as those people did not distinguish between one speech in individual and one speech in kind. The ultimate outcome of the people of heresy in speech was this nullification, unbelief, and unity, which the people of Oneness, Indwelling, and Unity say about the Creator and the creatures. Just as those who did not distinguish between the type of speech and its individual instance, and who said: He speaks with an eternal letter and sound, first said that He does not speak by His will and power, and that the bā' does not precede the sīn. Rather, when He called out to Musa and said: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14] ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-Qasas: 30], the hamza, the nun, and what is between them were existing from eternity, some of them accompanying others, never ceasing and never going to cease being necessarily attached to the essence of Allah. Then a group of them said: that eternal thing is the very sounds heard from the reciters.

Some of them said: rather, what is heard is two sounds: an eternal one and a temporal one. Some of them said: the shapes of the ink are eternal and everlasting. Some of them said: the locus of the ink is eternal and everlasting. It is reported of some of them that he said: the ink is eternal and everlasting.

Most of them speak using the word "eternal" without understanding its meaning. Some of them think it means eternal in His knowledge; some think its meaning is prior to other things; some think the meaning of the word is that it is uncreated; and some do not distinguish between what they say. These became Hulūliyya and Ittihādiyya regarding the attributes. Some of them hold indwelling and unity regarding the essence and the attributes. The ultimate outcome of both these and those was nullification (ta'til).

The correct position in this matter and others is the doctrine of the Salaf of this Community and its Imams: that (p-1738) He, glorified be He, has never ceased to be a speaker whenever He wills; that He speaks by His will and power; that His words have no end; that He called out to Musa with a voice Musa heard; that He called out to him only when he came, and did not call to him before that; that the voice of the Lord is not like the voices of His servants, just as His knowledge is not like their knowledge, and His power is not like their power; and that He, glorified be He, is distinct from His creation in His essence and attributes. There is nothing of His essence or of His subsisting attributes in His creation, and nothing of His creation in His essence. The statements of the people of nullification and unity who nullify the essence, the attributes, the speech, or the actions are false; and the statements of the people of indwelling who hold indwelling in the essence and the attributes are false.

These matters are expounded at length in other places, and we have expounded them in "al-Wajib al-Kabir." And Allah knows best what is correct.

(Taqi al-Din also said, in an essay of his on this subject): The first to openly deny that Allah speaks and that He took Abraham as a close friend was Ja'd ibn Dirham, at the beginning of the second century (AH). The scholars of Islam, such as al-Hasan al-Basri and others, ordered his execution. So Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Qasri, the governor of Iraq at Wasit, sacrificed him. He said: "O people, sacrifice, may Allah accept your sacrifices, for I am sacrificing Ja'd ibn Dirham. He claimed that Allah did not take Ibrahim as a friend, and did not speak to Musa directly. Exalted is Allah far above what Ja'd says, a great exaltation." Then he came down and slaughtered him.

Al-Qasimi's commentary on Surah 4, verse 164 (part 4 of 6):

Al-Jahm ibn Safwan took this doctrine from him (Ja'd ibn Dirham). He denied that God speaks, then fed the Muslims hypocrisy by affirming the word "speech," and said: "His speech is created in a substrate, like the air and the leaves of trees." Some of the people of *kalam* (scholastic theology, or dialectical argument) or *jadal* (disputation), among those who claimed to belong to Islam, such as the Mu'tazilites and their like, entered into some of the doctrines of the Sabians and the polytheists, following al-Ja'd and al-Jahm.

The origin of this was that the Sabians disagreed about creation in two positions. Some of them say that the heavens were created after they had not existed, as the messengers and the books of God, exalted is He, have reported. Others innovated and said: "Rather, they are eternal and everlasting. They have never ceased to exist, by the existence of the First, the Necessary Existent through Himself." Still others deny the Creator altogether. They have many doctrines, widely divergent, concerning creation, resurrection, origin and return, because they were not holding fast to a rope from God, exalted is He, that would unite them (p-1739). Conjecture does not unite people in matters of this kind, whose true natures human opinions are unable to grasp except by revelation from God, exalted is He.

They argue with one another only by means of syllogism, whose premises are taken from lower natural matters and the powers of natures present in earth, water, air, animals, minerals and plants. By these lower premises they wish to attain knowledge of God and knowledge of what is above the heavens, at the beginning and at the end. This is a clear error. Their own leaders have acknowledged that this is not possible, that they have no path to attaining certainty, and that they follow nothing but conjecture.

When the condition of these innovating, misguided Sabians, and of those whom they led astray from among the Jews and Christians, became known, and their speech had reached some of the people of *kalam* and disputation who had not been guided by the guidance of God with which He sent His messengers, they began to want to take up their methods, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) reported when he said: "You will certainly follow the ways of the nations before you, span by span and cubit by cubit." They said: "O Messenger of God, Persia and Byzantium?" He said: "And who are the people other than Persia and Byzantium?"

They argued for the createdness of the world by a kind of the methods of these Sabians, namely speech about bodies and accidents: that accidents are established, then that they are necessarily attached to bodies, then that they are originated, and then it is said: "Whatever does not precede originated things is itself originated." Many of the people of disputation relied on this in establishing the createdness of the world. When they saw that accidents, which are the attributes, indicate according to them the originatedness of the subject that bears the accidents, they committed themselves to negating them from God, because their establishment entails His origination. And the invalidity of the proof of the world's createdness, which they believed was the only proof, and indeed they often believed that no one's faith is valid without it, is known by necessity from the religion of Islam. These people oppose the Sabian philosophers who say that the world is eternal and that prophethood is a perfection that overflows onto the soul of the Prophet. For these speculative theologians are more correct and more closely follow rational and transmitted evidence, because their hearts were illuminated by the light of Islam and the Qur'an. Although they have gone astray in much of what the messengers brought, they are better than those in other respects in which they agreed with them. They agreed with those (the philosophers) that God does not speak.

Likewise they agreed with them that He has no knowledge, no power, and no attribute of the attributes. They held that affirming that He speaks requires that He be a body, and a body is originated, because it is among the attributes that indicate the originatedness of the subject. Indeed, according to them, speech indicates the originatedness of the speaker more than anything else, because it requires exits (of sound) for which other things do not require, and because it contains ordering, precedence and succession that other things do not contain. When they saw that the messengers agreed that He is a speaker, and the Qur'an is filled with affirming that, they sometimes said: "He is a speaker metaphorically, not literally." This was their first statement, when they were in their innovation upon natural disposition, before they fell into obstinacy and denial. Then they saw this as abominable and said: "Rather, He is a speaker literally."

Some of their theologians sometimes related a consensus, though that is not their actual position. Rather, the true essence of their doctrine and its root, for whoever has known it and originated it, is that God is not a speaker. They said: "The speaker is whoever creates speech, even in a substrate separate from Himself." So they interpreted "speaker" in the language with a meaning not known in the language of the Arabs or in any other language, neither literally nor metaphorically. This is the position of whoever says "the Qur'an is created." It is one of the two positions of the Sabians, who agree with the messengers about the createdness of the world. Although this (position) disbelieves in what the messengers brought, it is not in its disbelief like the first position. For these people do not say that God willed to send a specific messenger and to send down this speech upon him, which He created. They denied that He is a speaker in the manner indicated by the divine books and agreed upon by the people of sound natural disposition.

Between these people, who are the branches of the Sabians, and the believers, the followers of the messengers, a dispute arose. These people disbelieved in some of what the messengers brought about describing God with speech and with speaking, and they disagreed about the Book of God, believing in some of it and disbelieving in some. The believers followed what was sent down to them from their Lord, that God spoke through the Qur'an, that He spoke to Moses with direct speech, and that He speaks. They did not distort the words from their places as the earlier ones did. Rather, they rejected those people's distortion with the insights of faith, through which they knew the intent of the messengers in their reports of the message and speech of God. They followed this Qur'an, the Hadith, the consensus of the early generations of the Companions, the Successors, and all the followers of the prophets. They knew that the statement of these people is more vile than the statement of the Jews and Christians.

Ibn al-Mubarak, the imam of the Muslims, used to say: "We relate the speech of the Jews and Christians, but we cannot relate the speech of the Jahmiyya." The appearance of these people, who are the branches of the polytheists, and of those who followed them from the distorting Sabians, and then the distorting Jews and Christians, had become widespread in the early part of the second century and the early part of the third, during the rule of Abu al-Abbas, known as al-Ma'mun, because of the Arabization of the books of the polytheistic Byzantines, the Sabians who had been before the Christians, and those resembling them from Persia and India. The sciences of the Sabian astrologers and their like appeared.

It has already been mentioned that the innovated *kalam* in Islam comes from the branches of the Sabians, just as it is said: "The Mu'tazilites are the catamites of the philosophers." This doctrine appeared among the people of learning and *kalam*, and among the people of the sword and rule. Among its adherents were caliphs, emirs, viziers, judges and jurists, who used it to test the believing men and women and the Muslim men and women who followed what was sent down to them from their Lord and did not alter or innovate. This happened because most of them were deficient and negligent in knowing the true reality of what the Messenger and his followers brought.

* *

Section

Then there came a group of the speculative theologians of the Attributists (*Sifatiyya*), who supported that God has knowledge, power, sight and life, by rational arguments that agree with the prophetic texts. They distinguished between attributes subsisting in substances, which they called accidents, and attributes subsisting in the Lord, which they did not call accidents, because an accident is what does not endure and does not remain, or what subsists in something spatial or in a body. The attributes of the Lord are necessary and permanent, not of the same kind as accidents subsisting in bodies. These people, the analogical theologians among the Attributists, differed from those innovating, negating Sabians in many of their matters, and they affirmed the attributes that may be proven by rational analogy, such as the seven attributes: life, knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight and speech. They disagree about hearing, sight and speech: are these among the rational attributes or among the prophetic, reported, transmitted attributes?

They also differ about permanence and eternity, and about perception, meaning perception of what is smelled, tasted and touched. They also differ about the Qur'anic, reported, transmitted attributes, such as the Face and the Hand. Most of their earlier scholars, or all of them, affirm these, while many of their later scholars do not affirm them. As for what appears only in Hadith, most of them do not affirm it.

Then some of them turn the texts away from their indications because of the rational analogy that they hold opposes them, and some of them delegate their meaning (*tafwid*). The aim here is not to detail the doctrines of people concerning the rest of the attributes. The intent is only to speak about the message of God and His speech, which His messengers conveyed. So these people, between them and the people of prophetic inheritance, share a common ground in the correct paths they have acquired concerning the Creator's names and attributes. Thus in their doctrine about the message there is a mixture of the two inheritances. They mixed the right of the heirs of the prophets with the falsehood of the heirs of the followers of the Sabians, just as in the doctrine of the purely innovated *kalam* people, such as the Mu'tazilites, there is a mixture. There is no equivalence between the prophetic traditions and the Sabian traditions, but those (the Attributists) follow the prophetic traditions more closely and are nearer to the doctrines of the People of the Sunna than the Mu'tazilites and their like in many respects. For this reason many of the people of jurisprudence, Hadith and Sufism agreed with some of what these innovated, for several reasons:

The first: the abundance of truth that they state, and the prominence of the prophetic traditions among them.

The second: their clothing that truth in rational analogies, some of which were inherited from the Sabians and some of which were innovated in Islam, and the seizing by doubts contained in that, and their assumption that adhering to the prophetic traditions is not possible for people of reason and knowledge except in this manner.

The third: the weakness, among them, of the prophetic traditions that repel these doubts and clarify the path of guidance.

The fourth: the incapacity and negligence that affect those who claim to belong to the Sunna and Hadith. Sometimes they transmit what they know to be authentic, and sometimes they are like the unlettered who know not the Book except as wishful fancies, and they turn away from explaining the indication of the Book and the Sunna concerning the realities of matters.

Because this was their method, and they said that the Qur'an is uncreated, on the basis of what the texts and the consensus of the early generations (*salaf*) indicate on this (p-1743).
