In "al-'Inayah" it is said: The well-known reading of the verse is with the noble divine name in the nominative (raf'), and it has been read with the accusative (nasb) in the irregular readings (shawadh). End of quotation.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: The Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh narrated that a man came to Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash and said: "I heard a man reciting: 'And God spoke to Musa with speech (wa-kallama Allahu Musa taklimā),'" and Abu Bakr said: "None recites this except a disbeliever. I read to al-A'mash, al-A'mash read to Yahya ibn Wassab, Yahya ibn Wassab read to Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): ﴿And God spoke to Musa with speech﴾."

The anger of Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash (may Allah have mercy on him) toward the one who read in this way was intense because he had distorted both the wording and the meaning of the Qur'an. This was from the Mu'tazilah, who deny that God spoke to Musa (peace be upon him) or speaks to any of His creation. It is also related from some Mu'tazilah that one of them read to some shaykhs: "And God spoke to Musa with speech," and he said to him: "O son of the adulteress! How will you handle His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]?" meaning that this does not admit of distortion or interpretation.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 165 (part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people would have no argument against God after the messengers. And God is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾ [4:165]

﴿Messengers﴾ means: We sent all these prophets as messengers, ﴿bearers of good news﴾ of Paradise to whoever believes, ﴿and warners﴾ of the Fire to whoever disbelieves, ﴿so that﴾ (lest) ﴿people would have no argument against God﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. That is, an excuse by which they might plead, saying: "Why did You not send us a messenger to explain Your laws to us and teach us what we did not know of Your rulings?" This is because human power is too limited to grasp the particular details of what is beneficial, and most people are unable to grasp the universal principles of it. This is like His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs?"﴾ [20:134], and so on.

The term "argument" (ḥujjah) is used here, although it is impossible for anyone to have an argument against Him, glorified is He, regarding any of His acts; rather, He may do whatever He wills, however He wills. This is to draw attention to the fact that, in terms of acceptance before Him, exalted is He, an excuse, in accordance with His generosity and mercy toward His servants, is equivalent to a decisive argument that cannot be repelled. For this reason, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [17:15]. This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud.

In the two Sahihs, from al-Mughira: "No one is more fond of excuse than God, and for this reason He sent the messengers as bearers of good news and warners."

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿after the messengers﴾, that is, after the sending of the messengers and the revelation of the Books. It is connected to ﴿argument﴾, or to a deleted element that functions as a description of it. In this is evidence that God, exalted is He, does not punish creation before the sending of messengers, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [17:15]. In this is also evidence for the doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority) that knowledge of God, exalted is He, is established only through revelation (sam', the transmitted revealed texts).

﴿And God is ever Mighty﴾, meaning in His retribution against those who oppose His command and disobey His messengers; ﴿Wise﴾ in sending the messengers as warners.

* *

**Note:**

The verse points to the explanation of humanity's need for the sending of messengers and to their function, peace be upon them. The scholar Sayyid Muhammad Abduh, Mufti of Egypt, said in his "Risalat al-Tawhid" (Treatise on Monotheism) on this subject: Is it not from the wisdom of the Wise Creator, who established the affairs of man on the basis of guidance and instruction, who created man and taught him eloquence, taught him speech for mutual understanding and writing for correspondence, that He should make among the human souls a rank for which He prepares, by His pure grace, some of those whom He chooses from among His creation? He knows best where He places His message. He distinguishes them with sound natures, and He raises their spirits to such perfection that they become worthy of being illuminated by the lights of His knowledge and entrusted with the hidden secrets of His, which, if they were revealed to others as they are revealed to them, would overwhelm their souls or take away their minds because of their majesty and greatness. Thus they look upon the unseen by His permission, and they know what will happen to people in it, and they occupy in their exalted ranks a degree of those who act, the end of the witness and the beginning of the absent. They are in this world as if they were not of its people; they are the envoys of the Hereafter, dressed in the garb of one who is not among its inhabitants. Then they receive from His command, from His majesty, and from what is hidden from the intellects of the affairs of His exalted presence, in whatever way He wills that the servants should believe about it, and what He decides should have a bearing on their happiness in the Hereafter. They explain to people the conditions of the Hereafter that they must know, expressing it in terms that the capacity of their minds can bear and that are not far from the reach of their understanding. They convey from Him general laws that define for them their course in refining their souls and restraining their desires, and that teach them, of the deeds, what is the criterion of their happiness and their misery, in that (p. 1755) unseen order beyond their perception, whose knowledge clings in its generality to the depths of their consciences. This includes all the rulings related to the universal principles of deeds, outward and inward. Then He supports them with signs beyond the power of human beings, until the argument is established for them and conviction in the truth of the message is complete. Thus they become messengers from Him to His creation, bearers of good news and warners.

There is no doubt that He who perfected everything He created, who originated every being He made, who bestowed upon every living thing what it needs, and who did not withhold His mercy from any creature, small or great, must, out of His compassion toward the kind whose creation He perfected, and for which He established a capacity for knowledge that takes the place of the gifts He bestowed exclusively on others, rescue it from its bewilderment, deliver it from floundering in its most important life, and from error in its best state.

Someone may say: Why did He not place in the natural instincts what they need of knowledge? Why did He not place in them submission to action and the course of the path leading to the goal in the Hereafter? Is this kind of guidance and instruction not among the marvels of mercy? This is a statement that proceeds from the excess of reason and from heedlessness of the subject of the inquiry, which is the human species. That species, with what it has, and with what has entered into the constitution of its essence of thinking spirit, and what that entails of difference in degrees of preparedness according to the difference of its individuals, and that not every individual of it is prepared for every state by nature, and that the very existence of its being is founded on inquiry and reasoning, if it were inspired in its needs as animals are inspired, it would not be that species, but rather would be either another animal, like the bee and the ant, or an angel, not among the inhabitants of this earth.

Then he said: If man was created to live in a community, and was not given along with that natural disposition what the bee and some individual ants have been given, for example, of inspiration that guides them to what is necessary for that, but was instead left to his own thought to manage, just as he was created with a feeling of a Dominator to whom his soul is drawn against its will, yet knowledge of that Dominator's essence and attributes was not poured out upon him along with that feeling, but rather he was cast into the arenas of reflection, carried by thoughts in their courses, and driven by them to a place he knows and does not know, and in all of that there is affliction for his unity and peril to his existence, has this species been afflicted with deficiency and stricken with inability to reach what the weakest and lowest of animals have attained in the stations of existence? Yes, it is so, were it not for what the Wise Creator gave him in the way of his weakness.

Man is wondrous in his affair: by the power of his intellect he ascends to the highest ranks of the Kingdom (malakut, the realm of the unseen), and with his thought he reaches for the loftiest landmarks of the Dominion (jabarut, the divine sovereignty), and with his strength he rises above what is too great to be matched by the forces of the greatest universe. Then he diminishes, shrinks, and descends to the lowest depth of humility and submission whenever some matter befalls him, the cause of which he does not know and the source of which he does not grasp. That is due to a secret known to those who have insight and perceived by the souls of all people.

From that weakness he is bound to his desire, and from that lowliness he is taken by the hand to the nobility of his happiness. The generous Giver perfected for his whole kind what His wisdom required in singling out his species, by which He distinguishes it from others: that it should be lacking in its individuals. And just as He bestowed upon every person the intellect that directs the senses, so that he may look into seeking food, covering his nakedness, and protecting himself from heat and cold, He bestowed upon the whole what is more pressing for survival, more effective in protection from the dangers of misery, and more preserving of the order of society, which by consensus is the pillar of its existence. He bestowed upon him the true representative of love, or rather the one who brings love back to souls that had been barren of it. He did not break His custom in this, of building His creation on the basis of teaching and guidance, except that He brought to him, along with that, through the weakest aspect of him, which is the aspect of submission and humility.

So He established for him, from among his individuals, guiding and rightly-guided ones, and distinguished them from among them by characteristics in themselves that no one else shares with them. He supported that, for the sake of greater conviction, with dazzling signs that capture souls and take hold of the path upon the paths of intellects, so that the aspirant is humbled, the wild one is subdued, the intellect of the sensible strikes against them and returns to its right course, and the sight of the ignorant is dazzled by them and turns back from its error. They strike speech with thunderbolts from the command of God, and they astonish perceptions with dazzling signs from His signs, so that they surround minds with what leaves no escape from submitting to it. The owner and the slave, the fool and the poor man, the wise and the ignorant, the inferior and the superior are equal in their reliance on what they bring, so that submission to them becomes more like compulsion than like a free and reflective choice. They teach them what God wills to be of benefit to their livelihood and their hereafter, and what He wishes them to know of the affairs of His essence and the perfection of His attributes. These are the prophets and the messengers. Therefore the sending of the prophets, may the blessings of God be upon them, is among the completions of human existence and one of the most important of his needs for his survival. Their position in the species is the position of the intellect in the individual. It is a blessing that God perfected: ﴿so that people would have no argument against God after the messengers﴾.

Then he said, in discussing the function of the messengers, peace be upon them: It has become clear from what has preceded, concerning the need of the human world for messengers, that they stand among the nations in the position of the intellects among individuals, and that their sending is a need among the needs of human intellects. The mercy of the Originator, the Wise, has decreed its fulfillment, and it is a blessing from the Giver of existence by which He distinguished man from the rest of the beings of his kind. But it is a spiritual need, and everything in it that touches the senses is aimed at the spirit and its purification from the defilement of misguided desires and the straightening of its faculties, or at depositing in it what contains its happiness in both lives.

As for the detailed methods of livelihood, skill in the ways of earning, and the intellect's pursuit of comprehending what has been prepared for it to reach of the secrets of knowledge, that is something in which the messages have no role, except in the aspect of general admonition and guidance toward moderation in it, and establishing that the condition of all of that is that it must not create doubt in belief that the universe has one God, Powerful, Knowing, Wise, characterized by what proof has required Him to be characterized by, and that the relation of all beings to Him is equal in that they are created by Him and are the product of His power, and that their variation lies only in what some of them have been singled out for in perfection.

And its condition is that none of those deeds mentioned earlier should harm any person in his self, his honor, or his property, without a right required by the order of the common good of the community, as defined in its law.

They guide the intellect to knowledge of God and what must be known of His attributes, and they define the limit at which one must stop in seeking that knowledge, in a manner that does not burden one to be at rest in it and does not lift one's trust in what God has given of strength. They gather the word of creation upon one God, with whom there is no division, and they clear the way between them and Him alone. They rouse their souls to attachment to Him in all actions and dealings, and they remind them of His greatness through the prescription of various kinds of worship, at differing times, as a reminder for the forgetful and a continuous purification for the one who fears, strengthening what is weak among them and increasing the certain in certainty.

They clarify for the people what their intellects and desires have disagreed about, and what their interests and pleasures have contended over. They then settle those disputes by the clear command of God, and through what they convey from Him they support whatever serves the public good and does not forfeit private benefits. They bring the people back to harmony, reveal to them the secret of mutual affection, and draw their attention to the fact that in it lies the orderly unity of the community. They impose on them the striving of their own souls, so that it may settle in their hearts and be felt in their inner beings. They teach them that each should respect the right of the other, while not neglecting his own right, that no one should exceed his limit in what he seeks, that the strong should help the weak, that the rich should aid the poor, that the rightly guided should guide the misguided, and that the learned should teach the ignorant.

They establish for them, by God's command, general limits to which it is easy for them to refer their conduct: such as the sanctity of human blood, except by right, together with the explanation of the right that permits its taking; and the sanctity of honour, together with the explanation of what is permitted and what is forbidden regarding intimate relations. Alongside this, they legislate that they should refine themselves through virtuous qualities, such as truthfulness, trustworthiness, fulfilment of contracts, faithfulness to covenants, mercy toward the weak, boldness in advising the powerful, and acknowledging to every creature its right without exception.

They lead them to turn their desires away from fleeting pleasures toward the pursuit of lofty aspirations, employing in all of this a measure of both encouragement and warning, of threat and good tidings, as God, exalted is His majesty, has commanded them.

In all of this they explain to the people what qualifies them for God's approval, and what exposes them to His wrath.

Then they encompass their exposition with the report of the Final Abode, and of what God has prepared therein of reward and a good outcome for those who stop at His limits, adhere to His commands, and avoid falling into what He has forbidden. They inform them of some of the reports of the unseen that God has permitted His servants to know, things which, if the intellect found them hard to grasp in full, would not be difficult for it to acknowledge as existing.

By this, souls find rest, hearts are soothed, and the afflicted take refuge in patience, hoping for abundant reward or seeking to please the One in whose hand is the command. And by this is resolved the greatest problem in human society, which the wise have continued to strive to solve until today.

It is not among the functions of the messengers to do what teachers and instructors of crafts do. It is not part of what they came for to teach history, nor to detail what the heavenly bodies contain, nor to explain the variations in their motions, nor what is hidden in the layers of the earth, nor the measures of its length and breadth, nor what plants need for their growth, nor what animals require to preserve their individuals and species .... and other such matters for which the sciences were established, and in reaching whose subtleties minds have competed. All of that is among the means of gaining livelihood and acquiring the paths to comfort, to which God has guided mankind through the perception He has deposited in them. It increases the happiness of the sincere, and it decrees hardship upon the negligent.

However, God's custom in this is that He follows a method of gradual progress toward perfection. The laws of the prophets have come with what compels adherence in general terms to striving therein, and with what ensures that committing to it leads to the attainment of the stages of ascent for which God has prepared human natures (fitrah: innate disposition).

As for what has come in the words of the prophets alluding to some of what we have mentioned concerning the conditions of the celestial spheres or the configuration of the earth, it is intended only to direct attention to what it contains of indication of the wisdom of its Originator, or to direct thought to plunge into the depths to grasp its secrets and wonders.

Their state, upon them be prayers and peace, in addressing their peoples, cannot be above what those peoples understand, for otherwise the wisdom in sending them would be lost. For this reason, an expression may come that is addressed to the common people and yet requires interpretation and explanation for the elite. Likewise, what is addressed to the elite may require a long time before the common people understand it. This category is the least of what has come in their speech.

(p-١٧٦٠) In any case, it is not permissible that religion be made a barrier between souls and what God has distinguished them by, namely the readiness to know the realities of created beings to the extent possible. Rather, religion must inspire the pursuit of knowledge, demanding that it respect proof, and obliging souls to exert whatever effort they can in understanding the worlds that lie before them. Yet this must be accompanied by moderation, and by halting at the limit in the soundness of belief. Whoever says otherwise has ignorance of religion and has committed against it a crime that the Lord of religion will not forgive him. End of quotation.

When His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 163], and the verse, included the establishment of his prophethood and the argument against their obstinacy in demanding a book to be sent down to them from heaven, it is as if it were said: they do not witness that.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾ — of the Qur'an, the inimitable, which speaks of your prophethood. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of Allah's bearing witness to what He sent down to him is His establishing its authenticity by manifesting miracles, just as claims are established by proofs, since the Wise does not confirm a liar with a miracle.

﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ — that is, while He is Knowing of it and Watchful over it. So the phrase "with His knowledge" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject (the doer), and the sentence serves as an explanation of what precedes it.

﴿And the angels bear witness﴾ — that is, to this — ﴿and Allah suffices as a Witness﴾ to the truth of your prophethood, even if no one else bears witness. In this there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p-1761)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 167:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and avert [others] from the way of Allah have certainly strayed far astray.﴾ [167]

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., in that which Allah has testified to having sent down, while they are aware of its inimitability (i'jaz). ﴿And avert [others] from the way of Allah﴾, which is the religion of Islam, from whoever wishes to follow it. ﴿Have certainly strayed﴾, i.e., by what they did. ﴿Far astray﴾, because they combined going astray (dalal) with leading others astray (idlal).

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged [themselves or others] — Allah would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path [168]﴾

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged﴾ — i.e., [wronged] creation by leading them astray — ﴿Allah would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path﴾ — due to their lack of readiness for guidance to the truth and for righteous deeds, which are the path to Paradise.

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿Except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ [169]

﴿Except the path of Hell﴾ means: the path that leads to it, namely their acquiring of evil deeds. ﴿Abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ means: easy, not difficult for Him, and He does not consider it a great matter.

When He had established the matter of prophethood, and clarified the path that leads to knowledge of it, and the warning for those who deny it, He addressed people in general with the call, the establishing of proof, and the warning against rejection, so He, exalted is He, said:

(p-1762) The discourse on the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the explanation of the meaning) of His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord. So believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise.﴾ [170]

﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord﴾, i.e., with the guidance, the religion of truth, and the healing clarification that must be accepted. ﴿So believe; it is better for you﴾, i.e., believe, which is better for you, or adopt a course better for you than blindly following the obstinate ones. ﴿But if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., He is able to punish you because of the greatness of His dominion (*malakut*), or He is free of need from you, not harmed by your disbelief just as He does not benefit from your belief, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on earth all together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8] [Ibrahim: 8]. ﴿And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise﴾, in His making.

When He, may He be exalted, had answered the doubts (*shubuhat*) of the Jews and imposed the proof (*hujjah*) upon them, He turned the address specifically to the Christians, as a rebuke for them concerning the disbelief and misguidance they were upon. So He, glorified is He, said:

**The interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:**

﴿O People of the Book, do not exceed the limits in your religion, and do not say about God except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of God and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say "Three." Desist, it is better for you. God is only one God. Glory be to Him; (He is far above) that He should have a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And God suffices as a Guardian﴾ [4:171]

﴿O People of the Book, do not exceed the limits in your religion﴾, that is, by excessively elevating the status of Jesus, peace be upon him, and claiming his divinity. This is an overstepping beyond the rank that he was given, which was prophethood (risalah). It is thereby established that *ghuluww* (exaggeration, going beyond the limit) in religion is forbidden, and it is *mujawazat al-hadd* (transgressing the boundary).

In the Sahih, it is related from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not overpraise me as the Christians overpraised the son of Mary. I am only His servant, so say: 'The servant of God and His messenger.'"

Imam Ahmad said: Hasan ibn Musa narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, that a man said: "O Muhammad! O our master and son of our master! O our best and son of our best!" The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O people! Keep to your words, and let not Satan mislead you. I am Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, the servant of God and His messenger. By God, I do not wish that you raise me above my station which God, Mighty and Majestic, has given me."

Ibn Kathir said: He alone narrated it through this route.

﴿And do not say about God except the truth﴾, that is, do not describe Him with what is impossible for Him to possess, such as incarnation (hulul), union (ittihad), taking a consort, or having a child. Rather, declare Him free of all of that.

﴿The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary﴾: this is a description of him, indicating the falsehood of what they attributed to him, namely that he is a son of God, may He be exalted. ﴿A messenger of God﴾ is the predicate of the subject, namely "the Messiah," meaning that he is restricted to the station of prophethood and does not transcend it. ﴿And His word﴾, that is, he was brought into being by His word and command, which is "Be!" (kun), without an intermediary father or a drop of semen.

﴿Which He cast to Mary﴾, that is, He conveyed it to her and placed it in her by the breathing of Gabriel, peace be upon him. ﴿And a spirit from Him﴾, that is, by His creating and forming him like all other created spirits. He attributed him to Himself only as a mark of honour and dignity, as one says "the House of God" and "the she-camel of God."

It has also been said: the spirit is the breath of Gabriel, peace be upon him, into the collar of Mary's garment, and she conceived by God's permission. The breath was called a spirit because it is a wind that comes out from the spirit. He attributed it to Himself because it came into being by His command and permission.

Abu al-Suʿud said: "from" (min) here indicates the starting point of the act in a metaphorical sense, not partitive, as the Christians claim.

It is related that a Christian physician of al-Rashid debated ʿAli ibn Husayn al-Waqidi al-Marwazi one day. He said to him: "In your book there is what indicates that Jesus, peace be upon him, is a part of Him, may He be exalted," and he recited this verse. Al-Waqidi then recited: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾ [45:13]. He said: "Then it would follow that all those things are parts of Him, exalted be He far above that." The Christian was silenced and embraced Islam, and al-Rashid rejoiced greatly and gave al-Waqidi a lavish reward.

It has also been said: he was called a spirit because he gave life to the dead by God's permission. It has been said: because he gave life to hearts, just as the Qur'an was called that for this reason, in His saying: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [42:52].

It has also been said: what is meant by "the spirit" is the revelation that was revealed to Mary with the glad tidings.

It has also been said: it is customary that when they wish to describe something as having the utmost purity and cleanliness, they say that it is a "spirit." So since Jesus, peace be upon him, was formed by breath and not by a drop of semen, he was described as a spirit.

The mention of his being a messenger of God first, although in existence it comes after his being His word and a spirit from Him, is for establishing the truth from the outset with what is explicit in it and not open to interpretation, determining the outcome of what is open to interpretation, and closing the door to deviant interpretation. End.

﴿So believe in God﴾ and single Him out for divinity, ﴿and His messengers﴾, that is, all of them, and describe them as messengers, and do not remove any of them from their category by ascribing divinity to them.

﴿And do not say "Three"﴾, that is: the gods are three: God, the Messiah, and Mary, as His saying indicates: ﴿Did you say to people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"?﴾ [5:116].

Al-Sayyid ʿAbd Allah al-Hindi, in his debate with a priest of India, related on the authority of his opponent that a group of Christians called "Kuli Ri Dinis" used to say: "The gods are three: the Father, the Son, and Mary." He said: "Perhaps this matter was written in their manuscripts, because the Qur'an refuted them." End.

Or the implied meaning is: "Do not say: 'God is three,' that is, three hypostases (aqanim)." In their school textbooks now printed there is the following text: "The most particular of the secrets of Christianity is the mystery of the Trinity, which is one God in three hypostases: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. They are not three gods, but one God existing in three hypostases, equal in substance, and distinguished among themselves by hypostaticity. This is because they have one substance, one divinity, and one essence, and none of these three hypostases is greater, older, or more powerful than the other two, since the three are equal in greatness, eternity, power, and in everything except hypostaticity. We cannot fully comprehend these truths, because they are mysteries beyond the reach of human reason and perception." End of their words in their school textbook printed in Beirut in the year 1876 CE.

Look at this contradiction and obfuscation: they acknowledge that the three are gods, then they contradict their own statement and deny it.

The scholar Shaykh Rahmat Allah al-Hindi, in his book *Izhar al-Haqq*, quoted from the Christian author of *Mizan al-Haqq* that he said: "We do not say that God is three persons or one person; rather we say three hypostases in unity, and between the three hypostases and three persons is the distance between heaven and earth." End.

Rahmat Allah said: This is pure sophistry, because an existing thing cannot exist without individuality. If it is assumed that the hypostases exist and are distinguished by a real distinction, as he himself stated in his books, then saying that the three hypostases exist is exactly the same as saying that three persons exist. Moreover, in the twenty-ninth page of the Book of Prayer, circulated in the Church of England and printed in 1818, there is the following in my translation: "O you three who are holy, blessed, and exalted in rank, who are one." That is, three persons and one God. So "three persons" occurs explicitly in it. Likewise, it is full of expressions (p-1766) explicitly stating that Jesus is the son of God, that he is God, and that Mary is the mother of God and the wife of God, and they prostrate to her and her image with the prostration that is forbidden in their books for anyone other than God, just as they prostrate to God. We ask Him, glory be to Him and exalted, for protection, and we seek refuge in Him from abandonment and the deceptions of Satan.

The distinguished master Shaykh Rahmat Allah has indeed quenched the thirst in *Izhar al-Haqq*, where, in its fourth chapter, he presented the refutation of Trinitarianism with decisive proofs and compelling arguments.

Likewise, a considerable number of Muslims and of those who embraced Islam from among them have refuted them, in numbers beyond counting. Useful works on this have spread, praise be to God, and many groups from among them have also refuted them.

In the book *al-Ra'y al-Sawab wa Fasl al-Khitab* by the priest Jabbara there is the following in its form: The Unitarian Christians who appeared eighty years ago in America, who now have three hundred churches and hold the first rank in knowledge, schools, and literary gatherings, likewise have three hundred churches in England and numerous valuable compositions. They regard the Qur'an, as they regard the Gospel and the Torah, as divine books. They do not believe in the Trinity of gods; that is, they do not believe that Lord Christ or the Holy Spirit is a true god like the God who necessarily exists, but they believe that God alone is the true God. End.

In it also is the following statement: All the revealed books teach monotheism and deny the Trinity of gods, or that God is three, and they proclaim explicitly, in the clearest expression, that God is one, the Unique, and that there is no true god besides Him. End.

In the book *Susanna Sulayman* there is mention of many of their sects which came to deny the divinity of the Messiah and of the Holy Spirit. This book cites, from their ancient and modern sects and their disagreements, things that are astonishing, which supports what the Hafiz Ibn Kathir said, that they have varied opinions and conflicting statements. One of the speakers excellently said: "If ten Christians gathered, they would disperse into eleven opinions." End.

Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya said in *al-Risala al-Qubrusiyya*: The Christians scattered in Trinitarianism and union, scattered into a dispersion that no sane person would accept, and no transmission came except ambiguous words in the Gospel and what preceded it of the books, which were clarified by decisive words in the Gospel and what preceded it, all of which speak (p-1767) of the servitude of the Messiah and his worship of God alone, and his supplication and humble entreaty to Him.

Since the foundation of religion is faith in God and His messengers, and the matter of religion is the oneness of God and the acknowledgement of His messengers, the adherents of Trinitarianism in unity and of union in messengerhood have admitted into the very foundation of their religion corruption that is evident by the natural disposition (fitra) of God upon which He created people, and by the books of God which He sent down. End.

By God's praise, while writing these lines, I have gathered twenty works refuting them, all of which are printed and widely circulated, praise be to God. So there is no need to lengthen the discussion by quoting from them, since they are easy to consult.

Al-Mawardi said in *Aʿlam al-Nubuwwa*: As for the Christians, before Constantine the king became Christian, they were upon a sound religion regarding the oneness of God, may He be exalted, and the prophethood of Jesus, peace be upon him. Then they differed about Jesus after Constantine became Christian, and he was the first of the kings of Rome to become Christian. That is, the Romans had been Sabians, then Constantine compelled them to become Christian when he took power over them.

The early Nestorians said: Jesus is God.

The early Jacobites said: He is the son of God.

The early Melkites said: The gods are three, one of them being Jesus.

Then their later ones turned away from explicit statement of this reprehensible doctrine when souls rejected it and minds repelled it. They said: God, may He be exalted, is one substance which is three hypostases: the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, and that they are one in substance; the hypostasis of the Father is the essence, the hypostasis of the Son is the Word, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit is life.

They differed about the hypostases: some of them said they are properties, some said they are persons, some said they are attributes, and they said that the Word united with Jesus, and they differed about the union.

Then he said: These doctrines have no confusion that reason accepts, and their corruption is evident to reason.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Desist﴾, that is, from Trinitarianism, ﴿it is better for you﴾, that is: desisting is better for you; or: aim for something better than Trinitarianism, which is monotheism.

﴿God is only one God﴾, that is, in His essence, with no plurality in Him in any respect whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 171 (part 2 of 2):

By His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him; [it is far above His majesty] that He should have a son﴾, is a declaration of the exalted station of His Majesty, may His glory be great, above what they have attributed to Jesus' sonship, since they said: "He is God, and the son of God." What plunged them into this ruinous destruction and grave pitfall was the ambiguous wording found in the Gospel, such as "the Father" and "the Son." They did not interpret these words in the sense intended, but took them literally, and so they went astray and led others astray.

In "Munyat al-Adhkiya'" (The Desire of the Intelligent) there is the following text: As for what appears in the Gospel that exists now, of the application of "Son of God" to Jesus, peace be upon him, if it has not been distorted, then it is a metaphor, in the sense of "son of love," as one says: "So-and-so is one of the sons of this world."

A parallel to this is the saying of Jesus, peace be upon him, to the Jews when they claimed that they had one father, who is God: "If God were your father, you would love me." Then he said to them: "You are of a father who is Iblis, and you desire to do the lusts of your father." The Jews claimed that God Most High is their father, meaning that they obey Him as a son obeys a father. Jesus, peace be upon him, denied this and made them sons of Satan, meaning that they obey him. It is not hidden that "son" and "father" here are metaphors.

The application of the name "Father" to God Most High, and the name "Son" to a righteous servant, has been frequent in the earlier books. So it is either a result of error in translation, or it is to be interpreted in the manner we have mentioned, so do not be heedless.

However, this application has been entirely forbidden in the Muhammadan religion, as a precaution against misleading and falling into the polytheism of illusions, and this is the path of rectitude.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, is a reason for His transcendence above what is attributed to Him, meaning that everything in them is His creation and His possession, so how could part of His possession be a part of Him? For sonship and ownership do not come together.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, meaning: to Him all creatures entrust their affairs, and He is free of need of them. So how is it conceivable regarding Him that He would take a son, which is the condition of the weak and needy in managing their affairs, who require someone to succeed them and stand in their place? And His saying, Exalted is He:

(p-١٧٦٩)On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:
﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of God, nor will the favoured angels. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, He will gather them all to Himself﴾ [172].

﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of God﴾ is a resumed sentence (jumla mustanafa) confirming the earlier affirmation of God's transcendence. That is, he will not be too proud to be a servant of God, for his servitude is an honour in which one takes pride.

﴿Nor will the favoured angels﴾ disdain to be servants of Him, exalted is He. Whoever claims the superiority of the angels over the prophets has taken this verse as evidence.

Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said: That is, nor will whoever is higher than him in rank and greater than him in dignity, namely the angels who are close to the Throne (al-Karubiyyun), such as Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and those of their rank.

Then he said: If you ask, from where does His saying ﴿nor the favoured angels﴾ indicate that the meaning is "nor whoever is above him"? I say: from the fact that the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿani, the science of rhetoric) requires nothing other than this. The discourse was directed only to refute the doctrine of the Christians and their extremism in raising the Messiah above the station of servitude. So it must be said to them: Jesus will not rise above servitude, nor will whoever is higher than him in rank. As if it were said: the favoured angels will not disdain servitude, so how much less the Messiah? The specification of "the favoured" clearly and plainly indicates this, since they are the highest of the angels in rank and the most exalted in station. An example is the saying of the poet:

*Nor is his like one who matches Hatim in generosity, nor the sea with its surging waves, whose waters billow.*

There is no doubt that by "the sea with its surging waves" he meant something above Hatim in generosity. Whoever has taste (dhawq) should taste, along with this verse, His saying: ﴿Nor will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾ [al-Baqara: 120] [al-Baqara: 120], until he acknowledges the clear distinction. End of quotation.

Al-Baydawi (d. c. 685 AH) said: His answer is that the verse is a refutation of the worshippers of the Messiah and of the angels, so this objection does not hold. And if it is granted that the verse is specific to the Christians, then perhaps he intended by the conjunction (ʿatf) emphasis in terms of multiplicity rather than magnitude, like your saying: "The commander got up, and no leader and no subordinate opposed him." And if he intended magnitude, then the most it yields is the preference of the favoured angels, namely the Karubiyyun who surround the Throne, or those among the angels who are higher in rank than the Messiah among the prophets, peace be upon them. That does not imply the superiority of one of the two categories (jinsayn) over the other absolutely, and that is what is in dispute. End of quotation.

Nasir al-Din (Ibn al-Munayyir, d. 683 AH) said in *al-Intisaf* (a commentary-critique attached to al-Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf*): The disagreement over the superiority of the prophets over the angels has been extensive. The majority of the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari) held the superiority of the prophets. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr (al-Baqillani) from among us, al-Halimi, and a group of the Mu'tazila held the superiority of the angels. The Mu'tazila took this verse as their main proof for the superiority of the angels, on the basis of the reasoning that al-Zamakhshari used.

We, with God's help, will fully elaborate the issue from the standpoint of the verse. We say: the Ash'ariyya raised several objections to using it as evidence:

The first: our master Muhammad, upon him be the most excellent prayers and peace, is more excellent than Jesus, peace be upon him. So it does not follow from the angels being more excellent than the Messiah that they are more excellent than Muhammad, peace be upon him. This objection applies only if its raiser does not claim that every single one of the prophets is more excellent than every single one of the angels. Between our school and others there is disagreement on these extremes.

(The second objection) is that His saying ﴿nor the favoured angels﴾ is in the plural form, encompassing the totality of the angels. This requires that the totality of the angels be more excellent than the Messiah, but it does not require that each one of them be more excellent than the Messiah. There is also a point of scrutiny in this objection, because if its raiser proceeds from the premise that the Messiah is more excellent than each single angel, it may be said that this commits him to the view that he is more excellent than all of them together, just as the Prophet, peace be upon him, since he is more excellent than each single one of the prophets, is more excellent than all of them. None of those who wrote on this subject distinguished between excellence in detail (al-tafdil ʿala al-tafsil) and excellence in totality (al-tafdil ʿala al-jumla).

Some of our contemporaries distinguished between the two kinds of excellence, claiming that excellence in detail does not necessarily entail excellence in totality. This position is not confirmed as coming from him, and if anyone holds it, it is rejected on a subtle ground: the excellence intended is chiefly indicated by the elevation of the rank of the more excellent in Paradise, and the hadiths on this are abundant. In that case, either the rank of one of the lesser (mafdulin) is raised above the one agreed to be more excellent than each of them, or the rank of none of them is raised above him. The first is not possible, for it would entail raising the lesser above the more excellent. So the second is established, namely that the rank of the more excellent is raised above the ranks of the whole group by necessity. Thus it follows that his excellence over the whole group is established with certainty from his excellence over each one of them.

The third: He conjoined the angels to the Messiah with the particle "wa" (and), which does not imply sequence. As for citing the aforementioned example to show that the second always has a higher rank, it is countered by examples that do not imply this, such as the saying of the speaker: "Zayd did not blame me for this matter, nor did ʿAmr." I say: and like your saying: "Do not harm a Muslim, nor a dhimmi" (a non-Muslim under protection). For this order is the normal way of the discourse, and the second is lower and of a humbler rank. But if you reversed this, saying "Do not harm a dhimmi, nor a Muslim," so that the higher is placed second, you would have departed from the bounds of speech and the rules of eloquence. This example clarifies what is raised against the established rule, but truth is more deserving than contention, and there is no contradiction between the two examples.

We shall lay down a groundwork that removes the confusion and uncovers the veil. We say: the point regarding order in the two examples, whose contradiction is imagined, is one and the same. It requires in some places placing the higher first, and in other places placing it later. That point is the requirement of eloquence: avoiding repetition and avoiding descent. So when you adopt this, whenever it leads to your final statement being a descent relative to its beginning, or to the final part being subsumed within the first, having already conveyed it so that you are not in need of the latter, then turn away from that toward what constitutes an ascent from the lower to the higher, and a resumption for a benefit that the first did not include. An example is the verse under discussion. For if you were to take it that the Messiah is more excellent than the angels and higher in rank, the mention of the angels after him would be as if superfluous, because if the more excellent, namely the Messiah under this assumption, is a servant of God who does not disdain servitude, it follows that whoever is below him in excellence is more deserving of not disdaining being a servant of God, and they are the angels under this assumption. Thus nothing new is added by His saying ﴿nor the favoured angels﴾ beyond what preceded at the beginning of the discourse.

But if you assume the Messiah to be less excellent in relation to the angels, then you have ascended from the glorification of God, in that the lesser does not disdain being His servant, while the more excellent does not disdain this either. The non-disdain of the lesser does not necessarily imply the non-disdain of the more excellent. So there is a need to mention the angels, since the first does not entail the second. The discourse under this assumption thus has continually renewed and increasing benefits, and whatever is like this is what the Mighty Book must be understood to contain, for the goal of eloquence lies in this.

By this point it is necessary to say: "Do not harm a Muslim, nor a dhimmi," so that you place the lower after the higher, contrary to the order in the verse. For when you forbid him from harming the Muslim, it may be said: that is one of his special privileges, out of respect for Islam, so forbidding it does not entail forbidding it toward the non-Muslim, from whom this special status is withheld. So when you say "nor a dhimmi," you have introduced a benefit not present in the first, and you have ascended from forbidding some kinds of harm to forbidding more than that.

If you arranged this example like the arrangement of the verse, saying "Do not harm a dhimmi," the one addressed would understand that harming a Muslim is even more strictly forbidden, since the Muslim equals the dhimmi in the cause of respect, which is humanity for example, and surpasses him in a cause that is more sublime and greater, which is Islam. Thus this prohibition suffices him without the renewal of another prohibition against harming the Muslim.

If you say "nor a Muslim," you have not introduced any new benefit, and you have not informed him of anything other than what he already knew at first. Know that this is a single point, which sometimes requires placing the higher first and sometimes placing it later, and only the context distinguishes this for you. I have no doubt that the context of the verse requires placing the lower first and the higher later.

Among the eloquence that follows from this point is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra': 23] [al-Isra': 23], dispensing with forbidding them from striking them or anything beyond that, by implication of the lower. It is not fitting for the eloquence of the Mighty Book to intend a prohibition of something higher than saying "uff" and reproach (al-inhar, as written), because that is dispensed with, and the reflector on the verses of the Qur'an, together with the confirmation of other evidence, does not need anything besides them: ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38] [al-An'am: 38].

Since fairness required acknowledging what the verse implies for the superiority of the angels, and since the evidence for the superiority of the prophets was readily available to the one who holds that belief, the verse and that evidence were reconciled by restricting the superiority in the verse to a domain other than the point of dispute. That is, the superiority of the angels lies in strength, in the intensity of force, and in the breadth of capacity and power. He said: this kind of excellence is what suits the context of the verse, because the aim is to refute the Christians in their belief in the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him, on the ground that he raised the dead, healed the blind and the leper, and extraordinary things came about at his hands. Yet he does not disdain worshipping God, rather, those with even more extraordinary acts and more manifest effects, such as the favoured angels, among whom is Jibril, peace be upon him, who reached such strength, and such empowerment from God, that he uprooted cities and carried them on a feather of his wing, turning their highest part (ʿaliyaha) to their lowest (safilaha). Thus the superiority of the angels, in this sense, is not disputed: they are stronger, more forceful, and their extraordinary acts are greater. The disagreement concerns superiority in terms of greater reward, honours, and elevation of ranks in the abode of recompense, and there is no evidence in the verse for that.

Since most of what was confused for the Christians about the divinity of Jesus was that he was created, that is, brought into existence without a father, God informed us that this being who came into existence without a father does not disdain worshipping God, nor do the angels, who were created without father or mother. Thus their mention is delayed because their creation is more wondrous than the creation of Jesus. This is confirmed by the fact that God compared Jesus to Adam, peace be upon them both, comparing the strange with the stranger, and likening the marvel of His power to the more marvellous. For Jesus was created from a mother, while Adam was created without mother or father. This is why He said: ﴿He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] [Al 'Imran: 59]. The basis of this discussion rests on the point I have indicated. So whenever it is sound that what is mentioned contains a benefit not contained in the first, by whatever way, whether excellence or other benefits, then the reflection has been made firm and has matched the form of the verse. And God knows best.

In sum, the matter is one known by transmission (sam'iyya), and certainty concerning it is known by an explicit text that admits of no interpretation, and its existence is difficult to establish. May the blessings and peace of God be upon all of them. End of quotation.

﴿And whoever disdains His worship﴾, that is, refuses it and holds back from it, ﴿and is arrogant﴾, that is, exalts himself above it and considers himself too high for it, ﴿He will gather them all to Himself﴾, that is, He will assemble them on the Day of Resurrection for the appointment He promised them, and will judge between them with His just decision.

The Explanation of His, the Exalted's, Words:

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. But as for those who disdained and were arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any ally or helper.﴾ [173]

﴿As for those who believed﴾ — they were not arrogant toward His worship ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ — they did not disdain His worship ﴿He will give them their rewards﴾ — i.e., the reward of their deeds without any part of it being diminished ﴿and increase them﴾ — i.e., beyond their rewards, a great amount ﴿from His bounty﴾ by multiplying it manifold, emphasizing their honor.

﴿But as for those who disdained and were arrogant﴾ — i.e., toward the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic ﴿He will punish them with a painful punishment﴾ — this is the punishment of the Fire ﴿and they will not find, besides Allah, any ally﴾ — one who would befriend them to honor them ﴿or any helper﴾ — who would aid them and ward off the punishment from them.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [174]

﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord﴾: When Exalted is He had shown the falsehood of what the disbelievers, in all their categories, were upon, of the various kinds of disbelief and misguidance, He generalized the address and called all people to acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). He called him a proof (burhan) because of the decisive evidences (al-barahin) given to him, which bore witness to his truthfulness. Therein is an admonition to them that the argument has been completed by his being sent, so that after this there remains no excuse for one who would make excuses.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with its attribution to the pronoun of those addressed is to show kindness toward them, and to signal that his coming to them is for their nurturing (tarbiyah) and their perfection.

﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾: that is, a manifest radiance upon the truth, by which one is guided out of the darkness of misguidance, and it is the Qur'an.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.﴾ [175]

﴿As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him﴾ — i.e., they protected themselves through Him from what would ruin them, namely the deviation of Satan. ﴿He will admit them into mercy from Him﴾ — and this is Paradise. ﴿And bounty﴾ — which He will bestow upon them after admitting them into Paradise, such as gazing upon His noble Face and other of His sublime gifts. ﴿And guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾ — so He will lead them, by their adherence to the clear proof and the manifest light, onto the clear and direct way, which is Islam. And the mention of the promise of admission into Paradise before the promise of being guided to it — contrary to the order of occurrence between the two things promised — is for the sake of hastening to give the good news of what is the primary objective.

And His saying, may He be exalted:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 4, verse 176:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:

﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah (one who leaves neither father nor child). If a man dies leaving no child, and he has a sister, she receives half of what he left. And he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, they receive two-thirds of what he left. If there are brothers and sisters, men and women, the male receives the equivalent of the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray. And Allah is Knowing of all things."﴾ [176]

﴿They ask you﴾ i.e., concerning the inheritance of the kalalah. Its mention is dispensed with because it appears in His, may He be glorified, saying: ﴿Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah"﴾. Its explanation has already passed at the beginning of the noble surah. The one who asked was Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon me while I was ill, so he performed ablution and poured (water) over me - or he said: 'Pour (water) over him' - and I regained my senses and said: 'Only a kalalah inherits from me, so how is the inheritance?' Then the verse of the obligatory shares was revealed."

﴿If a man dies﴾ i.e., dies. The restriction of "halak" (perish) to a bad death is a newly arisen usage which is not relied upon, by evidence of the countless verses and hadiths. Because of the emergence of this usage, al-Shihab said in "Sharh al-Shifa'": it is prohibited to apply it to the Prophets, peace be upon them, and the original ancient linguistic usage is not relied upon, as is not hidden from one who is versed in the legal principles. And Allah knows best. Thus in "Taj al-Arus."

﴿He has no child, and he has a sister, she receives half of what he left﴾ i.e., the deceased, of the wealth.

Ibn Kathir said: Those who hold that the absence of a father is not a condition of kalalah, but that the absence of a child suffices for the existence of kalalah, have relied on this. It is a report from Umar ibn al-Khattab, which Ibn Jarir narrated from him with a sound chain. However, what is relied upon is the view of the majority.

Al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled that it is the one who has neither child nor parent. The evidence for this is His saying: "and he has a sister." Had there been a father with her, she would inherit nothing, since he excludes her by consensus. So it is shown that the kalalah is one who has no child by the explicit text of the Qur'an, and no parent by the text as well, upon reflection too, since the sister is not assigned half when there is a parent; rather she has no inheritance at all.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, that he was asked about a husband and a sister of full blood, and he gave the husband half and the sister half. He was challenged about this, and he said: "I was present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he decided this."

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that they both used to say (concerning a deceased who left a daughter and a sister): there is nothing for the sister, based on His saying: "If a man dies, leaving no child and he has a sister, she receives half of what he left." He said: So if he left a daughter, then he has left a child, and there is nothing for the sister.

The majority disagreed with them, saying (regarding this case): the daughter receives half by fixed share, and the sister receives the other half by agnatic residue, based on evidence other than this verse. This verse merely sets out what is to be assigned to her in this verse.

As for her inheritance by agnatic residue, it is based on what al-Bukhari narrated through Sulayman, from Ibrahim, from al-Aswad, who said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal decided among us, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), half for the daughter and half for the sister. Then Sulayman said: "decided among us," and did not mention "in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Also in Sahih al-Bukhari from Huzayl ibn Shurahbil, who said: "Abu Musa al-Ash'ari was asked about a daughter, a son's daughter, and a sister. He said: 'For the daughter is half, and for the sister is half; go to Ibn Mas'ud, for he will agree with me.' So he asked Ibn Mas'ud, and informed him of Abu Musa's view. He said: 'Then I would have gone astray and I am not among the guided. I decide in it by what the Prophet (ﷺ) decided: half for the daughter, and for the son's daughter a sixth to complete the two-thirds, and what remains is for the sister.' So we came to Abu Musa and informed him of Ibn Mas'ud's view, and he said: 'Do not ask me while this scholar is among you.'"

His saying: ﴿and he inherits from her if she has no child﴾ i.e., the brother inherits all of her estate if she dies as a kalalah and has no child, i.e., nor a parent; for if she had a child, the brother would inherit nothing. If it is assumed that with him there is one who has a fixed share, that share is given to him, such as a husband or a uterine brother, and the remainder goes to the brother, based on what is established in the two Sahihs from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give the fixed shares to their people, and whatever remains is for the nearest male relative."

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿If there were two sisters, they receive two-thirds of what he left﴾ i.e., if the one who dies as a kalalah has two sisters, two-thirds is assigned to them, and likewise whatever exceeds two sisters in its ruling. From here the majority derived the ruling for two daughters, as the ruling for sisters is inferred from daughters in His saying: ﴿If they are women more than two, they receive two-thirds of what he left﴾ [al-Nisa: 11].

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿If they are brothers and sisters﴾ i.e., those who inherit by way of siblingship ﴿brothers and sisters﴾ i.e., mixed ﴿men and women, the male receives﴾ i.e., among them ﴿the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ i.e., the equivalent of the share of two of his female siblings.

﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ i.e., out of dislike that you go astray in this, or with the particles (lam and la) supplied at both ends of (an) i.e., "lest you go astray." It was said: there is no omission or supposition there; rather it is the object of (yubayyinu), i.e., He makes clear to you your error which is part of your nature when you are left to yourselves and your inclinations, so that you may guard against it and seek its opposite.

Some preferred this view on the ground that it is of fine conclusion, and a turning back to the beginning of the surah, which is: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ [al-Nisa: 1]. For He commanded them to piety, and made clear to them what they had been upon in the Jahiliyya. When its detail was complete, He said to them: I have made clear to you your error, so fear Me as I have commanded you, for when evil is known it is avoided, and when good is known it is pursued.

The scholar Abu al-Su'ud said: You know that this is only fitting if His explanation was by way of identifying the points of error and misguidance without explicitly stating what is the truth and the right; and this is not the case.

﴿And Allah is, of all things﴾ among which are your affairs connected with your living and your dying, ﴿Knowing﴾, exceedingly knowledgeable, so He makes clear to you what contains your welfare and benefit.

* *

Notes:

First: Know that when He, may He be exalted, made clear at the beginning of the surah the rulings on wealth, He concluded its end with that as well, so that the end would correspond to the beginning. As for the middle of the surah, it includes debate with the sects that oppose the religion.

Second: Two verses were revealed concerning the kalalah: one in the winter, which is the one at the beginning of this surah, and the other in the summer, which is this verse. For this reason this verse is called the verse of the summer.

Third: al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from al-Bara' ibn Azib, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The last surah revealed was (Bara'ah) and the last verse revealed was (They ask you). And Allah, glory be to Him, and exalted, knows best, and He is the Granter of success and the Helper.

The completion, by His praise, may He be exalted, of what was facilitated of "Mahasin al-Ta'wil" of this noble surah took place on Friday morning, the first of Safar al-Khayr in the year (1320), in the upper right portico of the Sananiyya mosque, by the hand of its writer and compiler, the weak, humble, ignorant servant Muhammad Jamal al-Din al-Qasimi, may the Master forgive him and help him to complete it.

By His favour and generosity

Followed by the sixth part, whose beginning is: (Surat al-Ma'idah).
